- 2 - One last point on security concerns members using the Club when others are not present. It is important to leave the Clubhouse locked whilst out sailing or working in the boat park and when the last person leaves. Do not expect someone else will do it for you. I hope that everyone attending the Barbeque enjoyed themselves. The weather was kind to us, fortunately, after a changeable period leading up to the evening and there appeared a record number of midnight bathers this year. Good sailing (or swimming). John Weedon. MIRROR FLEET NEWS I'm very pleased to be able to report that about 10 Mirrors have take. part in races, either on Wednesday or Sunday, although we still can't manage to get more than 3 in a race - except on the one occasion on Sunday 5th July when we managed 4 in the afternoon race. I suppose one shouldn't complain when every newsletter reports an increasing number of Mirrors racing but - I've said it before and I'll say it again - what a pity we can't get more out at the same time. My grateful thanks to John Stringer and Fraser McPherson who very sportingly turned out on different occasions to bring the number of Mirrors 'signing on' to the minimum requirement of 3 boats for the Mirror Summer Points Series. I hope they'll consider joining us on a regular basis very soon. Naturally I'm grateful since, in the absence of Vic and Kim Braybrook, I managed to pick up two firsts, one of which was by a margin of about two feet over Robert Coy in a race in which the lead changed hands several times. Now, if some other Mirrors had been out as well, you might have picked up the first place 'spoons' instead of me. However, Vic's return on 5th July soon put us back in our places - obviously Vic's heavy weather technique is superior to the rest of us. Never mind, the more regularly we race, the better our sailing will become - I hope. A warm welcome to Karen Leeder, 12-year old daughter of Bob Leeder, who took part in her first Mirror race on 5th July with father Bob as helm. I gather Karen enjoyed it and father Bob is considering a partial return to the Mirrors to bring another youngster into the Cadet Fleet. Bob, of course, normally sails a Solo but - there's a lot of racing fun in a Mirror. Sarah Cant was kind enough to respond to my invitation in the May Navigans and volunteered as Assistant Race Officer for 6th September. Thank you Sarah. Any others like to volunteer? I'm hoping Sarah will be able to rejoin the Mirror Fleet very soon. I still remember how she swept past me (and Vic Braybrook) on the last leg of the last race of the 1980 season and I want to get my own back. On that occasion Sarah came second behind Caron Stuart (now sailing a 420 - often from outside the boat). Come back Caron - all is forgiven. Finally, I keep having a dream. It's a dream of lots of Mirrors with lots of young faces all screaming 'starboard' at me as we all race for the line. It may be a dream now, but wouldn't it be nice if it came true - it's really up to you adults. See you on the water. Mike Boreham. Mirror Fleet Captain. Sail No. 29015 LARS TINN.

- 3 - CONVERSATION PIECE (OR ALL'S WELL THAT ENDS - WELL ?) (a true-life story) ACT 1 - Somewhere on the River Blackwater (in a dinghy not a thousand miles from MSC) HE - Hoist the spinnaker darling SHE - Yes darling HE - Have you done it yet? SHE - I think so, but it seems to be twisted HE - Hurry up darling, they've dropped theirs in the water. We can catch them up. SHE - It seems to have tangled itself up HE - Then untangle it - dear SHE - I can't. You come and do it. HE - Don't be daft, I'm steering. Just get it untangled. Their spinnaker's still in the water. SHE - I can't I tell you, the *********** thing has tangled up HE - Then ************ well untangle it - you must be able to SHE - Don't shout at me. You always lose your temper. HE - I'm not losing my temper - I'm merely ... SHE - (with feeling) Oh! Shut up! HE - (also with feeling) Don't ********** bother. They've got their spinnaker up and they're flying. We might as well pack up. SHE - Oh! I hate racing. You always lose your temper. HE - I don't SHE - Yes you do HE - No I don't SHE - Yes you do HE - No I ... etc. etc. etc. ACT 2 - SCENE 1 - Later that Night SHE - Darling? HE - Yes darling? SHE - I wonder if we could have won today? SHE - Yes, probably. They had trouble with their spinnaker and if only you'd ... SHE - Well, I couldn't help it - it was tangled up HE - Oh, I'm not BLAMING you darling, but I can't see why you could'nt untangle it. SHE - I tried to but it wouldn't - AND YOU didn't help by shouting. HE - I didn't. As we now have a large number of boat trolleys of the four wheel steerable type, I think it is appropriate to give some quidelines on their handlinge For moving in the forwards direction the automatic steering works well provided care is taken not to try to steer too tight a circle. wheels can in some cases go "over centre" and require manhandling to get them back, so always restrict the steering angle as much as possible. Manual steering will limit this and the possibility of bent steering arms, but pedestrians must be very aware of the weight of the tow and avoid finger accidents. A supply of wheel chocks is advisable, For reversing a different set of problems arise. It is not generally recognised that it is impossible to reverse any great distance with the draw bar coupled in any way to the towing line. Trolleys being reversed down the hard must be steered entirely by hand until the trolley reaches the water; the draw bar may then be secured to the tow: line to assist removal from the water, It is always preferable to secure the winch wire or towing rope directly to a strong part of the trailer chassis. Steering bars are not normally as strong for taking the pull of the heavy load. It is strongly recommended, and at club sailing times essential, that a recognised tractor driver or winch supervisor be called in to help. The list of these names is displayed on the Club noticeboard. It is not the duty of an 0.0.0. to help here = he is too busy with other duties and may not be qualified to do the job anyway, so, out of season, please make prior arrangements. No other person may drive the tractor, it is not the same as a car and needs to be properly understood. The qualified operator will satisfy himself that the load appears safe, the gear appears fit for the job, and that the working team is sufficient for the job in hand. Onlookers are normally willing to help if asked but if not involved may become critical observers, All persons concerned with launching boats must be sure that no-one is infon the water in the immediate vicinity. Dinghy owners approaching the shore don't like to see lifeboats approaching from the shore! Less seriously but worth a thought, it would help if steerable wheels could be locked in the straight ahead position, just for when the trolley is in the water — they always slew round a bit otherwise. Trolley wheels should be as large as possible to assist rolling and as for conventional jockey wheels, they Frequently jam in the gaps between the blocks on our hard. How about engineering up a Mini wheel, non steerable, to replace it, /continued.

- 6 - Finally, concerning all trolleys, please try to arrange for the boat to be floated to its correct position without the need for either looking or feeling - these may be acceptable for light day boats but not for cruisers. A 'V' shaped frame-work in the vertical plane will often do the trick, so will a flat platform in conjunction with a pair of verticals which the starboard side of the boat may be secured to. When anywhere near No. 1 buoy watch your depth sounder carefully, you may be surprised! Good sailing, Russ Fuller, Cruiser Fleet Captain. Tel. Maldon [redacted]. 420 NEWS - BOOTHBY CUP - 1st ROUND. STANSGATE, JUNE 27th. The Boothby Cup is now held annually for two competing 420 teams. Although originally held for G.P.14 team racing at Maldon, with the demise of the G.P.14 Fleets, the cup is now contested between Osea S.C. and ourselves. This year it was hoped to include a third team from Maldon S.C. but due to previous commitments this was not possible. In future, however, it is hoped to increase the number of competing teams. Enough of the history - what about the sailing! The first race started in force 3/4 winds with the promise of some planing. At the first mark Marconi boats held 3 of the first 4 places, and using local tidal knowledge these positions were consolidated by the time the windward mark was reached. Places began to change over the following beat and broad reach, with an Osea boat moving into second place with the remainder looking menacing. It was noticeable that during the broad reach some Marconi boats were having considerable trouble with their spinnakers. At the mark at the end of the reaching leg more positions were lost and at one point Ron Greygoose, who had been in a favourable position was seen heading for the shore still carrying full spinnaker. The visitors steadily improved during the second lap and were gaining in confidence. Generous distances between boats reduced the use of team racing tactics and Osea finally gained 3 of the first 4 positions. The second race started in light winds and by the first mark it was obvious that the visitors were well placed. On the first leg it was pleasant to see tactics being employed when Colin Harper literally luffed an Osea boat off the water without loss of his own position. Positions remained fairly constant during the beat up Goldhanger Creek, the reach back to No. 1, and another reach to No. 2. The wind was steadily dropping and by the time all boats were homeward bound even the tell-tales were dropping. Race tactics were abandoned and all efforts concentrated on maintaining forward movement against the tide. As the fleet edged imperceptibly closer to the promontory Peter Chrystie and Colin Harper seemed well placed, but Pete overdid his search for thermals and was last seen sailing backwards towards Maldon. It was Ron, however, who scored by putting in a tack almost through the farm's front garden to get second position with Colin third. /continued.

"Since qualifying as a '420' sail measurer I have noticed that there are several 420's in the Club displaying sail numbers and emblems that do not comply with the Class Rules or the R.Y.A. requirements. The purpose of these rules is to ensure accurate identification; not just for the Race Officer, but more importantly, for the rescue services. So please ensure your sails are correct. If you wish to check your existing sails or plan to fix numbers to sails yourself, here are the requirements for the '420' Class:- 1. The 420 emblem and the national letter shall be placed under and in proximity to the upper batten, and the sail number under and in proximity to the second batten from the top. National letter shall not be in line with the sail number. The emblem shall be blue and not less than 480 mm high. Numbers and letters shall

- 3 - be red and of the following minimum dimensions:- HEIGHT - 300 mm WIDTH - 200 mm (except 1 & I) THICKNESS - 45 mm MINIMUM SPACE BETWEEN ADJOINING FIGURES - 60 mm. 2. The colour of numbers on the spinnaker is optional but it shall contrast with the colour of the panel to which they are fixed. 3. The national letters and sail numbers only, shall be similarly placed on both sides of the spinnaker, but at approximately half height. 4. On spinnakers made on or after 1st April, 1977, the national letter shall either be separated from the sail number by an horizontal line approximately 50 mm in length or be placed above the number. 5. The class emblem, national letter and sail numbers shall be clearly visible and shall be placed at different heights on the two sides of the sail, those on the starboard side being uppermost, to avoid confusion owing to the translucency of the sail. N.B. A yacht cannot be disqualified from a race for not complying with these rules without prior warning and adequate opportunity to make corrections. 420 NEWS Although August is a difficult month for fleet sailing I am happy to report that the number of boats competing has remained constant during the month. This can be attributed in part to the summerelike weather we've had. On a personal note, the camping week was undoubtedly the highlight of the year and although there was little wind for sailing I believe we all benefited from living in close quarters for a week (sorry about the noise, Lou!). The main event of the week started in what can only be described as unbelievable weather, with the Blackwater resembling the Meditteranean. The central theme was to have a 'tuneeup! session starting with some basic measurements on the boats, followed by a number of short races where helm and crew by a rota system sailed each participating boat in turn. The boat measuring aspect of the afternoon was intended primarily to establish a data base against which rig alterations and performance can be measured in the future. Oue to the difficult nature of some of these measurements (e.9. spreader deflections) some time was taken over them, and due to the high ambient temperatures it was noticeable that everyone except the fleet captain and John Chisnall disappeared for a swime However, the exercise was worthwhile and the details will be kept in a book which we can hopefully add to and upedate. Those not present at the session can have their own boats measured by prior arrangement. Six boats were raced in very light airs, in what turned out to be a mammoth racing session of about 34 hours duration. In fact, after the fourth race, several helms and crew were seen disappearing over the sea wall by the race box presumably to irrigate the cruiser park! The lady crews tightened their harnesses and managed to "hang ont (sorry about that Pete!) until the end of the session. All the race results were duly recorded by Robert Weedon (now affectionately known as Robitehead) in the race box for later analysis in the bar. The one thing that the session produced was a lively discussion of the results and the way in which future sessions could be organised. Several useful points emerged from the discussion:= 1. Since the aim was to quantify boats and helm/crew combinations, spinnakers were not used since they represented yet another variable in the analysis. Although this was falt to be reasonable at the time the consensus of opinion was to include them next time. 2e Since all racing was conducted in light airs the results are only applicable to those conditions. 3e Some participants infringed the sailing rules at times during the races without recourse to alternative penalties, (sorry about the green stripes, John and Murray!) and although these were overlooked at the time, future sessions will have to be more strictly controlled. 4e Awkwardly placed or dangerous fittings were pointed out by helms and improvements to centre board and kicker fittings suggested. To my knowledge these aspects were acted upon the following day = (yes, my boat is safe now!). Se 8y discarding the worst result the analysis showed that the best helm/crew partnership on the day was that of Janet Chisnall and John Weedon. The best tuned boat was found to be 41106 = "Wishful Thinking" (shortly to be renamed$), followed closely by 36372 = "Zoot", 29379 = "Boobs", and 27858 = "Blackbird", After further discussions it was felt that the next session should be held on a course that embraces all the aspects of sailing — due to the conditions, available time and courses, little or ma tacking took place. Finally the overriding observation and admission by some helms was their inability to start

- 5 - well and get clear wind. The only answer to this problem is to get out and practise, watch those who do it well and try reading Chapter 6 of "Start to Win" by Eric Twiname (I have a copy for loan). - 6 - Hi - de - Hi It started with a casual remark after dinner one night, as these things often do. "Darling, there's an article in the local rag about the Maldon Little Ship Club running a Radio course for Yachtsman". "You should do that", replied the skipper. "Why me?", said I, thinking of the sails and the anchor, the galley and all the rest. "Well, I'm too busy holding the bit of wood, and in an emergency, it would be you using the radio, and, anyway, it's all good experience". The result of this profound logic was that I attended the six week course and am now certified by the Home Office, to be competent in the use of a V.H.F. Radio, I hasten to add. The course was held in the M.L.S.C. Clubhouse on Maldon Quay for two hours on Wednesday evenings starting at 7.30 pm. Our tutor, Cyril Mansfield, a college lecturer and member of the Blackwater Sailing Club was the instigator of these short courses, an off shoot from when he was lecturing for Yacht Master Courses and had been asked on many occasions to go into V.H.F. Radio procedure in more detail. The outcome is that over 300 people have attended the lectures, many taking and passing the Home Office examination for the Certificate of Competence. The six lectures cover basic standard procedures, which channels are used for what etc., how to make a link call through a coastal radio station and how to contact your friendly neighbourhood Coastguard. Ample opportunity is given to practise as Mansbrite Electronics of Maldon provide two radio telephone sets, which are placed at each end of the lecture room and calls can be made and received. Each week, Cyril asked for a script concerning the procedure on making a certain type of call, Mayday, Pan, Pan, etc. The following session we would present our scripts using the radios and trying to be as realistic as possible. Imaginations ran riot and some hilarious situations were invented. At the end of six weeks we attended one sunny Friday afternoon for the examination. The course is cheap, cost £5., the exam isn't, the fee being £17.50p, but if you pass the Home Office send you a pretty certificate with your picture on it, that you can keep. The paper was a written one, there was no verbal test, and consisted of a selection of 20 questions from a possible 60. It took about an hour, and as we finished, the man from the Home Office sat down and marked them, there and then; not normal procedure, so I have been told. Twelve people out of sixteen passed, several being Marconi Sailing Club members. If you are interested in taking a Radio Course, the man to contact is Derek Steel, Commodore of M.L.S.C. Telephone Maldon [redacted] as they will be organising another series of lectures in the near future. If you would like to know more about Marine Radio, what is available on the market, how difficult they are to install etc., then come along to the November Cruiser Meeting at the General's Arms, Little Baddow, when Brian Ash and Bob Donaldson from Mansbrite Electronics will be there to show us their range of equipment, give advice and answer any questions you may have for them. Brenda Tate. 8/9/81.

MIRROR FLEET NEWS What a lovely week my family and I had camping at the Club during the August Sailing Week. In contrast to last year's excess of wind, this year had wind just right for experiencing the joys of meandering around by the simple means of wind upon sail = not going anywhere particularly = just sailing. I enjoy cruising in the Mirror just as much as I enjoy racing and I hope I'm never tempted to become so devoted to one that I forget the other, Now, you might ask what all this has got to do with Mirror news, and [I must admit = not a lot. However, during the week the mideweek handicap race saw six (yes =— SIX) Mirrors taking part. Our regular mideweekers of Alf Cottam and P.Collis were joined by Robert Coy, John Stringer, myself and David Green in his new Mirror which looked to be quite fast. It proved to be an interesting race and, for me at least, provided a number of lessons on how NOT to deal with the tides. BP, Collis had the right answers and I'm told by those watching on shore that he made up at least 150 yards on the leading boat between No. 1 and A mark by intelligent use of the tide. However, although first Mirror over the line, he came second of the Mirrors to Robert Coy on handicap since he was single handed. The Summer Points racing was resumed on Sunday 6th September and although the morning race was a bit of a drift (Vic Sraybrooke won after sailing for almost three hours — whilst I got fed up and retired for an early lunch), the afternoon race was very enjoyable with Vic and myself swopping the lead until the last beat when Vic pulled ahead to win by a few yards, You may get the impression that Vic and myself were the- only Mirrors racing and this is almost true. They needn't have worried since L manaoed to run full-tilt into a mooring buoy (cruiser attached) and come to a surprised halt. My crew innocently asked why I'd done that and I replied I didn't know — or words to that effect. The lesson is = don't be afraid of making mistakes = we all do it sometimes and we can only improve. Anyway, let's hope Margaret and Marie have another qo. I referred earlier to the very enjoyable August Sailing Week and was most impressed by the 420 fleet who organised a "tuning! session for S or 6 of their boats and then raced them in a series of short races with the helm and crew swopping boats for each race. For example, we could encourage each other to race and so improve our boat handling skills. We could hold a "racing rules session" before the start of the 1982 racing calender and perhaps try to arrange for a quest speaker to tell us the secrets of "go faster" Mirror handling. - 3 - SIR ERIC EASTWOOD Members will be shocked and grieved to hear of the sudden passing of Sir Eric on Tuesday, October 6th, at his home in Little Baddow, at the age of 71. The cremation has already taken place and a memorial service is due to be held on Friday, October 23rd in Chelmsford Cathedral at 2.00 pm. Older members will remember that in the early fifties he helped us to found the Club, taking the chair in his office at Great Baddow when he accepted our unanimous wishes that he should be our President, and it was only recently that he reluctantly resigned. Sir Eric was not merely a figurehead, he actually constructed a Fleetwind which he named "Nutsy May" and he often visited our modest premises at Heybridge and participated in our activities there. He frequently attended our Laying-Up Supper and always made some lively and stimulating speeches, and there is no doubt that his influence in the Company was in no small measure, responsible for the help we received with our Clubhouses as our activities increased. We extend to Lady Eastwood and her sons, John and Martin, our deepest sympathy in their bereavement; his loss will be greatly felt by us all. Eric Payne. Older members of the Club who enjoyed happy times at Heybridge when the barge-yacht Mamgu was our headquarters will be sad to hear that she has finally reached the end of her useful life and lies derelict at the end of the Maldon promenade adjoining The Maldon Yacht Club. In 1957 our Clubhouse was a shed on the seawall at Heybridge Basin and we were seeking more adequate accommodation when we heard that Mamgu was up for sale, the asking price being £2,000 which, at that time, was far beyond our means. However, the owner who had been living aboard whilst she was moored alongside the quay at Maldon, had taken up residence ashore, was anxious to sell the barge and we heard the whisper that an offer of around £500 would be acceptable. After prolonged negotiation, towards the end of 1957 we finally bought her and started fitting her out as our new Clubhouse. During this time we laid moorings at Heybridge Basin outside our shed on the seawall. /continued.

- 5 - On April 20th we arranged with Cecil Stebbens Senior, the Pilot and River Bailiff, to tow her round from Maldon quay to Heybridge, some of us taking the wheel during the voyage. By choosing suitable states of wind and tide, we managed to manoeuvre her bows-on to the beach outside our shed, adjusting the bow moorings on the seawall and the stern moorings which we had already laid. Access to the barge from the seawall proved to be quite a problem and we finally constructed a pier at seawall height extending to the bows of Mamgu, the final section being hinged to allow for the rise and fall of the tide, a matter of some 4 metres. We then proceeded to fit her out to suit our requirements as a Clubhouse, with changing rooms, saloon and galley, not forgetting the motor pump which was essential for keeping her bilges reasonably dry, and from time to time, caused us some anxiety. The barge served us very well for some five years but our main limitation was that we could sail for about only two hours on either side of high water, so we scoured the river for a more suitable site. After a considerable search, we finally decided on a site adjoining the summer residence of Tony Benn at Stansgate Abbey where there was a concrete hard which extended right down to the water's edge at low tide, thus permitting sailing at all states of the tide. A lease for the site was obtained and we bought a hut which we found right in the centre of Braintree, which we dismantled and transported to Stansgate, where it was reassembled and made into a very nice clubhouse. This was in April 1963 and it served us very well until we were treated to a permanent brick-built premises which we now enjoy. In the meantime, Mamgu was sold to the London borough of Newham for the same price we had given for her, and after a refit, it was used for training young people from that borough in the ways of the sea. However, the condition of Mamgu deteriorated to the extent that she had to be abandoned and another barge substituted, which is still giving excellent service and giving London youths a taste of the sea. Eric Payne. H O R N E T W O R L D C H A M P I O N S H I P S 1981 MONNICKENDAM, HOLLAND. The Hornet World Championships were held in Holland during the first week in August. Twenty-one British boats made the trek over to Monnickendam including three Marconi teams, these were:- Murray Todd and Ian Lindsey - K 2079 'Kyle' Colin Harper and Graham Williamson - K 2100 'Renaissance' Graham Mead and Mike Turner - K 2108 'Ultimatum' The remainder of the British contingent was made up of eleven Brightlingsea boats, and others from Stone, Weston, Downs, Sandwich Bay, Sussex, and Medway Yacht Club. /continued.

- 6 - It was disappointing that no Australian sailors turned up, but the previous championships had been held 'down under' over Christmas which could account for their absence. The fleet was made up to a total of forty-two by the twenty-one Dutch teams. Royal Wedding Day - Wednesday 29th July. Since both Murray and myself had to work on the 30th we decided to pack the boats on the Wednesday, 'Renaissance' and 'Kyle' had to be 'double stacked' on my trailer. Help given by Les, Sarah and Chris at this stage was very much appreciated. Friday 31st July. At about 8.00 hours we all congregated at Murray's, Mike Turner and Graham Mead and family travelled in one car towing 'Ultimatum' while Graham Williamson, Murray and myself travelled in Murrays car. Ian Lindsey and his wife Karen were due to meet us in Monnickendam - they had spent the week previous to the championships touring Germany and Holland. We arrived at Harwich with about an hour to spare after a journey which involved smashing the tail board light socket when trying to make a 'U' turn and the trailer mysteriously coming adrift from the car after someone had forgotten to push the trailer onto the tow-ball correctly! During the calm crossing, the other Horneteers aboard and ourselves were given an interesting tour around the bridge. The rest of the time was spent in the bar and cinema. When we arrived at the 'Hooke' we disembarked and the one hour drive to Monnickendam turned into a three hour mystery tour of Northern Holland courtesy of Mike Turner !!! We arrived during a torrential rain storm and were glad to get into warm comfortable digs. After having had a few beers in the championship marquee we returned to our lodgings to get a good night's sleep. Saturday 1st August. Saturday came with fine weather and upon arriving at the harbour/marina everybody was already busy rigging their boats in preparation for measurement and weighing. The sails were taken into the marquee and the hulls were weighed on a large crane. Having been measured the boats were covered up and round one of The World Series Volleyball Championships, (Helms v Crews), started. In the evening we discovered the fantastic 'Disco Babylon' where we received some very strange looks from the local 'smooth boys', and where the young ladies would not even speak to us!!! On returning to the lodgings it was found that we were unable to open the door, and after an hour or so the landlady was woken up (at 1 am) but she did not seem too concerned. Sunday 2nd August After a 1½ hour sail to the start I had got over some of my initial nervousness and was surprised to find myself in 2nd position half way up the first beat, and I wasn't too concerned when Graham Mead overtook me to round the windward mark 2nd behind the 'in-form' Jeremy Newman. After this Graham and myself were overtaken by one Dutch boat and three other Brightlingsea teams to finish 6th and 7th respectively. /continued

- 7 - Jeremy and Ian Newman would have won the race but bowed to superstition and failed to cross the finish line. Murray Todd recovered brilliantly from a bad first leg to finish 15th having been 42nd (LAST) at the first windward mark. We arrived at the welcoming service at the beautiful old cathedral five minutes before it finished which could have been a good move according to the British sailors who attended. Monday 3rd August. As the weather for sunbathing improved so the sailing conditions deteriorated, but the three Marconi boats went out with the confidence of a good practice race and proceeded to 'go down the pan'. The race was won by Duncan Nicholson of Brightlingsea, and Marconi boats were placed as follows:- 22nd - Murray 28th - Harper 29th - Mead. Feeling a little down, the younger members of the Marconi fleet 'wound a few down' in the marquee. The beer was served in ½ pint glasses so about four rounds were bought at each trip to the bar. In the sing-song that ensued, I am afraid the notorious 'Hornet Boys' were outsung by the 'Sharpie Sailors' who were sharing the venue with us and sailing their Europeans. We put this downfall in the singing down to lack of practice and went to bed. Tuesday/Wednesday 4th/5th August. LOADS OF SUN NO WIND NO SPEED NO GOOD Positions Tuesday - Mead - 28th Todd - 30th Harper - 27th (in no particular order) Wednesday - Todd - 30th Mead - 26th Harper - 29th ( in order ancient to youthful) (BOTH RACES WERE WON BY JEREMY NEWMAN) I did not write about these two races because I felt my comments would have been censored anyway. If I say that the fastest and most exciting point of both days was being towed out to the line, and having a swim before the start, perhaps you can see my point. Topless spotters on the committee boat certainly seemed to be very popular among the British contingent!! Perhaps you ladies who do the job at the regatta could 'bare' that in mind next year! /continued.

- 8 - On the Tuesday evening there was a very enjoyable Bar-B-Que and entertainment was supplied by a really terrible jazz band who were so bad that they were good. Thursday 6th August. The brilliant sunshine continued but a stiff breeze of about force 3 came up and with spreaders bent back in an attempt to flatten out the mainsail the improvement of the Marconi fleet was dramatic with results as follows:- Harper - 9th Mead - 10th Todd - 11th. Jeremy Newman was again first in this race where one saw crews actually trapezeing !!! and this meant that the championship was sewn up. The evening began with round 2 of the volleyball tournament and with the help of the slightest possible rule bending the helms team pulled back their early deficit to lead the series. The party in the Clubship in the evening was a great success with the Hornet and Sharpie sailors (who by this time had been re-named the'BLUNTIES'), joined together in a sing song which could be heard by Murray Todd (who was trying to get some sleep) in this digs about a mile from the festivities. Friday 7th August. The final race came and the Marconi boats decided to go for it in a big way! The wind was about the same as Thursday and the support team of Vic Tate and family and Pete Clayton had turned up to offer moral support. The race started after one general recall and was won by Kipper Stodel of Brightlingsea who finished third overall. Graham Mead was 7th and Colin Harper and Murray Todd 10th and 11th respectively. The prize giving dinner at a nearby motel was excellent, as was the after-dinner party in the Clubship. Overall places:- 1st. Jeremy and Ian Newman - Brightlingsea. 2nd. Malcolm Goodwin and Derek Gentry - Brightlingsea. 3rd. Kipper and Andy Stodel - Brightlingsea. 15th. Graham Mead and Mike Turner. 20th. Murray Todd and Ian Lindsey. 21st. Colin Harper and Graham Williamson. The volleyball was decided on the Saturday with the crews narrowly defeating the helms. A most enjoyable time was had by all. Colin Harper.

me Q = COXSWAINS REPORT 1981 As I write this, there are just two weeks to go to the last race and I'm glad I invested in a Thermotic suit: Looking back, it's been a season of ups and downs. The new 55 Hp Yamaha engine has been a delight to use but we were very unfortunate to have a major breakdown at the same time that the work boat was having its overhaul. A lot of nice things were said about our coverage of the Regatta and a lot of this good work was the result of cooperation with other clubs. Having just a few regular drivers means we've come to know the other drivers and recognise their voices over the Radio. Our Regatta has become a sort of club for us all to meet. We also had the help of the Police this year (at last they now have our Radio Channel) and they turned up in their new Even inflatable (still wearing peak caps!) Rescue crews get a lot of thanks when the weather is bad but I would like to thank all my drivers for turning up and for their patience during all the quiet days of July, August and September. Waiting for that last Mirror in a Force 2 when everyone else is in the bar is no fun. We did have one or two critisisms and these were discussed fully at Sailing Sub-Committee meetings and hopefully we learned from the episode. One example is that we now carry two 20 Metre floating lines to cut out the need to approach fragile dinghies in rough weather. In conclusion we are fortunate in having our small band of non-sailing drivers and I hope they will carry on being available. NORMAN KERRIDGE COXSWAIN P.S. The Commodore recently asked how we could quieten the enthusiasm of the Saturday night Regatta. Ray Harvey tells me that at the last Maylandsea Bay open meeting, they showed the film "Jaws 2" and the effect was quite interesting !!

MIRROR FLEET NEWS I wonder what sort of season the hedgehog who lives in our garden has had this year? Not long ago I saw him (or her) late one evening in the middle of our lawn, but by the time I found a torch he had disappeared and I haven't seen him since. I suppose, that, like myself, he is getting ready for his winter hibernation so that he can return next spring refreshed and ready to take on all comers at those things he likes best. My own preparations for winter have already progressed to stripping the paint from the hull of LARS TINN ready for repair and re-painting. Hopefully I will avoid my usual panic preparation a week before the start of the new season - this winter it will be different. This past sailing season has been both a pleasure and a disappointment. A pleasure because it's always nice to sail at Stansgate; a disappointment because not enough Mirrors took advantage of our facilities to race and sail in our company. However, all things considered, I'm delighted that we managed to keep the Mirror Fleet afloat, even if at times the effort seemed doomed to failure. Surprisingly enough, some 14 different helms took part in those races open to the Mirror Fleet. These were:- Cadets - Summer Points - Mid-Week Sarah Cant - Vic Braybrook - Alf Cottam David Evans - John Stringer - Peter Collis Robert Coy - Bob Leader - David Green Stephen Rutherford - Margaret Boreham - Dick Spilsbury Damian Boreham - Mike Boreham - – Some helms, of course, took part in all three categories whilst others could only manage one particular category of races. My thanks to them all for their help in keeping the Mirror Fleet on the water and my thanks to their crews for their part in the team. In addition my thanks to all those who volunteered for Mirror Fleet duties and thus enabled us to fulfill our obligations to the other fleets in the Club. Although the Spring Points Series was a complete disaster (no races at all), the Summer Points Series saw most of the races sailed and once again Vic and Kim Braybrook demonstrated their marked superiority over the rest of Us. /continued.

A number of clubs on the Blackwater organise one or more races during the season plus a team race, for the BJRC calendar. CRUISER FLEET NEWS The work boat will be removed from the water for annual overhaul on 15th November, so any mooring work must be done before that date. We are now laying-up more boats at Stansgate and this puts more pressure on our space, and more rush in the hauling out of boats in general. We shall have to clear obsolete trolleys etc. from the boat park so for this and other obvious reasons I would ask everyone please to NAME their trolley for identification both now and when it is not carrying its boat. At the same time it could be helpful to name ladders. I have been asked to point out that metal grids used in the boat park are private property, to my knowledge having been bought by Vic Tate, Stan Campbell and Stan Allerton. It is not recommended practice to nick them from under other peoples trolleys. I have written previously on the use of suitable trolleys at Stansgate - basically the first requirement is strength, including the vertical structure, the second requirement is the use of reasonably large wheels. Vic Tate or I will always be pleased to give advice and we recommend everyone to have their own trolley. However unmodified road trailers are not suitable for our exposed conditions with strong tides. I recently witnessed three operations involving standard road trailers:- a) the boat wasn't laid up but someone elses trolley was damaged b) the boat was laid up in a damaged condition c) an extremely large working party of volunteers was required and one person risked fingers and toes in getting the boat positioned. We can suggest improvements which make these trailers tolerable but for boats staying at Stansgate purpose built trolleys are far more suitable and much cheaper. /continued.

15 8] COXSWAINS VIEW OF THE PILOTS CUP The sailing sub-committee's decision to run the postponed Pilots Cup race to Mersea No. 5 in October was rewarded with ideal conditions with a Force 3-4 N.E. wind on a flowing tide. No problems for anyone of course but I know from comments from one anxious wife on the shore that they do worry when you leave the haven of club waters and I was out of sight of most of you for the day so here's how it was covered. The course was Mersea No. 5 to port, Marconi No. 4 to port. Entries varied from the fast Dart to the comparatively slow Solos and we weren't even sure if West Mersea No. 5 was still there. So, the-0.0.D. agreed to cover up river from the club when the faster boats returned and we proceeded down river - needing half speed to keep up with the Dart : Problem No. 1] the Solos will soon be out of Sight. "Stone Rescue 2 - this is Marconi Rescue - over " "Marconi Rescue from Stone 2 - Good Morning Norman - over" So contact had been made with Derek on Stone Rescue 2 and their two boats kept an eye on you through their section to Bradwell. We proceeded to the buoy half hidden amongst the dozens of participants in the Golden Cod contest and dropped anchor. My high visibility orange suit came into its own and was seen by competitors long before the buoy!! The Dart rounded 10 minutes before the Hornets and by the time the 420s arrived Stone were reporting the Dart back in their waters and the Solos were only just in sight at Bradwell. We then had a bit of luck. I spotted Steve in the Dabchicks No. 1 Rescue Boat at anchor fishing ! (They weren't racing until 2.30 PM). He agreed to watch the Solos and kept in Radio contact. We caught up the 420s and by this time the fleet was back in visual contact. All in all a good day out and for me at least a pleasant change from the usual triangles. A final message to shore based relatives. If you are at all anxious - get the 0.0.D. to call us on the Radio. We can usually put your mind at rest even if we don't appear to be in the right position. NORMAN KERRIDGE COXSWAIN Note from Ed. Thank you Norman for your words of assurance, now perhass the 'anxious wife’ will feel a lot happier whilst we iting = for her loved one to return from one of the longer races.

- 9 - SOLO FLEET NEWS I was made very aware of how much the Solo Fleet has grown over the years, when members assembled at my home for a fleet meeting. Had the few who were unable to attend been present the room would have burst at the seams. The meeting was called to discuss the points published in last months Navigans. However, before getting down to the main business of the evening, Ron Greygoose found himself proposed seconded and unanimously elected Solo Fleet Captain. Good luck Ron. The first point to be fully discussed was the Helmsman of the Year series. We all felt that the present series which is run as a number of morning handicap races, generally produces races that are too short for most dinghies due to the wide range of boat handicap numbers that are sailed within the Club. The Solo Fleet proposes that for 1982 the selection for the final should be based on results taken from 6 (or more) designated Class Points Races spread throughout the year. It was also proposed that consideration be given to allowing more than one finalist from each fleet. The format used for the final was thought to be very good and should therefore remain unchanged. If the proposed change to the selection format is unacceptable the Solo Fleet believes that Helmsman of the Year races should be held in the afternoon in order to increase the possibility of longer races. Afternoon race start time was discussed,with the result that the fleet would recommend a scheduled start time of 1400 HRS. However, this must not be used as an excuse for a short morning course and we would expect at least 50% of the afternoon races to be postponed by 30 mins. During this discussion it was suggested that consideration be given to starting the Mirror Fleet first (followed by Hornet, 420 etc.) in order to reduce the time on the water for our rescue crews. The fleet has not previously been noted for its attendance at open meetings. In order to encourage support for the local open meetings, it was unanimously decided to request that Solo Points Races be deleted from our calender where they clash. Finally we discussed the August race programme. It was noted that this year between July 5th and September 6th there was no full day devoted to points racing. We believe that this gap should be reduced and that points races should be scheduled for August. Since we also agreed that the total number of points races was about right the implication is that they should be spread more evenly throughout the summer. Our Fleet Captain is charged with taking the proposals from the meeting to the Sailing Sub-Committee, but I publish them here because I believe it would help if other fleets consider some of the points raised so that Fleet Captains can be briefed with a fleet view when the matters are discussed. Frank Savill, Ex. Solo Fleet Captain.

SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT -— 1981 The 1981 season started on the first weekend in April, with 10 crews competing for the first of the Spring Points, The series, 12 races in all, turned out to be very wet and windy, and provided plenty of work for the rescue boat. The Summer Points, by way of contrast, were sailed in mainly light conditions. Soth the Spring and Summer Series had increased support this year, with average entries up in most fleets. The Enterprise fleet has recovered some of its lost support and managed to compete in both series, but the Mirror fleet only managed to race a Summer series with an average entry of 3.18. The Cadet Series entry showed a small increase this year, with 5 races sailed, and the average entry was 5.8, Whilst on the subject of cadets I think it worth noting that for the second year running the Helmsman of the Year has been won by a cadet. The Ladies Cup had very poor support this year with only 3 of the 6 races sailed. The major event in the Clubs sailing calendar is the Regatta. This year it attracted 206 entries, which was very good considering how wet and windy the weekend was. The Clubs two open trophy races, the Dinghy Challenge Cup and the Cruiser Cup were both won by competitors from outside the Club, with the Dinghy Cup going to G. Palmer of Stone Sailing Club, and the Cruiser Cup to J. Littlewood of Maldon Little Ship Club. With an average entry of 19 the MideWeek race has proved to be as popular as ever. Indeed, one race had 33 entries, which is better than some SundaySe The Solo, 420, Hornet Open Meeting, held in September, again attracted a good entry, particularly the Hornets. As for open meetings outside the Club, we had no major successes this year, but a party from our Hornet Fleet did travel to Holland for the World Championships. The best placed Marconi Boat being that of Graham Mead and Mike Turner, who finished in 15th place. Finally, my thanks to the members of the Sailing Committee, Rescue Boat crews, Race Officer and all Club Members who have given up their time to help during the past year. Murray Bates, SECRETARY'S REPORT TO THE A.G.M. — 1981, MEMBERSHIP 1981 1980 Difference Ordinary 228 21S - 47 Associates 110 107 eS: Totals 338 382 44 A decrease of 44 members shows a continuing trend on last year's figures which showed a decrease of 23 members, COMMITTEE The Committee have met 11 times this year to conduct the business of the Club. - 3 - 420 NEWS I must hold more 420 meetings at home. This revelation struck me the morning of the day put aside for a discussion of next year's sailing. Firstly I noticed that the windows had been cleaned (evidence - slight smear bottom left of patio door) causing me to squint at the morning paper because of the high level of reflected light. Secondly, the pile of adult reading material had mysteriously vanished, Thirdly, my name neatly written in the dust on the bookshelves had been 'siliconed' away. Where will it end I thought, grabbing my coat before I too was polished. Well, unlike Howard Hughes I have survived this cleansing experience and the 420 meeting did take place with 12 of us discussing the following proposals:- 1. The general feeling of the meeting was that the 420 fleet would support any move to select the helmsman of the year from pre-selected points races. This would hopefully free race officers to select courses of a reasonable length according to class. In larger fleets (or fleets with a large turn-out) it was felt that perhaps more than one boat could be selected for the H. O. Y. finals. This selected could perhaps follow the same set of rules that are presently applied to the number of prizes awarded in points series. Although this move would require changed in the H.O.Y. finals format the event could perhaps become a club event held on a Sunday rather than held on a Saturday as at present. This latter point will require further debating by the Sailing Sub-Committee (as will all the points mentioned here) and will depend largely on the arrangement of next year's sailing programme. 2. Useful discussions were held on the arrangement and scheduling of points series. The concensus of opinion was that most fleet members would welcome a third points series as it is felt that at present there is a six week spell around August where points series are dropped. It was proposed that these series could be called Spring, Summer and Autumn, with probably more emphasis on the Summer Points (i.e. more races). Since at present the end of Spring points occurs at a natural break in the racing calendar (the week before the Regatta), this series is best left as it is. If the proposals are adopted then the end of the Summer Points could conveniently be arranged for the week before the August Bank Holiday. The meeting also supported a move towards scheduling the afternoon races for 1400 hrs. The main justification for this move was that less time would be spent sitting around getting cold (or drunk!) between the morning and afternoon races. One problem with the proposal is that race officers might set very short courses in the morning to make sure of starting the afternoon races on time. The meeting then launched upon discussions concerning the abilities or otherwise of race officers to which various points emerged. Firstly, since not all race officers sail 420's it was proposed that more fleet representation be made when courses are being set. It was felt that this could best be achieved through the fleet captain. Secondly, concern was voiced that perhaps more course guidelines could be issued to novice race officers, these guidelines to be based on existing race records. This information, however, could be difficult to collate and may well be a complex task since the time to cover a given course is a function of tides, wind strength and wind direction. Furthermore it was not known how well the race officers sheets are filled in! (I expect Malcolm can tell us!!). As an aside, Ron Greygoose is organising race officer instruction for those interested, as part of the winter meetings. Finally on this point there appeared no resistance to the proposal that the order of class starts be reversed in order to reduce the time on the water for the rescue crews. /continued.

3. It was proposed that next season the fleet should hold two or three team racing sessions. It was felt that our team racing tactics and skills are non- existent at present and that if we are ever to win the Boothby Cup we must do something about it. The format of these meetings is at yet undecided, but they will almost certainly be held on a Saturday since the normal sailing programme is usually full. On a personal note I think that these sessions could be a boost to getting a firm commitment to team racing from the more active crews. Remember that being a good team racer does not necessarily mean having the fastest boat —- so those of you that are interested in joining these sessions please let me know. 4. The holding of a 420 Open Day was briefly discussed. It was decided that having a single specified day would not necessarily reach the largest number of possible converts and could wastefully occupy crew's time and boats unnecessarily. A better solution would be to advertise through Navigans, that anyone interested in sailing a 420 could do so by contacting the fleet captain, who would arrange a suitable time and helmsman. Several boat owners at the meeting pledged their support (thank you Pete and Anna!). 5. Finally, the meeting discussed tuning sessions for next season. This year's session was held during the August camping week and although the benefits were difficult to quantify, it was felt that much experience in the running of the event was gained which could be used to produce a better organised and more beneficial (and more fun of course!) session next season. To summarise the discussions it was felt that perhaps two days were needed and that time should be given to boat tuning adjustments. This would necessitate two or more boats for instance, sailing parallel courses (but each in clear wind), at the end of which the slower boat alters boat tuning in a attempt to increase boat speed. If this is successful, then the initial fast boat may well have to alter her rig if she is now the slower. To obtain any reasonable conclusions from this approach, all points of sailing will require covering. This of course will require considerable organisation and monitoring! Some of these points have already been discussed in the September .Navigans so will not be laboured further. There will be a "weightlifting" sessionWJanuary at some suitable hostelry so we can formulate some ideas then. Well it's been a memorable year and I will be sorry to see John and Murray and Dave Harper leave the 420 fleet to join the Hornets, It would seem that the main qualifications required for joining the Hornet Fleet (apart from a Hornet that is) are that you are ‘slightly overweight, can drink enormous quantities of beer, know the words to countless rugby songs (if not be able to hum in a deep tone) and, as Kate Nicholson puts it, be 'mental', Of the first two qualities John and Murray rate highly and of the latter two only time will tell! Dave, I think, will have no problem in making the transition. Kate and I will miss John and Murray whose victories on the water are only surpassed by their repartee before and after races, I*m happy to report however that John and Murray's boat will still be seen on the water as it has been bought by Russell Jeffries who, through the Marconi Grapevine and thin office walls, is prophesying spectacular victories next season. Well, good luck John, Murray, Dave and Russell. Russell's boat has been bought by Nick Pavitt, so I hope we shall see him racing next season, and I wish him the best, Phil Gray. Fleet Captain.

- 6 - OUR TROPHIES For a Club which has been running for some thirty years, members must have looked with pride on the handsome trophies arrayed at the Laying-Up Supper and some of them may have been intrigued at the names given to them. The President's Cup was presented by one of our founder members, and first President, the late Sir Eric Eastwood, who intended it for Fleetwinds, a class originally favoured by us. We adopted this class because of its ease of construction and good all-round performance ; also we knew its designer, Alan Eckford from Stanstead Abbotts who helped us and gave lectures at the Club's winter evenings, which, at that time were held at The White Hart in New Street, before we had the use of our present fine premises at Beehive Lane. The Fleetwind was popular at the time and some of them found their way to Ceylon and are still sailing today. The Pilot's Cup was presented by the late Cecil Stebbens of Heybridge Basin, who was pilot and River Bailiff, and was intended to be awarded for an all-in long-distance race. He was very helpful to the Club and towed Mamgu from Maldon to its moorings and he constructed the access gangway from the top of the seawall to the barge. Mona's Cup was also presented to us for an all-in long-distance race by Mona Clark, who with her sister, Reena, ran the Jolly Sailor, which was handy for the barge and was much patronised by our members. For the first race we asked her to come aboard Mamgu and fire the starting gun and we also invited them both to our Laying-Up Supper. The Garrett Memorial Cup was presented to us for cadets by the wife of the late Fred Garrett who was our Secretary and because he attended to Mamgu, he was known as the ship's husband. He did a tremendous amount of work for the Club and he owned a cruiser named "Melody". He cycled to Heybridge from his home at Great Baddow each weekend and some evenings but unfortunately he suffered a heart attack and was unable to cycle, but, undaunted, he acquired a scooter so was still able to reach the barge until his heart finally failed. His daughter still works in the canteen at Great Baddow. The Boothby Cup was preented by Bob Boothby, Commodore of the Osea Sailing Club when they built a clubhouse on the seawall at Millbeach and were and still are keen sailors, turning out in good numbers, in all weathers. In their early days their members joined our Laying-Up Supper which was held in the New Street canteen, when some 60 of them occupied one complete spur of the top table, making an attendance of some 450 - an all-time record! The Mamgu Trophy is awarded annually for the best log or account of a member's cruise or adventures during the past season. It is a beautiful model of the sailing barge in her heyday and is correct down to the smallest detail. It was constructed by one of our founder members, Arthur Adam and there is a similar model in the Science Museum at Kensington. The Triple K may be something of a mystery to some; it was presented by Nic Tovey and Brian Partridge for Enterprises of which they were exponents. Their boats were named Kiora and Keel Kat respectively, and they were all spelt with Ks, hence the triple K. They seem to have taken it in turns in the early days to win their own cups. Eric Payne.

IDEAS SECTION As promised last month I will open this section with a description of how to mount the kicker lever under the thwart with little loss in efficiency. The figure (on Page 6) shows how the wires, pulley and lever are positioned. The two wires should be of substantial thickness (2 mm suggested) since the lever generates impressive forces. The upper half of the longer wire, above thwart height should be plastic sheathed to minimise damage to the crew (actually this system improves crew mobility during tacking). The main anchorage point for the system is at the aft end of the centreboard casing. This should be achieved by drilling a vertical hole through the casing and attaching a substantial eye bolt. Ensure that a washer is employed to distribute the load on the casing. Attachment of the wire to the eye bolt can be by shackle or by direct attachment with a thimbled eye in the wire. Since the rules allow only two pulleys with a lever, and since one of these pulleys is required on the mast, the second cannot be used to any mechanical advantage. However the length of the lever is not restricted and it is possible to employ a longer lever than is conventionally carried in the classic kicker arrangement. I have not found this to be necessary but for younger helms/crew this is worth considering. All dimensions shown in the figure can be varied by plus or minus one inch without any problems if the boom fixing is variable. If this is not the case the long wire length must be determined to suit your own boom setting. The modern 420 has a fixed gooseneck with sail luff tension controlled by the cunningham. If you have an older boat (e.g. Snapir) the gooseneck can be permanently fixed and the same principals of mainsail tuning applied. To prevent the lever slapping the centreboard casing it is possible to loosely mount the lever to the casing with a rubber bush. The mounting /continued.

- 6 - must allow enough movement for the rotation of the lever and should be placed as close to the centre of rotation as possible.
