- 9 - OUR TROPHIES Continued from previous Navigans. The Jackpot Cup was presented by Jack Bigden for a race for the over-forties. Jack did a tremendous amount of work for the Club and was largely responsible for the construction of our original wooden clubhouse at Stansgate; he also presented the Commodore Cup. The Costain Cup was presented by the late Sir Richard Costain whose firm constructed the M.A.S.C. clubhouse in Beehive Lane; he was told about our sailing activities in which he took a great interest and offered to present us with the said trophy. The Hornet Challenge Cup was presented by The Saltcote Sailing Club, in the ballast hole at Heybridge and has been won alternately by them and us. They are to be congratulated on their new floating clubhouse and their enthusiasm in turning out in good numbers in all conditions. We were pleased to welcome their then Commodore, Derek Gerkin and his wife Mollie at our last laying-up supper, in fact Derek proposed the health of our Club. The Twin-Flags Trophy was presented by the B.B.C's club known as The Ariel Sailing Club, whose clubhouse is at Teddington on the River Thames, and was won alternately by us and them. Sailing for these races was an interesting experience because, in their case, it involved dealing with flukey winds caused by buildings and trees, and when they sailed with us their experience of having to contend with choppy salt water! The Jonathan David Craig Cup was presented by Jack Bigden and is called after the name of his grandson. We are indebted to Vic Tate for producing the pictures of these trophies in the issues of Navigans for March and April 1974 when his wife Brenda was Editoress, and to Vice-President Nick Tovey for his painstaking research in supplying the names of the early winners, - his name being seen frequently amongst them. KNOW YOUR FLEET CAPTAINS Phil Gray's the boss of the 420 Fleet, No nicer guy could you wish to meet. Mike Boreham's head of the Mirror lot, Anxious to find what his lot's got. Ron Greygoose lords over the Solo-ists, Always scheming, and making lists. Murray Todd reigns over the Hornet 'crew', Hoots Mon! Och Aye! The Noo, The Noo. Stephen Perkins runs the Handicap 'mixture', 'He' and 'them', make quite a fixture. Derek Webb's bunch are last but not least, An Enterprising lot, rising like yeast.

- 10 - THAT WAS THE YEAR THAT WAS Well, my ears have only just stopped ringing from the calls of STARBOARD!, WATER!, and UP UP UP!, it seems that if nothing else, Hornet sailors can out-shout anybody on the river or in the bar! But despite my temporary deafness, "mine's a pint of lager", I have survived a very enjoyable year with a new boat in the Hornet Fleet and it's not called Stimulation for nothing, being a largermainedstiffriggedgybing-boardgofastershapedgoodwinhornet! Steering me round the buoys has been Simon Kenworthy, who has perfected his Jacque Cousteau impersonation despite 'all sorts of problems' depending on the wind(pardon). But as if to confound our sometimes brutal treatment of the boat, due to our unusual sailing techniques, it has proved to be very strong and resiliant. The fleet at Marconi is looking very healthy (boat numbers that is!) under the careful guidance of Murray Todd our Fleet Captain. The racing at the club has been excellent and Marconi boats have also done very well in other clubs' open meetings. Along with Colin Harper we competed in the Junior Nationals at Medway Sailing Club. The sailing was good but the social life(?) left something to be desired. The event was won by the Newman brothers with Div Mellor second, we finished 5th. and Colin 8th. We also competed in the Stone open meeting and finished 10th out of 38 boats. This together with a 7th in our own Regatta and a 4th in the Summer Points are good results, we feel, for the first year. We also competed in the Brightlingsea winter series, and although this is a closed event, Colin and ourselves were given temporary membership of the club. In spite of not managing any major success we enjoyed the sailing and our thanks go to the Commodore, Roger Robinson, and everyone at the club for making us so very welcome. The social life has been, and still is, the best of any fleet with great friendship extended by other clubs' fleets, much entertainment being enjoyed both organised and impromptu- "nice one moonie and steady dickie". So, eagerly looking forward to the new season, which starts for us with the Easter Egg at the Royal Corinthian Club, Burnham, on the 9th-12th April, we hope to see you there and we'll go for it in a really big way. Congratulations must be extended to Dave Harper, Murray Bates and John Chisnall for their excellent taste in joining the Hornet Fleet. Ian Stott. K 2093. General wave to the 420 Fleet.

- 11 - 1. 2. LOG OF COPERNICUS 1981 A Family Summer Cruise to Holland - Ijsselmeer and Friesland. The Concise Oxford Dictionary defines a lcg as a book with a permanent record daily made of all events occurring in a ship's voyage; it is also defined as a traveller's diary. Basic sailing details make dull reading for all but the purist, and I was not prepared to emulate Sir Francis Chichester who meticulously recorded for how long each sail was flown and how often it was changed etc., besides this was a sailing holiday but with the emphasis on "holiday". I have therefore, adopted a formulae which subdivides each entry or day into firstly, sailing details and secondly, a narratation of the events that took place. This is hopefully, a happy compromise between technical information and a more casual account of our wanderings; a Traveller's Diary. Friday 31st July Proposed passage from Stansgate to Levington Marina. Log Reading 7636. Trip zeroed at Stone. High Water Osea 13.30. 13.55 Shipping Forecast. Thames Variable 3 increasing to easterly 6, then decreasing to cyclonic 4. Thunder. Fog. 1750 Shipping Forecast. Thames North easterly 3-5. Fog, Rain. No sails set. The water and the sky were a rather murky shade of grey as, in company with Pete Clayton and Sandra on "Peace", we dropped the mooring just after 1.00pm and motored down towards Bradwell. The fresh breeze was on the nose and the water was increasingly lively as I attempted to sort out the boat. The first surprise of the holiday was to see the small coaster, the Alice P.G. layed up opposite Peewit Island. Steered by twin propellers instead of a rudder, her performance underway has earned her the nickname of "Miss Piggy", according to our son Robert, who crewed on her several years ago carrying china clay from Cornwall, and cargoes from Ireland to the Continent. Vic took some photo's for the record in between the bouts of heavy rain. Off the Nass the wind against the tide gave us a very lumpy sea and with the rain beating down there was a joint decision to run into Brightlingsea and leave Levington for tomorrow, hopefully, there would be an improvement in the weather. Motoring towards the Bench head I tried out my newly aquired radio expertise and attempted to make a link call through the new coastal radio station, Orford Radio. I was unsuccessful, as we did not have the required channel on our set, and Thames Radio were oblivious to my calls. Pete had a little trouble getting lines out onto the posts at Brightlingsea, but was eventually successful and we came alongside. The shipping forecast at 5.50pm bought more gloom, and our Avon unlashed from the cabin top and used by Mary to put out our lines was deflating quite well, so the skipper's mood darken and he spent the evening muttering about taking up some game called "golf". A very pleasant Dutch couple on a superb steel ketch came alongside "Peace" and during the course of conversation recommended a fish restaurant overlooking the town of Urk, in the Ijsselmeer. Vic took to the deflating Avon to take some photo's of "Arrk", a lifeboat he converted to a cruiser on his front lawn some twenty years ago. She had just changed hands, and was on a maiden voyage with her new owner. Outside the Anchor, the local Morris men were jigging in the rain, but on board we crept quietly into bed.

- 12 - 3. Saturday 1st August Passage from Brightlingsea to Levington Marina. Log Reading 7646. 10 miles. High Water Harwich 13.30. High Water Brightlingsea 14.30. 13.55 Shipping Forecast Thames North easterly 4-5 decreasing to 3. Mainsail and working jib set. A quiet morning, and our new cockpit cover slung over the boom was voted a great success. It allowed us to have the sliding hatch and cabin doors open without the persistant rain coming in. Pete and Sandra came aboard for coffee and shortcake topped up with Bailey's Irish Cream. Mary had the entire contents of the Rainy Day Box out and we spent the morning doing puzzles and trying to solve Rubick's cube. We left at 2.30pm and Copernicus' slick crew had main and jib set and we were sailing off Stone Point, Mersea, a record for us. Note to reader: Vic has a "thing" about keeping decks clear and so all foresails are stowed away while we are in harbour and bent on only when all mooring lines are clear. The sail past Nol and the Colne Bar Buoy was a pleasant reach and we waved cheerfully to John and Ann Smith on "Freya" as they passed by. Round Colne Point and across Priory Spit the sea started to become lumpy as we began the beat up the Wallet. I managed to contact on the radio, "Tijo" and "Beehive", who were sailing up to Levington from Stansgate and were about ½ mile behind our stern. Off Clacton Pier I dropped the jib and Vic started the engine as we were definitely overcanvassed, and we motored sailed tack by tack up towards Harwich. The wind was a good 4-5 from the north east and again the wind against the tide caused a confused short, steep sea that created very unpleasant conditions. My Bailey's thought it would like to make a second appearance but I managed to convince my stomach that it wasn't necessary. 7.00pm saw us off Shotley and everything totally different. We enjoyed a glorious "glide" under mainsail only with Mary on the helm, along the Orwell and were in Levington Marina by 8.00pm. The following hour brought "Tijo", "Beehive" and "Peace" safely into harbour, and we all celebrated with a drink on the Lightship at the close of the day. Sunday 2nd August Log Reading 7648 32 Miles. No passage undertaken. It was decided to spend Sunday drying ourselves out and spending a day together with everyone before we went our separate ways. "Tijo" and "Beehive" hoped to reach Lowestoft on their East Coast Cruise. A batten pocket and seam on the head of the mainsail needed repairing, and there was the usual pile of knickers and socks to wash out, so I had plenty to do. The weather was extremely hot and sunny and lunchtime found the Marconi party, lead by Vic and Stan Campbell, striding the mile and a half walk to the local hostelry. There to sit in the sunshine and enjoy a spendid Ploughman's lunch of salad, stilton and home baked bread, excellent value for 90p each, and washed down with some good beer or a light, dry Merrydown cider. The walk back was a little more erratic and one intripid party came across the saltings and mud flats back to the boats. After a lazy afternoon, the evening saw a repeat performance without the Ploughman's lunch and with the Hall's running a ferry service for everyone to the pub with their car. At the end of a glorious day we all jogged home by starlight. 4. Monday 3rd August Passage from Levington to Imuiden, Holland. Course: Buoys to Shipwash Light Ship, then 0.80M. 06.30 Shipping Forecast. Thames- Varaiable 3 becoming south westerly 3-4. Fog. High Water Harwich 02.27, 14.46. (B.S.T.) Pitching Ground Buoy Log reading 7673, trip 37 miles. 09.30 Cork abeam. 12.00 N.W. Shipwash buoy abeam. 13.15 N. Shipwash buoy sighted. 13.35. Shipwash Light Ship sighted. Log Reading 7696, trip 60 miles. 13.55 Shipping Forecast Thames- Varaiable 3. Fog. 17.50 Shipping Forecast Thames- Varaiable 3. Fog banks. The usual routine for our holiday, a cup of tea with the 06.30 Shipping forecast started the day, and this was the forecast we had been waiting for, slipped our lines just before 07.00am, the next stop Holland! The morning was bright and sunny with no wind and poor visibility. I checked the log at the Pitching Ground Buoy and we continued to motor up towards Orford and the Shipwash Buoys. Vic was not not very thrilled to find that the tide was against us and that we would have to sail against it until we reached the light ship. The visibility was so poor that by the time Shingle Street was abeam we had lost sight of the land. It took all morning to reach the Shipwash Light Ship during which time the visibility continued to lessen and so did the confidence of the crew! We heard the Light Ship before we saw her and I made a Safety Traffic call to the Thames Coastguard informing them of our departure. This then was our last contact with England and no other mark until we reached the Dutch coast over a 100 miles away. Early afternoon the breeze began to stir and we hopefully set main and working jib and cut the engine. The wind enabled us to sail at a fitful three knots, while on board we pottered around, Mary spun for mackeral and caught one so small we threw it back. Vic managed to get some sleep during the afternoon, while I did my "Clare Frances" bit on the tiller. At this time, Vic was relustant to put the Autohelm on as he was "saving" it for the night, so someone was always on the tiller and watching the compass like a hawk. With the darkness came a little more wind and we continued to sail on. However, there was a general panic when it was discovered that the compass light didn't work and couldn't be repaired, so that had to be monitored with the torch. I took the early watch (09.00pm to midnight), the visibility had improved but I saw no lights from any other shipping. Sitting in the cockpit, in the dark I began to wish I was any where but where I was! Oh! for Captain Kirk's transporter room and the ability to re-energise somewhere on dry land. Hypnotised by the compass and my mind filled with negative thoughts I didn't notice how close we were coming to "Peace" and I had to call Vic from his bed to come and sort things out before we collided. As Peace can sail much closer to windward than Copernicus and is a fin keel boat, while we have bilge keels we presumed that she would be the faster boat, but we were wrong and what ever I did, luff up, bear away or spill wind I could not keep astern of Peace and so we went in front for the rest of the night. Tuesday 4th August 06.30 Shipping Forecast Thames- Variable 3. Fog. 13.55 Shipping Forecast Thames- Variable 3. Extensive Fog banks. Midnight, and Vic came on watch. There was a fair amount of shipping around and on one occasion both boats had to turn to avoid getting to close to a large cargo vessel.

- 13 - 5. At 03.00am I came back on the helm, while Vic tried to get some rest. Our speed had dropped and by 05.00am Vic was out of bed again while we dropped the sails and started the engine. I stayed on watch until 7.00am giving Vic a little longer in bed after his very interrupted night (N.B. we worked three hourly watches), but by then I was dead dog tired and collasped into a deep sleep on the double berth in the main cabin. I awoke with a start an hour later, the engine had stopped. I looked up to see my dearly beloved with a grim expression giving the thumbs down sign. We had fouled the prop. Great! The North Sea was, luckily, flat calm but very cold as Vic donned his bathers and went over the side on the ladder and removed the remains of a tattered plastic bag from the prop with his toes! Ten minutes later we were on our way again, feeling very releived. As the day continued, the heat increased and by lunch time Vic was still in his bathers with a towel over his head to give some protection from the sun. Hats were the order of the day. Everyone had lost their appetite and the fog was gradually getting thicker until we were motoring on in a baking hot, shrouded world. We heard but did not see the ships passing astern of us during the afternoon but gave them a cacophony on our fog horns, Pete's sounded rather like a wounded cow. Our first landfall was a huge red and white checkered tower which we sighted about 04.30pm and on first sight we thought it was the bridge of a tanker about to run Peace down! We identified it as a gas pipe line station five miles offshore and much further south than we expected to be at Noordwijkerhaut. We turned and motored north the fifteen miles to Imuiden. The fog was now very bad, visibility down to 100 yards and at one point we lost sight of Peace but found her again by listening for the unmistakable sound of her Stuart 8. Pete decided to put up an extra halliard for his courtesy flags by tieing a shackle onto a line and heaving it over the cross trees. Ten minutes and a pair of broken glasses later, Peace was proudly flying the Dutch flag and the yellow duster. We sighted the lighthouse at Imuiden about 06.30pm and rounded the headland carefully as there were several big ships coming out and a dreadful tide rip. We locked through the Middensluis and then went up the Velserkom and thruned back to tie up alongside several other boats just outside the Kleine sluis at 07.30pm. We had arrived. Everybody was dead dog tired and suddenly hungrey, so somehow I managed to cook a meal before quietly passing out into a deep, peaceful sleep. Wednesday 5th August Passage from Imuiden to Amsterdam. Motor used only. Awoke to the sweet smell of sulphur fumes from the chemical factory the otherside of the North Sea Canal. I knew immediately we were in Holland, when a stream lined coach pulled up on the quayside and sounded its horn. This was a travelling supermarket and sold fresh bread, milk and vegtables as well as everything else one could need. Mid-morning we motored off along the North Sea Canal towards Amsterdam. Mary had a great time being towed behind the boat clutching a fender, while my mood became more and more thunderous as I tried to clear up the general debris scattered around in and outside the boat. I erupted when Vic stuffed a half deflated Avon down the companionway and asked me to stow it in the quarter berth, and for the rest of the holiday I was nicknamed the Avon lady. We reached Amsterdam by lunchtime and stopped at Sixhaven a small private marina, just north of the Central station. Lunch, showers and we were out to see the town by mid-afternoon. 6. Pete and Sandra very kindly offered to show us the way to the Rijksmuseum and we hopped onto a tram to travel the mile across town. The museum itself is the most imposing Dutch building I have ever seen, glittering with gilt and stained glass windows. The picture I had come so far th see Rembrant's "The Night Watch" was slightly disappointing, an anticlimax aftersuch a long wait to see it, I suppose. However, we picked the best place to go that day, as the weather was very hot and sultry and the museum deliciously cool. Wewandered back across the streets eating ice creams, listening to the street musicians and admiring the great range of goods for sale in the shop windows. Bought the inevitable post cards and then caught the free ferry that runs from the station across the canal to the Shell Research Centre, five minutes walk back to the Marina. Mary enjoyed a swim and we enjoyed a pleasant drink in the clubhouse before the end of the day. Thursday 6th August Passage from Amsterdam to Monnickerdam on the Ijsselmeer. Wind- north easterly 3-4. Main and working jib set. We left the Marina at 10.00am to try and catch the 11.00am opening of the road bridge just beyond the Oranjesluizen, which is the lock entrance from the North Sea canal into the Ijsselmeer, but we were unlucky and did not clear the lock until well gone 11.00am. I took the opportunity, while we waited for locks and bridges to mend a hole in the head of the mainsail, and by midmorning we were clear and sailing towards Marken. The weather was warm but the wind from the north east was blowing a gusty 3-4, so we had a beat up towards Marken lighthouse. There was a lively sea and conditions on Copernicus prevented me from boiling a kettle, sandwiches only for lunch. Visibility was poor and what we took to be a fleet of Hornet's racing ahead of us became a fleet of gaff rigged Sharpies as we came closer. We reached the Marken breakwater by 04.30pm and found the channel that goes into Monnickendam. We were surprised by the lack of water, only ten foot in the deepest part and a great deal of weed around. Pete caught us up and we were all tied up in the Marina by 05.00pm. The Marconi sailors competing in the Hornet World's were waiting on the pontoons to greet us and we had a grand get-together in the evening over a beautiful steak dinner in the local cafe. Friday 7th August Proposed passage from Monnickendam to Hoorn. Wind North-east 1-2. Genoa set. We decided to try and take some action shots of the Marconi Hornet fleet racing in the World Championships before making our way up to Hoorn. We said goodbye to Pete and Sandra, who had decided to stay put and have a lazy day, and motored out across the Gouwzee towards the Olympic course which had been set out off the breakwater in deeper water. The visibility was appalling, you couldn't see from one mark to the next, and Vic only managed to get a few shots before we realized we could be in serious trouble as technically we were a support boat, and if we interfered with anyone's racing the committee could disqualify the entire Marconi team; and we didn' think that the lads would be very pleased about that. Having been frustrated in our attempts to take photo's we were frustrated when we came to try and find the entrance into Edam harbour which was completely obscured by fog, and so in the end we headed for Volendam. The harbour was noisy, crowded and hot, and so was the town. We changed some money at the local bank, had lunch in a restaurant and bought some fresh food before deciding that we had had enough and dodging between the coach loads of tourists trundling through ten foot

- 14 - 7. wide streets, we came back to the boat. On Copernicus, several people were untying lines, tying up lines and generally charging about the decks, we quickly jumped aboard, untied all the lines and said bye bye to Volendam. By this time it was fairly late in the afternoon and we enjoyed a gentle sail under genoa back to Monnickendam. Mary grabbing the chance to go for a swim over the stern with her favourite blue fender. After dinner on board we strolled into the town to find that the most delightful evening market had been set up along the edge of the main canal and all sorts of goodies were on offer; even the children were selling off their old toys and books. Actually in the canal, a Dutch version of our Regatta Marquee pole climbing contest was taking place. Contestants had to swim to a pole, climb it and ring the bell at the top. Several people were successful, but there were many wet failures. The prizes were vouchers that could be exchanged in the local shops and while we were looking around a toy shop a very wet young boy came in and exchanged his voucher for a mini-radio. We had gone in to the shop to purchase a small plastic dinghy for Mary to play with; complete with oars it cost £7, which we thought was quite a good buy. We had to rush back to the boat to blow it up and Mary had a maiden row in the dusk before going to bed. Her aged parents then departed for the clubhouse, an old ship moored in a corner of the marina. After a quiet drink with Pete and Sandra, we were joined later in the evening by Murray Todds and Mike Turner, who had both returned from the Hornet Prize Giving Dinner held at a hotel some miles away. The talk and beer flowed freely until the early hours and a volumputous Dutch girl, called "Miss Piggy" by all the boys entertained all with her dancing. When we left at 2.00am the party was still going strong and we just about managed to stagger along the pontoon to bed. Saturday 8th August Passage from Monnickendam to Marken and from Marken to Hoorn. Wind westerly 2-3. Mainsail, genoa and sppinaker set. We awoke fresh for the day after a lazy lie-in and were joined by Colin Harper and Grahem Williamson, two young horneteers, who were rather subdued after the revelries of the night before. They had also lost Murray, very careless!! Several strong cups of coffee later Murray arrived and all the lads decided to join us and help sail the boat over to Marken, just for something different to do, after racing Hornets for five days. Great activity then ensued as the genoa and then the spinnaker were hoisted. Murray was on the helm and we had a pleasant gentle run down the channel and across to Marken harbour. Marken, orginally a small island on the edge of the old Zuider Zee is now joined to the mainland by a single road. Cars are banned from the island centre and many of the older inhabitants still wear the traditional Dutch costume of the area. Sometime in the 17th century the Dutch must have cornered the market in dark green paint as so many houses and buildings, all over Holland are painted in this colour. The old cottages around the harbour edge were most picturesque with green weatherboarding picked out with red and white. We wandered around mingling with the crowds of American tourists, or "Gee Thelma's" as we called them. All had little labels so they didn't forget who they were. After a snack lunch, Murray and Co. caught the ferry back to Monnickendam and we put to sea to sail up to Hoorn. Pete and Sandra came with us and for the first time we enjoyed the wind running free and had a lovely sail on the port tack under mainsail and genoa. Vic was so overcome with the excitement of a real sail, he fell fast asleep, probabely due to the effort of watching "Miss Piggy" dancing the night before. Mary was up forward catching up on her sleep after several late nights and I quietly enjoyed helming and counting the church spires along the 8. coast until we reached Hoorn round about 06.00pm. The harbour was absolutely packed and so was the marina but the harbour master allowed us to lie alongside the pontoon beside his office even after Pete gave it a hefty clout with "Peace". Mary was now full of bounce again and had discovered that there was a fair in the town. We all went to have a look round after dinner and Pete was persuaded to accompany Mary on one of the rides. This was almost a disaster as its effect on Pete's stomach was more devastating than anything he had encountered sailing. The standard of equipment and rides offered was extremely high, much better than anything I had seen in England. Mary's stomach was more resilent than any of her adult companion's and she enjoyed being hurtled round in space several more times before we trudged back to the boats. Sunday 9th August No Passage undertaken. Sunday morning we decided to have a lazy day and after moving from the pontoon on the outside into more comfortable marina berths, we settled down to enjoy Hoorn. Hand feeding the ducks was a favourite pastime. Holland has a large bird population, many of which are very tame. I had admired the herons standing on hoardings in the middle of Amsterdam. Gulls, comorants and grebe could often be seen fishing when we were out sailing and every marina had its own raft of ducks that beseiged the boats waiting to be fed, even the sparrows would hop over the decks and perch on the guard rails waiting for the odd crumb. We paid a visit to the local museum, housed in a very ornate four storied building in the main town square. It contained collections of china, glass, siver and furniture as well as some rather horrific paintings; but the most interesting pieces were the cheese press's and scales, used for weighing the finished cheese in the market. Vic had another little Rotella hunt, his favourite pastime. Checking over the engine in Imuiden he discovered the Potter was leaking oil, although the leak was cured by varying degrees during the holiday, our stock of oil was very low, and so far Vic hadn't managed to buy any to replace it, very annoying when we knew there was a gallon sitting on the garage bench at home. The day ended with a walk down to the harbour in the dark to admire a three masted square rigger, the "Elizabeth Smit" lying alongside the harbour wall. A Dutch ship, 100' in length, with a bowsprit over 30' long, she was on charter to a German party enjoying some palatial living. Dressed overall with lights, she was a magnificent sight, and Vic managed to take some reasonable photo's despite the long exposure required. Monday 10th August Passage from Hoorn to Enkhuisen. Wind North easterly 4-5. Main (reefed) and working jib set. After a hasty early morning shopping trip(knocking up the local tobacconist), we left Hoorn to sail up to Enkhuisen. The wind was blowing well and we decided that discreation was the better part of valour and I put four rolls in the main. We clawed our way northwards and had a bouncy and somewhat wet sail. The visibility for the first time since we had come into the Ijsselmeer was good and we could see the cars travelling across the top of the dam that cuts the meer into two parts as we came up towards the lock.

- 15 - 9. We came alongside the dolphins badly, hitting the boat forward and cracked the port navigation light and scuffed the varnish. The skipper was not amused! Locking in was accomplished without any further trauma's, although the lock was very crowded and even more boats were on the other side. After doing a turn round the harbour, we ran into the marina beside the railway station and managed to get a berth there. This, we discovered was a Royal Yacht Club and rather particular about its "customers", but like everywhere in Holland, being English boats we were made extremly welcome. The loo's and showers were palatial and dues were expensive by Dutch standards, 12.65 guilders or £2.60p per night. At the end of the afternoon we took Pete and Sandra to see the Zuider Zee Museum and its fabulous collection of traditional Dutch craft. A visit not to be missed if ever you find yourself in Enkhuisen. By sheer chance, we had met again our Dutch accaintances Hessel and Hopi Bakker whose company we had so enjoyed three years ago. They were still sailing their Cobra "Breewnyd" and the day ended with a lively discussion about Dutch and English politics aboard Hessel's yacht accompanied by large amounts of alcohol. Tuesday 11 August Passage from Enkhuisen to Medemblik. Wind- North easterly 3-4. Main (reefed) and working jib set. After the usual shopping expedition and a relaxed lunch we came out of the Marina and motored northwards to Medemblik. The wind was a fresh north-easterly occasionally gusting 5, so I set the working jib and shook one roll out of the main. Again we were on a beat and tacked out passed a fleet of dinghys racing off the point. Several tacks later we went out far enough to be able to lay the course for Medemblik close hauled. The waves were of nosignificant size but the fetch from the northly wind and the effect of the large dams, north and south, produced a nasty beam sea that lifted the boat on her starboard side screwed her round andleft her yawing badly. After two hours sailing I found the motion distinctly unpleasant. The weather was bright, sunny and fairly warm, a change from the dull clouds and drizzle we had had for the last couple of days. We sailed to just before the harbour entrance and once inside saw that again things were very crowded, (twelve boat trots), and decided to wait for the town bridge to open and lie inside the inner harbour for the night. By 07.00pm we were in and tied up alongside "Peace" lying outside an immaculate fishing boat. This presented problems to me going ashore, as there was a four foot gap between the boat and the harbour wall. Luckily, we found a boarding plank, which we quietly borrowed. The town, itself, is small and quiet with two dignified church towers and a railway museum. Vic took some photo's in the fading light, trying to catch the last of the sunset, and the glow of the harbour lights in the dusk. A mellow evening ended with a sherry in the cockpit before bed. Wednesday 12th August Passage from Medemblik to Staveren. Little wind. Genoa set. Quick action required at 08.00am, the fishing boat was going fishing, but we had resumed our places again a quarter of an hour later. The cloudless blue sky and bright sunshine promised a really hot day, and after shopping for fresh food and doing some hand washing, (spin drier provided free with showers and toilets), we chugged under the town bridge and through the harbour entrance. 10. There was delight breeze so wehopefully set the genoa and tried to sail eastwards towards Staveren. This quickly became a drift and as the sun got hotter and hotter we gave up the unequal struggle and took the genoa down. Pete managed to find the deepest part of the Isjeelmeer to anchor in (26'), and went for a swim. Vic and Mary joined him. The water was mirror calm but there was a thick film of duckweed that produced green loo's. We thought that perhaps the Dutch had not achieved the right chemistry for their inland sea. I indulged myself, and spent the afternoon lying out in the cockpit sun-bathing. Late afternoon we entered the lock at Stavern, very crowded again, and into the canal system of Friesland. The marina was only a short distance away and while paying our dues, we also picked up some diesel from the pump on the harbourmaster's pontton. The facilities were excellent, the main complex contained a bar, restaurant, supermarket and laundrette, while the showers were free and there was a sink for hand washing. The town was a little way away so we didn't make the effort to explore very far. Mary and I played tennis on the lawns while Vic chatted up a Shell tanker driver delivering fuel oil to the yard in his never ending search for Rotella. We celebrated his lack of success with a beer in the bar before retiring to bed. Isomewhat painfully, due to overexposure to the sun. Thursday 13 August Passage from Staveren to Hook. Motor used only. We left at 10.30am with no real destination in mind, but we would see what the day would bring. I had been very domesticated and strung a line of washing from the mast to the backstay, but that had to come down as the skipper said it obscured his view and we looked like a gipsy's encampment! It was beautifully sunny as we came along the Johan Frisco Canel and under the Warnserbrug to Morra Meer and Oorden. Pete followed a very large ferry giving day trips for tourists through the bridge and all the canals and meers were packed with craft of every conceivable shape and size, many of them sailing. We continued up the Nieuwe Vaart to Fluessen and into Heeger Meer. The day was ideal holiday weather, hot and sunny again, so we anchored just beyond the Betonde Geul and Pete bought "Peace" alongside. We all swam and lazed around. The water didn't have any weed but still somewhat murky and not very warm. After a wine and cheese lunch, a snooze became essential and it wasn't until late afternoon that we pulled up the anchor and came out of the Meer and into the small town of Hook. Pete managed to sail, but with so many boats around Vic found it too nerve racking. We were lucky enough to take the last berth beside the town quay and "Peace" lay outside of us. We paid our dues to a lady harbourmaster, who gave us not only a receipt but a small biography of the town printed in English and Dutch. Everything was extremely convient, the shops and post office only a stone's throw away, and we had fresh chips with our beefburgers for dinner and ice cream for sweet. Although our little corner of the quay was obviously the meeting place for all the locals, everyone drifted away by 11.00pm and we settled down for the night having spent the evening looking around the boat yards and large marina the other side of the canal. One yard specialized in building better yachts, another polythene dingys and windsurfers. Friday 14th August Passage from Hook to Terhorne. Motor used only. Friday began early about 01.00am!! when the bars closed and all the youngsters camping on day boats ahead of us came back and decided to have a sing song. One played the banjo quite badly, another the guitar quite well.

MIRROR FLEET NEWS FIRST, THE GOOD NEWS = the Mirror Fleet meeting at my home in Sillericay was well attended by eleven members, with another four members sending their apologies for absence due to illness or other unavoidable commitments. Since the four absentees have all raced and helped with Mirror duties in 1981, then I am encouraged by the response to this meeting and hope the fleet can carry it through to the racing programme in 1982, The meeting was arranged to hear a talk by Dennis Sristowe on Sailing the Mirror. Dennis is a well-known Mirror helmsman of national standard and (to borrow a theme from a well-known advertisement) his talk reached those theoretical parts that the text books cannot. reach. In other words, Dennis avoided the pitfall of merely repeating the standard text—book theory of sailing and instead gave us a more practical approach to solving the problems of mast rake, lee and weather helm, rigging, sail setting, spinnaker systems, hull painting etc. - in fact, all those subjects falling under the more general heading of "boat tuning". The meeting soon took the form of "question and answer" and I personally found the talk just right in: helping to bridge the gap between text=book theory (which I can understand). and practical application (which I can't). Now I'm counting the weekends to the time I can get the boat into the water to see if I can make it all work. One interesting piece of information to come out of the meating is that our own Vic Sraybrooke first introduced Dennis Bristow to the pleasures of sailing. - 9 - 11. By 03.00am I was threatening to throw a bucket of water over the banjo player but Vic thought I was being very antisocial. Things quieten down about 04.00am and I fell into a fitful slumber. This was shattered at 07.00am by the town dustcart emptying bins about three feet away from my left ear. At 08.00am the crew of the charter boat on the outside of Peace began to move all their belongings, one at a time, from their boat across Peace and Copernicus into an ancient car parked where the dust cart had been. This took over an hour of trudging across our decks. Soon after they left their place was taken by a large motor cruiser who from the number of people and shopping bags were going ashore to do their annual Christmas shopping. Enough was enough. We took the hint and left as soon as possible. Another idyllic day as far as the weather was concerned, we passed under the Jelteslootburg and along the canal turning left into the Prinses Margriet canal which opens into the Houke Slept and Sneeker Meer. The waterways were absolutely packed and it became rather like driving around Piccadilly Circus. It was a relief to anchor off a small island, the Roekoepalle, for a swim and lunch. Copernicus and Peace bounced about a bit and in fact we began to drag our anchor quite well, however, we were not likely to collide with anything and we were travelling in the right direction, so we let it be!! As on the previous day we lazed around and moved on at the end of the afternoon. Having passed thro' the flood barrier at the top of the meer, we found a quiet secluded, half-empty yachthaven, surronded by grassland and nothing else! This was situated just outside a place called Terhorne and was our turning point,as far north and east as we were going. Pete and Vic were most concerned over the amount of traffic on the canals and meers, steering required a great deal of concentration and there was no chance to relax; so they decided we would have an early start in the morning to avoid some of the traffic. The surrondings were perfect, quiet and peaceful. The water surronded by lawns and lines of willow and beech trees, set on the grass were bench seats and a children's playground with swings sandpit and a beam made from a tree trunck. After the hectic night in Hook, it was a welcome change. Saturday 15th August Passage from Terhorne to Sloten. Motor used only. We were away early, just before 08.00am. The Sneeker Meer was glassy clam and dotted with a few fishing boats but by the time we reached Houke Slept the barge traffic had began and at one point we counted five in close proximity. We retraced our route back towards Hook and turned left into a narrow canal that went down to a small town called Woudsende, which we corrupted to World's End. The town bridge was a toll bridge and we put our 1.50g into the clog that came swinging down on the end of a fishing line from the bridgemaster's office. We moored alongside the quay and spent the rest of the morning wandering around the back streets of this quaint little town. Much to his surprise Vic was successful in purchasing some of the elusive Rotella from the local garage. Pete and Sandra and I bought some presents for relatives and friends back home, while Mary bought some frites, the main part of her diet these days. At the end of the quayside was a magnificent, fully restored thatched windmill used as a Youth Sailing Centre. While we ate a sandwich lunch washed down with a very, tasty red wine, we watched several rowing skiffs go by. They were obviously being used for instructional holidays. One was crewed by an elderly gentleman determined not to forget which was port and which was starboard, the right sock was green, and the left red!! 12. We left about 01.30pm and motored down the canal, which was flanked by some very new individually,architectured houses, each with ite own berth for the family yacht. Once in Sloten Meer the breeze was enough for Pete to sail, but as again it was almost on the nose Vic didn't bother. The other side of the meer the canal ran down to the town of Sloten. On its outskirts the camp for the Cadet European Championships was beginning to be dismantled. Under another toll bridge, we thought we would lay alongside a small, tree-lined jetty at the back of a marina. Pete went first but went agroundtenfeet from the wall. We then had a go and after a bit of gentle manoeuvring, heaving on shore lines and trying to avoid tangling the aerial in the trees we managed to get close enough to get ashore; and by pulling Peace sideways fore and aft, as close to us as possible, we could all regain terra firma. On later exploration we discovered another thatched windmill and a town full of antique shops. Pete said it reminded him of Kelvedon! I should explain that these small towns that we visited had no particular tourist attraction. The focal point was the town canal which usually came from the maincanal in a the top of the town and then back again at the bottom. The canal was high street, mainroad and market place all rolled into one, flanked by broad cobbled pavements leading onto the shops. There were usually several bridges across and on one of these in Sloten, the presentation of prizes for the European Cadet Championships took place. Vic and I walked up to watch. I never did discover the nationality of the winner, but a lad from Stone Sailing Club was second sweating away in his thick navy yachting jacket, while a Dutch lad was third. All the Dutch team looked very attractive in cherry red sweat shirts and white denim trousers. After dinner Mary organised a tennis match staking out a court on the grass with some spare warps and two of Pete's boat hooks. After some energetic rushing around and collasping into heaps of laughter, pete was declared the winner. We celebrated with beer, shortbread and carrots! The carrots being the other part of Mary's staple diet at that time. We were all fairly tired, and when Mary threw some McInroe type tantrums, I quickly decided it was time for bed. Sunday 16th August Passage from Sloten to Lemmer. 17.50 Shipping Forecast. Humber, Thames, North-westerly 5-6, backing westerly 3-4. Showers. It was good weather as we left again fairly early to motor down towards the bridge that separated this canal system from the beginning of the main route into Lemmer. After breakfast I took the helm while Vic carefully did his housework and swept all the leaves we had collected in Sloten off the decks. We were disappointed to find the bridge didn't open until lunch time and as it was only 09.00am we decided to risk trying an alternative route through Brande Meer. We were worried about the depth, as the chart showed only 1.7 metres and "Peace" draws 4'6", but we were very lucky and with the echo sounder on crept across more by luck than judgement. The meer ran into the Stream Canal and by midmorning as we were going in the weather began to change and the wind got up and it rained heavily for a short time. Once into the main town canal we went through three toll bridges and locked out the other side, We were undecided what to do, our ambition was to reach Urk that day, the wind was definitely very strong and so we agreed to see if we could stay in the small marina by the lock for a couple of hours while we had lunch and sorted ourselves out. The harbour master was very helpful and allowed us to tie up alongside his pontoon.

- 10 - 13. He enthused about the Ipswich Town football team and also told us that there was a storm warning out for the Ijsjeelmeer. As it was only a quarter of an hour to the Scheveningen weather forecast we grabbed an early lunch and after listening to the radio agreed to stay put! There were gales all around. Lemmer was larger than the previous towns we had visited, and seemed to specialize in second hand shops. Vic was relieved it was Sunday and that they were shut. We had a long walk round the town and along the breakwater that gave a fine view of the harbour entrance. It looked very hairy out there, lots of white horses and plenty of boats running in for shelter. I tried a Dutch delicacy a "Niewe Herring" from a market stall, these are sold raw and should be eaten whole garnished with onions. I found it rather tasty but it did not dampen my appetite and back on board I set to and produced a three course Sunday dinner accompanied by Tony Blackburn and the Top 20 on the Radio. Just like home! Monday 17th August Passage from Lemmer to Urk. Wind Westerly 3-4. Main (reefed) and storm jib set. After persuading my husband to go bargain hunting and buying two T-shirts for under a pound each and some more presents we came back on board and listened to the 11.40am broadcast from Scheveningen Radio. The gales had abated and the wind was from the west; so it was agreed to sail down to Urk further south. I shook one roll out of the main, but we were being cautious, our main fault is that we are often over canvassed, and hauled the storm jib out of moth balls and set it. Once passed the headlands and several barges we were able to sail all the way on the starboard tack. The water had calmed down and we were able to navigate by sight as the visibility was good. Peace was sailing well behind us, and as we had time in hand, I dropped the main and Mary helmed the last few miles under jib only. We arrived at 03.00pm and tied alongside the largest fish market in Europe. Urk is a working harbour and there were over fifty trawlers tied up waiting to go out or being painted and repaired. The town, itself, was once an island and only joined to the mainland in 1942. It is like many small Dutch communities deeply religious and we were given some literature by a representative of the local church. We set out to find the restaurant recommended to us in Brightlingsea, that seemed light years away now, and found it just beneath the harbour lighthouse, which stands on top of the only hill I have ever climbed in Holland. Beside the light house is a memorial to all the fishermen who had lost their lives at sea. 1856 was a bad year, they lost 18, many young boys of 11 and 12. The sea still takes its toll today and in 1980 three men from the town lost their lives in the stormy waters of the North Sea. After Vic had taken more photo's of the sunset, it was beginning to be an obsession, we sat down to a fish and chip feast, small delicate plaice, sweet and dry with no grease, mountains of chips and mayonnaise, beer and icecream to finish. All very tasty and filling and reasonable for 13.50g per head, well under £3 each. Tuesday 18th August Passage from Urk to Muiden. Wind South to south-west. 4-5. Mainsail (reefed), storm jib set. We left reasonable early, as we intended to make the fairly long passage from Urk to Muiden. 14. The forecast said the wind was swinging round to the south, south west, on the nose again, and it was a good beat across the val van Urk towards the power station near Lelystad. We set the same sails as yesterday, the visibility was bad, very misty and there weren't many other boats out, only a few barges and an eel boat pulling up its nets. We motored sailed a few legs to catch up with Peace and after locking through at Lelystad reached the landing stage we had discovered three years ago in time for a late lunch. The wind was much stronger and we had quite a time getting lines ashore, Mary trying to heave in the boat against a good force 5. Despite increasingly severe weather conditions we decided to press on and left mid-afternoon. The sky had darken to a steely grey and the waves were short and steep giving us a bouncy wet time. We didn't bother to set the storm jib but motor sailed under main only. We tacked down and across time and time again, conditions were almost as bad as when we had sailed the same passage three years ago. Helming was very tiring, standing in the cockpit it was impossible to manage for more than an hour, and Vic and I took turns; it was always mine during the rainstorms as I always wear full waterproofs and Vic never wears a full set only a heavy duty anorak. Eventually, after what seemed like days we sighted Marken and the Pampus , a small island just north of the entrance into Muiden. We set the storm jib to dry it off and motor sailed at six knots instead of four without increasing the engine revs, perhaps we should have hoisted the jib sooner! It was interesting how quickly the rain flattened the water and the motionand speed of the boat improved.by the time we entered Marken, in the dusk, our navigation lights on, the water was relatively smooth - beaten flat by the rain. We managed to find a lerth and signalled Pete and Sandra in alongside us with a torch half an hour later. As always we were all starving hungry. Mary set to and fried some eggs on toast.Having eaten them Vic fancied a tin of curry and some new potatoes I had found in the food locker, this was gobbled down with relish. Ugghh!! Wednesday 19th August Passage from Muiden to Amsterdam. Motor used only. We spent the morning having coffee in the dungeons of the Muiden Schloss and took great pleasure in showing Pete and Sandra the giant carp swimming in the moat. I'm sure they thought we were telling another Tate tale but they were amazed to see one monster about 3' in length nicknamed "Nessie" by the locals. In the harbour the loos and shower block had been completely rebuilt since our last visit and were now very plush. Lunchtime we were away and bound for Amsterdam. We motored, although Pete (purist as always) sailed. We had to wait for the bridge tied up alongside the dolphins, once through it was an even longer wait for the lock, which was very busy. On the other side of the lock we lost no time in heading back to our place in the Sixhaven Marina. Peace seemed along way behind and when they eventually came in, the first thing Pete had to do was go swimming and clear his fouled prop. Late afternoon we decided to have a good lokk around Amsterdam. I, personally, found the city much cleaner than on our previous visit and less crowded with immigrants. We avoided the Red Light District, however, after discovering the Chinese quarter, which was most interesting we wandered by accident into what Pete so aptly described as the "spade squat area". The streets were narrow and dingy with boarded up houses and crowded cafes filled with Negro youths. At one point the road was blocked by a large American car the boot of which held a large urn containing what looked like stew being served to the men loitering around

- 11 - 15. We strolled by trying to look as inconspicuious as possible and quickly found the mainthroughfare. We dined at the frites stall opposite the station and headed back to the peace of Sixhaven, stopping at the clubhouse for a quick drink. The "quick drink" developed into a qiet party between the four of us, and a very pleasant evening was concluded by exchanging burgees with the "officer of the day". Sixhaven, he told us was a work's club for the Steel and Shipbuilders of the Amsterdam docks and there were many similarities between their organization and that of our own club, Marconi's. However, they had been helped by their companies who had purchased and dug out the site while the members had financed and built the clubhouse themselves. Thursday 20th August Amsterdam - no passage undertaken. The morning bought more rain and wind and the shipping forecast was gales from the north east. Several English boats came in during the day, one, Nordic Eagle from Woodbridge, whose skipper was the previous owner of Stan Campbell's Macwester "Tijo". He had crossed from England the previous day and had had a fast passage with an all male crew. While we were chatting on Peace, a large Rival attempted to berth nearby. Her skipper, a true blue Englishman of the "Hello, Rodney" school bellowed orders while her enthusiastic but novice crew rushed about in ever increasing confusion trying to understand the incomprehensible but voluble instructions being shouted in Dutch by the harbourmaster. Real, cartoon comedy stuff!! We ventured out in the wind and rain to do some shopping and found a variety of shops just behind the main city square ranging from supermarkets to botiques, stores to sex shops, all jumbled together. We visited the Hema, which is similar to our British Home Stores and bought two devices for making toasted sandwiches on a gas ring. We were so heavily laden with groceries and parcels, it was a struggle to walk back to the boat and we gladly stopped to have some more frites after bumping by chance into Pete and Sandra. Pete was beginning to feel very depressed, he had to return to work on the following Monday morning, and if the weather didn't improve within the next twenty four hours, he would have to abandon. The rain stopped at lunchtime but the wind continued to blow so I had a quick washing session which all dried fairly quickly. Mary and Vic wandered northwards and discovered some more shops that were much closer than the city centre. The evening was spent quietly, the mood of gloom was not dispelled. Vic was undecided as to what to do, although we still had a week's holiday left, a route home had to be planned in the near future. Friday 21st August Amsterdam - no passage undertaken. The early morning Shipping Forecast caused several decisions to be taken. Vic choose to take the canal route south and then cross the North Sea as soon as it was possible. Pete had reluctantly decided to abandon Peace in Sixhaven and return the following Bank holiday weekend to bring her home. So the day was spent with the Tates changing French francs into guilders and stocking up with provisions for a long weekend, while Pete and Sandra booked tickets for the train and the Hook to Harwich ferry. Pete very kindly lent us his inland waterway charts. We meet for a farewell drink and watched for the lasttime a pusher tug bringing a sand lighter through the canal lock, an interesting exercise in small boat handling. 16. We came out of Sixhaven at 07.00pm and down the North Sea canal into Oudehaven, where we lay alongside a Dutch motor-sailer until the road bridge opened half an hour later. Vic went up to the bridge house to pay our dues and discovered that the railway bridge had been broken but they hoped to have it repaired in time for the usual opening at 02.20am. Once in the Westerkannaal and tied alongside the wall, we had a meal and Vic was invited for a beer on board a Dufour just ahead of us. The owner was celebrating as he had only purchased her that afternoon and was taking her home to Braassemermeer. At 10.00pm a Westerly J24 came alongside and after chatting over a cup of coffee about the difficulties of Racing ratings in Holland and the Royal Wedding, we tried to get some sleep. Saturday 22nd August Passage from Amsterdam to Rotterdam. Motor used only. The railway bridge opened at 02.20am to the second and we began what was to be a very long day. 9 bridges later we tied up just outside the motorway lock to wait for it to open at 06.00am. The journey had been uneventful, with only six boats going through, and a head wind which made holding station between bridges easy. We were awoken at 05.00am by the sound of someone's engine and peered out of the hatch to see that the lock was open.Off again and we raced across Niewe Meer in the dark down to the bridge at Schipol. This we were told by our Dutch companions would open between 07.00am and 08.00am, in fact, it opened at 06.10am and my attempts to get any more sleep were totally unsuccessful. We motored down the Westiender plas under Leimuiden bridge and into Braassermermeer. Here we said good bye to the Dufour "Aeolus", which was berthed in one of the many private marinas there. We proceded down the canal to Woubrugge and Alphen aan den Rijn. Mary and I had a quick run ashore to buy some fresh bread at the bakery by the canal edge. We were familar with the geography as this was where we had stopped and met Hessel and his family three years ago. Vic managed to shut his eyes for a whole fifteen minutes but by eleven we were off again, through the town bridges and passed Gouwsluis, Boskoop and Waddinixveen towards Gouda. Using Pete's charts navigation was easy and of the "turn right at the next windmill" variety. The scenery was enchanting, gardens running down to the water's edge in the towns with ducks waddling amongst the flowers. Our only difficulty was in the Julianasluis just after Gouda, when we couldn't get the forward line on quickly enough for the skipper, and I thought we had lost Mary who had gone ashore to pay our dues and couldn't find a way back to the boat. In the Grouwe canal the scenery became much more industrial, the wind was blowing strongly from the south and Vic was very tired. By 03.00pm he had had enough and we berthed in the Capelle Yachthaven for the night. I gleaned some information regarding the bridge and lock opening times from the harbour master and we had just enough energy to feed the ducks and have a meal before going to bed and slept soundly despite squeaking fenders. Sunday 23rd August Proposed passage from Rotterdam to Bruinesse. Motor used only. We locked through the flood barrier above Rotterdam in solitary splendour at 07.15am, the only mishap was my dropping a fender over the side just before going in. (Retreived with a boat hook). Going down towards Rotterdam and round the Storm Polder we were beseiged by kamikarsse wasps dive bombing on board.

- 12 - 17. At Alblasserdam the 12 metre road bridge could have presented problems, as it was closed for the day, but the tide was low and with me clutching the bottom of the mast and trying to judge the distance between the top of the radio aerial and the girders (about 6"), we came under quite smoothly. The Dordrecht railway bridge opened at approx. 24 minutes past the hour and we were an hour ahead of shedule arriving at 09.15am. At 09.24am precisely the railway bridge was opened, a pusher barge came through from the south and a small yacht went through from the north. We went under the railway bridge and blew our fog horn as a signal for the road bridge that lies parallel to the railway bridge to be opened. Nothing happened, there was no sign of life in the bridge house, and it suddenly dawned on us that being Sunday, the road bridge was shut! Great! We tried going very slowly to see if we could get underneath guided by a Maluccan gentleman, who was on duty at the railway bridge, but it became apparent that we would lose the top of the mast if we went any further and so beat a hasty retreat astern, not wishing to get trapped between the two bridges. With a whirr of machinery the railway bridge descended, and with it our hopes of progressing any further that day. A chat with the Maluccan gentleman confirmed our fears that the road bridge wasn't manned at all on Sundays and the next opening was 5.41am Monday morning. Vic toyed with the idea of dropping the mast but decided against it I'm glad to say. We prowled along the main canal looking for a yachthaven, there were several, all their entrances barred by unmanned bridges that were closed. We came into a side canel and turned again by another closed bridge, we had earmarked a spot by a large blue steel ketch that looked suitable for lying alongside, when suddenly the bridge behind us opened, much to our surprise so we thought we had better be polite and go through! We found a berth in a pleasant marina and thought that we had better make the best of the circumstances and "do" Dordrecht. An hour's walk round the town revealed that everything was shut except the local park. This had an enclosure with goats, a turkey, peacocks and a donkey as well as a large number of ducks. Through the trees a pop group were setting up their equipment for a concert in the bandstand, and although the amplification was "fortissimo", the sound was not unpleasant. After lunch on board and a beer in the clubhouse we returned to the other side of the bridge and tied up alongside the ketch we had seen in the morning. We didn't want to get caught out again! I washed ten pairs of socks while Mary sketched the windmill opposite. There was a lot of swell from the motor boats ploughing up and down, obviously out for a Sunday afternoon joy ride. Luckily, everything quieten down with the dusk and we turned in for an early night. Monday 24th August Proposed passage from Dordrecht to Kortgene, Veersmeere. Motor used only. Up by 05.00am, that's 04.00am B.S.T. and discovered to our horror we were hard aground, but managed to get off by a great deal of pushing with boat hooks. We had completely forgotten that all these canals below Rotterdam are tidal, as they lead down to the shelts! I managed to drop another fender, must be something to do with getting up early but picked it up despite the darkness. No trouble with the bridges today, and dawn found us going down the Dordsche Kil and past Willemsdorp and out into the Hollandsch Diep. We followed the buoys down to Willemstad lock and were through by 09.00am. We had no detailed charts of this area until Bruinesse and this caused some confusion and a mini-divorce, after navigating us through the Volke Rak successfully, I lost my bearings and couldn't find Bruinesse. The visibility was good but my logic rather unsound when I mistook a cement factory for the town. However, after steering some rather odd courses we found the correct line of buoys at Bruinesse and eventually the Zuirizee bridge came into view. 18. The wind appeared to be on the nose which ever direction we were travelling in and we gave up any hope of sailing and motored into the Easter Schelde, crept across the edge of the flats to Zandcreek and the lock into the Veeresmeer. The short wait for the lock was spent chatting to a Dutch family aboard their delightful "yacht", which had been a service boat for ferries, now gaily painted in green, red and yellow she provided comfortable accomadation for holidays afoat, certainly something different! Once in the Veersmeer we agreed to carry on to Veere and not stop at Kortgene. We had time in hand and weren't feeling too tired despite the early start that morning. We hoped to pick up diesel and water at Veere but discovered that fuel was not available as the firm had gone bankrupt, a sign of the times! We continued onto Middleburgh and by 08.00pm, after delays in locking and buying fuel, we were inside the town canal. After feeding the starving hordes, we were invited for coffee on board the Prout catamaran alongside us. She hailed from Tollesbury, and her owner lived in Witham. It transpired that his brother, also on board, had built "Bluster" now sailed by Colin Leveridge from Stansgate. It's a small world! Tuesday 25th August Middleburgh. No passage undertaken. 06.30 Shipping Forecast. Thames- variable 3. Noord Hinder S.W.2, 5 miles. 13.55 Shipping Forecast. Thames- variable 3. High Fastnet moving east. 17.50 Shipping Forecast. Thames- variable 3. Extensive fog banks around coast. The weather was extremly warm again and we spent the morning in the coolness of the shopping arcades bargain hunting.Mary took the record for buying three pairs of kinckers for 20p! The afternoon was spent messing around, the female crew buying still more presents while Vic did did his homework with charts and tide tables and planned our route home. He was most concerned with the forecast of fog and wasn't prepared to take any chances with navigation. At dusk we went to admire the "Master Builder" which was tied up alongside the harbour master's office, being too big to come into the town canal. A group of folk dancers gave a display on the quay side and we watched them before retiring for an early night. Wednesday 26th August Passage from Middleburgh to Brightlingsea. High water Flushing 11.20 B.S.T. 2345 B.S.T. Log Reading Middleburgh 8127 Trip 490 miles. Flushing Lock 8131 494 miles. 06.30 Shipping Forecast. High fastnet moving east. Thames- variable 3 Fog. Noord Hinder West by north west 2. Visibility- 5 miles. B.P. 1128 rising. 11.00 Changed all clocks to B.S.T. Log reading 495 abeam windmill just before Flushing lock. 11.17. W12 buoy abeam. 11.25. WN 14 buoy abeam. 11.33. WN 12 buoy abeam. Working jib set. 11.51. WN 6 buoy abeam. 12.00. Trawle buoy abeam Log 500 Course 280° 12.30. Mainsail set. Sailing at 4 knots. 12.40. Auto helm set.

- 13 - 19. 13.55 Shipping Forecast. Thames- northerly 3 decreasing to variable 1-2 Fog. Noord Hinder. North by north west 3. Visibility 11 miles B.P. 1130. 15.00 Log Reading 513 miles. 15.45. Identified No 9 wreck buoy approx one mile south off course. 16.00. Jib down. Motor on. Log 515. 17.00 Log reading 520. 17.45 S.E.Thornton buoy, took back bearing 115°M. 17.50 Shipping Forecast. Thames North by north west 2-4. Fog. Noord Hinder North by northwest 1. Visibility 11 miles. B.P. 1130. 18.00 Log reading 526. 19.00 Log reading 531. 20.00 Log reading 536. Noord Hinder 1½ miles north abeam. After some more last minute shopping we left at 09.30am and it took several hours to reach Flushing but we were in the lock by 11.30am Dutch time. We tied up alongside the "Admiral Benbow" from Maldon preparing to make the same journey as ourselves. Her crew were busy dunking large hunks of bread into cups of Bovril,as if it was their last meal, did they know something we didn't? At 11.45 we locked out and all watches and chronometers were changed back to British Summertime, we were on our way home. We followed the buoys out towards the Deurloo channel and by noon there was enough wind for me to set main and working jib and maintian our course sailing at 4 knots. Conditions were good enough to set the Autohelm and George took over at lunch time and helmed for almost the rest of the way home. He had been put on for short spells on the way over but on the return trip proved to be an indespensible member of the crew. The wind was northerly force 3 but the gales had left a nasty cross sea that cork screwed the boat round and made her yaw. Eating became a desultory affair and Vic felt very sick after having to go forward to sort out the anchor chain which had been badly stowed and was banging around in its locker. Even Mary was bad adding a little tomatoe soup to the salty waters of the North sea, and for the rest of the trip we munched Crackerbread to calm our queasy stomachs. We were shocked to find by mid-afternoon how far the tide had set us south and altered course accordily. The wind became much more fluky and so the jib came down as it was only banging about but we left the main to try and steady the motion of the boat, which hadn't improved. The motor went on again, and by 08.00pm we sighted the Noord Hinder and Vic went on watch to take us across the shipping lanes. The visibility was good but Vic admitted afterwards he had been prepared to run back to the coast if there had been any sign of fog. I went below and slept for a couple of hours and was horrified on waking to see no husband in the cockpit. Heart stopping moments later I discovered he was on deck putting the mainsail to bed, a very silly thing to do alone and in the dark, that is how accidents happen. Thursday 27th August By 01.00am we had sighted the Galloper light and the shipping lanes were behind us. Vic waited until we could just see the loom of the Sunk light before turning in and I was left alone in the dark but this time with George zipping away merrily for company. He had to come off for ten minutes while I avoided colliding with a tug coming down from the north across our bows but that was the only event which caused me any concern. By 07.00am I was chilly, stiff and weary, we had sighted the Gunfleet Tower as I went below for some sleep but an hour later I woke up to find that with the dawn had come the fog and visibility was down to 100 yards. The fog became thicker and thicker, George came off and the echo sounder on. Vic had taken a back bearing from the North east Gunfleet buoy and set a course for Clacton pier, when the depth was only 10' we thought we had better anchor before we landed on the beach. Just as I was dropping the CQR over the side there, 30 yards ahead 20. was a triangular mark rising out of the murk. The chart and the odour confirmed that it was a sewer outfall mark ¼ mile south of Clacton Pier, with the engine off we could hear the waves breaking on the beach. During breakfast, the fog lifted for long enough for us to see the shore line and the Helter Skelter of Butlin's Holiday Camp. The fog had clamped down again as we set off using the echo sounder to follow the contours of the sea bed around Priory Spit and into the Colne. We were all beginning to feel a bit frayed around the edges by now and progress was obviously extremely slow. We passed a channel marker buoy, several yachts and a sailing barge before we found the deeper water which was the edge of the Colne channel. We found the entrance buoy to Brightlingsea and crept towards the "Master Builder's" mooring and then it was as if a curtain had been lifted, the sun blazed down, I could see across Cindery Island and there were the trots ahead of us. We came alongside a Mirage and I handed the lady on board a rope for a running line which she promptly tied on to the guard rail! Muttering "Charter boat" under my breath to Vic, I suggested that the rope might hold us better round the cleat aft, disenguaging herself from several small, screaming children, she agreed it was quite a good idea! Ashore by 11.00am, we dropped our Clearance forms off at the Customs House before phoning my parents and walking to their house for a fish and chip lunch. Afterwards Vic collapsed on the spare bed for some well earned rest while Mary and I lay in the sunshine on the lawn and told my family some of the many incidents of the last month. We returned to the boat in the evening and agreed it was better to make a passage in the dark than in fog, and as fog was forecast for the next morning we were off again by 09.00pm on the last leg home. The night was clear as we came down the Colne to the Inner Bench Head then cut across the corner of Mersea Flats towards Bradwell. The ships laid up in the estuary were a blaze of glory, all except the "Alice FG", which was lit by one flickering anchor light. The familar shoreline came closer, the Stone pub with the Thursday night disco going full blast, the Stone Sailing Club and then the end of the Stone moorings, where with the aid of a searchlight we found our own, just 500 yards from the house and home. The Log Reading was 616 miles. The famliy agreed we had had a very successful and enjoyable holiday but that we had been too ambitious in the distance covered. Only having overnight stops at each port of call is very tiring. We were lucky that no one suffered from even a minor ailment and the boat behaved beautifully throught out. Mary at eleven has become a capable crew member , her agility at jumping ashore and setting lines was a great asset. Vic got all his sums right and took us there and bought us back safely. I, responsible for navigation on the inland waterways, had no great difficulties, except for losing Bruinesse for a while. We found Holland similar in climate to England, but fuel, food, fags and facilities are much cheaper than here, Brightlingsea cost the same as Enkhuisen and offers no facilities at all by comparision. Our holiday this year cost less than a cruise on the East Coast two years ago. We look forward to returning to Holland next year, but our plans will be more modest; we shall sail to the Veersmeer and, hopefully, laze in the sun. Brenda A. Tate. September 1981

Saturday 29th May ) Sunday 30th May ) Regatta Monday 31st May ) EDITORIAL The season has started with a bang (well anyway, a hoot!)! Didn't Ron do well in getting the Solos on the water. It was a lovely sight to see so many sails on the water for the first race. Of course, preceding this was the Fitting-Out Party which, although small in numbers was large in success - sorry to have missed it. Now our thoughts must turn to our biggest event of the year - the Regatta. Those of us who aren't sailing, must help as much as possible in the running of it. Mary Greygoose. COMMODORE'S NOTES Now that the Fitting Out Party is behind us the season is officially launched, and it is time to emerge from hibernation. It was very pleasing to see a good number of members entering into the spirit of Pirates and Castaways by wearing some excellent costumes and this helped to make it an enjoyable evening. Did anyone get lost in the fog on the way home? If you have tried to contact me at work recently and have been unsuccessful it may be because my office is now in Building 46 at New St. (Internal Telephone No. 9374, External 723) or it may be that I was just not there anyway for various reasons. However it is always possible to ring me at /continued.

- 2 - home and if I am not there, leave a message. John Weedon. SOCIAL NEWS The Fitting-Out Party was not so well attended this year, however, many more members were in fancy dress. The two prize winners were:- Jackie Manning and James Court. Thanks go to Shirley Orchard for her efforts on the night and also to the ladies who helped prepare and serve the food. Our next event will be the Regatta on 29th/30th/31st May, with a disco on Saturday evening and a James Bond film on Sunday evening! Both of these events will be held in the marquee. Pat Harper, Social Secretary. DINGHY PARKING On reading the March issue of NAVIGANS I was concerned to find items which indicate a trend of opinion which cannot be allowed to go unchallenged. The contributions in question refer to the re-allocation of space in the dinghy park and clearly imply that racing helmsman should be given prioity over those who do not race. I have no axe to grind as to how people make use of their sailing time whether it is to race, cruise or potter but it has always been recognised that, unlike some other clubs, the M.S.C. is not a purely racing club. It should also be remembered that those dinghy owners who do not appear to sail very often are still contributing to club funds and are therefore making it possible for the more enthusiastic to organise their racing. Those who spend little time at the club are the losers as they are not making the use of the facilities to which their subscription entitles them. It may be a sad fact to the racing committee but an examination of the club's statistics leads one to the conclusion that the racing members are in fact a minority of the membership. Under these circumstances why should a racing helmsman have priority regarding parking position over the next? I have always in the past been reluctant to make criticisms of the club's management as I am only too aware of the valiant work they do and what little contribution I make to their work (also some are my friends?). On this occasion, however, I must point out that such a move constitutes a change in club policy which to my knowledge has not been referred to the membership. All dinghy owners who pay the same subscription must have equal access to the club's facilities. Doug. Paynter. Editor's Comment - I have been advised by the Committee that there has been no change in policy over dinghy parking as could be construed from the item in the /continued.
