-—= 9 os The following article came into the hands of our President, Mr. Jack Pateman, from an unknown source:= "MARINE CASUALTY = A report sighted by Captain G.P. Byth (1940). Dear Sir, I write in haste in order that you will get this report before you form your preconceived opinions from reports in the world press, for I am sure that. they will tend to over=dramatise the affair. We had just picked up the pilot, and the apprentice had returned from changing the 'G* flag for the *H', and being his first trip was having difficulty in rolling the 'G* flag up, I therefore proceeded to show him how, coming to the last part I told him to ‘let go', the lad, although willing is not too bright, necessitating my having to repeat the order in a sharper tone. The Chief Officer overhearing from the Chart room, and thinking that it was the anchors that were being referred to repeated the ‘let go' to the Third Officer on the forecastle. The effect of letting from the the port anchor drop ‘pipe’ while the vessel was proceeding at full harbour speed proved too much for the windlass brake, and the entire length of the cable was pulled out ‘by the roots? I fear that the damage to the chain locker may be extensive. The braking effect naturally caused the vessel to sheer in that direction, right towards the swing bridge that spans a tributary to the river up which we were proceeding. The swing bridge operator showed great presence of mind by opening the bridge for my vessel, unfortunately he did not think to stop the vehicular traffic. The result being that the bridge partly opened and deposited a Volkswagen, two cyclists and a cattle truck on the foredeck. In his efforts to stop the progress of the vessel the Third Officer dropped the starboard anchor, too late to be of practical use for it fell on the swing bridge operator's control cabin. Up to now I have confined my report to the activities at the forward end of my vessel, aft they were having their own problems. At the moment the port anchor was let go, the Second Officer was supervising the making fast of the after tug, and was lowering the ship's towing spring down onto the tug. The sudden braking effect on the port anchor caused the tug to 'run in under! the stern of my vessel, just at the moment when the propellor was answering my double ring Full Astern. The prompt action of the Second Officer in securing the inboard end of the towing spring delayed the sinking of the tug by some minutes thereby allowing the safe abandoning of that vessel, It never fails to amaze me, the actions and behaviour of foreigners during moments of minor crisis. The pilot for instance, is at this moment huddled in the corner of my day cabin, alternately crooning to himself and crying after having consumed a bottle of gin in a time that is worthy of inclusion in the Guinness Book of Records, The tug captain on the other hand reacted violently and had to forcibly be restrained by the Steward, who has him handcuffed in the ship's hospital. I enclose the names and addresses of the drivers and insurance companies of the vehicles on my foredeck, which the Third Officer collected after his somewhat hurried evacuation of the forecastle, these particulars will enable you to claim for the damage that they did to the railings of number one hold. I am closing this preliminary report for I am finding it difficult to concentrate with the sound of police sirens and their flashing lights. Had the apprentice realized that there is no need to fly pilot flags after dark, none of this would have happened. I am Sir, Yours faithfully, MASTER.”

- l]0. REMEMBER = COLD CAN KILL Extract from R.Y.A. Publication = G 16, Hypothermia is the most dangerous of conditions caused by exposure to cold, and is a condition best avoided} Indeed, cold is probably. the main threat to life during prolonged immersion in any waters other than trapical ones. It is therefore sensible to assess the risks before sailing on cold water and take all possible precautions to avoid becoming chilled. when the water is very cold, say around 5 C (41 F) a man of ordinary build would be hypothermic and helpless in half=-an—hour or less. He would be reduced to the same state within one or two hours if the water were 15°C (59°F) although these times may be doubled by the wearing of conventional clothing and even more if special clothing is worn. Some sailing clubs insist on their members wearing "wet-suits" when water temperatures are below 5°C(41°F) and this is a very wise rule because, quite apart from hypothermia, immersion in cold water can cause sudden death and because the shock of immersion makes it difficult to breathe: normally. Avoidance — Avoiding hypothermia therefore resolves itself into a matter of wearing a sufficiency of warm clothing with a wind=proof and waterprooff outer layer. When in the water it is preferable to float quietly and wear gloves or mittens whenever possible to minimise the chance of cold injury to the fingers. Ignorance — There seems to exist a considerable ignorance about the dangers of immersion in cold water, or alternatively, there is a reluctance to accept that the hazard is important. Measures are taken to avoid ordinary physical injury and drowning and, indeed, most sportsmen and others are familar with the first aid treatment of these conditions. Oddly enough, the universal acceptance of approved life-jackets has probably increased the danger of death from hypothermia, though only because drowning is delayed long enough for cooling to take place. Drowning occurs very rapidly after immersion in cold water because of certain respiratory reflexes and the fact that very few people can swim for more than a few minutes in very cold water, More and more enthusiastic sailors, canoeists and others use their boats all the year round, even when conditions are extremely cold. In general, such activity should be encouraged, but with reservations, because there is no doubt that there is an appreciable hazard, although the risks can be reduced to an acceptable level by sensible appreciation of the simple actions necessary to reduce the possibility of injury by cold, and the reasons for them. Your committee strongly advise all dinghy sailors to wear wetsuits when sailing particularly in the Spring and Autumn Series. WINTER MEETING = VIDEO SHOW = 1980 ENTERPRISE WORLDS. M.A.S.C. LOUNGE. 420 News I am writing this with sticking plasters on certain fingers — this being a sign that the season is well under way and that excellent winds have prevailed (except for one Sunday that is). Three 420's turned out for Spring Points 1 in force 3/4 winds, but very low temperatures, The race was won by Caron and Heather Stuart even though Heather went for a swim during the race. Well done girls and don't forget that you get a free night out with the Fleet Captain every time you win (Notes— two free nights out with the F.C. for those coming second$$). The Easter Series were held in ideal 420 conditions with winds of about force 4 from the north (hence very cold$) and the water was fairly choppye On the Sunday 9 boats started, of which 3 were 420's. It was obvious from the morning start that it was a 420's day, as the Solos and Laser were left behind in the spray. Russell Jeffries was out with his newly acquired boat and he rapidly discovered new found power that led to a few encounters of the fishy kind$ The race finished with Heather Stuart and myself taking first place with Pete and Dave Sayer a close second. The afternoon was virtually a repeat of the morning with a slightly shorter course due to the extreme cold. Easter Monday arrived with almost identical conditions to the Sunday with the exception that the water was a little flatter. In the absence of Heather Stuart (come back Heather = all is forgiven!) Malcolm Stuart kindly crewed for me. Malcolm and myself went into an early lead after a good start but on the first spinnaker reach the spinnaker pole snapped and we capsized. Malcolm landed on his back on the half extended centre=board waving his legs in the air. How he achieved this position defies logic and in my startled condition I thought he was either signalling to the rescue boat or had assumed his famed vasectomy position! However, by the time the boat was righted Pete and Dave Sayer had taken the initiative and had sped past to win the race. So it was all down to the last race with lots of sailing psychology being applied in the bar at lunchtime. The race proved to be very exciting with Pete and Dave getting away to a good start leaving Malcolm and myself to restart after crossing the line before the start signal. Some lost ground was made up on the leading 420 but no amount of effort could prevent Pete and Dave coming home first and winning the series. Well dorelads, and I hope those two large Easter Eggs make you fat! Fleet Duties. By the time this is published a list of fleet duties up to August llth will have been posted on the 420 notice board. The list is not completed yet, but as more boats are registered it is hoped that these duties will be finalised. If you cannot make your duty due to previous arrangements please make alternative arrangements with another member of the fleet without recourse to the F.C. and then record the change on the board. - 9 - HORNETS AT BURNHAM Three Marconi Hornets went to the Easter Egg meeting at Burnham and the event provided these boats with an oportunity to gauge their progress over the past year. The fleet was disappointing with only 12 boats competing the gruelling 4 day, 5 race series. The weather over the weekend was mostly pleasant with winds varying between force 2 and a fresh 4 on the final day. The meeting was dominated by Nick and Tony Smither from Dover in their brand new, dayglo yellow boat,"Suspect Device". There didn't seem to be anything "suspect" about it - Nick and Tony won all five races. Graham Mead & Mike from our own Club finished second overall, and on this form should be looking for at least a top ten place in this year's Worlds - well done Graham. Uncle Jessie Todd and Ian in the "big rig" Kyle had speed to spare, power to spare and also new for 1982, "Hunter-Killer Submarine" Impressions - all this before the start of the first race! Murray and Ian finally got their acts together and did very well to finish fourth. Meanwhile, I had borrowed my dads new boat, borrowed Sidney's crew winkle, and after much gear failure and Jacques Cousteau Style Capsizes. We finished 6th. All in all a good fleet performance - let's hope we can keep up these placings at Thorpe Bay and subsequent Meetings. On the home front, it is good to see much more open racing. Of the five club races completed at the time of writing there have been three different race winners. I hope we will see a trend towards many more boats being in contention than we have seen over the past 3 or 4 years - this can only be good for the fleet as a whole. It was good to see so many Solos out on the first race - well done Ron - you certainly seem to have got your boys in order, which is more than we can say for our dear friend Phil. I would have thought that with the cream of your fleet defecting to the Hornets (how wise), more 420 sailors would be out there trying to stamp their authority on the fleet!!! So come on lads lets all go for it this year. Finally, I was talking with Miss Tenroh the other week and she asked me to thank the Editor for "Capturing her Article in such a darling manner". For those of you who don't know her, Miss Tenroh is the tall, slim blonde often seen with the lads of the Hornet fleet. Good Sailing. Colin Harper. (OFFICIAL HORNET SCRIBE)

- 3 - The First Time A Nearly True Story. Well, there was I, the owner of a motor cruiser, and suddenly the cost of my trips poodling up and down the river were beginning to get quite frighteningly high. It was then that a friend suggested that what I was doing was not real boating, and offered to introduce me to sailing. He took me sailing in a Wayfarer on an idyllic summer Sunday evening with a puff of wind blowing now and then, and we cruised down to the local hostillery and drifted back somewhat more ballasted than when we went. That was the moment I decided that this sailing was for me. I decided that I would like to build a popular fibre-glass dinghy because the local dealer was very close, and I was sure he could advise me if I got into trouble, but to cut a very long story short that was an absolute disaster, because, not only was the dealer an incompetent fool, who eventually delivered to my home enough resin and matt to build two Morning Clouds (the gel of which was the wrong colour anyway), but as the moulds (hired from the imcompetent fool) were being delivered, one half fell off the trailer and was last seen apparently trying to overtake a police car on Blue Bell Hill. After that I decided to look through the magazines, try to find a second-hand boat, and suddenly there she was, an Enterprise, called Wild Times, trolley, trailer, cover, and all go fast gear. What else could I ask for (I didn't even know what size an Enterprise was!) but the owner proudly told me of the races she has won and the thought of getting to the hostillery somewhat quicker than the Wayfarer spurred me on. I took delivery on a day that was to be somewhat of an omen. A tremendous thunderstorm was in progress, complete with lightning, hail and torrential rain. A bedraggled man rang the door bell and asked if this was Mr. Noah's house, handed me a soggy envelope with a "certificate" in it and disappeared into the wettness forever. So Wild Times was mine. That weekend I thought I'd sort out all the ropes and wires and funny looking gear and it took several lengthy phone calls to my friend with the Wayfarer to rig the mast, but finally we made it and decided to hoist the sails - whereupon the boat promptly blew over, and looked most undignified lying on the next door neighbours car, so we very hurriedly righted her before it was noticed (my neighbour is a very big bloke, and has no sense of humour!). I think it was then that I noticed these silver things in the bottom of the boat. I rang my friend and again "it's okay, those are the elevstrom bailers", "just part of the sophisticated bailing system". Then I noticed two perspex flaps in the flat end, I rang my friend again "what are the windows for", I asked, "just part of the sophisticated bailing system", he said, and this time I detected a touch of impatience in his voice. I then noticed something else which I didn't understand, but decided not to ring my friend as maybe I was straining relationships a bit far. So the big day arrived. Michael Fish said it would be force 3/4 and sunny and warm - and so it was. My wife and son rigged the boat while I took one more glance at my "teach yourself" sailing book. It is at this stage I should explain that the better half of my marriage was not relishing the maiden voyage of Wild Times, and with lifejacket, water wings and Rosary at the ready climbed aboard. A good shove from me and we were sailing."Beautiful - now I think the pub is that way". It was then I wished I had strained my relationship with my friend to one phone call more, because there were these two holes in the transom letting in water like the Murda Dam after 603 Squadron had finished. The crew drew my attention to the fact and I informed the crew that it was all right - probably just part of the sophisticated bailing system and when we really got going the stern will lift and the Elevstroms would take the water away". Well, it didn't happen quite like that. In fact the water got deeper and deeper and crew got more and more agitated until I wasn't sure whether it was my blood pressure causing the screaming in my ears or the crew requesting - no demanding - that I do /continued.

mt kk = somethinge Fortunately, just across the river to where we had launched is an island, and we headed like a wounded wallowing water buffalo towards the beach with the finger of the crews glove in one drain: hole and my bobble hat jammed in the other. We landed, and with the crew standing with arms akimbo (the classic mother-in-law pose) demanded I empty the Medway back into the Medway. “What with?", I asked, meekly. "You work it out — you're the skipper", came the acid reply. I looked around for something to bail with — nothing — not a thinge There was only one thing to do — I took off one of my wellies and started to bail. This was too much for the crew who broke into uncontrollable hysterical laughter. Somebody said that being a skipper is a lonely business so I took. no notice. I got the boat relaunched with my hankie ripped in half, and, with a big knot tied in each, rammed into the drain holes. - 5 - Spring Points 7 was sailed in force 5-6 and once again Vic Braybrook and Kim showed a marked superiority in heavy weather technique in FLAMING PEST. No. 8 was on the same day in similar winds and could be described as a comedy of disasters. Shortly after the start I ran aground whilst trying to tack too close into shore, and was almost immediately joined by Vic suffering from a broken forestay strop. Whilst I tried to persuade Vic we'd be better off in the clubhouse bar, Bob Leeder in DOUBLE TROUBLE sailed off into the lead but, with a new, untried, boat and novice crew, didn't push things too hard and was eventually overtaken by Vic and myself. The last beat saw a close tacking duel between us and I eventually took 1st place by no more than 12 inches with the Race Box giving only one "hoot" to share between us. In the battle towards the line, our port jib fairlead pulled out of its fixing. I thought my request to Maggie to use her foot to bear on the port jib sheet (in order to set the jib) was relatively calm, calculated and polite under the circumstances. Her reply that she'd need legs six feet long to comply was, I felt, a little unhelpful but she gallantly set the jib as best she could until we tacked for the line. They don't come much closer than that - it was exciting and I hope we get more of them. In contrast No. 9 was not sailed due to lack of wind, whilst No. 10 was sailed in light wind on a short in-shore course. Now, we have all heard of tactical psychology being applied in sailing, and I reckon I was the victim on this occasion. Maggie sailed LARS TINN, David Green sailed his boat (no name - perhaps that is what he should call it) and I sailed BIGINUFFTOO BUMBLE. Maggie said she was worried about taking out LARS TINN so I promised to keep an husbandly eye on her:- "Don't go too far away" - she says. "I won't" - I says "You'll come back to help me if I get into trouble?" - she says "Yes, I will" - I says. She then proceeded to lead from start to finish and beat me into 2nd place by 100 yards. I still think I was conned. Spring Points No. 11 was sailed in "normal" wind and Vic Braybrook had a runaway victory. No. 12 was literally a comedy act. With light wind and adverse tide, only Vic could make it round the 1st mark. Bob Leeder, David Green and myself caused considerable mirth and merriment to the watchers in the clubhouse as we tried for 20 odd minutes to get round the mark. Eventually Bob and David did get round, but I never managed it and retired for an early shower. All-in-all, I'm pleased we managed to sail the Spring Points Series. David Green, Bob Leeder, Vic Braybrook, Maggie and myself have been the racing helms, whilst I also spotted Alf Cottam, John Stringer and Frazer McPherson shaking the winter creases from their sails, and also had the pleasure of meeting Chris Thorne whilst he was getting his boat ready for the coming season. I hope more Mirrors will join us in the Summer Points Series to share our fun, our "rough and tumble", our small personal triumphs and minor disasters but, most of all, to share our sailing. Rule 50 states that a yacht whose entry has been accepted and which sails about in the vicinity of the starting line between her preparatory (i.e. 5=minute) signal and the starting signal shall rank as a starter whether she starts or not. I've always understood that this requirement is satisfied if a yacht is actually in the water at the 5eminute signal, even if merely being held stationary by a member of the crew, and still ranks as a starter even if held after the starting signal or indeed never actually crosses the start line at all. In one race this year, it appeared from the race box that one yacht was still on the hard at the Seminute signal and, in accordance with the rule, did not rank as a starter, In fact the yacht was still on the hard at the start signale The yacht in question then got afloat, sailed up to and crossed onto the pre—course side of the line, and started "correctly" (if that is possible for a yacht not ranking as a starter!}). This rather confused the race officer who was now assailed by doubts as to whethers= (a) the yacht should rank as a starter by the mere fact of having "signed on" ? (b) since the start had been towards the west (ise. towards A mark) and the yacht approached the start line from the course side, should she have been regarded as a premature starter and the class flag left at the dip ? (c) would the race officer be held up to public ridicule had the yacht subsequently "won" and protest ensued ? In the event, the yacht conveniently capsized (no harm done) and "retired", but had she completed the race in a winning position (more=than=likely possibility) then an interesting protest meeting might have resulted. Why not use Navigans as the medium to impart your pearls of wisdom! Unfortunately most potential contributors are too busy sailing to put pen to paper but somebody has to make a start = so here goes} There are many excellent books available on boat tuning and the sailing techniques and tactics necessary to win races, but the Tiro can easily become confused by the detail and get his priorities all wrong, e.g. the finer points of tuning and having the best equipment only marginally effect performance whereas what really matters is Helming Ability, or as it is sometimes said, the nut on the end of the tiller. How does one obtain this Helming Ability? Obviously there is no substitute for hours spent on the water, nevertheless there are bad practises which need to be unlearned and good practises which must be followed at all times if you are to get amongst the race leaders. Probably the most difficult skill to master is the ability to sail to windward. It is here that most races are won or lost. Sailing to Windward Getting to the windward mark first depends on a combination of speed and directiane Direction is a matter of choosing the shortest route by making use of /continuede

- 7 - the wind and tide but it is no good going in the right direction if you are not getting there fast enough. Real improvements in speed to windward may be obtained if certain basic points are understood and mastered. It is the relative trim of the sail and centreboard which determine how well you sail to windward. If the boat is not to slide sideways through the water the centreboard must generate a sideways force equal to that exerted by the sail. N.B. In order to generate drive and sideways force it is necessary for both the sail and the centreboard to be set at a small angle of incidence to the wind and water respectively. Priority 1 - Keep the boat Upright. Both the sail and the centreboard operate at maximum efficiency when the boat is absolutely level and the mast and centreboard are vertical. Centreboard theory. The force generated by the centreboard (F C.) is proportional to the square of the speed of the boat through the water (S) and the angle of incidence to the water (A), i.e. F C. ∝ A.S². The angle of incidence is in fact the angle at which the boat is slipping away to leeward. Every effort must be made therefore to keep this angle to a minimum. Remember A ∝ F C. and 1/S². If the boat is to be kept upright all the heeling forces must balance. Let us consider a typical situation. (Any resemblance to a SOLO is purely intentional). F S Centre of Effort d 1.0 m 2.7 m 3 m 0.3 m F C Crew Weight W .75 m Centre of Lateral Resistance If the boat is not to accelerate sideways the force generated by the centreboard must equal that provided by the sail i.e. F S. = F C. The boat is prevented from heeling solely by the balancing effect of the weight of the crew. It follows therefore that the maximum force that can be handled depends on the ability of the helm/crew to sit out for long periods, i.e. F S. = W x d, e.g. a 12 stone helm sitting comfortably on the side deck (d = .75m) will only manage a driving force equal to that of a 9 stone athlete sitting well out (d = 1m). Obviously the Force (F S.) that will be generated by the sail depends on the wind strength but once the wind gets up to above force 3-4 there is normally more /continued.

Having grasped the buoy it still takes several seconds to belay the mooring rope round the bitts, while to haul in the chain to the required length and flick it vigourously to remove most of the mud, may take minutes and a lot could happen in this time. The operation can be facilitated by splicing a loop of strong line into the main mooring rope at about one metre from the buoy. It is then an easy matter to haul in the buoy over the anchor chain rollers just far enough to secure this loop round the bitts. The skipper can then relax and return at leisure to the cockpit to stop the engine or release the sheets, which have an uncanny habit of fouling on these occasions. But don't forget to haul in the chain and secure it before going ashore! Incidentally, it is much easier for the boat hook to take the loop rather than the thick strop or the buoy itself. - 9 - SUMMER CRUISE 1981 S. Crisp. BEEHIVE Sat. Aug. 1st. Beehive and Tijo left Stansgate for Levington Marina with Margaret Cambell from Tijo stating that as she had six people on board, namely Ian Campbell and his fiancee Kim and Jimmy Campbell and Jackie Hall as well as themselves plus all the extra food stacked quite high, they were going to have a steady sail and were not going to push it too hard. The wind was a northerly force 4 gusting 5, right on the nose and while sailing with wind over tide in the wallet I watched Tijo being thrown all over the place and realised, not just from the way my stomach was trying to escape from my mouth, that we were doing exactly the same thing. While keeping my back to the bow of the boat and trying to concentrate on what the first thing was that I would do when discarding with my wet oilies Vic kept me informed of the state of each wave in short form, M.W. (medium wave) L.W. (long wave) and F.W. ( which he assured me was a freak wave) With wind over tide it took 9 hours to reach Levington Marina where we met up with Brenda, Vic and Mary Tate of Copernicus and Sandra and Peter Claydon of Peace who should have been in Holland but were held up by unfavourable weather. The following day (Sunday) we were all held up by very favourable weather when the sun beat down on us and the only relief had to be the nearest watering hole at Levington, so there we were outside the local pub, taking up most of the seats and tables lunchtime and again the evening and what an enjoyable day that was. Mon. Aug. 3rd. Still glorious sun but winds barely force 2. Copernicus and Peace had left very early that morning for their destination in Holland and we set motor for Southwold. According to Mr Trigg, the harbour master, our boats would be able to enter the Southwold entrance at any state of the tide. We approached the entrance at about 7.15 p.m. and low tide was about 8 p.m. We saw Tijo who was just ahead of us looking slightly stationary for just a few seconds and when we followed we realised why, we bumped a few times but made it in okay. At least we know now just where the bar lies. On tying up at the quayside we were delighted to find that the pub there was serving fresh fried fish and chips - bonus - especially for me who had ran out of calor gas that day and had been looking forward to a mere sandwich that evening. It was the freshest fish and chips we'd tasted for a long time. Whilst in the town the following day (Tuesday), Tijo's scouts spotted a fellow member, Bill Penkham of Sirius but although we made our way to where the sighting had taken place, he had obviously gone to ground or perhaps we'd passed him on the way, anyway we returned to our boats in readiness for our sail? to Lowestoft the next day. At this point, Margaret discovered that Tijo's loo was completely blocked to which we all discussed the possibilities of the cause of such a thing while Stan, looking a bit down in the mouth knew that he was going to have to do the curing of it. Weds. Aug. 5th. Still hardly a puff of wind, plenty of sun and some fog banks. Vic and I were sitting having our breakfast in the cockpit, marvelling at the still glorious morning when other sounds caught our ears coming from Tijo -

It was Stan, banging and retching whilst clearing his blocked loo = suddenly, up came the forehatch cover and one at a time out jumped the four inhabitants who had been sleeping only seconds beforehand, gasping for air as they came. The job done and up came stan, bucket in hand and proceeded to throw the contents overboard - on our side = oh well, we werent that hungry anyway. Before leaving Southwold we met up with another Macwester called Penelope Jane, the owners were schoolteachers on holiday and had sailed down from Humberside, so before leaving there were hurried inspections of each others boats. The weather conditions were so calm en-route to Lowestoft it was hard to believe that this was the north sea, and it seemed Jimmy Campbell didn't believe it either and leapt overboard to investigate, attached to a warp and a buoy - although we rather suspected that Margaret and Stan had that many on board they'd been eaten out of a boat and a dinghy so they'd cast Jimmy overboard as live bait - but the fish didn't want to know. Reaching Lowestoft, was for me, absolutely wonderful - although our main intention for this holiday was to go to Lowestoft I somehow had the thought in the back of my mind that weather conditions would not allow it in the two short weeks that we had - me of little faith. We had been forewarned that the mooring charges would be £6. a night for our boats in the outer harbour, but if we had chosen to wait until the road bridge was lifted we could have gone up river for a mile or so and the sailing club there would have let us use their moorings for £1.50 a night, but as we did not want to be dependant on waiting for the bridge to be opened for coming out we rafted up in the outer harbour where, with quite a lot of other boats, especially Dutch, spent a few not too comfortable days of snubbing and not too easy times getting onto the ladder up onto the quayside. The Royal Norfolk and Suffolk Yacht Club however was very welcoming and very comfortable, we proudly left a Marconi burgee to be hung amongst the other club burgees in one of the lounges. Fri. Aug. -7the Left Lowestoft for the Butley River, once again hardly any wind but the sea had some nice rollers coming in and when Tijo and Beehive were both in a ‘downer’ we could only see each others masts, In spite of the fact that we were having to motor again it was a very pleasant trip. On passing Southwold the Macwester we had previously met there called Penelope Jane re-joined us and stayed in our company for the following week. — Sat Aug 8th. Left the Ore making for the Deben and Woodbridge Marina. Passed Ron Phillips of Vanellus making for Lowestoft and Ann and John Smith of Freya making for the Ore. We were to meet up with Wendy, Jean and Peter Hall (and one plastered leg) of Jappa in Woodbridge and their guests for the weekend, John and Shiela of Two's Company, where we spent a very pleasant weekend. A very reluctant John and Shiela had to leave Woodbridge by train to go home on the Monday and I Don't think that the rest of us waving them off and jumping up and down at the station made them feel any better. Monday night the men had our five gallon water container half filled with real ale in readiness for the bar-b-que the following night. Tues. Aug. IIth. Prepared to leave Woodbridge Marina for the Rocks, weather glorious again and a calm day. Vic had rather a long walk into town to get petrol before we could leave as only diesel fuel is available in the Marina. On reaching the Rocks we walked to Ramsholt and collected wood on the way back in readiness for the much awaited bar=-b=que that night. It was Kims birthday as well so it was to be a celebration, and we certainly had a terrific celebration the singing round the fire that night was pure harmony - well it sounded so at the time although we did start a few wolves howling somewhere in the distance. /to be continued in September.

CRUISER FLEET NEWS At the August Bank Holiday weekend five of our boats went to the Medway to visit B.P.Kent Yacht Club where we were joined by a further three boats from Marconi Avionics. We had a most enjoyable time at Colemouth Creek where we were given very sheltered moorings and excellent hospitality. Our trip to Kent was in warm weather with calm waters and we made a 5 knot average easily in spite of my water pump - thanks to Vic for a quick tow . Yes, a filter will be installed very soon. Two of our boats made a rapid passage back to the Blackwater on the Sunday in force 5-6 breezes while the rest of us had a cruise in company on the Medway in the same south westerly winds. On Monday we then had a gentler but excellent return passage arriving "home" about 6 pm after a mainly fine day with favourable breezes from Medway to Swin Spitway followed by a spell of motoring straight into the westerly force 4 plus including the most fantastic squall that would have been embarrassing but for the warning of its approach, giving time to get everything ship shape before it hit us. Our thanks to all who helped to make the weekend so successful and enjoyable. /continued.

Five Marconi boats entered the World Championships this year at Highcliff Sailing Club. Dave Harper crewed by Murray Todd, Colin Harper crewed by Danny Lumley, Simon Kenworthy crewed by Ian Stott, Graham Mead crewed by Mike Turner and Pat Black crewed by Caron Stuart. After a good journey down to Highcliff, the boats were unpacked, measured, weighed and then entered, this taking all of the Saturday. However, with 70 boats to be done and with nice sunny warm conditions, the wait did'nt seem all that longe All the boats were passed fit, but a little on the heavy side, and we all looked forward to an eventful series on large Olympic courses. Sunday Practice Winds light, Westerly, Variable. The fleet started first time and on time on a very long line start. Colin Harper 2100 sorted out the wind shifts on the first beat to arrive 7th at the windward marke Simon Kenworthy 2093 started late, after being line shy, to reach the mark in the pack with Dave Harper 2078 not far behind. The first reach developed into a run allowing the back of the fleet to overtake the middle of the fleet. MIRROR FLEET NEWS CAMPING/CADET WEEK (TWTWTW) - That Was The Week That Was - and what a most delightful time we had at the camping week this summer. Phil Gray worked extremely hard to organise an activity week which both cadets and adults enjoyed to the full - aided and abetted by his brother Bob Gray who gave all those interested a first class introduction to the art of canoeing. On behalf of the Mirror Fleet my thanks to Phil and Bob and to all those others who contributed to a wonderful week, including Frank Savill who helped us prop up the bar by pulling the pints on the other side. (Mirror) Fleet Cruise - I got my cruise in after all, thanks to TWTWTW during which a combined fleet cruise was arranged to Heybridge Basin. A fleet of some 13 dinghies included four Mirrors helmed by Robert Coy, Maggie, Philip Taylor and myself. The wind was, to say the least, a bit patchy and most of us had to hitch a tow from a couple of passing cruisers. However, Philip Taylor (son of Mick Taylor) and Jim Coy (GP 14) both showed they had a nose for smelling out what wind there was and got to Heybridge way before we other poor souls drifted in. After a mild liquid lunch at the local ale house, we had a nice beat back to the Club and finished with a feeling that it was a day well spent. My thanks to Ray Ball and Murray Bates who sailed cruisers to act as guard boats. I must say I thoroughly enjoyed the cruise and wonder whether one or two "officially sponsored" dinghy cruises couldn't be included in future sailing programmes. Racing Backwards - one of the events during TWTWTW was an obstacle race on both land and river. The last time I did anything like this was on basic training at RAF Padgate many years ago - and I think I'm a bit out of practise. Stephen Jeffries (11 years) proved quite conclusively that he can run much faster than I can during the 'land' part of the race, whilst Maggie proved she can beat me sailing backwards as well as forwards during the "river" part of the race. Considering the times I've managed to sail backwards accidently during normal races, an inability to sail backwards over the finishing line on this occasion was close to being irksome. Racing Forwards - the Mirror Fleet continues to enjoy some good competitive racing even if our numbers are disappointingly small. In one race, Vic Braybrook and myself were so intent on tactical manoeuvres upon each other that we missed out "D" mark and had to sail some considerable distance back to round it correctly. In the meantime Bob Leeder had kept himself well clear of our fun and games and sailed through to take a clear and well deserved win. There must be a lesson there somewhere. Although I have not yet seen the official results, Vic has obviously /continued.

om am won the Summer Points Series — congratulations Vic} We now look forward to the Autumn During the summer sailing John Stringer managed to break his tiller, and the very next week my tiller broke whilst tacking shortly before the start of a race. I actually started using the stub of the tiller but that also gave way after a few tacks and I took the hint and retired for an early shower. Like the fisherman and the one that got away, I'm certain I would have been on a winning streak that day = anyway that's my tale andI'm sticking to it. Capsize Drill - I'm glad my youngsters attended Phil Gray's cadet classes during the winter and the practical Saturday afternoon capsize practise earlier this year. Maggie and I peered over Phil's shoulder as he instructed the cadets and thereby provided ourselves with some useful revision. Consequently, when Maggie and I capsized recently during heavy weather we were able to right the boat without much difficulty. I reckon the capsize was caused by my crew standing up when I called “Gybe Oh" and consequently ending up leeward of the mainsail. Maggie reckons it would help if I gave the commands before the event and not afterwards. Anyway, her cry of anguish and shock as she disappeared below the cold waters of the Blackwater did introduce a comical element into the situation — at least from where I was sitting shortly before I, too, slid into those self=same waters. Helmsman of the Year Qualifier — much to her relief, Maggie will not be the Mirror Fleet representative this year. Although I haven't seen the official results, I believe the Mirror Fleet will be represented by Vic Braybrook. Racing Stop=Press — Autumn Points 1 and 2 have seen the welcome return of Mick Taylor to the Mirror Fleet. He scored two very convincing firsts to present Vic, Bob Leeder and myself a problem to ponder upon until Nose 3 & 4e A warm welcome to his crewedaughter Helen and crew-son Mark. Let's hope more adult/child teams will emerge to join our racing fun. WANTED =— CARAVAN Anyone thinking of selling a 4 berth Mike Boreham, caravan? I'm thinking of buying one and may be interested Mirror Fleet Captain. in yourse [redacted], CADET WEEK I have just calculated that I have spent twenty days under canvas during August. I know this to my cost as I have lost weight, am a mass of cuts and bruises and find difficulty in sleeping in a warm soft bed. Apart from the fact that there are grounds for a divorce in the Gray camp I would not begrudge one of those days. Cadet Week will remain in our memories for some time and whilst we sit by our winter firesides with the snow gently carpeting the landscape, we will harken back to those halcyon days of warm sun, blue seas and insect bites, My fondest memory of the week (apart from a full bottle of whisky brought to my tent at a moment of dire need) is the sight of scrubber Mike Boreham making a fool of himself in the diving competition. I didn't tell you at the time Mike, but I thought you were better than that idiot in a stupid shirt who eskimo rolled off the board} Another fond memory will be the sight of Murray Bates' face when contestants in the treasure hunt kept pestering him for his autograph. Murray didn't_ appear to make as many beers out of this activity as I did from another part of the proceedings$ /continuede

- 8 - Congratulations must be extended to the Pete, Bob and Stephen team for noticing that the flags at the racebox were in fact hoisted at the yardarm and not at the masthead. However, it did not help them to win! Further congratulations are also in order for Damian Boreham for producing the smallest crab ever seen on the Blackwater. In fact this very same crab can be seen through an electron microscope at the Natural History Museum. There was a marked absence of wind during the week (apart from that coming from Kate's tent that is) and although this curtailed some of the planned sailing activities it appeared at times that we had forsaken sailing for canoeing! My only memory of the canoeing races is that of suffering pains in places where I didn't even know I had places! If the Obstacle Race is ever held again the rules will be changed so that I can win something! It showed me two things - firstly I do not sail backwards well and secondly that for those intrepid single handed sailors in a two man dinghy who do in fact raise the spinnaker (well done John in the Hornet and me in the 420) - these should be rewarded with a longer spinnaker leg (weather permitting that is!). I observed several things during this epic event. Firstly during the capsize exercise, on leaping over the side I found that Kate had not put the centreboard down!!! (what are crews coming to these days). Secondly two man (or one man, one girl or one boy, one girl, etc.) lasers came first and second, and thirdly we appear to have an olympic swimmer in the club who can swim from A mark to Osea faster that a dinghy can sail the same distance! Anyway, everyone joined in the spirit of the event and I'm thinking of joining the Hornet Fleet to learn how to sail backwards. The innumerable games of volleyball, rounders and football once again brought out the competitive spirit in everyone. The volleyball produced a superstar in Janet Chisnall whose spatial awareness and her dexterity close in to the net was sheer poetry. (Janet - I was a little disappointed that you didn't keep falling on me this year!) The mixed football proved to be very physically demanding with some impressive tackling and dribbling (I had forgotten my handerchief!). Power struggles eventually started between the Gray Brothers and a duo of Robert Weedon/Little John Chisnall and the game was only finished when Lucy Boreham stopped an almost certain winning shot from Bob Gray, with the back of her head. Well done Lucy, and keep taking the pills luv. What a great game rounders is when you have a left hander on your team who can whack the ball into the ditch and then stroll round for one rounder. Even with this advantage, the final outcome was very close and apart from a few obvious cases of obstruction, (worth half a rounder I believe) very little rule-bending was evident (shame!). Man overboard drill for the Cadets went with a splash with scenes reminiscent of the Marie Celeste. Some cadets were seen re-entering the boat over the stern and this is to be discouraged as even a big cadet like myself can get over the side! (enough of the serious stuff!). To those of you who enjoyed the week, on your behalf I would like to thank the following. Cheers John and Murray for the support and something like ten man-hours of work (hard work) in constructing the deathslide. Thanks to Bob and Russell for their help on the Sunday and to Bob for all the canoeing instruction and the nightcaps. Thanks to the Sailing Sub-committee for their finalcial support and the authorisation of the splashing out on prizes (they haven't had the bill yet!). Thanks to Mike Boreham for the prize-giving ceremony (see list of prize winners at the end) - you lucky devil Mike, I hear you got two kisses from Kate. Special thanks from Bob and myself to all those that so generously contributed towards our second favourite pastime. Finally thanks to all those that joined in the spirit of things and for anyone that may have been bored for the odd hour or two - you had better watch out next year! /continued.

NATIONALS AT LLANDUDNO The Marconi Fleet and families descended in force on the Brig-y-Don Hotel at Llandudno for what turned out to be a very windy and curtailed event. Of the 49 entrants 4 were from Marconi, and the results were as follows:- 1. Geof Carveth - Littleton S.C. - 2¾. 2. Martin Payne - Salcombe Y.C. - 7. 3. Guy Bradbury - Dover Y.C. - 7. 17. Ron Greygoose - 42. 18. John Salmon - 43. 25. Roger Smith - 55. 42. Geof Josey - 118. Ian and Sue Shaw arrived and entered at the last minute, and finished 10th and 20th respectively. Only 2 races were completed in the series. A last desperate attempt was made to run 2 races on the last day, but this was abandoned after the start. Half the fleet managed to get afloat through the surf, but some (me included) didn't make it. Many boats suffered damage and broken tillers were the order of the day. The lack of sailing did have compensations as we were all able to spend time together and make a real holiday of our stay. Other notable items were:- 1. John managed to up-end Jack Holt on the promenade! 2. Roger was leading Ian Shaw in the final race before it was abandoned! 3. Geof never stopped eating scones and searching newsagents for a plastic mac. 4. Margaret's hairdrier did not set the hotel on fire, despite any rumours to the contrary. The Hayling Island Club took the team prize - we thought we could be in the running at one stage. The final departure was marred by an unfortunate accident when Caroline was knocked down by a passing car. Roger, Wendy and Grandma, had to stay on for a few days until Caroline was well enough to return home. We were all very relieved to see her (well on the road to recovery) at Stansgate. - 6 - MARCONI SAILING CLUB Code of Practice for Launching and Recovery of Cruisers Large Boats - Boats above 27 ft length will NOT be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. The tractor is more suitable than winches for heavy boats but see below concerning ropes. Tractor - Only to be operated by authorised drivers. It is extremely dangerous for non key holders to operate the tractor. Winches - When Club organised dinghy events are in progress the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies. The OOD will be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for information of dinghy sailors. At other times the following code should be observed:- When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed. Avoid sharp bends in winch cables - shackles should be used for attachment to trolleys. It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strong team of helpers. If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the boat owner must provide a rope or cable of suitable strength and sufficient length that the tractor may remain on the level and always clear of loose shingle. Boat Trolleys - If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to other boats. Work Boat - This may be operated by any club member after obtaining permission from Peter Clayton who will advise upon its use. A team of at least two people is necessary for work on moorings. - 2 - OUR COMMODORE'S NOTES Having recovered from the annual withdrawal symptoms once again it is time for the autumn activities. The Laying-Up Supper (which we hope is successful) at the Chancellor Hall, and the A.G.M. which is usually well supported, come close together. The committee are very reluctant to put up members' costs but our expenditure over the last few years has been rising and there is no choice but to increase members' contributions. There were no increases in fees last year when the Club made a loss of a few hundred pounds, thus reducing our reserve to just over £2,000. This year we expect this to fall to around £1,000 which is considered to be the lowest acceptable level. With projected increased expenditure we have to look for extra income next year. Increases in our running costs which are mainly rates, rent, fuel and maintenance are continually rising and unavoidable. Unfortunately membership has fallen over the last few years, but this is the trend nationally so we are no exception, which all means increased fees but we hope you will be aware of the reasons and support the resolution. I wish to thank the many members who turned out at the recent working party and ask that you continue your support as I say my farewell as Commodore, and pass you over to Frank Savill, may Frank's team be a happy one. MIRROR FLEET NEWS If you haven't managed to get your boat down to Stansgate yet - you're too late 'cos the season has ended. Yes, the winter season for the ritual "Sunday Morning Lay-In" has arrived but you'd better make the most of it while it lasts. With Christmas only a few weeks away, it will soon be new year and time to get the boat ready for the '83 season. I'm already getting ready to strip our spare bedroom of such excess paraphernalia as beds, wardrobes, and ornamental gazzunders so that I can get to work on BIGINUFFTOO BUMBLE with secret "go faster" ingredients for the Spring Series '83. My only problem is Maggie. No, she doesn't object to my using the bedroom to work on the boat - only to the fact that if I'm in there, she cannot get in to work on LARS TINN. I guess there's no real way out but to get a bigger house. Either that or we'll just have to get used to eating breakfast off the bottom of an upturned Mirror in the kitchen. Although still relatively low in the number of regular sailors, I feel the Mirror Fleet has been more active and much stronger in spirit in 1982 than in 1981 and consequently has provided some very enjoyable racing. Some 15 different helms have taken part in those races open to the Mirror Fleet. They are:- Peter Collis Vic Braybrook David Green John Stringer Robert Coy Maggie Boreham Dave Beckett Bob Leeder Damian Boreham Len Graves Mike Taylor Fraser McPherson Dick Spilsbury Alf Cottam Mike Boreham We have sailed all three series of Spring, Summer and Autumn races as well as taking part in the mid-week handicap series, and this is a particularly pleasing feature of the past season. I won the Spring Points series by the narrowest of margins from Vic Braybrook. Vic made a come-back by taking the Summer Points series by a rather more convincing margin, whilst Mike Taylor white-washed us all in taking the Autumn series with 100% wins. However, even Mike might not have things all his own way next year. In Autumn Points 5, Maggie was leading all the way until the last leg when Mike came through to beat her by 34 seconds, whilst Autumn Points 6 saw me leading all the way until the last leg when I managed to throw it all away by running well and truly aground. Mike's presence in the Autumn Series was certainly very much appreciated and welcome, even if the margins of his wins in races 1 - 4 were so large as to stun us in rather the same manner that an icy-cold shower takes your breath away. Anyway, I'm looking forward to next season for some keen racing between Vic, Maggie, Mike, Bob Leeder and all those others who will undoubtedly be joining us next year. Make your mind up now to join us "on the sea in '83". My thanks to all those who volunteered for Mirror Fleet duties and, in /continued.

Chelmsford [redacted] Many apologies to Sylvia Crisp for having to wait until now to see the completion of your Summer Cruise 1981. Weds. Aug. 12th. Yet another sunny day. We spent the morning re-cooperating Stan organised the cleaning up of the debris from the night before, heard the news that Peggy and Jimmy James of Sonya had sailed past our boats earlier that day while we were all out for the count and only Peter Hall was up and about to hear them..Now as Peter had his leg encased in plaster, the best way for him to get ashore the night before was to put insulating tape round the foot of his plaster and then put his leg into a plastic bag to keep the plaster dry while rowing ashore. The trouble came very early that morning when Peter woke Jean to say he was in agony because they'd bound the tape too tightly, so while Jean fumbled for the light switch she also unwittlingly put their clock forward one hour, and when later that day we sailed up to the river Ore, Peter was entering one hour earlier than the rest of us, saying to Jean that he was convinced we'd worked the tide tables wrongly, why else was he taking so long to clear the entrance. We made for a mooring at Aldeburgh that evening but being Wednesday it was early closing so we were disappointed about not being able to get fish and chips for supper. Thurs. Aug. 13th. We made our way for Orford where we spent a few leisurely hours looking round the castle before going back to the Butley river. The castle has an old well covered by an iron grid, and with Stan Campbells natural charm with children he obliged them by letting them know how deep it was by daintily spitting into the well and the kids listened intently with their heads on one side waiting for it to land. By evening we were back in the Butley and once more found our feet taking us in the direction of the Boyton Bell and spending another happy evening in good company, besides, Stan was quite dry after all that spitting. Fri. Aug. 14th. Left the Butley for Levington Marina, Winters Maid and Myth of Mynto were already there after returning from their holidays in Holland. Now I like to think that coming into a marina presents no problem for me as long as I'm not helming, so I didn't foresee any difficulty this time until on reaching the rest of our boats in Levington, in readiness to go alongside I suddenly realised that we were going to have to back Beehive in and she does do some odd things when in astern, anyway there were lots of hands there to help us and I think that most of us were to our sleeping bags early that night ready for our first very early start the next morning at 5 a.m. The operation by our Marconi fleet, casting off whilst our eyeballs were still protesting at being woken so early was probably done with great skill - I never noticed - it was all done so quickly but I wont mention the boat who was trying to take the pontoon with him with his stern rope still tied onto it - no better not - he might mention the fact that he was too busy noticing that Tijo was trying to motor off and we still had her tied to our bows. Well for Beehive it was back to the mooring at Stansgate and after such a lovely holiday we were quite sad to leave her - I wonder where we will be going next year?

Facilities are good, other members nice and friendly, and last but not least the sailing can be terrific. (If only I could pluck up the courage to try it!). Ron has received a letter of apology from Rob Bassi of the Ocean Youth Club. He said his mini van would much have preferred the easy run down the A12 rather than the rally stage to the clubhouse. Letter received from the Maldon & District Branch of the R.N.L.I. :- "I am writing to you on behalf of the Maldon and District Branch of the R.N.L.I. in order to let you know that we have fixed a date for our Annual Bar-be-Que and to express the hope that you might be able to arrange your late Summer/Winter programme to include a mention of this function. The Bar-be-Que will be held on Saturday, 3rd September, 1983 at Cardnell's Yard, Maylandsea and, as usual, all boats are welcome to come along and tie up free of charge for the night or take advantage of the plentiful moorings which are available. Alternatively, plenty of car parking space is available for those who wish to travel by road. Although September seems far off at the turn of the year, we do hope your members will make a note of the date and that we will see as many as possible on the night. Wishing you a safe and happy sailing year. Yours truly,(Signed)Patricia Connell." Hon. Secretary. Front Cover - Peter Clayton and Sandra working hard! Typed: Wednesday, 16th February, 1983. CRUISER FLEET NEWS At our February meeting we had a very entertaining show and discussion when Mr. Terry Cooke gave us various hints and tips concerning our boat painting problems and introduced several new products. Although a small meeting it was certainly a good one. Next month will be a film evening similar to previous ones held recently, while for April we are hoping to have a slide presentation by both Jack Pateman our President and Dennis Byatt our former Commodore. Both have been doing some exciting sailing recently so it should be a good show. Both these meetings are at the General's Arms on the first Wednesday, starting around 8.30 pm. Those people who have paint to collect may do so any time from my home - best to give a call first. I shall also aim to have some with me when I'm at Stansgate. Russ Fuller, Cruiser Fleet Captain. Mike Boreham, Mirror Fleet Captain, [redacted], HORNET FLEET NEWS I am happy to report that my second attendance at a Hornet Get-together (The Ship, Stock, 25th Feb.) was rewarded with a good turnout. Unfortunately I have not yet seen the assistant F.C. at any of these gatherings (mind you, I have only attended 66.66% of such meetings — well two out of three anyway!). A very enjoyable evening was spent disposed about a large round table and the only person who appeared to be missing was — yes you guessed it = Guinevere! Great pressure was brought to bear on Murray Todd, to hold a party on the weekend of the Dinghy Exhibition. Afterseveralminutes Murray succumbed and by the time you read this you*®ll have to "reach" back into your subconscious to remember it! Judging by conversations during the evening, boat preparation is being left to the last minute so let's get our fingers out and get to it lads! The fleet working party (March 6th) was extremely well supported — so well in fact I was reduced to insulting the assistant F.C. (yes, he does exist after all) for lack of something to doe The "greater" half of the fleet (interpret this as you wish) assembled at the race=box to witness a revolution (not the boat design) in the making, whilst the remainder distributed layers of paint (sometimes on the race marks). The revolution at the race=—box was the brain=-child of our new young Race Equipment Officer whose name escapes me for the moment. It involved the fitting of a semi-automatic continuous halliard flag raising system (otherwise known as SACHFRS). The principal of operation was basically sound but the implementation generated two schools of thought. There were those who argued the case for splicing (minority) and those who argued the case for knots and whipping (majority). I myself belong to the whipping school, but I am always open to suggestion. I had not realised that the simple act of tying a few knots and splices could be the catalyst for so many new relationships. Malcolm Stuart and Geoff Josey (once Solos) were caught in flagrante delicto whilst attempting to seal their frayed ends with burning matches, whilst Sarah and the unknown gent in the flares (sorry I didn't rise to the bait Colin) held intellectual conversations. /continuede

Phil Gray, Cadet Skippere “TM re et 1983 YEAR BOOK I should be grateful to receive any comments you may have on the format of our Year Book. Some of the changes this year are obvious and will I hope make it easier for new members to understand. Other detailed changes I should like to bring to your attention are:= PRIZES: Recently 2nd and 3rd prizes have been awarded for all races on the same basis so the special arrangement for open and closed races is deleted. COURSE INSTRUCTIONS: Following a Protest last season the instruction has been clarified so that Race Officers are free to change courses for standard fixed club line starts if weather conditions change after the course has been displayed at the signing on point. The Course displayed on the front of the race=box at the Class Warning (10 minute) Signal is the one that counts. FINISHING LINE: A clear statement is now made that there is no ‘long line’ finish except for the Marconi Cruises Cup which is sailed to BIRD course instructions. /continued.

PERSONAL SAFETY: For all races sailed before the Whit Regatta Wet/Dry suits must be worn by all competitors. Failure to do so will result in disqualification. SIGNING ON AND OFF: Much confusion exists between clubs on what to call race sheets. A declaration sheet can be for signing on or off or both. This year you will have new race sheets and all references are standardised on the most direct description, i.e. Signing On Sheet = Signing Off Sheet. COURSES: Although space did not allow inclusion of a map covering the whole of the river the Year Book does now make reference to the long distance courses traditionally used for All-In and Cruiser races, Details of these courses are available on a new "4 double sided map which will be available at the signing-on point in the club house. DESCRIPTION OF MARKS: The new mark at the East end of the outer cruiser moorings is included as Mark Fe Responsibility for this mark may be taken over by the Fisheries Protection in which case its description will change. E Mark is traditionally off Osea to the East of the Pier, The Speed Limit buoys are often used or alternatively our Orange Inflatable Buoy. Or sometimes as happened last year, we caused confusion by using both, Consideration is being given this year to sailing a triangular course for one or more races in which case E buoy may be positioned anywhere with respect to two other fixed River or Club marks. To avoid last year's confusion and to allow for new courses the description of E mark this year has not specified it by type or position. Therefore any courses using E mark must add the description on the board at the signing on point. LADY PERSONS: Finally I have set out to remove the last vestiges of chauvenism from the Year Book — now we are all helms together. Mike Boreham, Mirror Fleet Captain, [redacted], HORNET NEWS I hope this reaches Mary alright as I'm writing at the eleventh hour as they say. Well, things are hotting up in the sailing world (not the weather I notice) and it has been rumoured that people have actually been sailing! This month started with the Dinghy Exhibition at Crystal Palace and Murray's party. Marconi were well represented at the Exhibition in the form of Mike/Colin/Sarah (the pretty one) and company. The pristine Hornet of Graham Mead apart from being a repository for Hornet balloons, attracted many admirers. Some Marconi Cadets (bless their little cotton socks) complained at the lack of helium in the balloons but this was soon solved by attaching a helium filled Merlin Rocket balloon to the cheaper imitation. Also seen on the stand was a Hornet with an automatic (well semi-automatic) spinnaker pole system. This system appealed to my engineering sensitivities as it appeared to be well thought. out and remarkably economic in its use of blocks, fittings and ropes. It's rumoured that John and Murray may be fitting this system this year as they are convinced that the majority of their swims have resulted from the pre=spinnaker launch balancing act that takes place. The system may well suit us helms with lightweight crews (84 stone naked!) so I shall be watching with some interest (other boats that is!). Anyway well done all those who supported the Hornet stand. The same weekend saw the annual Hornet party once again hosted by Murray Todd. Sue and I had heard so much about these parties that we started training several weeks before. I contented myself with evening runs round the estate to build up my stamina and Sue got cracking on the sausage rolls, eventually producing a round one hundred. I bet you all think I am going to make some really cheap joke here at the expense of Murray but as you now know I am not like that. I would like to thank Murray for a very relaxing evening (sorry Murray, couldn't resist that one!) and a stimulating video show. I couldn't actually see one of the video films as David Harper had his face pressed to the screen = I believe it was something to do with Hornets sailing at Stone. Talking about Stone, don't forget our first race with them is on May lst, 10.30 am start. News is trickling through of a Marconi success at the Burnham Easter Eqq and I hope a report appears in this issue of Navigans or failing that, next month. Now it's slap wrist time. Hands up those of you who attended the last get-together at The Ship. I am reliably informed that Murray Bates (not so Rear Commodore) was the sole attendee on this occasion. In recognition of Murray's devotion to duty I suggest all those members who are 35 years or older buy Murray a drink when they next see him. /continuedo

HORNETS AT BURNHAM ( ANYONE FOR A G & T?)... Three Marconi Hornets entered the 32nd Easter Egg meeting at R.C.Y.C. Burnham. The event attracted a disappointing turnout of only eleven boats. Graham Mead and Mike Turner in 'Ultimatum' had an unfortunate start to the weekend when, on the first leg of the first race, Mike's trapeze harness broke and he spent quite a considerable time hanging on to a mooring buoy before being rescued by the less than adequate rescue service. There was Marconi success in this race however because Colin Harper and Ian Stott in 'Renaissance' won the race by a considerable margin from the only other finisher in the severe conditions which prevailed during the race. As a result of the incident in Race 1, Mike Turner sustained an injury to his finger which prevented 'Ultimatum' from taking any further part in the event. Race 2 on the Saturday was held in winds of about force 3 to 4 northerly, and was dominated by Nick and Tony Smither from Dover who had won the event in 1982. Colin Harper improved from a bad start to finish second, narrowly holding off a challenge by the other Marconi boat 'Gingernuts' sailed by new member Dave Berger with his crew Kim Ridge. Sundays race was held in very light conditions and Colin Harper and Dave Berger found themselves towards the back of the fleet but fortunately the leading group sailed the wrong course allowing 'Renaissance' to round the final mark in 3rd position with 'Gingernuts' not far behind and after a long run against the tide with many changes of position the race was won by Neil Hutton and Margi from Weston S.C., Nick and Tony Smither were second and Colin Harper and Ian Stott managed to hold onto 3rd. Sunday afternoon saw the first ever Hornet Open Meeting snowball fight in which the joint team of Marconi and Datchet took on all comers and remained unbeaten, Sarah very skillfully pretending to be with the opposition and hitting people on the side she was standing (or was it really accidental?). [redacted], HORNET NEWS Kate and I are very disappointed in the Hornet Fleet. We were under the impression that it was a very competitive, lively and go-ahead fleet famed for its massive turn=—outs and bawdy socials. Come on lads, I can assure you the estuary is nice and warm now} Six intrepid sailors made Spring Points 3 and 4, the first Hornet class race of the season. They were Graham/Mike, Graham/Murray (F.C.), and Phil/Kate. The first race was held in wind strengths of 0 to force 1 from a N./NeW. direction. The two Grahams made good starts with "Stimulation" fighting the current armed with the knowledge that all those sheets must do something and eventually making the start line about one minute later. Mike/Graham in "Ultimatum" immediately stamped their authority on the race rounding 'E' mark with the Mirrors and a substantial lead. This lead was maintained throughout even though "Stimulation" forsook the northern route from C to Breezy (very slow run against the flood tide) and opted for a reach to the race box and then a course out of the tide to Breezye This course to be a mistake on the crews part] After a pint and a sandwich, Spring Points 4 was started in even lower wind strengths. The start was with the tide and the first mark = A to port. "Ultimatum" arrived there first only to find the leg back over the start line and then on to Breezy was to be a very protracted affair. All three Hornets were soon involved in a tussle for windward position (albeit out in the wicked tide), but "Stimulation" opted for a shore hugging position and with the help of a foot over the side to avoid a breakwater soon established a small lead. The other boats soon followed this example and an orderly progression made its way to Breezy. Graham/Murray rounded first and established a good lead to Noe 1 with "Ultimatum" moving into second place. After gybing in order to lay "A" mark Graham/Murray Overstood and immediately made a bee line to the shore and out of the current. "Ultimatum" and "Stimulation" stayed out in the current and at 10 yards from the finish all three boats were in line abreast, and despite all the pumping and Flatulence aboard the other boats "Stimulation" creamed over the line followed fractionally later by Graham/Mike and Graham/Murray. a 3/4 and then a course back to Noe 4. THORPE BAY YACHT CLUB -— 30th April = lst May, 1983. Thorpe Bay Yacht Club hosted the annual Two—Pint—Pot meeting for Hornets. The entry of twenty four boats included three Marconi teams. Saturday's race was sailed in medium winds and sunshine and the olympic course was set very accurately which made for some very close racing. Nick and Tony Smither (winners of the faster Eqg meeting) and Sally Allyard dominated the race and soon got well clear of Chris and Andy Bines who were unchallenged for third place, The following oroup of four boats contained two from Marconi; "Ultimatum" (Graham Mead and Mike Turner) and "Renaissance" (Colin Harper and Ian Stott). This group remained close together for the whole race (about 2 hours), with Graham making up for his poor upwind performances with very fast downwind legs. Eventually however, both Marconi Boats lost out to the other two in the group and Graham and Colin finished 6th and 7th respectively. The race was won by Sally Allyard who was sailing her last hornet event Since she intends entering the ladies World Championships in which she will sail a laser. After the race most of the younger competitors went down to Southend to the Kursal where great amounts of time were spent arranging group discounts /continued.

on the various rides. We all returned to the club for a ‘Chicken and Chips! supper which some people ate and others ended up wearing. The disco which followed was enjoyed by all who stayed and finished with a rapturous chorus of a few well known songs! Sunday Morning's weather was dismal with torrential rain and very little wind. There was an encouraging forcast however and by the time the race started the rain had stopped, but the wind was still very light. (IDEAL FOR PHIL). Colin and Ian made a poor start and tacked out on port to gain clear winde In doing so they picked up a good wind shift which allowed them to lee=bow the tide on the starboard tack and the whole fleet crossed behind them. Peter Bennet and Giles Weston from Sussex Yacht Club just overhauled Colin by the windward mark and these two got well clear of the following group. Bennet pulled away and Colin and Ian dropped back into the bunch. After this, the race became a little processional until a force 5 squall came through to allow Colin and Ian and Nick and Tony Smither to go from 5th and 6th to 3rd and 2nd in the space of one two sail reach. Bennet won the race convincingly with Smither 2nd and Colin 3rd. Both the other Marconi boats had disappointing results in this race, The gruelling third race in a strong force four to five began soon after the end of race two and Dave Berger and Kim Ridge in ‘Ginger Nuts! from Marconi displayed excellent upwind speed on the first leg, but he was unable to maintain this performance throughout the race. Nick and Tony Smither got well clear of the field in the conditions to which they are ideally suited and Peter Bennet sailed well to finish second. Graham and Mike capsized on the final run whilst lying Sth and decided to retire. Colin and Ian finished 6th after capsizing at the first marke The race finished at around 6.30 pm. - 5 - CADET NOTEBOOK - 1 SAFETY CAPSIZE DRILL - THE R.Y.A. METHOD - (LEEWARD CAPSIZE). Stage 1 - Crew (c) and Helm (H) fall into the water, each checks that the other is O.K. and then they both move towards the transom (Fig.A). Stage 2 - Helm checks that rudder is secure, crew frees the mainsheet. Stage 3 - Helm moves to the back edge of the centreboard using the mainsheet as a safety line (Fig. B). If the centreboard is not down crew moves into the boat and lowers it. CAUTION - crew should make sure that the helm is not struck by the centreboard! Stage 4 - Crew throws jibsheet to helm who acknowledges its receipt (Fig C). Stage 5 - Crew lies in the boat facing downward supported by the water (NOT the boat) Fig D). Stage 6 - Crew informs helm that everything is ready. The helm climbs onto the centreboard using the jibsheet and leans back (Fig. E). The boat will come up slowly (Fig. F) and in doing so scoops up the crew. Stage 7 - The boat is upright and the crew uses his/her weight to balance the boat. Stage 8 - Getting the helmsman aboard is achieved in several ways:- (A) The helm might be able to climb in unaided as the boat comes upright. (B) In boats with high freeboard (i.e. 420's) the crew rocks the boat boat towards helm, grabs his/her hands, and rocks back pulling him aboard. (C) In boats with little freeboard it may be necessary to bail out some water before the helm comes aboard. REMEMBER: Do not enter the boat over the transom. Stage 9 - Open self bailer, transom flaps or bail out the water and sail away. Phil.

os 8 — Letter to Editor [redacted], Rayleigh, Essex, [redacted] 22nd May, 1983 Dear Mary, In the 'Navigans' - anf excellent publication, I think; - and for which many thanks to you all the effort you must put in each month - there is one particular point with which I feel I'd like to take issue. May I refer to the article in the March Issue entitled 'Calling Willing Ladies'? As a mere male I have many times been grateful for the care and concern shown by ladies, and it is always very nice to be on the receiving end of such ministrations, — but why is it always considered the 'normal' for men to have their ladies prepare and serve their refreshments, - and wash up afterwards! Surely nowadays there is no discrimination in the kitchen, galley, or what you will - or if there is, what are the ladies doing about it? More to the point, perhaps, what are the men doing about it? Are we incapable of cutting sandwiches, or making tea or coffee - and of washing up afterwards? — Fuex poke ahead? Many ladies nowadays sail with a great deal of expertise, and no one thinks it is strange that they do. No one apparently finds it strange to see a man behind the licenced bar. Would it be too strange to have men working in the refreshment bar? — and notice the word 'working'. That's what happens there - from start to finish with very little respite, respect, or even appreciation, especially at Regatta Time. I would like to suggest that one member of eeth fleet in turn wee- bo made responsible for refreshments = to be aided by a cadet. After all they get all the benefit of tuition and experience from the Club, and they should be prepared to give something back - No doubt they are. If the idea is acceptable, perhaps we shall not again have such notices as ‘Ladies — Don't Forget to Volunteer to Work in the Galley, Will You?' - Why should you? After all, isn't your leisure as precious to you as your male's is to him? Of course, if doing your thing is serving, etc., ... That's great! The jobs that need doing include:- Inspecting for damage, repairs to the GRP, rubbing down and varnishing woodwork, repairing/replacing damaged fittings, repairing trolleys, sail mending etc. Clearly some experience is required to ensure that essential jobs are identified and completed satisfactorily, but most of the work can be done by inexperienced people. It should be an opportunity for the novices amongst us (and I am one) to learn about boat maintenance and for those without boats of their own to feel the satisfaction of a job well done. The easy way is to spread the load over several people and throughout the winter, so that's what I want to arrange. The idea is to have a different team responsible for each boat with one person in each team responsible for that boat. That person gets to be called a Boat Captain - sharp, huh. The Boat Captains inspect their boats at the end of the season and arrange with their teams to carry out any work needed some time between then and fitting out.
