6 - SADLER SHAKEDOWN There we were, George and I, in the middle of the main shipping channel at Harwich/Felixstowe harbour, We were motor sailing intending to clear the harbour entrance as quickly as possible. I had already noticed a floating block of flats being towed by three tugs bearing down on us from our stern. Looking ahead I saw a Townsend Thoresen ferry start to leave Felixstowe, soon a huge white bow wave grew in front of it and was heading our way, then out of the blue, the engine's warning bleeper started, setting my heart racing. Was it the oil pressure?, was it the temperature? was it I called to George to helm whilst I started to check. There were no warning lights illuminated on the console, but not having any gauges I could not check whether it was a malfunction of the bleeper, a malfunction of the warning lights, or prelude to engine seizure. The engine did not smell hot and kept a steady beat. To stop the engine would have been suicidal as the light wind was blowing directly towards the Felixstowe harbour, the very direction that the Floating block of flats was heading. The Townsend Thoresen Ferry kept forging OUr Waye George called to me that a Sealink ferry was just rounding the corner and heading towards us. There was nothing for it but to turn out of the channel and hope the engine would take us out of trouble. With the warning bleeper becoming louder I increased the throttle. The engine responded and we were soon surging out of the main channel and away from being run down by the two ferries. We stopped the engine and sailed on. The floating block of flats was in reality 15,000 tonnes container ship — it was enormous, or seemed to be in those confined waters. Once clear of imminent danger and with the tide under us we sailed up the Orwell towards Pin Mill, JI checked the oil lever, it was correct and the oil was not burnt, I checked the water inlet, it was not blocked. I gingerly started the engine, no warning came from the bleeper, it ran smoothly. I then checked the water flow, the delivery pipes were running full bore, nothing wrong there. In fact there did not seem to be anything wrong with the engine at all, Of course there should not have been, the engine was almost brand neu, having only run approximately 10 hours. We were on the first cruise of my new Sadler 29 = I had just spent the last year building it and did not expect any troubles apart from minor adjustments. I had tested the engine on short trips previous to this cruise, We fetched up at Pin Mill, picking up a mooring buoy. The tranquility of the mooring soon made me forget the near panic situation just a short time ago. We cracked open a couple of cans of beer, I was at peace with the world once again. That evening we were cordially entertained at the Pin Mill Yacht Club, by some of the members of that club. On returning to our dinghy we found it to be a very long way from the water's edge! We had arrived at high tide earlier that evening and now it was low tide. The hard at Pin Mill has a very small rise from top to bottom, consequently the tide recedes very quickly leaving a long hard. We staggered back to the water carrying the dinghy. George stepped off the side of the hard into the mud. We both started to laugh as neither of us could see where we were, (It's very difficult to direct a torch when carrying a dinghy!) covered in mud we rowed back to the boat, Next day we sailed back to Tollesbury, having a very pleasant sail without any drama. Next day I telephoned the engine's main agents. “what age is your engine", the engineer enquired, "When did you buy it"? My reply was that it was /continuede

- 7 - new and came with the boat. "Oh yes", he said "your engine is in the series that needs a modification, I will send you one in the post". To my surprise and delight the modification turned up by return of post. It consisted of a new terminal strip with two resistors and a diode soldered on to it. This was easily fitted and the old terminal strip returned to the agents. The fault that had occurred in my installation was that the diode had been leaking a voltage across the terminals and this had operated the bleeper. The fact that this only happened when the engine had run for some time was due to the diode warming up. When cold the installation was perfect, but on running for a period the bleeper would operate. The moral to this tale is that although warning lights and bleepers bring one's attention to a fault in the engine, they do not tell the full story and only a set of engine gauges can be used to actually know what is happening inside the engine. Needless to say, I am now fully instrumented, the little bleeper will not worry me again! D. Field. THIS IS THE 420 NEWS In the absence of Peter and Anna (you remember them, they are the ones always seen low down on the horizon) who have temporarily deported (sorry departed) to Australia in search of didgeridoos, I thought I might emulate Phil Gray's inimical prose and write a load of old rubbish on the 420 sailing events. First, the Summer Points - John Weedon immediately stamped his authority on the series and left no chance for anyone else to win the series. We had him worried at times though as occasionally we were almost close enough to see his sail number. This left second place to be contended between myself and the indomitable duo of Alan Mack and his ace crew Julian Brown. With equal points and one more race to go I used my secret weapon (my wife as crew, not wings on the centre board) and had a really exciting race with Alan, narrowly beating him by a mile at the last mark (sorry Alan). Julian was seen to be heavily bandaged after the race. Seriously though, Alan and Julian had an excellent mid-week win, storming ahead of the fleet and intimidating Phil Gray into retiring. The Mona's cup was won by John Weedon and Damian Boreham. Damian also crewed for John in some of the Summer Points races. Are these two really invincible? Phil Gray ex=420 only came second! Those 420 sailors who have not sailed lately will not have experienced the new hazard to blissful 420 sailing. It's called the blue peril. A certain type of boat seems suddenly to ap;ear to windward creating massive holes in the wind leaving the poor hapless 420 sailor bemused, sails flapping, spinnaker collapsed, speed zero and spray kicked in ones face, (enterprising sailors will have guessed the class by now)e The only known cure for this malady is for more 420s to sail and regain our oun fleet start, The real highlight of the season was David Hall's visit. 420 sailors who missed this really must kick themselves. David instructed us on the theoretical and practical handling of the 420 and imparted many useful ideas and tips on topics such as rig setting, spinnaker handling, barbar hauling and tacking. I will not go into further details as I feel sure that Peter on his return from holiday will want to write a separate report on David's visit. I would like to thank David on behalf of the 420 fleet for sharing his valuable time, knowledge, and experience with us. As I work in the same office as Phil Gray — no violins please - I have instructed him on some of the techniques learnt from above, so the next time you see him on the water, keep clear, he's still learning. I apologise for numberous references to Phil (who is this guy anyway) and assure you that it won't happen again as the next 420 news will be in the erudite hand of our intrepid pommy fleet captain ably assisted by his Sheila.. (you remember, she's one of the prettier 420 crew/helms). RF. Jeffries. PeSe Rumour has it that Sue Gray is to be our next Editor. Sue, who has a classical bent (it is left as an exercise for the reader to work that one our) will bring a new dimension to satorical editing. This change was necessary in order to censor the numerous insidious innuendo's about Phil's inability to keep a Hornet upright. I am able to say that this is the real reason he may join the Mirror fleet and not the one reported in an earlier Navigans. [redacted], CADET WEEK 1983 Now that the cuts, bruises and scars have healed (all except Neil Pembleton's that is!) we can look back and reflect on this years' cadet week. The Sunday evening treasure hunt supplied the usual surprises, one of which was that a live crab can survive ina pint of beer! I was disappointed that no-one produced an octopus (although one was seen alive and well later in the week?), although there were a lot of poor imitations. By the way, the answer to the last question was any number between 20 and 25. It's unbelievable but one team wrote 35 and another wrote "very ancient", To reduce the fire risk due to long dry grass the cadet skipper arranged for a moderate fall of rain during Sunday night! Monday dawned with more rain and high winds which proved to be a realistic background for capsize drill, Malcolm Stuart kindly offered his services as a proving ground for potential 420 crews wishing to learn the art of trapezing. I use the word ‘art' loosely as many aspiring crews appeared to spend a large amount of time under the water. These crews I should add were mainly parents and the mirth they caused was only topped by Malcolm's demonic laugh as he dunked one after the other in the soup — well done Malcolm! Tuesday saw an improvement in the temperature and a lessening in the wind strength. The morning was well spent in learning and practising how to start a race, Four practice starts were made and each one was video-taped from the racebox by Pat Stuart. The tapes were later played back in the lounge and proved to be very constructive. It was plain from the tapes that most boats got a good start once but no-one got it right all of the time. However, it was noticeable that the three Mirrors taking part showed considerable and sustained improvement throughout, In fact, so good was the general improvement that when the Cadet Skipper made his final run for the start line in the Wednesday evening race he found the line blocked with Mirrors$ Race 1 for the Cadet Series was held on Tuesday afternoon in fairly light winds. Ten (yes, 10) cadets took part which in itself must be a record judging from the last few years' performances, The race was won convincingly by Damian with Kate second. Race 2 was sailed on Wednesday morning in very light airs and with the /continued.

crew of 420, K.41106 looking slightly the worse for wear. Conditions were difficult because of a tight leg to No. 1 against an ebb tide. The faster boats made agonisingly slow progress whilst the Mirrors were slowly drifting seaward. 41106 retired with sun-stroke and hangover (the boat was also sinking — yes, honestly!) and the race was abandoned after 1 hour 55 minutes to allow Bob in the fisherman to rescue the tailenders. As the abandon flag was being raised a zephyr of wind appeared and Penny (crewed by daddy) who was by now virtually on the northern shore of the estuary began to move and eventually finished the course. Well done, Penny - hope you enjoyed the "After-Eights" luv. As a bit of light relief and because of the rapidly rising temperatures, on Wednesday afternoon a Super Teams competition was held. This involved the various skills of cycling, dribbling (with a football that is!), running, tug-of-war, throwing the welly, throwing the ball, cartwheels and canoeing. The dribbling produced a play-off that resulted in a draw between Robert Weedon and Robert Gray. The cartwheels were included when it was found that there were so many budding gymnasts on site and Damian showed us that he can do other things besides sailing. The cycling race required stopwatch timing to 1/100th second and it was during this event that Adam Bloomfield decided to audition for the next James Bond film by arresting the motion of a bike and rider doing Mach 2 by merely placing his body in the path of the machine. Well done, Adam - hope the hand, arm, leg etc. are better. The canoeing event provided its usual thrills and spills with something like a span of eight years separating youngest and oldest. The event was won by Steven Gray (youngest) whilst Andrew Sharp (oldest) canoed three quarters of the course and then decided to swim the remainder. If you can remember whose team you were in then the final winners were team C captained by Robert Weedon. Cadet Race 3 was sailed Thursday morning and this time a fairly old looking cadet called Frank (or Uncle Frank as he is now known) sailing a Solo (sail number withheld!) joined in, and in fact managed to win} Now seriously the winner was Keith Boyles followed 34 seconds later by Alec Pembleton. Alec by this stage in the week had ditched Dad and his "Graduate" for a slightly up-market boat and a younger crew (that will cost you a pint Malcolm!). The final Cadet race was sailed on the Friday morning and once again the wind was very light. The windward mark (S8reezy) was reached quite quickly by virtue of a strong ebb tide but the beat to C was to leave only three boats in contention. They were Keith, Kate and Alec. Alec showed very good boat speed (and sailing skill) and when he rounded C mark the other two boats were 400/500 yards ‘yw behind in lightening winds. The duel for second place raged over the next two legs with Kate easing past Keith on the Osea shore and then making a late break for A mark with the tide. Alec was first home with a 22 minute gap before Kate with Keith a close third. In the final reckoning Alec won the series with Keith second. Uncle Malcolm can now boast that he has crewed a winning boat in a series (give me a call sometime Malcolm). About 20 participants tried Phils walk along the seawall on Thursday evening and made it to Steeple Bay sailing club where they were picked up by the Mariner, a Leader and a cruiser for the return journey. Those lucky enough to join Lynn (I hope that's how it's spelt!) in the Mariner experienced a brisk and damp sea passage home with the golden orb of the setting sun kissing the world goodnight (good stuff eh!). Well, what a change Saturday was! Winds force 4 and where had the sun gone? The plan had been to cruise up to the "Jolly Sailor" at Heybridge, get outside of a few Cokes, have a spot of lunch and cruise back — but it was not to be. However, a few intrepid souls did manage a picnic on the lee shore of Osea Island with a little help from Malcolm and Lynn in the Mariner. One final event (I used this word loosely) was the paper chase held .in. an attempt to clean our site of rubbish. If there were any rules at the start then /continued.

(c) if anyone gets squeezed out of their allocated space to use the marked overspill area. EDITORIAL The cake competition was "magnificent", or rather the entries were. So much hard work must have gone into them - the standard was very high. Also, you should have seen the proud look on the faces of the competitors. We had two sessions of judging, one Saturday 24th Sept. and the second the following day. For the Saturday we were lucky to obtain the services of Betty Beavins and Connie Bigden ex Galley Ladies (20 years ago), and what a truly professional job they made of it. After much marking and conferring they pronounced Damian Boreham (12 years old) the winner with his super sponge decorated in blue and white with the Marconi flag. (Well done Damian). A close runner-up was our clever Sailing Secretary with his scrumptious chocolate sponge, and third was one of Ron's boys, Dennis Dear. On the Sunday we had another set of judges who also did a grand job. They were Ann Bates and her mother. They followed the same rules as Betty and Connie, and, because they found the cakes to be of a very high standard, made their choice finally by taste. First was Stan Campbell, with a lovely fruit cake, second Phil Gray (another fruit and nut case) and third, Murray Todd with a sponge decorated with - yes, you've guessed - a hornet. I jumped at the opportunity and started training at some open meetings. The Marconi Regatta was one of them. This was all easy going with not too much wind at any of them, but it was a different story when we arrived at Mounts Bay for the Nationals. Sailing Club News Over the weekend of the 13th/14th August, two boats made the long trip from the Marconi Club on the Blackwater River to the MAv/BP Club, at Colemouth Creek, Grain. The boats making the visit were "Roanoke" crewed by Denis Byatt, Malcolm Stuart, and Marconi Club Commodore Frank Savill, and "Blucett" sailed by the Bingley family, Skipper Ben, 1st mate Christine, 2nd and 3rd mates Mark and Shape. The crews had very good conditions to sail down the Essex Coast with the wind N/E force 2/3. Having first encountered the lovely old sailing barge and the Olau Line ferry vying for line honours at Garrison Point, they arrived at 7 o'clock at Colemouth creek, where they joined other overnight visitors "Puff Dragon" (Trio West) and "Lady Amanda" (Brian Herring). A social evening had been arranged by the MAv/BP Club members. Pauline Beldham and her stalwart lady helpers again provided the excellent buffet. The evening proved an enormous success with the guests in great demand. Roanoke sailed on Sunday morning at 06.00hrs in very light winds, Blucett having left slightly earlier. They rendezvoused at the Warps buoy and together they made the Spitway by 11.30, the wind then died completely and they were forced to motor to the Marconi Club and their moorings, arriving at 14.15. The MAv/BP Club members wish to thank their visitors for making the long trip and they look forward to the return visit and sailing match next year in the early summer. 420 FLEET NEWS First of all I would like to say a big "thank you" to the Hornet Fleet for the way they organised the 420 Open Meeting. Everything went very smoothly - apart from some completely unfounded mutterings about the competence of the Race Officer (thanks Phil, moving E mark to the opposite side of the river was a really good idea, we should do it more often). Thanks to Ann Bates for chasing up those notorious entry fee dodgers as receptionist and to the ladies who organised and ran the galley. Luckily somebody volunteered for the arduous task of running the bar =— thanks Colin. The Open Meeting itself was very well attended, attracting 18 competitors (six from M.S.C.). Saturday dawned Foggy, grey and drizzly with practically no wind at all. However, it soon improved to be foggy, grey and drizzly with some wind. As the wind was southerly it was very difficult for the R.O. to arrange a beat, and, in fact, by the time we had reached what should have been the windward leg the wind had shifted and it was a reache The visitors soon showed the Marconi Fleet their heels reflecting our lack of practice against good opposition, and this is shown in the positions of the Marconi entry of llth, 12th, 13th, 14th, and 16th out of 16 entries, Paul Springett won this race closely followed by Dave Hall after the lead had changed several times during the race, Sunday was much better from the point of view of the onlookers (in that the sun was out, the water was blue and visibility was well over the 100 yards of the previous day). However, the wind strength was less and dropped gradually throughout the course of the first race. The wind was now straight out of the west and so the first leg was a beat with everyone trying to keep close to the shore to be out of the tide. This made for an exciting beat up to the corner off the Club with the air ringing with shouts for water at the shore, at cruisers and for starboard boats. Much to my surprise we didn't hit anything! After the point, however, things eased off as the visitors pulled away again. Springett and Hall again tussling for lst and 2nd places. Unfortunately they were both disqualified for being over the start line and so first place went to Geoff Lynch from Hickling Broard. Marconi men again bringing up the rear, The final race started in very light airs and was really a repeat of the morning race as far as positions went, with Paul Springett and Dave Hall monopolising the lead between them. Despite the fact that Paul spotted the new position of 'E! mark first and made a long leg on starboard tack to reach it first (we thought he must be on a really good wind shift) at the finish line Dave Hall took first cannon with Paul taking the second. Again the Marconi entry maintained their positions. These results meant that there was a tie for lst place between Paul and Dave as they both had identical results (one lst, one 2nd and 1 disqualification) and Geoff Lynch was 3rd. - 7 - I was going to write a tremendously witty piece this month about "Three Petes' Race" which I took part in recently (when I entered the Handicap Race in the Autumn Points due to insufficient 420s being about). HORNET NEWS Right, hands up all those Hornet sailors who saw John Mager's deliberate mistake during the third race of the M.S.C. Open Meeting. Well donethose who actually spotted John leading the field for a couple of marks. No seriously though, we had a large turnout for the open both from outside the club and within. The race was over two hours long and after all the beer at lunchtime the fleet were relieved to get ashore. Sunday dawned with warm and sunny weather but little wind. The third race produced the second general recall of the weekend when half the fleet appeared to be walking their boats over the line. A clean start was eventually made with John Mager well away and a few lengths clear at the first mark. The reach up Goldhanger creek split the fleet, the most favoured route being south of the rhumb line. In the latter stages of the race the middle and tail end of the fleet bunched together off Osea shore in disappearing airs and much place changing occurred in what was now a strong ebbing tide. MSC-DOC-1983-10-mamgu-trophy-log-sian-ii: SIÂN 11 GOES FOREIGN Introduction The following is an account written in 1983, of the cruise of Siân 11 to Holland. Modern technology has provided the means to copy the log, the text has been rearranged so that the photographs taken on the trip could be included. The Log Our plan for the 1983 Summer Cruise was to take our boat Siân 11 to Holland. The skipper had done the crossing before, but only as crew on other boats, but it would be the first crossing for Carys (mate, deck hand, cook and all other tasks allocated by the skipper). Siân 11 is a 28ft. Twister, which was bought as a hull and deck in 1980 and fitted out by ourselves in the back garden, she was launched in 1981. Due to domestic complications of having to find 'cat sitters' for our 23 year old cat (eventually solved by bringing my mother and aunt from North Wales to perform the task, however they could only stay two weeks ) we decided to take two weeks holiday from July the 9th to the 24th inclusive, and attempt to sail the boat to Holland in the first week and spend the second week relaxing and cruising Holland, and then leave the boat in Holland and take another week later on to fetch the boat and sail home ---- the plans of mice and men. Since our experience of night sailing was limited, Carys having not done a night passage before, it was decided to start from Levington, and so at midday on July 9th we set off from Bradwell, our home port. Out in the river visibility was not good, and we were beating against an Easterly wind towards the Bench Head Buoy, visibility became worse, we never did find the Bench Head that day, the trip to Levington was abandoned and we headed for Pyfleet to anchor for the night. There we met Stan and Margaret off Maldon Aries, Jack and Jackie Off Winters Maid and Albert Shirley, Jeff and Lesley off Myth of Mynto, all from the Marconi Sailing Club, they were heading for Ramsgate enroute to Normandy and had aborted the journey for the same reason as ourselves. Sunday morning (July 10th )was even worse, visibility was less than the day before, so we decided to sail to Rowhedge for a pint, we left Maldon Aries and Myth of Mynto at Pyfleet and took Winters Maid and Siân to Rowhedge. We sailed back in brilliant sunshine and tied up at Brightlingsea, later to be joined by Maldon Aries and Myth of Mynto. Walking back from the pub that evening saw us all very exited since all the fog had gone and all the stars were clearly visible. On Monday (July 11th ) we said goodbye to the ' Marconi ' fleet they were heading for the Spitway and we were heading for Levington, the wind had backed Northeast and we had to beat up the Wallet. We always seem to be beating in the Wallet, Carys remarked that she should have married a gentleman, since according to Russ Fuller gentlemen never beat to windward. We arrived at Levington about an hour before low water and ran aground about 50 feet from the visitors pontoon. We had our evening meal on the mud and eventually tied up against a boat called Storyville, from the Deben, for a few hours sleep. 1

Tuesday ( July 12th ) quarter past midnight weather forecast was wind NE force 4 with fog patches, this was good enough for a start and at half past midnight we left Levington, wind speed was 3 knots and variable. The main was hoisted and we motored towards Harwich, we noticed a sailing boat, also under engine, coming up behind us, they caught up to ask where we were bound for, it turned out that they were heading for Oostende, the boat was called Mach Fluff and we promised to keep in touch by radio throughout the journey. At 1.40 a.m. we hoisted the jib and switched off the engine, the wind had picked up slightly and the log was streamed, log 00.00. By 3.00a.m. Siân was putting her shoulder in and speed had increased to 6 knots. We were surprised that we could not see the Sunk Light Vessel, but we could see Mach Fluff's stern light about half a mile ahead. At 3.30 a.m. Siân was beginning to surf, we were by the yellow No. 2 buoy, when there was a loud crash from below, on investigating we found six broken eggs on the floor, the cabin sole was like a skating rink, the cupboard door could not have been clipped properly, anyway we should have stored the eggs in one of the lower lockers where they could not fly across the boat. Cleaning the mess took a good ten minutes and the result could only be described as barely adequate. Back in the cockpit we noticed that Mach Fluff's stern light had disappeared, but where on earth was the Sunk?. At 3.45 a.m. we heard the Sunk and suddenly we were in fog, we assumed that this was one of the fog patches mentioned in the weather forecast. By 4.05 a.m. we were by the Sunk altering course towards the Galloper, wind speed was 20 knots and we were making 6 knots. Because the surfing was making steering a compass course difficult we decided to take it in turns to steer, half an hour on and half an hour off. I decided against using the Autohelm as the seas were terribly confused and it was difficult to imagine how the Autohelm could cope. At 6.00 a.m., we had just finished breakfast, hot chocolate and marmalade sandwiches, when we made radio contact with Mach Fluff but when I mentioned breakfast he signed off rather abruptly. While we breakfasted the Autohelm was switched on and it coped very well so it was left on, it did make life easier. The weather forecast at 6.25 a.m. was wind Force 4 NNE with fog banks, big these fog banks, we had been in one for the last 25 miles!. At 7.00 a.m. we found the Galloper, we heard it first, and had to alter course to get to it, we were a bit South of our dead reckoning position but only by about half a mile. We again made radio contact with Mach Fluff, it turned out that when I mentioned breakfast he had to call off to be sick, the three men on board were all sick with the one female member on board left in charge. Course was changed for Oostende and Siân was really surfing making more than 7 knots, with the wind speed exceeding 20 knots but still in fog, visibility was less than half a mile. I tried to get bearings from the RDF, a Hitachi combined RDF and radio, the radio worked but not the RDF-----what a fine time to find out!. At 8.00 a.m. we saw a rather watery sun but it soon disappeared, we made contact again with Mach Fluff they had managed to get a good RDF cocked hat position, we estimated that they were North of us. We calculated our position to be three miles from the South bound shipping lane. At 8.30 a.m. we estimated that we were just entering the shipping lanes, visibility was bad, we did not see any ships but we could hear their fog horns, it was not very pleasant, there was one of them very close. The next two hours kept us on full alert, we kept on seeing shapes that were not there. I think the shapes were due 2

to the fact that we kept on looking at the pulpit and when we looked away an image left on the eye was carried when we turned our heads. The confused seas and the surfing continued, and at 11.00 a.m. the log read 50.29 miles and the visibility was still very bad. At 12.25 a.m. we heard the West Hinder Light Vessel but it was North of our dead reckoning position. This was puzzling but there was no doubt that the signal was the West Hinder, the next minute a large container ship came towards us from the fog, she was called 'Gertrude H' travelling eastward, I tried to call her on channel 16 to ask for a position, but they did not reply. We deduced that if the ship was in the shipping lane and the West Hinder was to the North of us, we were also in the shipping lane, no place to be in the fog. I did a running fix by taking bearings off the horn of the West Hinder and plotted a course to arrive 5 miles off Oostende. The theory was that we ought to see the traffic or the buoys off Oostende, we would be unlikely to miss everything. At 2.00 p.m. I estimated our position to be about 10 miles off Oostende and visibility if anything was getting worse. Carys was getting a bit anxious but the skipper assured her that we were definitely in the Southern North Sea. It was decided to call Oostende radio to have a visibility check, the theory being that if the visibility was three miles from the shore we could close in, if not we could carry on hoping to see a buoy or some traffic. Contact was made with Oostende, and when I asked what the visibility was like?, they replied "We haven't that information sir". At this point I would have swopped the VHF radio for any crude RDF that worked. Whilst I was below cursing the VHF as a safety aid, Carys said "I can see a yacht ahead" and when we were about to change course to ask for a fix she said " I can see a green buoy" I said "You little darling" and gave her a wet salty kiss on the cheek. Twice the green buoy disappeared in the fog but at 2.15 p.m. we knew we were at the Middelkerk BK green buoy, log reading 67.85. Course was changed for Oostende and at 3.03 p.m. we identified the Brittenstroombank North Cardinal but still no sign of Oostende At 3.35 p.m. we saw land about a mile away, but where were the block of flats that you should be able to see 15 miles away?. Suddenly we saw yachts and fishing boats all gilling about outside the pier, we were there!. The problem was that we were still surfing at 6 knots towards the lot of them, it was time to slow down, the jib was dropped but the speed did not drop significantly. Lights were flashing on the pier so the engine was switched on, and the log pulled in recording 76.4 miles. Taking the main down was another problem, the seas were huge, Carys remarked afterwards that she had not seen a wall of water before, the boat was rolling ±30°. I found the only way was to take in the main on the roll to port and hang on for grim death whilst the boat rolled to starboard, Siân's sail was never stowed so untidily. Suddenly everybody was making a dash for the entrance, the flashing lights had gone off, we followed and noticed that the locals had the main sails hoisted and took them down in between the piers. We were showing our inexperience!. Inside the harbour we turned right just before the ferry terminal and saw that the green light was showing that we could enter the Macator dock, we had already decided on a day's rest at Oostende and the Macator is much quieter than the North Sea Yacht Club. The wind was blowing right behind us into the lock and Siân was sailing in under bear poles. On reaching the lock applying reverse power produced the inevitable result, Siân went right across the lock. The lock keeper remarked "First time in the Macator Siân 11" and I replied " Yes, isn't rather obvious". Two Dutchmen helped us out and one remarked "Long keel 3

yah!", it said it all. We were berthed and tidied up by 5.30 p.m. and the sense of achievement is almost impossible to describe. There is nothing like taking your own boat foreign for the first time. The problem of being too far South of our course bothered me a great deal, the only explanation I can think of is that due to the surfing the Autohelm only tried to correct at the end of the surf and not when the surf starts as when the helm is operated manually. As a result we were being set South by the continuous surfing. MECATOR DOCK SIÂN II IN THE MECATOR 4

Wednesday (July 12th) saw us in a rather foggy Oostende, at least we could see the top of the block of flats, we had a Vivacity called Opus 111 in the berth next to us owned by a friendly Belgian couple called Pete and Fenandel, they gave us some very good advice not least to recommend a little restaurant called Petit Paris, the fish was delicious. Whilst walking to the pier we saw Mach Fluff moored in the North Sea Yacht Club and we went to see them, for up to now they had only been voices at the end of the radio. It turned out that the skipper ( John ) was a Concorde pilot, which accounted for the boat's name, Mach being the speed of sound and Fluff being a Fat Little Ugly F--Flyer, his crew was his wife Sue, a German called Friedle and another pilot who had left for the UK to fly Prince Andrew to the USA. Friedle's wife Erica was joining them in Oostende for the rest of the cruise. When they entered Oostende, on reaching the inner harbour the lights started flashing so they turned to go out again, only to find a ferry coming in, so they turned to go in again. At this point a voice from a loud hailer said " English yacht I do not care where you go but get bloody lost ". Like us they planned to go to Flushing the following day and we agreed to keep in touch on the way. We had a drink at the North Sea Yacht Club and talked to Ron and Ness and their son Martin on a boat called Indecision from Lawling Creek, they were leaving for home the following day. On the way back to Siân we noticed Storyville in the harbour. It turned out that they had left Levington four hours after us but abandoned their trip outside Harwich harbour because the fog was too thick, they had a relatively good passage that day visibility being no less than two miles. That night we got to bed at two o'clock in the morning convincing ourselves that it did not matter as we did not need to make an early start that day. Thursday July 14th, weather forecast was winds West 3 to 4 , visibility moderate, ideal for our trip to Flushing, our start was a mad rush. contrary to all other advice received, the harbour master at the Mecator would not take English money and we had to make a dash to the railway station to get some change. By 3.00 p.m. we were outside Oostende sailing a course of 060° magnetic with the wind from the North North East, so much for the weather forecast. LEAVING OOSTENDE 5

At 3.30 p.m. we changed to the No 1 genoa and by 4.00 p.m. the wind had dropped off altogether and the engine was started, we also made contact with Mach Fluff who had left Oostende before us. At 5.20 p.m. we were off Zebrugge and the seas were very confused in spite of the light winds. At 5.35 p.m. we were by the Wilengen Buoy changing course to 085°M heading for Flushing, the wind picked up and we had a super sail along the coast. ( Sailing from Oostende to Flushing is easier than sailing from the Blackwater to Harwich, plenty of buoys and no sandbanks.) At 7.00 p.m. we again made contact with Mach Fluff and we told them our position they said that they could see us, we altered course towards them and we sailed in company into Flushing harbour. APPROACHING FLUSHING 6

Our log was switched off and we noticed that the reading was considerably less than the distance on the chart, showing the importance of working the tides along this coast. It is also important to remember to fit your fenders at water level in the lock as the wooden surround is at water level. We tied up at the marina at Flushing at 9.05 p.m. and felt that our holiday had now really started. Mach Fluff invited us on board for supper, and several glasses of wine later we collapsed into our bunks at 1.00 a.m. in the morning. Friday July 15th, and we did not bother with the early morning shipping forecast, sheer bliss, came to about 10.00 a.m. and left for Middelburg at 11.30 a.m. encountering lifting bridges for the first time, these presented no real problem, but in planning a passage ample time should be allowed to pass through the bridges, the one outside Middelburg kept us waiting three quarter of an hour. LIFTING BRIDGE AT FLUSHING 7
APPROACHING MIDDELBURG SIÂN II AT MIDDELBURG MIDDELBURG HARBOUR 8

We planned to stay at Middelburg that night so that we could visit friends, and sail to Were the following day. Mach Fluff decided to only stop long enough to do some shopping and move on to Were that day, so we said our goodbyes and agreed to keep radio contact at 11.0 a.m. the following morning. Middelburg is a delightful town and the day was spent sightseeing. After supper we went to see our friends, but they were out, we would try again in the morning. We had one or two, or was it three or four or five or -----------? drinks at the Yacht Club, we returned to our berth and when we saw Siân we both had the same thoughts. " How could we have set out with a plan that ment leaving her in some foreign country ?." We decided that if it was at all possible Siân would be bought home at the end of the fortnight ------the plans of mice and men!. Saturday July 16th, we were woken up in the middle of the night, actually it was 8.15 a.m., by someone singing the Max Boyce song "Hymns and Arias". I remember thinking I must be at the Arms Park in Cardiff. It was John and Cath Morle in their boat Tea Tetua from Bradwell, we helped them tie up. Our friends from Middelburg also turned up, they are also friends of John and Cath, and invited the four of us to supper that evening, how could we refuse?. We had a smashing time. MIDDELBURG TOWN 9

TOURIST TRANSPORT IN MIDDELBURG The following day, with Tea Tetua in company we motored to Were and sailed on the Veersmere, they say that there are a million surfboards in Holland, ninety thousand nine hundred and ninty-nine must have been on the Veersmere that day, they were everywhere. APPROACHING WERE 10
WERE HARBOUR SAILING ON THE VEERSMERE 11

DUTCH BARGE UNDER SAIL NORTH SEA DAM We made radio contact with Mach Fluff they were on their way to Goes. It was decided that avoiding surfboarders was not a good pastime and we tied up to the landing stage on one of the islands in the Veersmere called the Haringvreter Island. It is very pleasant walking on the island, with horses, cattle and deer as company. 12
WERE FROM HARINGVRETER ISLAND HARINGVRETER ISLAND 13

We were joined by friends of John and Cath in their boat Splash and over coffee that evening we decided to have a barbecue on the island the following day. The Dutch provide free barbecue sets on the island. SIÂN, SPLASH, TAI TETUA, TIED UP ON THE ISLAND ON BOARD ROSA MARIS 14

11 Monday July 18th, we all sailed in Siân to Were and phoned our friends in Middelburg inviting them to the barbecue, they accepted, and said that they would sail up in their boat to join us. One must be careful at Were, because if you decide to tie up along the town pontoon there is very little water on the east side of the pontoon. Although we managed to tie up, we found that in the swell of passing boats we were touching the bottom, and it is very hard. Whilst the ladies were preparing the barbecue, the men did a bit of boat maintenance, and John notices that he had more water in the bilge than normal and found to his dismay that one of the engine mounts had sheered. We had a discussion and decided, that rather than go to the Ouster Schelde the following day, we would sail back to Middelburg with John, in case he would need a tow and see if we could get some engine mounts in Holland. If we could not John would sail back to England with us, where he knew he could get the mounts and go back to Holland by ferry. Having decided on our plan we enjoyed a superb barbecue. JOHN MORL PREPARING SUPPER LEAVING THE VEERSMERE Note length of barge

Tuesday July 19th, saw us back in Middelburg. John managed to locate engine mounts and our friend took him by car to collect them, they were back by 3.00 p.m. John with myself as handyman, had the engine lifted, engine mounts fitted and the engine running by 8.00 p.m. We enjoyed our supper that evening and decided to return to Flushing the following day. Wednesday July 20th, we made radio contact with Mach Fluff at Goes, they were off to Zierikzee that day ready to sail home the following day, we wished them a safe journey home and signed off for the last time on this holiday. We got our shopping done and when we returned we saw Storyville in the harbour, they were also going to Flushing that day. We agreed a time of departure of 2.30 p.m. We said our goodbyes and got under way. The weather forecast at 5.55 p.m. was variable 3 becoming NE 3, visibility moderate to good. That evening we spent having a drink on Storyville, she is a Colvic Countess 33, compared to our Siân she is enormous, and fitted with a Decca navigator, most impressive. Thursday 21st, we motored into the lock at Flushing at midday, the lock was full of sailing and motor boats, this gave us confidence that we had worked the tides correctly. With the tides running as strong as they do along the coast, everybody tends to leave at the same time, if you find your in the lock alone, it is worth your while to check your tide calculations. We locked out at 1.00 p.m. and heard somebody shouting "Siân II, Arthur ", it was Dave and Joan Thomas on Marinero, they were just going into the lock; we heard later that they had a big piece of tarpaulin around their prop. LEAVING FLUSHING It was nice and sunny with the wind NE about 12 knots and under No 1 genoa and full main we enjoyed a soldiers wind towards Zeebrugge. At 4.30 p.m. we were off Zeebrugge and changed course for Oostende we could clearly see the block of flats some 15 miles away. When we arrived off Oostende the light was flashing and we had half an hour wait, rolling about outside the entrance, it was surprising how 16

strong the wind and tide were when we eventually were allowed to go in. This time we moored at the North Sea Yacht Club as it was our intention to leave for home the following day. It was very crowded in the harbour, with boats rafted nine deep. Because of our narrow beam we were given a fore and aft mooring which made life a little easier. Whilst we were mooring we missed the weather forecast at five to six, everybody we asked said that it was not good. We decided to leave at 6.30 a.m. the following morning provided the forecast was favourable. NORTHSEA YACHT CLUB Friday 22nd July, we were up at six preparing for the off,the 6.15 a.m. weather forecast was wind East 5 or 6 locally 7, with fog banks, we went back to bed. We spent the day waiting for weather forecasts and walking. The 1.55 p.m. forecast was wind East 3 or 4 locally 5, thundery showers, visibility moderate becoming poor. The 5.55 p.m. forecast was East 5 locally 6 becoming cyclonic 4, thundery showers, visibility moderate to poor. We decided on a 4.00 a.m. start. In between weather forecasts we went to listen to a jazz concert in the open air. The band was the one that played in the funeral scene in the James Bond film "Live and Let Live", they were very good. Nick the skipper of Storyville was a keen jazz fan, hence the name Storyville, and was anxious to have his photograph taken with the leader of the band. Carys went and asked if this was possible and the leader said "Let me meet this guy", he seemed very old to me but it made Nick's day. 17

OOSTENDE JAZZ FESTIVAL CARYS TALKING TO THE LEADER Saturday 23rd, what a grotty place Oostende is at 4 o'clock in the morning!, especially when we realised that there was a Dutch sailing boat tied up to our aft mooring and we could not get out. A knock on the hull brought a quick response and he soon moved and was very grateful as he could occupy the slot we had just vacated. Our problems however were not over as there was a raft of boats across the entrance to the North Sea Yacht Club blocking it completely. On the outside was a large British motor cruiser with four men sitting in the cockpit. When we asked them to move we realised that they had been sitting there all night drinking. What followed could have been a scene from a Carry-On film, the motor cruiser under full power moved off but was still attached to the raft. When it was eventually sorted out, we apologised to the boat immediately attached to the motor cruiser, and with typical Dutch diplomacy he said "Perhaps it is not your fault". By 5 o'clock we had cleared Oostende harbour, the wind was right 18

behind us and we were rolling from side to side unmercifully, it was terribly uncomfortable. and no combination of sail setting seemed to help, we left the engine on. The weather was dry, and visibility was moderate, we could see a thunder storm to the North East of us, the lightening was quite spectacular. The rolling continued, but as we were approaching the Middrlkerk Bank Green buoy the wind veered South, the rolling stopped, and we were sailing. As we were approaching the East Dyck buoy, at the edge of the east bound shipping lane I went below to check the chart, Carys remarked that the wind speed was increasing and the next minute we were flattened as a squall hit us. Carys did her best to get Siân's nose to the wind but not before she saw the dodgers being covered in sea water. The next few minutes were taken up in getting safety harnesses on and putting a reef in the main. I went forward to put a reef, wearing a track suit over my shorts, and got saturated by the spray and the waves, the elastic in my track suit could not hold the weight and I arrived back in the cockpit with a sodden track suit around my ankles, not looking at all as your well dressed yachtsman should. The wind speed was 35 knots and we were close hauled. Siân is a wet boat at this point of sailing, we had waterproof tops on but the rest of us was saturated. There were breaking seas everywhere, and we were in the shipping lanes, but the visibility was good, we had to tack twice to avoid shipping, by the time we reached the West Hinder the wind speed had dropped to 25 knots and veered South again. We were sailing comfortably in confused seas. Carys went below to change and I shall never forget the sight of a bear bottom in a red jacket being thrown about below trying to get her trousers on. we were doing a comfortable 6 knots under a reefed main, heading for the North and South bound shipping lanes. By the time we had reached the North bound shipping lane we had the reef out, the fog was closing in and it was raining hard, but the visibility was not too bad, we could at least identify ship shapes a mile away. Half way across the shipping lane the wind died away completely and the rain was torrential, the engine was switched on and was left on to clear the shipping lanes. From the shipping lanes to the Galloper was the most frustrating two hours of the whole trip, it consisted of jib down genoa up, genoa down jib up, reef main shake out reef, jib down genoa up and by the time we were approaching the Galloper we were under jib and full main sailing comfortably in fog, visibility was less than a quarter of a mile. It took some time to find the Galloper we had sailed passed it, we could not believe that it was North East of us, but it was. The sail from the Galloper to the Sunk was uneventful, the weather improving all the time, we could hear the Sunk ahead of us but could not see it as we were looking directly into the sun. At 5.35 p.m., log 66.6 we had the Sunk on our port side and we were steering a course of 260° magnetic heading for Clacton. We were under genoa and full main, Siân had her shoulder in and we were sailing at 6 knots in a calm sea, and at 6.45 p.m. we spotted the Wallet No 2 buoy and we could see land. 19

THE SUNK LIGHT VESSEL It was interesting to note that looking at the Sunk with the sun behind us, we could see it 7 miles away. At 8.15 p.m. we were off Clacton, changing course for the Knoll, the red sunset was well worth coming home to see, the wind however was right in the nose, we dropped the genoa and switched on the engine, this cruising is making a gentleman out of me!. At the Knoll the engine was switched off and the jib set, the wind speed increased again, we were on our last leg home. Off Bradwell we unshiped the log reading 93.51, and by 10.45 p.m. we were having a drink at the bar in the Club. We were glad of our bed that night, and remembered in the morning that we had not phoned the customs before going to bed, one should phone within two hours of arrival. Looking at Siân II in her berth the following day we could not help but feel that she had done everything asked of her and could no doubt do much more. Unfortunately the joy of having made the trip and gone foreign for the first time, was dimmed by the fact that when we phoned home to say SIÂN II IN DUTCH WATERS 20

that we had arrived, we learnt that our old cat had died, anyway that's life I suppose up one minute down the next. POSTSCRIPT The log won the Mamgu trophy at the Marconi Sailing Club in 1983, unfortunately we were only allowed to keep it for twelve months, it looked nice on our sideboard 21

- 2 - COMMODORE'S NOTES I should like to thank all members who attended the working party in October. We got a lot of work done and the club is now reasonably tidy for the winter. The good turnout was helped by the marvellous weather, but might have been even better had we been able to advertise the day's entertainment. For those not present the entertainment was caused by us when we decided to burn rubbish on the foreshore, including a fibreglass hulk from the dinghy park. Before we knew what was happening we were invaded by the coastguard, two fire appliances, the police launch, and finally a police car - all this triggered by radio calls to the coastguard from boats on the river. I suppose, had it been the stubble burning season no-one would have taken any notice. Elsewhere in Navigans you will find the A.G.M. Agenda. Please come - it is probably the best opportunity you have in the year for giving your view on how the club is run. Mary Greygoose has now finished her second three year stint as Editor of Navigans, the first being from 1969 to 1972. She leaves the post having set a high standard for Sue Gray to follow. THE GLITTERING PRIZES Another season is over, and by the time this is printed and read we will have enjoyed the gourmet delights of the Laying-Up Supper and the presentation of the annual club prizes. In preparation for the big night I was scrabbling around in my wardrobe the other day, when I came across a rather tatty evening bag, and an even tattier prize list for last year. Idly glancing through the titles I noticed that many could be interpreted more literally, particularly if the emphasis is put on cruising rather than dinghy sailing. Enlarging on this theme, I would like to present the "Alternative Prize Winner's List for 1983, Cruiser Fleet Style". PILOTS CUP - a pilot is defined as one who shows the way, and this year this award must be given to John Todds in "Chimo", who, during the summer holidays, sailed from the Blackwater via the Kiel Canal to the Baltic Sea, a first for John and the first time a Marconi boat has cruised this area. MUD RACE - was heavily contested this year, (well, we all went up the Alde, didn't we). Quasar, Aces and Eights, Copernicus and Maldon Aries were all strong contenders, however, the undisputed winner, without doubt is Albert and Shirley Pearce in "Myth of Minto". They really explored the depths of Abraham's Boson (look it up in Cootes), it took half an hour to tow them off! MARCONI CRUISER CUP - Joan and David Thomas in "Marinero" who cruised France, Belguim, Holland and the Channel Islands this season in one trip that lasted 3½ weeks and covered over 800 miles. BARNACLE POINTS - too many entrants for this event, the winner Nick Tovey in "Tirzar" for giving his boat the opportunity to collect the most barnacles on her hull. Did Nick leave the mooring this year? Answers on a plain postcard please. MUG'S MUG - for the crew of the year, Mug's Mug is just the thing for that evening cup of tea and toast, Joyce! (Ann Bates' Mum). JACKPOT - an award for the over forties, and proving that you can still cruise well over forty is Bill Buchanan, still sailing regularly from Stansgate. MOANER'S CUP - the junior crew of Clara Anne, they can and they do! HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR - one skipper with some health problems has been determined to enjoy his boat to the full and has done so with great success. Cruising Helmsman of the Year - Jimmy James. Brenda Tate. 3.11.83. /continued.

DAY TRIP JO FRANCE After getting up at 5.30 am, we managed to be ready at 6.30 am and were waiting for Ron and Mary Greygoose who arrived about 6.45 am. Our coats and bags were put in the car boot and we were off. Less than two hours later we arrived at Dover's booking hall and bought five tickets to Boulogne. Mum and Mary got their Identity Cards — they both hated their photographs. We got back into the car and drove to the dock entrance, where we gave the officer our tickets. He tore a bit out and gave them back, then we drove along to the passport office. The officer was reading a book, and when she saw our car arrive she opened the window of her office, took our passports, looked inside them and gave them back, without looking at us at all. She just closed her window and carried on reading. We then drove off again towards the ferry, where another officer told us to park next to the two coaches. We had plenty of time to go to the cafe to have a drink, returning to the car at 9.30 am to find more cars in the queue. A few minutes later we drove onto the M.V. Tiger, a P & O ferry. We were one of the first cars on the boat, and, having parked close to the exit, went upstairs where we found five seats in the lounge before looking around the ferry. At just after 10.00 am we left for Boulogne. After reading for awhile Dad and I went for another walk and had a look at the radar. It was fairly rough and when I sat down again I began to feel travel sick. I had one of Mary's tablets and went with Dad to stand on deck and look at the horizon, which by now was the French coast. Half an hour later we were told to go to the car, and after about ten minutes the front of the ferry opened and we were let out. Before we left the dock we had our passports checked again. Leaving the dock we turned onto the road (on the right-hand side). The second car we saw we all thought was a mad driver. We drove through the town to the old part of Soulogne, and had a look in a small shop. Then we found a nice restaurant. We were taken upstairs and saw at least a dozen people all eating at one big table, but they were English. I think we hoped they would be French. It took two hours to eat our meal. The ice cream at the end was the nicest part. On the way back to the car I bought a Boulogne doll from the small shop we had looked in before, Leaving Boulogne we drove to Calais, and from the road we could see the white cliffs of Dover. When we got to Calais we went to a hypermarket. Dad, Mum, Ron and Mary bought all the wine they were allowed and I bought chocolate, chewing gum and some other sweets. At about 6.00 pm we drove back to Boulogne. We were just in time to catch the ferry, and were the last car on. It was a 7.00 pm sailing and as soon as we drove on the boat we started moving. lt was dark, so we could see both sides of the channel because of the lights. We arrived at Dover just before 8.30 pm and were let through customs. wWe all slept a little in the car on the way home, except Ron, of course, who was driving. /continued.

o« OF =m We were dropped off at home at about 11.00 pm, and I went straight to bed exhausted and drifted off to sleep, thinking about what had happened during the day. Thankyou to Ron and Mary for a great day in France, from Clare (Savill). John Wade, Fleet Captain. * * * BLUE PERIL NEWS It seems a long time since Steve (my crew) said those immortal words "I'm just testing the toe stra.....aps", and went for the early bath before our first Spring Points race, and I realise that I haven't contributed an article since then. A truncated Spring Points Series was contested by myself (in my old boat), Steve Evans and Mike Wellington. Individual race details are now lost in the mists of time and modesty prevents me from relating the series winner here. It was around about this time that that enterprising couple, Nick and ‘Catherine Pope, produced a new lightweight crew — young Christopher. (Apparently bath times indicate a strong liking for the water and he is expected to go into training soon). _ Eleanor Witter and myself had a lovely time in the team race against Rochester, we spent so much time chatting and not thinking about sailing that we managed to do quite well. Steve Evans and myself went in for the Regatta, sailed in light or zero wind conditions, and enjoyed the excitement of big fleet sailing. We shall be there again next year hoping for an improvement in our results and for a bit more wind. The Summer Points Series was contested by six boats in light winds (again!) and reached an exciting climax with the final result hanging on the last race of the /continued.

- 10 - series, Steve Evans or myself standing to take the cup, but once again modesty prevents me recounting the winner. Wednesday nights were well attended by Enterprises and some cracking sailing was enjoyed with some very competitive spirit introduced by Fred Terry's boat, a very welcome, if overdue, sight - keep it up next year Fred! The Autumn Points Series started with a good breeze but I was the only Enterprise there for the first race, when after much nail biting not helped by Alan Mack's crew reciting those daunting lines from Treasure Island, "Them that dies'll be the lucky ones", we shot out and tore about for half an hour before coming in relieved that the rescue boat was not running - a very good excuse. Anyhow, to cut a long story short, Steve Evans won the Autumn Series with John Walker second and me last. Well done chaps! There is no trophy for the Enterprise Autumn Series yet, and anyone wanting to donate a suitable family heirloom or any other trophy is most welcome (a mooses head on a plaque is not really suitable - or is it?). During the high winds of the Autumn, several boats blew over and had to be lashed down, remember - it is a club rule that boats be securely tied down and in our new dinghy park space we are very much more exposed. 22 June 1983 - it = SAILING ETIQUETTE It was one of those rare hot, sunny Sunday afternoons and we were having a lovely run-back up the Blackwater with the tide under us. We had anchored for lunch in a sheltered spot in the mouth of the estuary and, with a fresh NE blowing there was no point in hoisting more than the working jib for the return trip. It would also give a chance for my non-sailing friends to take a turn on the helm since, in the morning it had meant hard tacking down river into very short lumpy seas. My MacWester 27 didn't quite look like a carnival float but with two families plus a friend on board, Blucette's foredeck and cockpit were groaning under the weight of 5 adults, 3 growing children and good lunches. Hardly in racing trim! We had manoeuvred safely through two legs of a dinghy race and: were managing to leave plenty of room for a stream of racing cruisers to pass with spinnakers flying when, uh-ho! The upwind leg of that race? Here he comes, hard on the wind, crew way out on the trapeze, going like the wind and he has us on starboard! I'm standing on the companion steps and my wife calls from her reclining position on the foredeck. "See the one to Port?" "Yes" I say. He'll pass ahead of us I had decided, so best leave the hehksman alone as he had been steering a good steady course. Now what's happening? The approaching craft had altered course and was now aiming to go clear under my stern. I was secretly glad I hadn't gone to port to cross under but I still came back into the cockpit, stepping over the maze of legs, and reached behind me for the tiller. That was the best move I had done all day as - you guessed it - he altered course yet again and, with a very few yards now separating us was obviously aiming at my sink outlet 6 inches or so above the waterline just abaft the after chain plate! At that moment he called "STARBOARD" and I hauled the helm hard over and 4 tons at 4 knots did a reasonable impression of turning on a sixpence. "Not that way, you stupid B----r!}"; "Oh, B------ y hells"; "Who taught you to B------ y saili"; "Oh, They went down my starboard side with 6 to 8 feet to spare shouting all sorts of abuse, something about rules and parentage and the number of arms and legs I didn't have, which continued way into the distance... Now, turning as I did to Port mean't I only had to turn 45° or SO; reduced the time to pass; kept the jib flying (it was out to starboard) and didn't knock my helmsman overboard (he was standing to port of the tiller). Turning to starboard - I suppose that was what he mean't, or was it reverse - would have mean't 135° of turn; an increase in the time to pass, thus allowing the tide to set me across him; backing the jib, reducing directional control, and would have given my helmsman indigestion, with a stout tiller in his stomach so goon after lunch. Maybe I could have argued that the almost inevitable. I a se

12 = would have been his fault as he was then the overtaking craft Needless to say I had a barrage of questions from my guests. Of course we should not have got into such a tight situation but he could have held his initial course and passed clear in front of us with room to spare. In the ideal world we wouldn't need any collision avoidance regulations, (I won't bore you with the chap who tacked in front of me in the morning and I just avoided using his towed inflatable as a fender). In fact one of my friends was SO impressed with the day out he's now talking of taking up sailing! Sailing is fun, and most of the time very friendly. In my six years of sailing I have never been shouted at like that before, except when I've been racing as well. Then if I catch you on starboard -plug your ears - unless of course you are just out for a cruise. Those that attended the race training session this year will know most of it as it is basically going to be a summary of what Dave Hall told us. (Not necessarily in order of importance). The first item concerns the jib sheets. I expect this is old hat to a lot of people but it was new to me this season and, having tried it, I've found it an improvement. The basic idea is that, instead of fixing the centre of the rope that forms the jib sheets to the jib, both ends of the same rope are attached, so forming a continuous system. When I was shown this my initial reaction was that the rope would not now be long enough for the crew to go out on the trapeze. In fact, this is not the case. Using this system means that the crew always has the jib sheet to hand instead of having to reach across the boat. This is particularly useful should the jib need adjustment when the spinaker is being flown. B= COMMODORE'S REPORT 1983 This report for the 1983 season is my first as Commodore and I start by thanking my Committee for the support given to me during the year. Our Sailing Secretary, Malcolm Stuart, will report on the year's sailing activities; however, I must make some comment about our Regatta and Open Meetings. Although we will remember 1983 for the glorious summer, you may need reminding that the weather prior to the Regatta was generally wet and cold. This resulted in a lower than average turnout of boats and an even lower than average turnout of camperse Income was down and this was particularly noticeable in the Regatta bar. In an effort to overcome the problems caused by bad behaviour, it was decided to cancel the disco and in addition arrange for the Police to be on site for the Saturday evening. Unfortunately, plans for an alternative entertainment fell through, with the result that we still had a minority causing problems. However, we believe that we must find a way to combat these problems, because there is no doubt that the majority attending events like our Regatta are well behaved and we cannot allow a minority to spoil this great event. We also had a behaviour problem at the Disco evening held during our September Open Meeting, but, again, it is our intention to continue with these events. For our Barbeque we also provided additional security cover following a threat of trouble, but, in the event, there were no problems and I hope everyone enjoyed the evening. My own sailing activities were over very quickly this year. Having made a late start, within a few weeks I managed to trap a nerve in my neck, which put paid to my activity. Qur colleagues from Rochester visited us as usual this year and two of them returned with their families to camp with us later in the season. For once we planned a return visit. 1 went along as one of Dennis Byatt's crew, enjoying my first cruise out of the Blackwater. Later you will be asked to vote on a proposal to increase subscriptions. ‘The aim of the suggested subscription increase is to increase our income by approximately 10% in order to keep our income end expenditure account in the black and increase our reserve to cover future replacement of capital equipment, (radio, tractor, rescue boat, etc.) as well as provide the large sum that is needed every few years to cover road maintenance. The proposed increase has been added in such a way that members making the most use of the Club, i.e. the sailors, will bear the major share of the increase. Your Committee feel that this is not only fair but necessary in order to encourage new non=-sailing members. I do hope you will support this Committee proposal. We started the season with no one nominated to organise the Galley. My thanks go to those involved in keeping it going during the early part of the season and, of course, to Maureen Ball for later accepting the post of Galley Organiser. I am glad to see that most of the team have accepted nomination for the coming year, and at the same time I thank the retiring members: Vic Crisp, our Treasurer, Mike Cerey and Tony Cockrell, for their past effort. Two junior Officers retire this year: Phil Gray, our Cadet Captain, who has done a magnificent job motivating our youngsters, and Mary Greygoose, who ends her second term as Editor of Navigans. Sue Gray (Phil's wife) has offered to take on this job and I wish her every success. Finally, may I say to all who have in some way helped the Club run smoothly during this year, thank you. Frank Savill Commodore

- 10 - SAILING SECRETARY's REPORT 1983 INTRODUCTION I will outline this years sailing activity drawing special attention to a significant reduction in the numbers of boats sailing. But first I will take you back to this time last year when we started to put together the 1983 sailing programme. SAILING PROGRAMME The sailing year starts with the appointment of officers at the AGM. By that time details will have been collected on tide times and dates agreed through the BJRC on the major sailing events for the following year. The December Committee meetings then put together the basic sailing programme, allocating duties and trying to avoid conflicts with other sailing events and social activities. Inevitably it proves impossible to avoid all conflicts but the aim is to produce a balanced programme from the beginning of April to the end of October. The 1982 season had seen the successful introduction of an Autumn Points series for dinghy racing but a lack of support for the Ladies and Cadets series of six races spread throughout the year. It was decided therefore to perpetuate the Autumn Points series and replace the Cadet races by a series to be run during Cadet Week. The Ladies series reverted to the original formula of a single race and it was planned to extract results from a new Figure of Eight race to be sailed round Osea and Northey. The basic sailing programme for 1983 was therefore constructed round the three points series taking notice of suggestions made in previous years that racing should continue through the summer since not everybody took their holiday during August. Also all points races were programmed as morning and afternoon pairs since complaints had been received when only one points race was scheduled. Although a Spring Points series was introduced as far back as 1969 it was not until this year that the change from one premier series was fully recognised in the Year Book. It was anticipated that the new format for displaying the Clubs awards would encourage fleets to present new trophies to fill the now obvious gaps on page 2 of the Year Book. Did you all notice that this year saw the last postage of male chauvenism removed from the Year Book. Now we are all Helms together in eager anticipation of one of our ladies carrying off the Costain Cup. DINGHY POINTS SERIES The season has been an unmitigated disaster for the three dinghy points series. An overall reduction in points racing of 36% compared with 1982 affected all fleets as the statistics show:- FLEET - TOTAL ENTRIES – - 1982 - 1983 - Change Mirror - 89 - 71 - - 20% Hornet - 149 - 72 - - 51% Solo - 194 - 140 - - 28% '420' - 122 - 50 - - 59% Handicap - 125 - 85 - - 32% Enterprise - 79 - 48 - - 35% Dart - – - 22 - – Totals - 758 - 488 - - 36% Notes 1. Handicap excludes Enterprises and Darts (1983 only) 2. 34 races scheduled both years but one Abandoned in 1983

- 11 - Activity seems to have fallen off after the Regatta:- POINTS SERIES - Average Number Boats/Race – - 1982 - 1983 - Change Spring - 18 - 13 - - 26% Summer - 26 - 17 - - 34% Autumn - 23 - 13 - - 45% Overall Averages - 23 - 15 - - 34% Having presented the bald and unpromising statistics the next step is to seek some convincing explanation. Club membership fell this year and was reflected in a 20% reduction in boats entering any race in the points series:- FLEET - Boats Entering Any Race – - 1982 - 1983 - Change Mirror - 11 - 7 - - 36% Hornet - 12 - 9 - - 25% '420' - 16 - 11 - - 32% Solo - 18 - 13 - - 28% Handicap - 10 - 6 - - 40% Enterprise - 7 - 6 - - 14% Dart - (1) - 8 - N.A. Total - 75 - 60 - - 20% The basic sailing programme changed very little and in both 1982 and 1983 there were 34 points races scheduled. A superficial examination of the number of races sailed in each month appears to show a difference in the distribution of races in the Summer months until one remembers that a month can have either 4 or 5 weekends. At this point the exercise becomes too difficult and one is tempted to say that comparison of statistics from only two consecutive years is a mathamatical nonsense. Afterall we know what a difference weather conditions can make to our sailing. 1983 one argues was a classic balmy English summer and we all opted for a lazy year. Whether or not this is true, and who is hoping for bad weather next year to prove it, the fact remains that the average entry for a points race was only 15 dinghies. (By conincidence entries for Wednesday evening races also averaged 15) Fleet as opposed to handicap racing remains remarkably popular at our club and runs against the trend at other local clubs. However when you consider that we currently try to support 7 fleets each needing at least 3 boats on the water to make a race, then our average entry of 15 dinghies doesn't indicate a healthy state of affairs. To support this mini-armada of 15 dinghies on race days we have to organise about a dozen volunteers acting as duty officers looking after the clubhouse, the race box and the rescue launch as well as assisting with the Galley and Bar and totting up the results. Then there is Claude Emerson who clears up behind us. We have often debated the organisation required to run our Regatta, but this, for some 200 dinghies, seems well worthwhile compared with the effort we put in each weekend for a meagre 15 boats. One aspect not considered above is the National trend in dinghy racing. It is claimed that the advent of Sailboards has reduced the number of dinghy sailors and there is some evidence from attendances at National events that this is true. More optimistic forcasters reckon that the total sailing activity will increase with Sailboarders turning to dinghies as they get older or wiser. There are few sailboards registered at our Club and there has been no demand for organised racing, but we may have an artificial barrier to sailboard membership in the way in which we make up our fees when one considers the minimum facilities required to launch a sailboard.

a 32 ws So long as sufficient people come forward each year to pay their membership fees the Club will remain financially viable, but can we continue to gain respect as a sailing club with so few sails on the water. REGATTA Although the total entry was 30% down this year, this was largely due to the atrocious weather preceeding the weekend, which discouraged camping. Marconi entries remained steady at 24 dinghies but we didn't get any nearer to the prizes. The event remains remarkably popular with our visitors who this year had to put up with light and variable winds which played havoc with our starting and finishing procedures. As a result the Regatta Sailing instructions were altered after the second race to allow for a committee boat finish, and this facility was used in the final race to stop the Mirrors and Toppers at Breezy. The detailed procedure will have to be refined somewhat for 1984 because the assistant race officer who was hastily conveyed to Breezy got her wellies full of water. OPEN MEETINGS The three Autumn open meetings were well supported and actually showed a small overall increase on last year. Entries FLEET 1982 1983 ‘420! 20 18 Hornet 26 29 Solo dé 13 Totals 58 60 The Hornet open meeting was particularly successful being the best attended of the meetings in their 1983 Calendar. SAILING MATCHES The only successful match of the year was the Rochester visit when the BP/MAV contingent brought six dinghies and took away both the individual Colwyn Stone Trophy and the team win, albeit by a small margin of 872 to our 882 points. Perhaps the most remarkable feat was that despite light winds and flaming June weather a Sheerwater Catermaran made the sea passage from the Medway without the assistance of the infernal combustion engine so beloved of the 43 knots or bust approach. The other sailing matches planned this year failed to materialise. No Boothby Cup since neither Osea or ourselves could raise a '420' team. No Solo team matches with Fishers Green, although we did support each others Open meetings. Finally plans to sail joint fleets of Hornets with Stone SC got no support. CLOSED RACES Overall statistics show support for the closed races was poor but despite the failure to sail for the Pilot Cup or Ladies Cup some encouragement can be gained from the continued success, despite reduced numbers of Hornet Buoy and Jackpot, and the undoubted success of the Cadet Week series.
