CLOSED RACES Contd Jackpot was as enjoyable as ever this year. The racing up to the Jolly Sailor at Heybridge and back with the tide is always interesting, but the added spice comes at lunchtime. It is invariably sunny and one sits on the sea wall quaffing ale, trying to give the leader of the morning race a special handicap for the return leg, but basically just sitting around and waiting for someone to provide the entertainment. This year the prize went to a lady who appeared out of nowhere to create havoc in our moorings. The poor innocent lady, who owned the large wreck that our geriatrics had tied their dinghies to, was overwhelmed with male helpers, one of whom managed to capsize his Solo in his eagerness to display his gallantry. In the best Jackpot traditions said gallant helm was awarded the trophy, despite the fact that he won. This years Hornet Buoy was sailed in very strong winds and despite many spectacular capsizes there was no expensive damage. This event consistently generates some of the best Hornet sailing of the season. The organisation of a 4-Race series for the Payne Cup sailed during Cadet Week attracted 10 dinghies and showed itself to be a great improvement on the previous formula of a six race series spread throughout the season. It was impossible this year to organise sufficient Mirror's for all helms and with a very young batch of helms on our hands at the moment some were still handicaping themselves with geriatric crews. With this years winner being only 10 years old, I think we can look forward to a Cadet fleet growing in Significance for the rest of this decade at least. TRAINING I have mentioned the promise that our Cadet fleet shows for the future and much credit must go to Colin Leveridge who again took on the Winter instruction sessions which attracted 20 cadets. Phil Gray put a tremendous effort into organising the Cadets this year particularly during camping week. Having seen his sailing performance deteriorate after Cadet week, I propose that all future Cadet Captains should be able to claim average points for the rest of the season. The use of video equipment to help training on starting technique was so successful that we wondered at the time how long it would be before all our starts came under the close scrutiny of a camera. In order to keep ahead of these fledglings some of the older members also had training sessions. The '420' fleet had a very successful day organised by Dave Hall and until the Autumn Open meeting, the whole '420' fleet were convinced they were going faster. Although no formal training took place in the premier fleet the friendly and persistent instruction of Solo tail enders continues relentlessly. POT HUNTING The Hornet, Mirror, Solo and Dart fleets went out into the wider world for a little pot hunting this year. Most successful being Robin Smith (Dart 2606) who brings to the club its first National and European championship since Roger Hance won the Enterprise Nationals in 1973. Neil Salmon crewing for Dave Sherwin of Leigh on Sea SC (Mirror 64203) helped him come 2nd in the National Cahmpionship and then mopped it up by winning the Mirror Worlds. Colin Harper (Hornet 2100) did the round of Hornet Open meetings winning at Weston Sailing Club and coming 4th overall in the Hornet Travellers series whilst Graham Mead (Hornet 2108) came 16th in the Hornet World and National championship.

POT HUNTING Contd Three members of the premier fleet entered the Solo Worlds at Hayling Island but as in previous years their final positions were still into double figures but then standards are so much higher in this fleet. CRUISING Some 80 cruisers are laying up at Stansgate after a year which indicated once again that there is little demand for organised Cruiser racing. The three Barnacle Points races organised for Saturdays were abandoned, no cruisers entered the club all-in races and we had only one entry in our own Marconi Cruiser Cup. Next year it is proposed that we extract results for Barnacle Points from Mona'S Cup, Pilot Cup and the Cruiser Cup. Dinghy sailors may be forgiven for gaining the impression that cruiser activity is limited to scrubbing, painting and launching. To dispel this myth I will chronicle this years epic voyages. John Todds notched up a Marconi first by taking "Chimo" to the Baltic via the Kiel canal. Joan and Dave Thomas did 800 miles on their Channel Islands trip taking in Belgium and Holland en route. As for the rest of the fleet, a company of eight cruisers went up the East Coast as far as Aldebugh during August. Finally we must not forget the two Marconi Cruisers who made it round to the Medway to sample Rochester's muddy reception. CLUB BOATS We now have a total of eight club boats:- Working Boats Pleasure Craft Mariner Rescue Launch Brazil Rowing Tender Idle Vice Fisherman Cadet Work Boat Graduate A mooring raft is to be added to this fleet over the winter to release the Work Boat from handling increasingly heavy mooring gear. The cost of running club boats is high both in financial terms and the effort expended in routine maintenance and emergency repairs. We are indebted to those members who take responsibility for a particular boat since any boat which was merely club property would soon deteriorate. It remains to be seen next year what use will be made of our four pleasure craft particularly by the Cadets. After some major repair work on the Mariner Mitsui outboard this season, the engine should be good for a few more years. However we are aware of the Mariner's limitations as a rescue launch and it is felt that we should start looking round for a more satisfactory replacement. It may prove impossible to combine the function of speed with that of stability in one vessel but the aquisition of a mooring raft will allow us to review the role of all the club working boats. SAFETY AFLOAT An increasing awareness of safety comes to all of us with experience and whilst it must always be the responsibility of individuals to avoid putting themselves into dangerous situations we can as a club do something to minimise the risk. The 1983 Sailing Instructions introduced a new rule encouraging dinghy sailors to wear adequate clothing for the Easter Series.

SAFETY AFLOAT Contd ah Our Cadets are taught safety afloat and have to demonstrate their ability to right a capsized dinghy but we have no formal training for novice adults. A natural tendency for beginners is to come down to Stansgate when it is quiet and make a fool of themselves in private. Whilst this is very understandable it is alas pretty dangerous in a tidal estuary. We should therefore encourage all beginners to contact their fleet captain who will arrange basic training as necessary. One of the easiest and safest ways to begin sailing is to join in at the tail end of a race, and follow the fleet round (some of us go on for years doing just this) Seriously though it does make it easy to decide which way to point the wretched boat and the rescue launch is always on hand if you to for a dip or want a tow back. We have an excellent team of regular rescue launch drivers now who are not complacent about their skills and subject themselves to bouts of further training. For our major events such as the Regatta and the long distance races we are indebted to the support given by the Cruiser Fleet in providing mother ships at the remote ends of the course. The need was brought home to us this year when we had to abandon a Hornet at Bench Head in the Rum, Tub and Bung race which further demonstrated the limitations of our Mariner in rough seas. THE RIVER Subtle changes take place in the Blackwater each year and the first sail of the year becomes a search for the new gravel banks. The more obvious things to avoid whilst sailing are the river marks and this year has seen No 2 (Lawling Creek) edging out into the main channel and sprouting a light. The North Doubles (No 7) also received a light, but our local river mark Goldhanger (No 1) had its light discontinued. Our "F" buoy marking the eastern end of the cruiser moorings is being replaced by a Fisheries Protection buoy which will be lit. The ground tackle from "F" buoy has been recovered and will be used to locate "D" buoy more accurately on the start line for next season. TROPHIES We are indebted to the donors for four new trophies this year. To Norman Kerridge for the "Jack Kerridge Trophy" which is awarded to the winner of our new Figure of Eight race in memory of Jack who loved a ride on the rescue launch, particularly when we went up river. To Ron Greygoose for the "Captain's Trophy" awarded to the winner of Solo Autumn points. The beautifully hand made model solo has a helm bearing a striking resemblence to its maker. To Richard Spillsbury for the "Spring Fever Cup" awarded to the winner of Mirror Spring Points, and finally to Mike Boreham for the "Autumn Reflections Cup" awarded to the winner of the Mirror Autumn Points. An interesting point came out this year as we prepared the trophies for prize giving, when we realised that the Pilot Cup has always been incorrectly referred to as Pilot's Cup and the Mugs Mug was first mispelt in 1968 and has remained so ever since. CONLCUSION The 1983 sailing year was not an unmitigated disaster, our Cadets and the Autumn Open Meetings saved us from that. However, I would ask you to reflect on the general fall off in sailing activity and let me have your considered and constructive views on whether this is a problem to be solved or do we accept it as a fact to be faced. Either way your comments can influence the construction of the 1984 sailing programme. Malcolm Stuart Sailing Secretary

John Salmon Solo Fleet Publicity Director SOLO AND WHAT I FOUND IN IT Not exactly in it you understand; more, the sailing properties thereof. It was ten years in a Mark IX Merlin Rocket and crew problems that led me in search of a single hander. Many a boat did I try, some with trapeze, some with sliding planks, but my attention repeatedly turned to a pretty 12 footer designed by Jack Holt with the idea that lightweights and heavyweights alike could compete on equal terms. The rig was so versatile that I decided to give it a chance, but with reservations that it would hold my interest after such a machine as Merlin Rocket. So, off to purchase an old Solo I'd heard about living in long grass down at Fishers Green which, on trial, proved to be a poor example! So, the building of a new composite Solo was the order of the day, with a view to entering it in the Nationals at Southend. It was finished the evening before the meeting and was launched with due ceremony in fading light off the Harlow jetty, appropriately named 'Shiver'. So there was I, of Merlin Rocket fame, all set to make my debut and maybe my name in this new chosen class. Lesson one: don't sail it like a Merlin Rocket. There was I gamely powering this little fat boat straight through the waves and wondering why I was slower than most. It took me until the end of the week to realise that Solos are to be coaxed, sailed free, kept upright, and not to tack with the tiller extension up your sleeve! Since then, some ten years ago, various Solos and I have had a good relationship, rewarding me when I get it right and reprimanding me when I do not. For this most sophisticated of single handers has so much to offer: the very strong hull and rig that withstands many a capsize; freedom of choice where fittings and layout are concerned; the standard of sailing within the class, but most of all the guys and continued ... John Wade Fleet Captain HORNET FLEET NEWS My New Year message to the Fleet is - let's do it more often in 1984. The crew of "Stimulation" only stopped doing it on the 18th December and intend to start again the very first race of the season, so let's see you other Hornets out there joining us on that day. It is said that Hornet sailors have a propensity to get wet on the inside as well _ as on the outside, and after watching the R.N.L.I. rowing race on 2nd January at Maldon, I can only agree. After the arduous business of rowing the "isherman, the crew (Murray Bates, Peter Clayton, Ian Lindsay and Graham Mead) got on with the demanding task of replacing lost body weight in the bar of the Maldon Little Ship Club! Mind you, they had earned a little relaxation since they had collezted 2350 between them in sponsorship and were rewarded with a bottle of the "water of life". They were ably assisted in this task by a certain Scotsman wishing to test the alcoholic content of this elixir, Well done, chaps - I wonder where the “premier fleet were? I have a feeling (and have had since I was 14) that this year is going to be the year of the Worlds. With a bit of luck and the grace of the Bank Manager, the M.S.C. Hornet Fleet could have 5 or even 6 boats represented at the Worlds in Holland. Here's a few dates for your diary:- 7th May - Fleet Captain's Birthday(27) 9th June - Boothby Cup, Stansgate 16th June - Boothby Cup, Osea S.C. 6/7th October - Dart/420 Open - Fleet Duty. See you at the Hurdlemaker's Arms and the Barn Dance. Love, Phil

A mutually acceptable date is still to be arranged. Useful hints this month is concerned with the crew, or rather the crew-helm roles tionship. I know I have to be very careful here as this is a very touchy subject (no "double entendre" is intended here). Suppose, however, your crew turns to you at a crucial point in the race and says something like, "What on earth are you doing? That boat that's just overtaken us is not only 10 years old, but it's crewed by a 12 year old girl!" Whilst this may well be justified criticism, I would say that this is not the time to come out with it. The atmosphere in the boat will now be strained and the mental attitude of the helmsman at least will not be one that enables him to get the best out of the boat. It would be better for the crew to have kept quiet here, waited until the boat had shot past another on plane and then said something like, "That's great! We're really shifting now. Let's go for it!" _ Not, I hasten to add, that I would actually like any crew of mine to use these exact words. The atmosphere in the boat will now be harmonious and therefore conducive to better performance. This is all pretty obvious, you may think, but it's surprising how many people come almost to blows in the course of a race. The same ideas apply to the helms- man as well. A good helmsman should praise a crew for doing things correctly and only criticise constructively, and preferably after the race. This is obviously a subjective point, as some people may be able to sail fastest when they are shout- ing at each other all the time. Speaking for myself, I like to enjoy the sail as well as the race and rowing (as in having an argument) spoils both for me. Next month I shall list the points, in order of importance, that I think have helped me to sail faster over the past two years. I would point out here that I am not trying to claim that these ideas are my own or that they will work for everyone, but I am convinced that they have helped me. Ron Greygoose Fleet Captain SOLO - A RECENT LOVE AFFAIR It was back at the tail end of 1979 when, having resolved to join M.S.C. because of the enjoyment gained from crewing an Enterprise with Geoff Josey, I looked around for a suitable class of dinghy to buy. I wanted to try my hand at helming a racing dinghy but knew of no-one mad enough to risk sailing with me, so the choice was simple. The only single-handed fleet at the Club was Solo. Picking up a second-hand glass-fibre boat, I suppose I must have made a fairly lucky choice, for it subsequently proved fast and reliable. It seemed appropriate to name it Greenfield for, apart from the obvious connection with its dark green decking, the name also represented the street name in Dearborn, U.S.A. where we had stayed for the previous two years - the trip which provided me with the funds for boat buying, a luxury we certainly could not have afforded previously. Launching then, with my newly-acquired green machine, into the virtual unknown, I started to learn the necessary skills and judgement the hard way, which involved the involuntary gulping of large quantities of Blackwater and frequent tests of the efficiency of my life-jacket. I was not, however, without considerable help and advice from some of the more experienced Solo helms at the Club - notably, John Rutherford and Geoff Josey, to whom I remain indebted. It was only as I slowly and somewhat painfully began to climb the learning curve that an awareness of the virtues and potential of the Class which I had so haphazardly selected gradually developed. Whilst fundamentally a young man's boat, demanding as it does a high level of athleticism, fine balance and physical endurance but offering in return high performance, responsiveness and excitement, it also has the unique quality among single-handers of having a very adaptable rig. This means that with careful choice of rig and sail, and tuning to match, it is possible for people of vastly differing weights, age and technique to be competitive at Club level. This of course is exactly where classes such as Laser and Topper fail to measure up as practical club boats, and it is perhaps appropriate here to acknowledge the great debt which M.S.C. owes to Frank Savill for pioneering this splendid class at the Club. Frank has served the Club very well in many respects, but to my mind none more so than in his excellent choice of single-hander. A well-prepared wooden-decked Solo is a beautiful sight, both ashore and on the water, but for those who prefer the relatively low maintenance demands of glass-fibre boats they have the satisfaction of knowing that both types are very closely matched for performance, and quite competitive boats of either type can be picked up for under £500. Small wonder then that the Solo class has for years been the best supported and most dynamic class at the Club. Anyone fed up with handicap fleet racing or crew problems could really do no better than take up the challenge offered by what must surely be Jack Holt's greatest masterpiece. John Salmon SOLO, THE FLEET WHERE THE CAPTAIN BUYS THE BEER

John Wade Fleet Captain [redacted] ENTERPRISE FLEET NEWS The fleet meeting held in November was attended by representatives from four Enterprises and two welcome guests from the premier fleet, Eleanor Witter and Malcolm (any excuse for a drink) Stuart, our hard-working Sailing Secretary who attended all the other fleet meetings. Lively discussion ensued with items on the agenda from the "Get John Witter A Wetsuit Fund" to "Next Year's Sailing Programme". Malcolm assures me that our recommendations are being implemented into this year's sailing programme, so let's give it our full support this season, particularly as we will have our own start. I forgot to mention in my last missive that I attended a seminar early last year and I am now a qualified Enterprise measurer and can measure boats, sails and do the yearly buoyancy endorsements. I have been competing in the Maylandsea Bay Winter Series with Steve Evans and Nick Pope crewing (my regular crew is letting his lash wounds heal) and we have enjoyed some very competitive sailing in an eight race series, with an average turn-out of six boats. My last memory of the series is planing home in a Force Four with the sun shining warmingly from a bright blue sky - better than many a summer's day! We even managed to scrape into the prizes by finishing third overall just to complete a cracking series at this very friendly club. I recommend that you get your boats ready and yourselves fit for their opening meeting on 28th/29th April, not to mention our own Easter Series. Issue 2 7.1.84. Marconi Sailing Club Code of Practice for Launching and Recovery of Cruisers Large Boats - Boats above 27ft. length will not be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. Tractor - Only to be operated by authorised drivers. Winches - When dinghy events are in progress the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the [redacted]t[redacted]t half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies. The O.O.D. will be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for the information of dinghy sailors At other times the following code should be observed: When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed. Avoid sharp bends in winch cables-shackles must be used for attachment to trolleys. DO NOT shackle winch wire back on itself. It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strong team of helpers. If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the boat owner must provide a rope or cable of suitable strength and sufficient length that the tractor may remain level and always clear of loose shingle. Boat Trolleys - If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to other boats. Authorised tractor drivers and winch supervisors. The following is an extract from a letter received from Maldon District Council: “SAFETY OF NAVIGATION There are many moorings on the river which are inadequately buoyed, and are poten- tial hazards to vessels using the river at night and during the winter. In an continued

2 endeavour to reduce the problem the Council is recommending to all their licensees that they provide a minimum size of mooring buoy, as follows: For moorings which are adjacent to a navigation channel, the buoy should be not less than sixteen inches in diameter; For moorings not adjacent to a navigation channel, the buoy should be not less than ten inches in diameter, Mooring buoys should be of sufficient size and buoyancy to ensure that at least half of the buoy shows above water at high tide. The use of disposable plastic bottles or similar containers is not satisfactory as they puncture easily, become brittle with age and are often not capable of supporting the weight of the mooring chain. In the interests of safety, any mooring that is inadequately buoyed and could be a danger to navigation WILL BE REMOVED." Please note that, as a covenant to our moorings lease, we must be seen to comply with the above recommendations. Phil Gray Fleet Captain (Phone nos. on front page) 420 FLEET NEWS After all that nonsense last month it is perhaps fortunate that this month there is very little Fleet news. The only idea I would like to float is one that came out of the Fleet Meeting. It is this. In order to achieve a larger turn-out for racing, certain Sundays of the year will be designated as "special race days". These will be days when sailors make a special effort to get down to the Club. For example, if we choose, say, the first Sunday of every month as a "special race day", then those people who can't make it every weekend, due to family commitments or whatever, could “book up" to come down to the Club on those days. The first "extra special" Sunday is therefore ist April, which happens to be the first day of sailing this year!!! Book it up. See you then. 420 HELPFUL HINTS This month, in the last of the series, I am going to jot down some of the things that I think have increased my boat speed over the past two seasons. I am sure that not everyone will agree with the ideas expressed here, but I remain convinced that they have helped me! Factor affecting speed Importance rating (out of 10) (1) Wind shifts 10 (2) Keeping boat level 8 (3) Tacking well (roll tacking) 6 (4) Mark rounding 4 (5) Tactics (6) Boat tune 2 (1) Wind shifts - I have given this by far the most importance. It can be shown that when two boats are travelling at 4 knots and are both tacking for the windward mark, the boat that ignores a 5 wind shift will be over 45 feet down wind of the one that tacked on the shift after only one minute. It is therefore possible to lose more ground by ignoring windshifts than by any of the following methods. There are, however, many times, especially in our tidal waters, when it is far more beneficial to tack in order to keep out of the tide. (2) Keeping the boat level - Most people would agree, I think, that the best boat speed can be obtained by doing this. It is particularly important when going to windward, as this is when the full centreboard is needed and any heeling is effectively reducing the depth of the centreboard. It is there- fore surprising how many people allow their boat to sail heeled over at an angle. I think the main reason is that it feels more comfortable, in that the boat is less likely to capsize on top of you. (3) Roll tacking - Especially in light winds roll tacking can gain you a lot. Even if you can't do it very well, it causes the sails to make a lot of noise and can disconcert other competitors who aren't trying it. (4) Mark rounding = Now we are getting to the bottom end of the list. There will probably only be about 10 marks on a given course, so it is only possible to lose a small amount of ground by poor rounding. One thing, however, that has been convincingly demonstrated to me is that you should always try to round a mark on the inside. If someone has an overlap on you and is calling for water, it can be beneficial, though not always possible, to deliberately slow up and round the mark behind him but close to the mark. This is especially true if there is more than one boat inside you. By doing this you will lose a lot less ground than if you allowed yourself to be pushed away from the mark by the other boats. (5) Tactics - Except in team racing, these should normally be restricted to keep- ing clear of the other boats and their dirty winds. Luffing matches only serve to slow down the boats involved. (6) Boat tune — Beyond basic setting up of mast rake, I don't really understand this subject! Pete Chrystie

- 4 - 420 FLEET NEWS Many thanks to Rumpole of the Hornet Fleet for his comments last month on the new 420 trophies. Any doubts he may have unwittingly aroused concerning the seaworthiness of the fleet were dispersed on the occasion of the first organised sailing of the season (April 1st). The sun was shining and the wind was blowing - unfortunately at around Force 6 and the R.O. made a wise decision to cancel the planned racing. It was decided, however, to test out the new procedure of launching and recovering the rescue boat each weekend. As soon as the rescue boat was in the water, a bevy of frustrated Solo sailors generously launched their dinghies in order to give the rescue crew some practice. Two 420s were also launched and gave a convincing demonstration of high speed sailing. Anna and I only lasted about 15 minutes as my head had gone numb (yes - more numb than usual) but the Sayers didn't seem to notice the cold and planed back and forth for about half an hour. Back on shore there was plenty to do, picking up bits of Solos and their bleeding crews (a literal description - nothing personal, Malcolm) and, after some hot soup from the very efficient Galley, there was general agreement - we were all mad. So - the sailing season has started, and with a bang! Six boats were out on that first day - 4 Solos and 2 420s (not enough to race anyway). The less sturdy, more highly tuned fleets will no doubt be out when the weather improves sufficiently but, if you own a 420, why not make use of its excellent high-wind-sailing capabilities and extend your sailing season? See you at the Club. Pete Chrystie Fleet Captain SOLO NEWS Four Solos (well, their mad helms, anyway) were ready for Spring Points 1 and 2 on Sunday, April 1st. Roger, Malcolm, John and Ron (of course) were raring to go. Roger, Malcolm and John had the added incentive of a free drink - Ron didn't need one - incentive, that is! Racing was abandoned, but the 4 Solos and 2 420s joined the super-looking Marconi Rescue Boat on the water and gave the onlookers something to watch. - 5 - MORE SOLO NEWS Latest news from Club and Country about that most elegant and under-rated fleet - the Solo. STOP PRESS - in a recent article in the Solo Class Association National Newsletter, Marconi Solo Public Relations Officer hinted at mammoth transfer fees to boost East Coast Solo competition. When interviewed by your Navigans reporter, J.S. stated that he wanted to improve local competition by concentrating active Solo sailors and reviving the Eastern Area Championship. Who knows? Dabchicks might emulate Ipswich Town and import a brace or two of Dutchmen for their Open Meetings (who needs more competition?) NATIONAL NEWS - from the Solo Class Association, a controversial motion to introduce a more bendy mast reputed to help lightweight sailors in heavy weather was rejected, by those who remained awake, as being against the principle of a one design boat. (Quite right, too - at Marconi and Fishers Green the lightweights need no extra help!) On next year's agenda - helium-filled lifejackets to allow helmsmen with fuller figures to compete in light winds. The meeting did accept a motion to enlarge the size of the hole in the transom. Rumours that this was originated by MSC to assist in more vigorous rudder-waggling action have been denied by the Hon. Sailing Secretary. J.R. - no, not the one with the big hat - says larger holes are available from Yacht Equipment, Danbury, at 45p per square inch (ADVERTISEMENT). FROM OUR GOSSIP COLUMN - despite the fact that it did not cost him a bomb last year, there has been no repeat of Hon. Fleet Captain's offer to buy all Soloists a pint if they turn up for the first day of the season. According to J.S. this is because he expects such a large turnout resulting from the recent publicity that he would have to take out a second mortgage to pay, even at post-budget interest rates. Finally, to reduce the standard of this magazine to appeal to the masses of frustrated Solo sailors, a new competition is introduced. No, not spot the ball, not even spot the Solo, but invent a caption for this picture. If more witty, topical and succinct than the others, your entry will win a drink at the Club bar. - 6 - LOCAL KNOWLEDGE When we sail to other waters we read the pilots and charts for the area concerned and very frequently see a recommendation along the lines "local knowledge should be sought before attempting to cross the bar" et cetera. Sometimes the need for local knowledge arises even closer to home. Unfortunately, we have experienced the damage of two Club boats during the March winds. The owners were unlucky - or were they? We recognise that our waters can be rough at any time of the year, and especially so in Winter. The alternative to taking the boat out is to move it to a sheltered location - Heybridge Basin, Maldon, Lawling Creek or one of the marinas; they are all used by members as an alternative to laying-up at Stansgate. On occasions, owners have been unable to deal with a boat themselves, so friends have helped in some way. No-one likes to see vessels coming to harm, but equally if Stansgate becomes known to Insurers as a bad risk, we shall all suffer increased premiums. While we sympathise with the present unfortunate owners, let us all be reminded that local knowledge says "don't leave your boat afloat at Stansgate for the Winter". Russ Fuller

Clarke Solo - 2nd - R. Greygoose 3rd - J. Salmon 4th - R. Smith 5th - D. Dear Despite the weather, race management this year went smoothly. The family Simms ran the racebox like clockwork, promoting their youngest daughter to 2nd assistant translator this year. A new problem in heavy rain with a Northerly wind appeared in the form of a racebox window completely obscured by thick waves of water so, in between hoisting flags, Alistair Simms had to clear the window with a squeegee. Pat Harper, Pat Stuart and Ann Bates were locked in the Reception garage again for the Regatta with a new recruit this year - Mary Greygoose, promoted from Galley Slave. The only problem here, apart from the usual batch of eccentric parents of competitors, was the weather which threatened at times to reach the back of the garage. - 4 - 420 FLEET NEWS I expect you all noticed a gaping hole in Navigans last month - yes, the 420 Fleet News was missing. Many apologies to those of you who searched the hallowed pages in vain. No such luck this month, however, because now there is some news. First, and most important, is that Dave Hall has again agreed to come and give us another race training session. Dave is one of the top 420 sailors in the country and consistently qualifies for the Worlds (as he has this year). He is a very busy chap, as his job at A.D.G. Water Sports occupies 6 days a week and sailing his 420 takes up most of his free Sundays, so it is very good of him to give up his time for us. The important date to remember for the session is Sunday 29th July, start at 9.30 a.m. We will begin by rigging the boats on shore and Dave will make appropriate comments on what is right and/or wrong. We will then practise a method for gybing - on land - and then get on to the water to put theory into practice. Last year this was a very useful and stimulating session, so please do try and come along to support it. The Summer Points Series has not got off to a good start. The first three races were not sailed but then - in the fourth - we has an entry of six boats. This may well be a record for any Fleet this year, if you discount those funny little snub-nosed single-handers - well done, Fleet! Unfortunately, this race was later abandoned due to lack of wind. The Wednesday evening series has seen a very good turn-out - a minimum of four 420s in every race so far. From my soundings the pursuit race format is very popular, as you know you have to be in the lead at 2013 hrs. if you are going to win; or, if anyone at all overtakes you, you haven't won. Returning to the race training session on 29th July, you may be thinking that 9.30 a.m. is a bit early; this is the time requested by Dave to make the best use of the day. However, you may not have realised that this is the last weekend of Camping Week and the Club Barbecue is on the previous evening. An easy way of having a good time on Saturday night without having to worry about driving, and being ready at such an early hour on Sunday, would be to bring a tent or caravan and camp on Saturday night. - 6 - SOLO NATIONALS: 29 JULY - 3 AUGUST 1984 This year the Solo Nationals were held at Brixham, South Devon, in a joint Championship with the Seafly class. A disappointing entry of 36 Solos was explained by the fact that a large UK contingent had travelled to the Netherlands two weeks earlier for the Worlds, and that Brixham was a long way from the Solo centres in London and the Midlands, especially in the peak of the holiday season. John Salmon and Roger Smith were the Marconi representatives. The practice race and the first two points races were held in light, changeable winds with the water in Torbay fairly choppy. The Wednesday saw a two hour delay before the start, which with the race and the journey out and back meant seven hours on the water. The race finished in a force 4 which made racing a little more exciting. Strangely, on Wednesday and Thursday the two Marconi boats finished within a boat's length of each other, which seemed to make the journey to Brixham rather unnecessary. Friday's last race was much more exciting with a force 5 - 6 and some bigger waves. Overall, however, the two Marconi boats were not in good finishing positions with John Salmon 21st overall and Roger Smith 24th. The overall winner was S. Cray (3406) from Hollowell SC with Craig Moffet second. Geoff Carveth, who had retained the World Championship in Holland, did not compete. The Solo A.G.M. was held at Brixham on 2nd August 1984 and this year there were no long arguments about masts, rudders, etc. The most eventful subject was a vote on the election of president, with the incumbent Gordon Walls being challenged by Craig Moffet who won the vote. The next most eventful subject, which for some reason caused much hilarity, was a proposal that where the Nationals are held amid interesting scenery the programme should include a "lay day". The gentleman's lady friend endorsed this proposal. I was pleased to see that there were quite a few young helms at the Nationals as well as the old faces, which is a good sign that the Solo is attracting young helmsmen who find it an easier boat to handle competitively in heavy weather compared to the Laser. Roger Smith CRUISER FLEET NEWS The voyages of our boats have been far-reaching this year. Chimo had an extensive cruise to Denmark and Heligoland. John Wade Fleet Captain Maldon [redacted] HORNET WORLDS 1984 Four Marconi Hornets set "sail" for foreign parts on 3rd August. The "sailing" was done in a Townsend Thoresen ferry bound from Felixstowe to Zeebrugge, and thence to Hoorn, Holland, where we would be joined by the fifth Marconi boat with Colin Harper. The Fleet were soon found esconced in the "Viking" bar and savouring their last taste of English beer. The sailors comprised Grahame Mead/Mike Turner, Pat Black/Tony Cockerell, Murray Todd/Keith Boyles and Phil Gray/Kate Nicholson. The supporters consisted of Sue Gray, Barbara Mead (her first mention in Navigans), Laura, Becky and Geoff. After landing at Zeebrugge, we flashed our newly acquired (and expensive) Small Ships Registers at unsuspecting and slightly confused Customs Officials and then drove the 200 miles to Hoorn. The majority of the Fleet looked and felt the worse for wear after this first exhausting day and when, in the failing light, we finally found our hotel we just collapsed into the nearest chair with a beer. The Fleet (minus Colin Harper) had taken over all but one room in a small hotel only ten minutes' walk from the boat park. The proprietor, who spoke better English than Murray, was called Basil by his friends after his uncanny resemblance to a certain T.V. character. We were able throughout the week to change in the hotel and he didn't mind us walking in and out in wetsuits. This proved a boon, as the Hoorn Sailing Club facilities were a little stretched. continued ...

«f= The first day was taken up with boat measurements, sight-seeing and a welcome by the Mayor in a local church where free wine and beer was served! Sail meas—- urement gave several crews near heart attacks when two sets of brand new Hood's sails failed and two new Hyde genoas failed to satisfy the Dutch measurer. The Hyde genoas were quickly passed when it was established that the English rules were applied at World Championships in cases of measurement discrepancies and since the Hyde sails conformed with English rules, they were 0.K. after all. The Hood sails, however, were too large whichever rules one applied and a fair amount of on-the-spot surgery was carried out before they were passed. The sailing was held over a triangular course some 2 = 3 miles offshore and the race instructions said we would race over 10 nautical miles. In fact, I can advise my readers that a Dutch nautical mile is probably twice the inter- nationally accepted distance. Generally, as one sailed up and down the start line to determine if there was any bias, one could not see the windward mark. The Race Officer did a fine job of setting an accurate start line for all six races and there was only one postponement for a course change and only two General Recalls all week. The longest time spent on the water was approximately five hours one day, with the shortest race (race 6) being about 14 hours when the course was shortened (probably due to worsening conditions, but possibly because the Smithers brothers were winning their first race!) The number of boats competing was 45, of which 22 were British, the remainder being Dutch. Our Dutch hosts were very pleased that so many of us had made the journey and spent the whole week enquiring as to our well-being, etc. I was surprised as to the gentlemanly way the boats raced, especially at the start line where it was always possible to find a spot with a hole to leeward. The racing conditions were superb right through the week, with wind strengths generally between force 3 and 5. The average water depth is only about 10 ft in.the area, so these winds produced a heavy chop which made beating difficult for the inexperienced crews. Racing through the chop with spinnaker up on a reaching leg proved to be the most exciting point with many spectacular cap- sizes to be had. With the exception of Grahame and Mike, all the Marconi boats capsized at various times during the week, but none so unluckily as Colin Harper, who capsized just before the finish line in one race when he was lying in fourth position. As the week advanced it became a test of endurance (both on end off the water), a test of the boat and its fittings (Colin's mast fell down during one race!) and a test for the support teams who were fed up with all the sailing, the children (bless their little cotton socks) and supplying food and drink after the sailing. I'm sorry to say that Sue did not get her promised trip to Amst- erdam, which is a good excuse for us to go back to Holland one day. However, it was a lovely sight to see Sue and Barbara (second mention in Wavigens) wait- ing patiently for their loved ones (Ed's. note: And Phil and Grahame) as the exhausted sailors came in from the troubled waters, The new World Champion is Peter Bennett from Shoreham SC and since the Chanp= ionships he has subsequertly won the Nationals, The Marconi boat positions were as follows: 12th "Ultimatum" Grahame Mead & Mike Turmer 15th "Renaissance" Colin Harper & crew 28th "Kyle" Murray Todd & Keith Boyles 32nd "Stimulation" Phil Gray & Kate Nicholson 38th "Ultimate" Pat Black & Tony Cockerell Phil Gray Fleet Captain

— : MARCONI SAILING CLUB SAILING SECRETARIES REPORT = 1984 I have set out this year's report chronologically picking up the successes, disasters and light relief as we progressed through 1984, JANUARY: The year started with a huge success for Marconi. We raised a total of £500 in sponsorship for the RNLI rowing race, the £350 raised by our official entry was the highest for any one boat, although it was left to our unofficial entry rowed by two St. Trinians old girls to win the race. The first of six Cadet Winter Meetings run by Derek Hall started in January. The meetings held at M.A.S.C. between 6.00 and 7.00 pm on Saturday evenings were well attended and the benefit to our Cadet Fleet became obvious as the season progressed. FEBRUARY The 1984 Year Book came out with the promise of lots of new trophies:— ww Points Series Trophy Donated By 420 Spring Jumbly Trophy Pete Chrystie Mirror Spring Spring Fever Cup Richard Spillsbury Hornet Autumn Leaf Trophy Mike Turner Enterprise Autumn Autumn Blues Trophy Steve Evans Mirror Autumn Reflections Cup Mike Boreham 420 Autumn Seaweed Trophy John Weedon Only one failed to meet the Laying—Up Supper deadline but Mike Turner gave himself another year by winning Autumn Points and promised to turn over a new leaf next year. Steve Evans was seen to be handling the Autumn Blues Trophy with some trepidation. His wife revealed later that the glue was still wet. MARCH The main working party attempted to get Stansgate ready for another season in heavy rain. Aside from the early burly of the routine fun jobs Pete Chrystie aw and a small slave gang erected a totem pole to protect sailboards. The Sailing Sub-Committee came up with an excellent idea to offer the use of our gravel covered hard to Tillingham Fire Brigade for routine pump tests. The request got to them a little late for this year but the idea is worth a repeat. APRIL The first dinghy race of the season was scheduled for All Fools Day = 6 turned up. The wind matched this effort by blowing Force 6 with occasional sleet. Commonsense prevailed and racing was cancelled for the day so that we could concentrate our resources on a first trial of the Mariner launching and recovery procedure. The launch procedure worked perfectly in the adverse weather conditions and the 4 solos and 2 "420's" joined the Mariner in its new high visibility livery for a short thrash. MAY Spring Bank Holiday Monday was devoted to the somewhat novel pursuit of safety traininge Leaving the drowning activity till later in the season, when hopefully the river would have warmed up, we concentrated on perfecting the recovery of capsized dinghies and sailboards using the Mariner. After trying out everyone's fanntiniiod

as Se theories we concluded by making the following recommendations Capsized dinghies lying with sails on the water are most effectively righted by the rescue launch working towards the dinghy from the top of its mast. This was shown to allow better control and to minimise the risk of damage. - Practice towing showed that dinghies towed most successfully from a stern line, although care had to be taken not to put any snatch load on forestay fittings which are designed for mainly vertical loads. The tow line should be clipped or looped either side of the forestay to damp down yawing whilst any snatch loads are taken back to the mast or a thwart. - Sailboards should be de=rigged in the water-first bring the board over the side of the Mariner followed by the rigging after releasing the clew outhaul and collapsing the boom against the mast. - The safest method of beaching the Mariner was demonstrated using a buoy close inshore from which the Mariner was pulled or quanted ashore after raising the outboard. On the Regatta I must first remind you that it was the coldest and wettest Whitsun Bank Holiday on record. Not surprising therefore to find total entries down to 110 compared with 158 last year and 223 in 1982. We can draw some consolation from the atrocious weather, it gave excellent sailing conditions and, judging from comments made by competitors, must have been one of our most successful Regatta sailing programmes. I feel this has given us a healthy base on which to build a really good 1985 Regatta and a little publicity to those friends we have made at past Regatta’s will prove well worthwhile. It was appropriate that the first Wednesday evening race this year was sailed in Regatta week for the Mud Trophy. JUNE The end of Regatta camping week brought the Rochester visit and some decent sunny weather. Rochester took the team prize by a convincing 182 to 35 points margin whilst Peter Belcher from Rochester won the individual Colwyn Stone Trophy with two firsts in his Laser. The visitors concluded that an unusual(sic) wind direction had puzzled the home team more than: the visitors and that we had missed crucial wind shifts. The following day we entered four teams in the Maylandsea Bay Challenge Cup extracting our results for the Jack Kerridge Trophy. An excellent race this, round Osea and Northey Islands with a multitude of individual and team prizes at stake. We failed to reecapture the Boothby Cup this year. After a closely fought first leg at Stansgate we failed to get a team together to contest the second leg at Osea. A big disappointment in recent years has been the relunctance of some of our better helms to compete for the Club. We have the talent and ability to win many of these events but so often fail to rise to the challenge. Summer Points 4 gave rise to an interesting debate on race abandonment procedure and it demonstrated that the Race Officer must exercise some care when seeking to abandon a race under Rule 5.1. Certainly where the situation arises because of insufficient wind it is very difficult to abandon a race where a competitor demonstrates his ability to complete within the timescale. The safest course for Race Officers is to keep an eye on the weather conditions and if necessary shorten the course either at the race box line or from a committee boat at any rounding marke The Rum Tub and Bung went off without a hitch this year attracting 38 cruisers and /continued.

- 6 - 28 dinghies. Summer Points 5 scheduled for the afternoon was cancelled because of the late finish of R.T. & B. The trial inclusion this year of points racing on days allocated to traditional races failed on this and other occasions to attract more entries to the traditional races. JULY This month brought problems with the Marine Band radio at both the clubhouse end and on the Mariners "Seavoice". A starting problem was identified on the Mariner engine but the true cause was not found until the engine was stripped down for its winter service at the end of the season. I am pleased to report that despite the extensive electrolytic corrosion the bill for winter service will be little different to last years. The best trained fleet in the club again persuaded Dave Hall to come along for a one day session. This year he concentrated on spinnaker gyberipokery. The "420" and Enterprise fleets in a somewhat desperate attempt to maintain fleet racing nominated certain Sundays when they would make a special effort to ensure at least three boats made it to the start line. Unfortunately this had little effect on numbers but nevertheless seems to be a good commonsense idea. AUGUST This year's Jackpot was as enjoyable as ever and unmarred by past excesses. Nobody had to be poured back into their boat after lunch, none of the geriatrics lost their teeth and the ladies of Heybridge escaped any overwhelming displays of gallentry. The Pilot Cup was somewhat unusual with a Cruiser only entry. We had two Barnacle Points races this year and we seem to have arrived at the right formula of four races with results extracted from Mona's Cup, Rum Tub and Bung, Pilot Club and Marconi Cruiser Cup. On Pilot Cup day the dinghy fleet chose to wait for Summer Points 16 despite weather conditions which would have favoured most dinghies. I have been surprised how reluctant some of our better dinghy helms are to enter one-off races. Perhaps we could encourage more entries by simply pointing out how much easier it is to win a trophy for a traditional one-off race than the long haul involved in the Points Series. Robin Smith managed to gain some good publicity for the club by winning the Dart Nationals at Worthing. The Hornet Fleet avoided any adverse publicity over in Holland and with five boats they formed the second largest contingent after Brightlingsea S.C. at the World Championships. The premier fleet had two representatives at the Solo National Championship. Their finishing positions were explained by the fact that the Solo is now attracting young helms who find it an easy boat to handle competitively in heavy weather. The August Bank Holiday Series saw the resurgence of a real Cadet presence at Marconi. For many years we have nurtured Cadet helms with adult crews but at long last the chickens are leaving the nest. Neil Salmon and Clair Savill won the series and another cadet pair, Damian and Lucy Boreham came fourth. Hopefully next year we can encourage more pairings and start to do battle with our neighbouring Cadet Fleets particularly Maylandsea Bay and Blackwater who both use Mirrors for Cadet racing. The August Bank Holiday weekend gave us the opportunity to continue the safety training. Two of our more athletic rescue drivers spent an interesting afternoon /continued.

- 7 - fishing a very game Claire Urry out of the water by every conceivable method. Claire's life saving qualifications making her performance very real. For an unconscious casualty the optimum method evolved was to drop off the rescue crew who gave support in the water, cleared the casualties airway and gave the first vital inflations of the lungs. Meanwhile the driver brought the Mariner alongside with the ladder down on the port side, which is clear of the engine controls, then with the engine idling the crew climbs aboard to help the driver bounce the casualty over the side. We may only get an unconscious casualty once in ten years, but when it happens the rescue driver and crew of the day must be prepared to respond efficiently. SEPTEMBER The Marconi Cruiser Cup this year gave us some organisational problems with a 9.a.m. start from Thirslet Spit and a long line finish at Stansgate on what turned out to be a very popular weekend for river traffic. Criticism of our ability to identify finishers reliably led to a B.J.R.C. proposal to start and finish the race at Thirslet Spit. We have countered this by proposing a start at Osea Pier with a short line finish at Stansgate but inside a committee boat rather than 'D' buoy to avoid too much action inside the moorings. A last minute switch of dates by the Hornet Fleet took everybody by surprise but the organising Dart Fleet coped well with what turned out to be the best attended Hornet Open of the year with 29 entries. The Solo Open only attracted three visitors largely due to a conflict of dates which kept the Fishers Green contingent away. However a good turnout of nine Marconi boats and Force 6 winds kept up the interest particularly when beating down Goldhanger Creek at the bottom of an exceptionally low tide. Capsizing in a gale with only an inch of water to lubricate the hull is an experience only bettered by trying to get sailing again. OCTOBER The Dart/"420" Open Meeting was organised by the Hornet Fleet who were grey with fatigue by the end of the weekend. Their task was made more difficult by not having the support of an O.O.D. which led to the first problem with keys, then the committee boat turned out to have no obvious place to hoist flags. The rod that broke the back of these wasp-like insects was the additional burden of organising Autumn Points 9 and 10. Despite the problems the visitors thoroughly enjoyed their racing particularly the Dart Fleets quick flash round Osea and Northey Islands which nearly ruined racing at the up-river clubs as everyone stopped to watch. Entries were 18 Darts (7 Marconi Boats) and 14 "420's" (4 from Marconi). The formula of a long first leg true beat created by a Committee Boat start followed by an interesting chase round the river buoys provides an attractive course for our visitors giving them some relief to the open water Olympic courses. Helm of the Year final was sailed in Lasers of which Pete Moseley had managed to scrape together four club boats including his own. The four races turned out to be an endurance test ending in a sudden death one lap run-off between Ron Greygoose and Pete Moseley who tied for first place. In the end the overall result hung on the crucial decision of when to tack for 'A' Buoy on a fast ebb tide. Putting the club into mothballs at the end of the racing season we reviewed the use made of the club boats and whilst "Idle Vice" had been used extensively and "Brazil" occasionally, no use had been made of the Cadet or the Graduate. It was decided therefore to dispose of these last two and consider acquiring a training sailboard. /continued.

NOVEMBER With dinghy racing at Stansgate over for another year and setting out to give a polished performance at the Laying—Up Supper I noticed that whilst Cruising Prizes are listed in the Year Book none have been awarded since 1975 and few members could recall what they were for. John Witter was able to turn up his note from September, 1965 Navigans which clearly identified them as intended for a members first cruise and not as some had thought a sort of runners-up prize in the Mamgu stakese One obvious contender, which should have been recognized last year, was Ann Bates! log for their first cruise up the East Coast. I was pleased to be able to rectify this omission on Ann's birthday at the Laying—Up Supper. Whilst keeping Ann's prize a surprise I did suggest to our Rear Commodore that since half our members owned cruisers, and the Laying—Up Supper was supported more or less equally by the Dinghy and Cruiser Fleets, we should give more awards for Cruising. Murray Bates was in the middle of finishing off some 65 hand made trophies at the time and I was perhaps lucky not to have ended up in the hot water bath with the screen prints. Nevertheless it is worth thinking about for next years; we may even see the Sea Wife's Prize back again. Despite its title and camnatations of creature comforts I understand it has more to do with climbing ew masts and remaking halliards in the teeth of a North Sea gale. The 6 trophies, 28 prizes and 8 spoons not collected at the Laying—Up Supper will be presented at a date to be arranged, but most likely the New Year Working Party at Stansgate! SAILING FUTURE Looking back over the year reminds us of all the things we intended to do and of lessons learnt. A further 16% reduction took place this year in dinghy points racing on top of last years 36% reduction. Whilst the average entry for Wednesday evening races remains around 15 the Points Series are only attracting an average of 10 boats per race compared with over 14 last year. It is interesting to compare this with attendance at Committee Meetings = the Main Committee meeting alone averages 16 and the Sailing Sub-Committee has on average more people sitting round a table talking about sailing than we see on the water the following weekend. yy Certain changes have already been instituted for next years sailing programme with the main objective of encouraging activity on the water. For 1985 the Summer Points series will be abandoned and Spring Points extended to the end of June. In July and August many Sundays will be occupied by traditional races but where there is a gap a half—handicap pursuit race will be run in the morning, along the lines of the popular Wednesday evening races, and in the afternoon there will be Handicap Races split into one, two or three handicap classes depending on the days weather conditions and numbers of entries. The Summer Points Club Trophies will be re-designated as the Clubs premier trophies for each dinghy class and will be awarded on the total racing programme of Spring Points plus Autumn Points plus any other relevant closed races. REFLECTIONS It was 1981 when Murray Bates took on the Sailing Secretaries job after making me promise to help with some of the donkey work. I have enjoyed our four years together looking after the Clubs sailing activities, but will always remember our half-term doubts when we sat down together and wondered what if anything we were achieving I think the moment of gloom had been brought on by yet another hole in the Regatta marquee. I pulled Murray out of this abyss by pointing to some of the things that seemed /continuede

Yu to be going right. Starting gently on a non-controversial issue he had to agree that we were getting the Year Book to press a little earlier each year and in sight of getting it printed in time for issuing with membership renewals. The Autumn. Points series was introduced successfully in 1982 and Wednesday evening sailors have welcomed the new pursuit race formula. Perhaps the most significant and long lasting improvement in the last few years has come from an increasing reliance on Fleet Captains to find the resources to cover major activities. What we are finding now is that fleets have accepted an on-going commitment to specific activities making the organisation from one year to the next so much easier, However, a group activity such as that provided by the fleets is not always appropriate to a specialist task. The sailing activity is equally dependant on the individuals who turn up quietly at the appropriate time and get on with what they have made their own job. Few of these individuals are on the Committee, or any sub-committee for that matter, so I should like to end by paying tribute to their help and by encouraging all club members to look around for some task, however small, that they can make their own. - 10= 420 FLEET NEWS This will probably be my last piece for Navigans, as Anna end I will soon be moving away from the Essex area. Perhaps this is just as well, as it looks as if the hall- owed pages are to be desecrated - I mean decimated = in order to save a few pounds. In many ways this is a shame because a lot of people get a great deal of pleasure from the present format, although it is also true that a great many people don't even read it! However, I digress (something that won't be allowed in future?) The 420 annual Fleet Meeting took place at my home on 5th December 1984, First item on the agenda was to elect a new Fleet Captain. Unfortunately, the person singled out to be cajoled into the position must have got wind of it and cried off coming to the meeting at the last moment. However, undeterred, we elected him anyway and so the new Fleet Captain is Alan Woods. Alan's main worry about taking on the job was that he will not be around for a few months of 1985 and so it was agreed that Len Graves would join with Alan t© give the Fleet the considerable benefits of Joint Fleet Captaincy. A lively discussion then ensued on how to arrange the duties. It was felt that the best way was to send each fleet member a list of duties required and ask them to take on as many as necessary. This would minimise the amount of swapping required and therefore make the turn-out for duties more reliable. There was majority supp- ort for the new format of the Wednesday evening series. A weekend cruise was svgg= ested and it was agreed that some sort of cruising activity would be arranged for 1985. The possibilities of persuading cruisers to participate as support (e.g. to carry gear and provide a measure of safety) would be investigated. It was felt that a boat tuning/ race training day or days would be of use. The Dave Hall sessions were very successful but it was felt that it would be imposing on Dave's good will to ask him back for a 3rd year. Perhaps something could be org~ anised in conjunction with Maldon S.C. or maybe a "self-help" practice day could be organised. It was agreed to advertise the willingness of fleet members to take out any other Club members, on request, in order to encourage new members and those thinking of changing class to for the 420. This offer to be repeated on a regular basis throughout the sailing season. There was criticism of the new rescue boat procedure. Not so much because it was a nuisance to launch and recover but more because it so often caused delays to the start of racing. Also, it does not seem to have helped the engine. It presumably has solved the problem of the double skin filling with water. The Laying-Up Supper was very poorly attended this year - this presumably means that the present format is unpopular with the majority of Club members. The Fleet thought it woule be a good idea to hold the prize-giving at a more popular event, say the January Barn Dance. Most people would welcome a break of about 30 minutes at half-time and the prize-giving would fit nicely in here. Well, that sums up the 420 4.G.M. It only remains for me to thank the members of the Fleet for their support during my 2 year stint. I would also like to take this opportunity to thank all the Club members who have helped make our time with such fun. Most of all, I would like to thank whoever it was who had the foresisht to persuade M.A.S.C. to buy the Stansgate site. Teo my mind, it is the best site on the River Blackwater.and with the facilities it offers, makes M.S.C. one of the best clubs in the country. Look us up if you are in Devon - our collection of sailing toys will be at your disposal, Pete Chrystie Ed's note: We'll miss you!

- 2 - Since reporting to you in the December issue of Navigans, we have had the Cruiser Christmas Party on Saturday 15th December, held at Stansgate. The area immediately behind the dustbin space on the ground floor under the Galley is being increased in size by removing part of the wall of the Bosun's locker and part of another wall to provide access to the space previously not utilised under the main stairs. The doorway to the Bosun's locker has been bricked up (thanks to Albert Pearce) and an up-and-over garage door will be fitted to the outside wall. I must admit that although I was concerned when this scheme was first suggested, the end result is very pleasing and adds warmth to the previously somewhat drab entrance of the Clubhouse. Dick is also undertaking and/or organising many other minor improvements and repairs. 3. The brambles and rubbish have been cleared from the area around the Race-Box and action is in hand to convert the old "blockhouse" (on which the Race-Box stands) to a secure store for use by the Cruiser Fleet. Even sea-facing windows are being incorporated! Maybe the spotters for the Regatta could use it if the weather is anything like 1984. 4. The provision of five double 13 amp. electric power points, strategically positioned, in the Cruiser Park. A power supply to the Race-Box is also included. This task is being co-ordinated by Malcolm Stuart. 5. Work has started on the clearing of ditches and the sides of the road. We are trying to encourage the surface water away from the road, so as to prolong its life. We intend holding another Working Party on Sunday 3rd February in order to complete the above tasks. John Salmon Acting Scribe ROBIN'S RIPPLES (THE CAT FLEET) Month after month I scour the pages of Navigans looking for the Cat Fleet Section, but to no avail. Could it be that the rest of the Dart Fleet, like me, spends so much time sailing that they too rarely get time to put pen to paper? If the "Premier Fleet" is such a great Fleet to belong to, how come they always meet the press deadlines? There are those, admittedly dinghy sailors, who seem preoccupied with the statistics of falling numbers racing. If they sailed a Dart they would realise that you don't have to race to have fun on a modern Cat. How often do you see the dinghies going out when the conditions are vigorous, when there is no race on, just to thunder up and down the river all day for the hell of it? I would guess that, apart from the Cruiser Fleet, the Cats clocked up more hours on the water last year than any other fleet, and had more excitement into the bargain. When those of us that travel regularly to Open Meetings return to the Club on Sunday mornings to find yet another boring points race scheduled for a start somewhere near mid-day (when the best part of the morning has gone), the call of continued .....

- 7 - the sea is often too much, and we opt to do our own thing, exploring the estuary one way or another. West Mersea, Brightlingsea and Clacton are all within easy sailing distance on a Dart. What better on a glorious summer day that to wave the wife goodbye at Stansgate and then head down to West Mersae beach - "just had to pop ashore, dear, to adjust a couple of battens!" Here is the challenge for 1985. One marvellous Sunday afternoon last July, the Stampede passed Brightlingsea Creekmouth buoy heading West at 1605 hours, two out on the trapeze, and we stepped ashore on Stansgate hard at 1640 hours, during which time we had a minor diversion somewhere off Bradwell while we burned off a Dart! If anyone can beat that under sail in 1985, then the drinks are on me! Back to the December Navigans. If two boats are considered a team, then the second stage of the Boothby Cup at Osea S.C. was most certainly contested. Barry and Linda Palmer sailed their Dart up to Osea, accompanied by Steve Dodgson and myself on the Stampede. We certainly raced and signed off correctly, and I suspect the Stampede easily won on handicap in the conditions. We didn't stop to find out because the Osea dinghies were not even half-way round the course when we finished and we needed to get back to pack the Cat up for a regatta next day. Thanks to Malcolm for the mention of our Nationals victory last season. Two other Marconi Darts also attended, David Broise and Peter Lay, but I do not have the final results to hand. Peter and Liz were appointed Dinghy Park Guards and were allowed to park their caravanette in the boat park at night to safeguard the Darts. Naturally the rest of the Dart Fleet took up the challenge and there were nightly competitions (usually after the bar shut). How many Darts can be equipped with "No Waiting" cones on top of their masts? How many nights in succession can the club Mirror sails be hoisted up "Shooting Star's" mast? And, finally, can a long piece of rope be tied around Peter's van through all the door handles without them noticing? The answer was "yes"! Finally, trumpet-blowing time! The Marconi flag was flown far and wide last season and this is by way of an explanation as to why we don't sail at the Club very often. January 1st. Grafham Grand Prix - Dart - 1st. April 7th/8th. - 8 - July 14th. Totnes to Torquay Long Distance Race - Stampede - 1st Cat. August 4th/5th. Shoreham S.C. Cat. Open - Stampede - retired with broken toes! August 12th/17th. Dart Nationals, Worthing - 1st (both on and off the water)! August 25th to September 1st. Dart Europeans, Toulon - 5th (150 enties). September 8th/9th. Eastney Cat. Open - Stampede - 1st. September 29th/30th. Highcliffe Cat. Open - Stampede - 9th (79 entries, light crew, heavy wind)! October 6th/7th. M.S.C. Dart Meeting - 1st. October 20th/21st. Grafham Water Cat. Meeting - Dart - 1st. December 26th. Leigh Brass Monkey - Stampede - disqualified (either over line at start or cuddling crew after 5 minute gun)! December 30th. Grafham Grand Prix - Dart - 4th (on handicap, 1st Dart). All that petrol! I think I'll do something cheaper this year, like Formula One car racing! Seriously though, already planned for 1985 is a visit to the Dee Sailing Club on the Wirral for our most northerly ever Dart Open. There will also be a return visit to La Rochelle and possibly La Baule in the Stampede. The Dart Nationals are at Paignton in July, while we go back to Lake Garda in Italy for the Europeans in September. At Easter there will be an attempt at Grafham Water to break the 24 hour distance record for sailing craft using three Stampedes. At present the record is held by an Osprey dinghy, which covered 181 miles in New Zealand some years ago. Obviously we are at the mercy of the wind on the date set, but we have high hopes of the Stampede easily breaking the record. I hope to find time to see you on the water at the Club in 1985 and look forward to further growth in the "fun and exhiliration" Fleet. Remember - Dart sailors do it with one in the air! 7a COMMODORE'S NOTES It is with profound regret that I report the sad and sudden loss of our dear friend and colleague, Eric Payne. On Monday 4th February several members, including Eric, had assembled ready for the February Main Committee Meeting; Eric was talking, then peacefully passed away. It was a dreadful shock to us all. The M.S.C. members send sincere condolences to Mrs Payne and her family. The Committee Meeting was postponed to the following Monday (and has not yet been held at the time of writing). Continuing my aim to keep members informed of activities, since my last Jan- uary issue report we have continued to make much progress in readiness for the sailing season:- A.meeting was held at M.A.S.C. on Wednesday 23rd January during which Mr G, Wignall, M.A.S.C. Club Manager, and I discussed:- 1. The problem with the water supply at Stansgate —- M.A.S.C. have agreed to replace the old pipework and aim to complete the task before Easter; 2. Our advertising campaign — to increase the size of membership, parti- cularly dinghy sailing members; 3. The annual contribution paid by M.S.C. to M.A.S.C. Following the above, an Executive Meeting was convened on 29th January during which a letter was drafted to once again highlight our objections, et cetera, to the excessive levy. In parallel with all the above, we have been in contact with the Crown Estates Commission to seek approval to extend our Cruiser mooring towards Stone. Another successful and well attended Working Party was held on Sunday 3rd February = this has been a great encouragement to all the Executive Committee members. Progress was made on the Cruiser Park “Electrification Scheme"; the hedging and ditching party have broken the back of their task. If any member knows of a secondhand metal door, size 7' x 6'6", please inform Murray Bates. DATES FOR YOUR DIARY Friday - 22nd March - Solo Fleet Meeting, Wheelers Restaurant, Maldon. - 8.15 p.m. Sunday - 24th March - WORKING PARTY, Stansgate. - 10.00 a.m. Saturday - 30th March - Fitting-Out Party, Stansgate. - 8.00 p.m. to midnight. At the time of writing, the start of the dinghy sailing season is only four weeks away - Easter Series on Sunday 7th and Monday 8th April. The next Working Party will be held on Sunday 24th March in readiness for the start of the season. We still have many tasks to complete - maybe Bernard Payne and Peter Foreman and their team of "specialists" will further the hedging and ditching project. 3 = GALLEY The Galley will start operating again from Easter Sunday onwards, and I begin the season once again by asking all members to support the work of the Galley by taking a turn behind the counter. Maureen Ball Galley Supervisor C'ford [redacted] * * * all ls mw RACE MANAGEMENT SEMINAR On Saturday 23rd February our Club acted as hosts to the B.J.R.C. one day seminar at M.A.S.C., Beehive Lane. Our able Commodore chaired the occasion with his B.J.R.C. hat on and a surprising attendance of 69 people was achieved. They represented 15 different clubs from the Blackwater area and slightly fur- ther afield. The speakers were Tim Hockin and Nicol Robinson = both members of the R.Y.A. Race Management Committee and it was soon evident from their presentation that both could call upon a vast amount of experience of race organisation at all levels. The material was presented in an informal style and with a dry wit which was certainly well received, the day being rounded off by a lively question and answer session. Altogether the attendees were given a very informative and enjoyable day for a modest fee with coffee and lunch provided, and all those concerned with its organisation deserve congratulations. - 5 - SAILING PROGRAMME 1985 As you will probably have noticed from your Year Book, there is no Summer Points Series arranged for this season. Over the past few years the entry for this series has been low in comparison with those held in the Spring and Autumn, so a new format is being tried this year. The Spring Series has been extended into June and the Autumn Series into September. The Summer Points trophies are to be awarded on the basis of points extracted from the handicap races held on Sundays during the Summer months and those closed Club races which all helms are eligible to enter. For the purposes of points extraction only, there is no minimum limit on the number of boats competing from any one Fleet, e.g. if only one Mirror enters and finishes a race in accordance with the sailing instructions, first place points will be awarded in the Fleet Series. Retirement and disqualification points are derived from the whole series, as normal. To qualify as a Fleet Series, a minimum of three different helmsmen must have taken part in any of the valid races. I have to report two amendments to the Year Book. The first is that the Dart Fleet will start at 11.25 a.m. and 13.55 p.m. The second is that the Dart/420 Open is to be held on 12th and 13th October and the Helm of the Year Final is to be held on 5th October, while Autumn Points 9 & 10 are to be sailed on 6th October. Fleet and O.O.D. duites are also swapped accordingly for these events - Cruiser Fleet, please note. I apologise for any inconvenience this may cause and look forward to seeing you all at the Club and on the water. Steve Evans SAFETY ON THE WATER Just a few notes to remind any who may need it that our sport is not without hazard, particularly at this time of year when even on a warm, sunny day the water remains very cold. I would offer the following points for your consideration: Dinghy sailors at this time ofyear must wear wet suits or equivalent; Check every part of your boat thoroughly before the start of the season and replace any gear which is suspect; - Discipline yourself to re-check your boat with care from stem to stem each time before you use it; - Dinghy owners must pay particular attention to buoyancy, both personal and boat. Check it carefully yourself and get a qualified measurer to certify the boat, even if you do not intend to compete in Open Meetings; - Do not assume rescue facilities will be on hand to help you. They are usually somewhere else, so your salvation must always be in your own hands; - If inexperienced, or unfamiliar with our sailing environment, please ask advice from the 0.0.D., Fleet Captain or other experienced helms; = One of the most sinister aspects of hyperthermia is that rational thought becomes impossible. If you reach that stage, you are really in trouble; so, if you feel cold and tired - get ashore. There's always another day. Take care and have a great 1985 sailing season.
