wo es SAILING — SPRING 1985 (SO FAR) The season started this year with the Easter Series. The weather on the Sunday, rain and a Force 5 Southerly, was braved by 2 Solos and an Enter- prise who were unable to race due to the lack of rescue facilities. Undeterred, the three boats went for a “thrash" anyway, resulting in Roger Smith looking as though he had been five rounds with Frank Bruno! Monday's weather showed little improvement with the wind even fresher than the pre- ceding day. Two Solos, a Hornet (briefly) and a Dart entered the morning race but Ron Greygoose in his Solo proved to be the only survivor. Three Solos entered the afternoon race which was sailed in a wind of increased strength, resulting in a total "wipe-out" with no finishers. Spring Points 1 and 2 were cancelled due to bad weather. Enterprise, Solo and Handicap fleets sailed Spring Points 3 and 4 on a day which started with light airs, gradually increasing to a nice sailing breeze by the end of the day. The Solo "lads" were the only sailors to raise a fleet for races 5 and 6, but were joined by a Laser and a Fireball who went along for the ride. These races were Sailed once again in strong winds and Malcolm Stuart was seen plodding round sporting his specially modified reefing mainsail, which en- abled him to survive where others didn't. Solos were the dominant species sailing races 7 and 8 and were kept company once again by Enterprise and Handicap fleets. The afternoon race called heavily on the Rescue service with capsized boats spread out gybe marks, Steve Evans in particular causing confusion by hiding one of these marks with the upturned hull of his Enterprise. Speaking from personal experience, the water is gradually warming up now and this should encourage more of you to join in the thrills and spills and beauty of sailing at Stansgate. See you there. Derek Webb Sailing Secretary HUNGRY ON WEDNESDAYS? That's caught your attention, hasn't it? The good news for all you hungry Wednesday night sailors (and supporters) is that a Galley service will start on Wednesday 5th June (that's Midweek Race No. 2) for a limited period of 3 weeks to judge demand, run by yours truly. In any event, there will not be a service on 26th June (Race No. 5) as I'm on holiday. This service will offer sandwiches, some cakes, sweets and hot drinks from 6.00 pem. to 7.00 p.m. and again from 8.30 p.m. to 9.30 p.m. I'll be closing while the race is on so that I can watch the fun and put my feet up! Anyone who is accustomed to using the Galley on Wednesdays should please be undeterred by my presence and carry on as usual. See you at the Regatta.

- 6 = SOLO NEWS 1. Off the water, the Solo fleet had a meeting at M.A.S.C. where we dis- cussed the way we get round a course, delving into the Rules as and when necessary. We tried to keep off deep discussions of Rule interpretation, et cetera, but inevitably we had some disagreement over quite basic rules. It proved a popular topic, with 15 people turning up. Overall, the meeting seemed to provide a useful forum and we will try to do it again. Ze On the water, we had our “warm up" sail on 31st March; Ron Greygoose was the only boat to complete any race of the Easter Series, only to lose his mast on the final race. Well, he didn't actually lose it - just reduced its height somewhat. In fact, there was one point on Easter Monday when I wondered if we would have a Solo fleet to start the season proper. Ron was going towards Stone without a mast, Bob Anderson had disappeared into Stan- sgate Bay trying to emulate a submarine and, having tried to swim the course, I retired. There must be a prize for the most number of accidental capsizes in a day} 3. We have had a fleet for each race so far, although of course one week's racing was cancelled and we spent our time picking up boats in the dinghy park. On 28th April, we had 3 boats racing — Malcolm Stuart with his “itsy- bitsy, teeny-weeny" sail. Two Soloists were in Race Box and Rescue Boat and 3 more boats arrived for a "tune up" sail in the afternoon. Come on, you other fleets - if you can't beat us, join us! 4. With all the rough weather lately, we do appreciate the presence of the Rescue Boat which makes our sailing possible. or Final note! Don't forget to tie your boat down securely with stakes either side of the boat, completely flush with the ground to eliminate hazard to boats, lawn mowers, children, et cetera. The boat should be secured to the stake on either side, not just looped over. Make sure the stakes are firm. Remember, it's not just your boat that you may damage! Roger Smith Fleet Captain DART FLEET NEWS Firstly, a thank you to the captain and crew of the cruiser "Suppose" for their valuable assistance with the Rescue Boat when the Dart fleet were on duty. We promise not to use your buoy as the start-—line again. The Easter weekend winds were not ideal to start the season but were useful to Robin Smith and his team sailing a Stampede to create a new World Record for the greatest distance sailed in a 24 hour period. While Robin was breaking the record, some of us were making our own records sailing Darts upside down, so we were very grateful for his timely advice at the Marconi Dart Teach-in. oe Strings". We hope to see everyone at the Regatta weekend, which promises to be a good "Cat" get-together. Anne Duckmanton CRUISER RACING Now that the Cruiser fleet within our Club is so flourishing, I feel sure that there are many members, like myself, who would like to compete in some of the local B.J.R.C. events. Our dinghy fleets have been well respected on the River Blackwater for many years and, with the depth of experience in our Cruiser fleet, now is the time to take some of those Cruiser cups. Over the next few weeks I will be looking for those members willing to race at least some of the B.J.R.C. races and pressing them for the £3.00 registration fee. Mike Turner Cruiser Racing Representative SAILBOARD SAFETY With the advent of more sailboards at the Club and recent problems encount-— ered rescuing people from other clubs, the Main Committee would like to ask all sailboarders to operate their own safety code. The Club does supply rescue facilities in the form of the "Mariner" but this is usually tied up with the dinghy racing programme. Since it is not obvious to the Rescue Boat when a boardsailor might be in trouble and since their priority is to check on capsized dinghies (more conspicuous), it is important that board sailors are aware of their own limitations in the range of tide and wind conditions. So, please, if you are a beginner, stay near the Clubhouse and keep up-tide with respect to the Clubhouse. If you are an expert (or an aspiring one), ask yourself whether you are not too tired to get back unaided.

COMMODORE'S REPORT The Regatta is over and now we wait patiently for some good weather so that we can all enjoy the various Club sailing events. I would like to take this opportunity to sincerely thank all Members who helped us with the pre-planning preparation, the many tasks during the weekend and for the clearing up operation following the event. As those Members who attended the Regatta will know, we were blessed with very variable weather. I think most of the visitors enjoyed themselves (at least some thanked us personally!) but, once again, it was very disappointing to witness a very poor representation by the Club dinghy sailors. During the weekend we had the usual problems to attend to, namely sewage disposal, shortage of spotters and insufficient hot water for the showers. We were also subjected to some aggravation from a few visiting sailors and supporters alike, no doubt caused by excessive intakes of alcohol. As you are all aware, we have been wrestling with the problems associated with the showers and low water pressure for some time and,the week before the Regatta, M.A.S.C. organised a major re-plumbing exercise, which included the installation of a new water heating boiler. I had so many complaints after the first race on THE EDITOR, NAVIGANS. c/o MR.P.J.GRAY, K BLOCK, BADDOW. continued ...

2 = Saturday regarding the temperature of the shower water that we had to involve M.A.S.C. and the heating contractors, who arrived only to establish that the wrong size of boiler had been installed. I am pleased to report that this problem hopefully has now been resolved = no doubt we will find out how off- actively in the immediate future. On the Thursday before the Regatta, we had a Company safety inspection on the Stansgate site. Although we are grateful for such checks, we would have preferred the visit either after or long before the Regatta! However, all tasks highlighted by the Inspector were carried out on the Friday and on Saturday morning. Normally we hold Main Committee meetings on the first Monday of every month, followed by the Sailing Sub-Committee on the Tuesday of the following week. These were held in reverse order this month, so that the Sailing Sub-Committee Regatta debriefing report could be considered by the Main Committee during their meeting on Tuesday 11th June. (Ed. This is why this month's issue is late, as I had to hold the front page!) The consensus of opinion of Executive and Main Committee members assembled at the last meeting is that the future of the Regatta in its present form is questionable. To be quite frank, we do not have sufficient interest from our membership to support and administer the event, and we now question the sense of continuing same. The financial viability of the event, even when very good bar sales are taken into account, is also not very attractive The Executive Committee are obviously extremely concerned about this state of affairs and, immediately following the Regatta, decided that the Sailing Sub-Committee should consider the formation of a separate Regatta Sub-Comm- ittee to organise and administer the event. Unfortunately, at the time of writing, it appears that there is not even sufficient support from the Sailing Sub-Committee for this suggested revised method of operation. At our last meeting your Main Committee therefore decided that, unless we have positive commitments to organise and administer the 1986 Regatta by the end of September this year, we will not hold next year's event. Maybe we can consider alternatives which would be less demanding to organise and less taxing on our limited resources. One example would be to invite only selected Clubs to a camping/sailing week. No doubt we will debate this topic further at forth- coming meetings. At the last meeting we also decided not to host the Hornet Open Meeting later this year.— the reason being the demise of our own Hornet Fleet and the behaviour of certain Hornet sailors at the Regatta. Pat Black, our Secretary, has already written to the Hornet Association in order to give them a long notice of the cancellation of the event. We have, however, agreed to host the Hornet Junior U.K. Championship on 28th and 29th September, as previously agreed. The Sailing Sub-Committee, chaired by Peter Clayton, our hard-working Rear Commodore, has been considering many aspects and certain criticisms of the safety factor of our dinghy racing operation. This has been an emotive sub- ject for many years and one which has caused me much personal concern. One- solution promulgated is so labour-intensive (while extremely safe, I agree) that I think we would probably have more members involved in Rescue and back- up operations, et cetera, than would be racing. Obviously, we must come to an amicable solution, therfore Murray Bates and I have agreed, if possible, to attend the next Sailing Sub-Committee meeting to assist Peter and his team to reach a conclusion. Looking forward to seeing you all at Stansgate in the near future. David Harper

5 GALLEY Regatta My grateful thanks go out to all the many helpers who worked so hard for the Galley during the Regatta. Our breakfast team, sandwich-makers, servers and washers-up all worked well. We certainly had considerably more customers than last year, our food stocks had virtually sold out by the end of the last day. Without my team of ladies, one chap with a beard, and an ll-year-old part time sweet shop proprietor, it would have been an impossible task. Thank you all, More Seriously: IS THE GALLEY SERVICE GOING TO CONTINUE? IT IS UP TO YOU TO DECIDE. At the time of writing (29th May) there are 5 Sundays in June for which there are no volunteers for Galley on the Rota. By the time you receive this Navigans at the end of the month you may well have found the Galley closed when you had expected it to be open. Please will all members whether they sail dinghies, cruisers, or are even non-boat—owners give serious thought now to giving up one Sunday during the season to help provide this service for their fellow members, The Galley actually earns money for the club and helps towards the cost of providing and maintaing the good clean facilities we all enjoy at Stansgate. I suspect that, with a few exceptions!, most ladies are like me and wouldn't relish the thought of digging trenches to lay power cables, pumping out the cess-pit, knocking down walls, building up walls,doing plumbing repairs, installing electrical equipment, etc., jobs that are done by some of the lads probably unseen and unnoticed by most of the members who come to the club on a Sunday. Ladies can however make sandwiches, tea and coffee and sell them along with the sweets and fizzy drinks stocked at the club, They already have the necessary skills, and once they have done a session in the Galley they know the job pretty thoroughly. A day in the Galley can keep 2 people quite busy, especially on a nice day when there are more members and visitors on the site, but if it only has to be done once in the course of the year it can be quite enjoyable, and also gives you a chance to get to know some of the other members, If you don't want to take the plunge on your own, try joining in the next time you see the Galley open. You can learn a lot if you go in and do some washing-up and watch how it is all done. RESCUE SERVICE The strong winds encountered during the Spring Points Series and the capsizes occurring as a result have made it apparent that some members are unclear in their understanding of the role of the rescue service provided by the Club. The rescue service is primarily intended to ensure, as far as possible, that the sailors taking part in organised racing at the Club are prevented from being exposed to any unnecessary personal danger when they are in difficulties. The emphasis is on the safety of the human - the dinghy is of a secondary con- sideration. It must be made clear that, on windy days, when there may be more than one dinghy capsized at any one time, the rescue boat cannot be expected to tow dinghies back to the hard. This time-consuming process will prevent it from ensuring the safety of other sailors. On these occasions, the rescue boat will check whether the crew of a capsized boat is in trouble; if it is, the sailors will be advised to leave the dinghy which will be anchored, if possible, by the rescue boat crew. If the dinghy crew is not in difficulty, or if the sailors refuse to leave the boat, the rescue boat will leave to attend to the other capsized dinghies, returning to check on the original boat if it is obvious that it is still in trouble. Abandoned dinghies can be attended to once any danger to personnel has passed. Members of the Sailing Sub-Committee are to be trained in the use of the workboat in order to expedite recovery of abandoned dinghies. Two important points should be remembered; these are that the final respons- ability for safety always lies with the dinghy crew (who ignore the advice of the rescue boat coxswain at their peril) and, secondly, that dinghies are in- sured and therefore the decision to abandon can be made more comfortably with this fact in mind. Finally, just a commonsense note to new 0.0.D.s = ensure that the radios are switched on and that two-way transmissions are carried out between the rescue boat and theClubhouse and between the rescue boat and the racebox prior to racing, when the rescue boat is on the water. I hope these notes will serve to clarify any misunderstandings of the role of the rescue service. Moorings: The question has arisen as to the liability of a mooring owner who allows another member of the Club to use his mooring. It would seem well-established practice that a member of a club using another member's mooring accepts all risks of accident howsoever arising. Even where moorings are hired out on a commercial basis, it is normally on the understanding that the boatyard disclaims all liability. The only advice I can give, therefore, is to use your own mooring. If you have to use another member's mooring, remember that if anything happens you are likely to be liable. Sorry for the moans, but I'm only passing it on. John Wade DINGHY CRUISING NEWS Initially, I didn't think that dinghy cruising would stimulate too much interest, but recent events have shown just how wrong I was. Several people have already contacted me expressing interest and even greater enthusiasm was shown at the New Members' Evening. This article will, I hope, be the first of many to tell you what is happening, when and where. The objective of dinghy cruising is "to promote and encourage all forms of (safe and enjoyable) cruising in dinghies and similar small craft". (Dinghy Cruising Association words, not mine). The activities currently envisaged are:- Flotilla sailing in the Estuary; - Creek crawling; - Picnicking trips to such places as East Mersea or Sales Point; - Barbecues; - Aquateering; - Camping cruises to "distant" sites, such as Brightlingsea. Because such events would only be organised in a loose sense, safety is of paramount importance. We probably would not, for example, be able to count on the rescue boat being available, therefore a guard boat will be essential. To ensure that suitable safety standards are not only formulated but under- stood as well, a "package" of cruising safety notes is being compiled and will be available shortly. If anyone is interested in dinghy cruising, please let me have your names, addresses and details of your boat. continued

The dinghy team was sailing for the Colwyn Stone Challenge Trophy. The Roch- ester team was Richard and Sharon Stone (Wayfarer), Maurice and Pam Chapman pee Meg and Pat Fitzgerald (condor) and Gordon Belcher (Laser). Enterprise), Mark Chapman (Topper), Alastair Macfadyen and Alick Jamieson The wind was North West, Force 2 with occasional lulis and patches of Force 3. The course consisted of beats with the tide and very broad reaches and runs against the tide; conditions which favoured the Wayfarer and the Fireball. Richard Stone and Alastair Macfadyen took full advantage to chase the Condor round the course; Richard won and Alastair scored well on handicap. Gordon Belcher in the Laser benefitted from the gusts to stay close and was well placed on handicap. Overall, Rochester scored well, to go into lunch with a healthy lead. After lunch the story changed. M.S.C. decided enough was enough and, with good sailing by the Solos and Mirror, they attacked the Rochester lead. With a similar course, the Catamarans, Fireball and Wayfarer led at the windward mark and , in a dying wind, bore away against the tide. In the lee of Osea Island progress for the later boats was slow. On the second lap, the wind increased and backed, to give some planing on the broad reach. This allowed the planing boats to make up some of their handicap but not enough to prevent Richard Stone from winning the race and the trophy. Alastair Macfadyen was equal second with Mike Boreham, the Mirror's spinnaker keeping it in contention. Ron Greygoose and Roger Smith had a private battle in their Solos, which spurred both of them to be well placed. Gordon Belcher was in sixth place, whilst the Enterprises suffered by not having sufficient sail power to plane on the last reach. The Catamaran duel was won by the Fitzgeralds'Condor, which kept out the Dart. Mark Chapman had good boat speed, but missed a buoy and had to return, thus losing any chance of a good place. COMMODORE'S REPORT It is now many weeks since I last wrote to you, so I will attempt to bring you up to date with significant developments at the Club. First, no comment about the weather! However, let's hope for an improvement for the remainder of the month and early October so that we can really benefit from all the pre-season efforts. There is a mixture of good and bad news, so I will deal with the good first. The Barbecue, held on Saturday 20th July, was one of the best I have attended. Despite the weather, all 400 tickets were sold - bar sales were a record for the event! I thank all those concerned with the organisation, et cetera. The Barbecue was at the start of the Camping/Cadet Week, which continued through to the following Sunday. This was a great success - approximately £700.00 taken for camping fees and £1,000.00 bar sales. THE EDITOR, NAVIGANS. c/o MR.P.J.GRAY, K BLOCK, BADDOW. continued ...

2 = Once again, many of our members were involved in the planning and organisation of the event, but particular thanks to Derek Hall, who did a fantastic job teaching the Cadets. Many of the participants have thanked us personally and the Cadets look forward to the next event. Due to the revival of enthusiasm of the Cadet Fleet, during the last Executive Committee Meeting we decided to allocate No. 3 Garage to the Cadets for a Games/Recreation Room. This was agreed at the last Main Committee Meeting. Dick Papworth has agreed to liaise with Claude Emerson about painting the walls and already we have been given a dart board and table-tennis table - donations of any other sensible items would be most welcome. Incidentally, we are also looking for a carpet, size approximately 20' by 8'. After considerable deliberation, we decided to purchase a new lawn-mower cost- ing in excess of £500.00. This will be used exclusively by Claude Emerson and securely locked when not in use. By doing this we aim to reduce the problems and costs associated with grass cutting, and improve the general appearance of the site. The next important social event to consider is the Laying-Up Supper, which this year will be held at the County Hotel, Chelmsford (yes a new venue!) on Saturday 16th November. We have been lucky to obtain a Saturday booking, which we feel will be more acceptable to our members. Sheila Wade, our Social Secretary, has already started work for this function - please watch for her announcement and book early as numbers are restricted. Our aim is to intro- duce a less formal function and, as previously mentioned, only present sigma- ficant prizes, thereby allowing more time for the dinner and the social side of the evening. Membership is growing we now have 400 members. This is a very rewarding result to an advertising campaign earlier in the season. Now the bad news! Unfortunately, at the end of the Camping/Cadet Week we experienced a problem with the Mariner's outboard engine (that's the Rescue Boat). The quotation for the repair is £1,300.00. You will now realise why we have not rushed to resolve this problem. Much discussion has taken place at the Executive and Main Committee Meeting and s we have charged the Sailing Sub-Committee with reconsidering our rescue/dinghy racing support operation and then reporting back to the Main Committee as soon as possible. At the end of the day we may decide to sell the Mariner and introduce a new form of Rescue Boat. Progress is being made with the cesspit problem. Dick Papworth is liaising with Maldon Council re a proposed alternative scheme and we hope to meet the Council representatives at Stansgate later this month. Hopefully, some of the work can be carried out by our members during the Winter Working Parties, thereby reducing the cost to -the Club. Thinking of Sue, who has to type this, I will stop writing. (Ed. Thank you.) I look forward to seeing you at the Club during the remaining weekends of the season. David Harper

The Sailing Side of Cadet Week — Weather-wise Cadet Week gave us a bit of everything this year. Tents were pitched and put away in the rain and in between we had windy days, calm days, sunburn days and cold days. The main object of the week was cadet training under the leadership and guidance of Derek Hall. The week started with ‘dry' capsize drill and instruction on rigging and reefing the cadets' dinghies (mainly Mirrors). A windy Monday afternoon added: realism to the cadets' capsize practice, carried out off the hard using 'Idle Vice’. Thanks go to the stalwarts who spent all Monday afternoon in the water holding "Idle Vice' for the youngsters in increasingly uncomfortable conditions, Tuesday was a fine hot day. The cadets were given some basic sailing instruction on land, (the sea wall makes a good lecture theatre) and then spent the morning reaching to and fro across the river. Later in the morning they sailed’ off up-river escorted by the work boat, Unfortunately the wind then died away completely and a tow home was needed. Shades of Dunkirk, ten or so dinghies returning to the hard being towed by the workboat and Murray Bates' 'Candy'. The calm afternoon enabled the cadets to have some rowing practice and a swim, The wind returned on Wednesday and with it more instruction and sailing for the cadets which was continued on Thursday morning, By now the cadets were handling their reefed dinghies confidently in the increasing winds (well, most of you were!). The wind had increased sufficiently by Thursday lunch time for the proposed sail round Osea to be abandoned in favour of a frontal assault on the island, straight across the river under jibs only. All the cadets arrived safely, although one young lady did forget to jump into her dinghy after pushing off from the hard. However she was promptly retreived from the drink and popped back into her boat to continue the voyage with the others, (I bet 'mum' still doesn't know who she was and I'm not telling). The cadets were escorted by the Mariner, workboat, fisherman, and George Robinson's Freyag A fair number of Mums, Dads, friends etc. thumbed lifts in the safety boats, and there was a good gathering on Osea beach for the afternoon. (To tell the truth we spent most of the time sheltering from the cold winds behind a big clump of gorse bushes), The trip back to Stansgate was brisk and bumpy but all boats made it in good order with plenty of opportunity to apply the knowledge gained during the week. Friday morning was devoted to heaving-to and man-overboard drill. A fair degree of competence was displayed although a lot of the men-overboard, (half-filled plastic bottles) were retrieved whilst sailing by at full tilt! Not quite what Derek had in mind I suspect. The final treat(!) was a sail down to Thirslet, round the beacon and land on the spit for lunch, All the cadets plus a few others followed the workboat down to Thirslet in a brisk, cold wind, with the fisherman bringing up the rear, The Mariner popped back to the Club to collect Derek who had the morning off to scrub his boat and to collect a few packed lunches that had been left behind, I don't suppose I will ever know who decided on Thirslét as the lunch-time venue (someone in the Camping Club Boating Group I think!) but lacking the friendly gorse bushes of Osea we all stood around like penguins trying to keep warm until it was time to sail back. (It was fun though, kids, wasn't it?) The trip back to Stansgate was a long beat along the edge of Thirslet spit and one or two helmsmen learnt another lesson, (What is lee-way, David?). The last activity of the afternoon was cleaning and putting away of boats, Derek's final duty took place on Friday evening when he presented each cadet with a small prize and they in turn presented him with a bottle of his favourite tipple. In concluding this account it must be said that the very real and noticeable progress made by the cadets during the week reflects great credit on Derek Hall for his skill and patience as instructor and on the youngsters for sticking with it even when wet Contd.e.e

~4- and cold. I am sure that I speak for all the cadets’ parents when I say 'Thank you very much’ to Derek for giving so much of his time for the benefit of our budding sailors, On a more general note thanks are also due to the club officers on site who, while nominally on holiday, had to deal with all the usual problems that arise when there is a large gathering at Stansgate, Thank you all for a most enjoyable week, Ray Ball, GALLEY & CAMPING Each evening during Cadet Week the Galley sweetshop was opened and run by Janet Boustred and her friend Alison, thank you both for giving up your time. - 6 - SOLO NEWS Solo Worlds, Pevensey Bay - see Bob Anderson's graphic account of this event - my hands are still shaking. The beaching technique at Pevensey is designed to avoid making your trolley wet. As you near the beach they shout, "Sail it in hard!" Unfortunately, that is just the moment that the beach wind shadow takes the wind out of your sails; nevertheless, you sail in and a number of people in the water grab your boat and run up the beach, having pushed the helmsman over the transom. They leave it on your trolley and all you have to do is get it up a soft shingle bank at 45°. If you are Dutch your boat is borne, shoulder high, directly into the dinghy park accompanied by chants in strange tongues. The event was won by Ken Falcon; Dick Batt was runner up in a borrowed boat; Geoff Carveth third, also in a borrowed boat. Skipper's Cup and Vet's Trophy were won by Tony Catchpole of Hayling Island. My position? See Solo Class Newsletter or next year's Year Book (that means it's no good). Jack Holt had the new fibreglass sandwich boat there which he has just built using the Omega mould. It feels very stiff and he will announce price et cetera in about a month's time. It was a shame not to have another Marconi boat there, but it was great to have the support of the Andersons - thank you, Bob and Elsie. Actually, Bob has picked up some useful tips in the dinghy park and should be considered honorary M.S.C. (Marconi Solo Consultant). The dressing romms at Pevensey revealed some strange sights; one chap stuffed football shin pads under the front of his wet suit; another pushed vast quantities of foam down the back to prolong the agony, so to speak. Some of the Dutchmen even had little strap on attachments to protect their thighs! It made them look like cowboys going for a shoot-out in the O.K. (wash my mouth out) Corral! We had a second barbecue on August 26th; again, the weather could have been better, but it could have been worse. Congratulations to Cathy and Dave Nixson on the birth of Daniel on 5th August. Stuart Pullen went down to the Chichester Harbour Federation week sailed from Hayling Island and acquitted himself well in quite windy weather. Don't forget the Halfway Open on 14th/15th September; our Open on 21st/22nd September and Fishers Green on 6th October. Also, we are organising the Hornet Junior Nationals on 28th/29th September - please turn up and help. Roger Smith 1985 SOLO WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS PEVENSEY BAY, SUSSEX It was during the week 26th July to 2nd August that Pevensey Bay S.C. were hosting the Solo World Championships and Elsie and I decided that we would go to "sunny" Sussex to join in the delights of the week (as spectators, of course).

ow: si I am now glad to say that I was not competing: winds between Force 4 and Force 7, with more than the occasional gust of 8 plus, set the conditions for most of the week. Not ideal for the faint—hearted. Following Monday's race the dinghy park was littered with broken and bent masts, with numerous collections of other gear failures. And so it went on for race after race. One competitor, who had to purchase a new mast, said he'd never been more terrified in his life. While on the run riding a 12 foot wave, he heard a roaring sound behind him and looked back, only to observe an even bigger wave fast approaching. He said that he had been “pitchpoled" many times, but had never hit the water burgee first before. Listening to the conversations at the bar after the races, many similar tales were being told. Roger will tell you how he was fifth round the windward mark and how we are now clued up on how to race tune a Solo rig (small consultancy fees to the Barbecue). As a novice to Solos myself, I felt nothing but admiration as each day the competitors made for the start line in seas which, at times, only revealed the tops of the sails to those watching from the shore. I believe it was a total surprise to the organisers that Soloists were prepared to sail and survive in such conditions. The beachuastersaid that he was amazed at the high standard of seamanship demonstrated by those he described as "pond Sailors". I am sure that full details and race reports have already been seen in the yachting press; this is just a note of a few of the observations that I made during the week to give me the confidence to cope with the occasional 2-3. Who knows? Next year Bob Anderson CRUISER FLEET NEWS Your attention is drawn to the plan for cruiser leying-up, which will be displayed on the Clubhouse Noticeboard. - 2 = COMMODORE'S REPORT Since writing my September report, we have at long last received a reply from M.A.S.C. regarding the M.S.C. contribution. As M.A.S.C. had to spend approx= imately £1,600. to improve our water heating system, they have instructed us to pay a contribution for the current year of £4,500. For next season, they are asking £5,000. Immediately upon receipt of the M.A.S.C. letter confirming the above, an Executive Committee meeting was held in order to re-examine our financial position, review our capital budget based on a five year plan and consider Committee proposals for the A.G.M. All these items will be debated at the October Main Committee Meeting, which has not been held at the time of writing. We are now attempting to work more closely with M.A.S.C. one landlord/tenant basis, as per their instructions. In light of this new relationship, we have replied to M.A.S.C. and tabled our capital budget requirements, which include the following significant items: 1. Sewerage disposal. 2. Road resurfacing. 3. Site security. 4. Hard -— much concern in view of recent accelerated deterioration. 5e Rescue Boat - the engine is a write-off and we are.currently examining our rescue operation. 6. Tractor - it is envisaged that a replacement will be required in the next few years. | We have requested that M.A.S.C. provides the funding for items 1 to 4; in connection with items 5 and 6 we have requested an interest free loan, repay- able over a five year period. Much thought has also been given to the future of the Club and in particular to the future lines of succession for Flag Officers and other demanding roles on the Main Committee. Our proposal is to change the rules in the M.S.C. constitution so that Associate Members will be able to hold such posts. Our proposals will be debated at the October Main Committee Meeting and, if agreed, will be tabled at the A.G.M. on Sunday 3rd November at 2.00 p.m. at Stansgate. The Executive Committee feel that we cannot continue as a dynamic sailing club without the active participation of our Associate Members in Club management. Tickets for the Laying-Up Supper are selling very well. Please make sure you have booked your tickets if you wish to attend. Remember that there are limit- ed numbers this year. Mr Charlie Stock has accepted our invitation to be principal guest this year and I feel sure that his short presentation will be most interesting and infor- mative. Pat and I look forward to seeing you all at the Club, the Working Party on Sunday 27th October, the A.G.M. on Sunday 3rd November and at the Laying-Up Supper on Saturday 16th November. Maureen Ball C'ford [redacted] SAILBOARD NEWS All sailboard members - if you have any problems or needs concerned with the Club, please contact me, Ian Savage, or Alan Polley on the telephone numbers below, as we are your representatives on the Sailing Sub-Committee. As you may be aware, we now have a Club board, a vinta solo, which is available for use by any member. It is kept in one of the front garages and can be used when there is a Duty Officer in attendance at the Club, the key to the garage being obtainable from him. Please exhibit caution in its use. If you are a beginner, do not use it in strong winds, offshore breezes or strong tidal conditions. Also, let somebody know you are going out. If starting for the first time, it is advisable to attach a long line to the towing hook and have a friend on shore holding the other end, and please always wear a buoyancy aid. If anybody needs guidance on how to sailboard, any of the regulars or myself would, I'm sure, be able to offer assistance, but please bear in mind that the Club is not the safest place for beginners and a course on an inland lake to start with would be advisable. If you do use the Club board, please hose it down with fresh water after use and store back in the garage, but do not roll up the sail when wet - either wait till it's dry or leave it draped over the board. With increased numbers of sailboarders using the Club, I have had a couple of reports of accidents involving boards and boats in collision and of a swimmer being hit by a mast, so please could we all exhibit care, especially when launching and retrieving on beach areas, and please keep away from the hard area and sailing marks when racing is in progress. Also, be aware of the rules of rights of way, since we do not want to find restrictions being placed on our movements. Finally, if anybody would be interested in some open races or a fun day - nothing too serious - let me know. Ian Savage C'ford [redacted], Alan Polley C'ford [redacted] SEA CADET BOATWORK COURSE - JULY 21ST TO 27TH Fifty Sea Cadets from Essex units as far afield as Walton, Southend, Colchester, Harlow and Tilbury enjoyed the facilities of the Club for their annual Boatwork Course this year. continued ...

as Ot They arrived, towing a motley collection of trailers heavily weighed down with their 165 ft. ASC dinghies, which in turn had tents, Mirrors, cooking gear et cetera packed within, and were soon encamped in rows in the camping field. For many, their regular sailing areas had been ponds, lakes or reservoirs, so, for some, the Blackwater must have seemed like a veritable ocean! Sunday was spent mainly setting up camp and rigging boats, but a short sail in the evening in a good breeze soon broke the ice. Monday, however, was quite a different kettle of fish, with Force 5 winds, gusting 7 at times. It soon became clear that, however deeply reefed the boats were, any further Sailing that day was out of the ouestion. During the afternoon a GP14 cap- Sized with three cadets aboard and in a heavy swell in the narrows just off Osea very soon turned turtle. The rescue dory at the time was having its plug "dewhiskered" (or whatever it is that "pugs" outboards at the most inopportune moments) and to our amazement a lone Mirror sailor (Peter Skeeting, we think) who was with the Camping and Boating Club plucked off the three lads who were by then decidedly frightened, and deposited them safely ashore! No mean feat and one for which we were extremely grateful. Monday night was even more exciting .... the wind had not abated and at one stage we had some twenty or so people parascending with the mess tent! By Tuesday forenoon four cadets sadly decided that enough was enough and left for home, whereupon Sod's Law prevailed and the weather began to improve; the rest of the week provided first class conditions for sail training. In terms of results obtained by way of R.Y.A. Certificates, the Course was an undoubted success - but probably of equal value was the experience of operating from a sailing club where folk operate by cooperation and mutual assistance rather than by a more rigid discipline. Since many of these young men, having been bitten by the "sailing bug", will probably have their ow boats in later life, this will have been a useful introduction to club life. Saturday afternoon saw groups of somewhat weatherbeaten boys stuffing their dirty gear into their kit bags to take home to Mum, and striking camp, but it was unanimously agreed that all would come again next year, given the opportunity - please! a SAIL A MIRROR FOR A NEW EXPERIENCE OR MIRROR MANIA AND MIRROR MANIACS Just like British Rail, we (the Mirror Fleet) are getting there, so, look out, "premier fleet" - our fleet is catching you up! We haven't made double figures yet, but next season could be the one for us if the Autumn Points Series is anything to go by. At the time of writing, the fleet has sailed 7 out of 10 races scheduled(the other 3 were abandoned) and the last three races have seen 6, 7 and 8 Mirrors participating. After several years of Boreham clan domination (in numbers, that is = not results!), a race can now be held without us. In fact, we can now stand on the sea wall as on- lookers and enjoy the spectacle. I was such an onlooker on Sunday 6th October, when 8 Mirrors signed on for the morning race, with winds gusting up to Force 5. Neil Salmon, crewed by Clare Savill, had a great start and shamed the rest by flying their spinn— aker over the start line (it was a reaching start). Unfortunately, it flew too well and they capsized just @ few yards start. over the Damian Boreham, crewed by Peter Brown, also had a good start; in fact, so good that they thought they were the culprits who were “over the line" and had to thread a somewhat precarious return journey through the fleet to start again. Pity really; the real culprit was another Mirror who appeared to be checking the lights on "F" mark when the starting gun went off. Never mind, Damian and Pete -— put it all down to experience. The fleet sailed down in close company to Breezy where a gybe was required, Dennis Dear rounded first, crewed by young John Dear, and was followed by Peter Collis who promptly capsized. Mike Boreham touched Peter and had to waste time doing his "720" and a certain amount of chaos threatened as Jack & Diane Rusbridge, Mike & ‘Janet Battle and Damian & Pete all managed to avoid both Peter and Mike and set off in hot pursuit of Dennis towards Goldhanger,. Dennis, now thoroughly hooked on Mirror Mania (yes, the “premier boat" has been left to sulk under its cover in the boat paxik), led all the way over to Goldhanger on a broad reach. At Goldhanger, Phil Gray and Kate Nicholson decided to set the fleet a poser by capsizing just before the mark and drift-— ing into the path of the onrushing stream of Mirror Maniacs. This time, chaos not only threatened but actually occurred and out of the melee emerged my dearly beloved husband, Mike, crewed by Lucy Boreham, scarcely able to believe his luck at going from 5th to 1st in one fell swoop (of a Hornet)! Mike Battle was close behind (in "Battleship", would you believe) and these two remained in that position around "A" mark and into the second lap. Eventually, by dint of much hard work and superior windward Sailirig, Mike Battle took the lead and led around "A" mark by a few yards, only to lose it again to Mike Boreham, who blew into his sails a little bit harder and reach- ed the finish line just two feet ahead of the "Battleship". Jack & Diane Rusbridge sailed a good race to take 3rd place. In the meantime, other exciting things had been happening on the course. for a start, Chris & Stephen Thorne's gaff fell down, Peter Collis again capsized and Neil & Clare also lost their gaff. Finally, Damian & Pete cap- Sized and, all in all, the rescue boat had quite a lot of work to do. I think Mike Wellington (rescue crew) actually enjoyed his swimming as a rescuer more than his swimming as helm the day before, when he took part in the Helmsman of the Year Final. DATES FOR YOUR DIARY Wednesday 4th December - Cruiser Winter Meeting, Committee Room, M.A.S.C. - 8.00 p.m. Saturday 21st December - Cruiser Christmas Party, Stansgate. - 8.00 p.m. EDITORIAL A bumper edition this month owing to the various A.G.M. reports, list of prizewinners, results, et cetera. At the very back (I hope) of this issue you will find your membership renewal form. This is now 3 sides long, and is much clearer for those myopic members (like me). Russell Jeffries, our Membership Secretary, has asked me to point out that renewals received after 28th February 1986 will incur the joining fee! Also, please check your total carefully - apparently a large number of cheques had to be returned last year for correction, and this incurs a lot of additional cost, not to mention work. Russell would also like all three sides (i.e. two sheets of paper) returned. Thanks. End of lecture. Deadline for next month is Wednesday 4th December. Sue Gray COMMODORE'S REPORT FOR A.G.M. Since taking over as Commodore last year, I have at least achieved one personal objective; that was to improve communication by keeping the membership totally informed of all developments. THE EDITOR, NAVIGANS. c/o MR.P.J.GRAY, K BLOCK, BADDOW. M.S.C. membership has been significantly increased and I am sure you will agree that we have re-introduced a better sense of belonging in the Club. continued ...

mn Oa I take this opportunity to thank the Executive and Main Committee members for their support and encouragement, and I also extend my thanks to the other Club members who have assisted us in achieving our objectives. Every sailing club has problems; we are no different. My approach has always been to consider problems as opportunities and thereby reduce hard- ships. The following comments relate to significant Club events in chronological order. At the start of the season we were concerned about the decrease in interest in dinghy sailing and the increase in subscriptions to M.A.S.C. and M.S.C. necessary to balance our books. We soon realised that our solution to both Situations was to increase the size of our membership. Consequently, we mounted a recruitment drive and, in parallel, started negotiations with M.A.S.C. re our section levy. I was also burdened with the task of chairing the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee and running a Race Management Seminar for them. I am indebted to Pat and Malcolm Stuart for their support in this direction. As it happened, we used the M.A.S.C. facilities for the seminar; 69 delegates attended and we gained much publicity for M.S.C. The winter/early season working parties were very well attended; this gave us much incentive to work harder on behalf of the Club. The Cruiser Christ- mas Party on 15th December 1984 was most enjoyable and a New Members' Evening was introduced. Both events were well attended. At the end of the pre-season working parties we had provided ourselves with another garage: converted the "blockhouse" under the race-—box into a large, secure storage area: organised five 13 amp. double power sockets in the Cruiser Park; and cleared most of the ditches and the sides of the road to the Club. An early decision was to make more use of the site - hence the venue here today. To reduce costs, we no longer have a front picture on "Navigans"; maybe we can debate this later under "Any Other Business". The Barn Dance on 26th January was another success. I must thank Sheila Wade for a most excellent term of office as Social Secretary. Just before our Main Committee meeting on Monday 4th February a dear old friend, Eric Payne, died. Eric has been a great loss to the Club. February brought problems with the water supply. We also had further dis- cussions with M.A.S.C. about our levy. Application was made to the Crown Estates Commission for permission to extend our Cruiser moorings towards Stone. Early in the year Claude Emerson and Dick Papworth completed much painting inside the Clubhouse and we are generally quite pleased with the result. By early March most jobs had been completed and on Sunday 24th March we held our "Fitting-Out' working party. During the winter two of our members, Peter Sayer and Arthur Hodges, spent hundreds of hours refurbishing the tractor. A microwave oven was purchased and the installation co-ordinated by Dick Papworth. Essex Police telephoned me about thefts on the Bleckwater. Action was taken to inform all members. The replacement of our magnetic card lock system is now high on the list of priorities for capital expenditure. We exhibited at the National Dinghy Exhibition once again - my thanks to continued ceecee

-3- Derek Webb and Steve Evans for organising same. Several new Associate Men-— bers joined the Club as a result of this exercise. The Fitting-Out Party on Saturday 30th March was also another success. The Regatta was excellent from the sailing point of view, although we would still have liked to have seen more Marconi dinghies participating. However, the event brought some problems. Just to mention a few:- 1. Sewerage; 2. Shortage of spotters; 3. Not sufficient hot water; 4. Snags with the toilets; 5e Aggravation from certain (albeit a small percentage) of visiting dinghy sailors and their spectators. 6. Problems with the telephone and electricity supply. 7. Lack of interest from Club members. Just prior to the Regatta, h.A.S.C. (Gerry Wignall in particular) organised a re-plumbing exercise for our hot water system and to overcome problems due to low cold water pressure. Unfortunately, the wrong size boiler was instal- led, but this was soon corrected and has worked satisfactorily ever since. A safety audit just prior to the Regatta was about as untimely as one could ‘have wished. At the last Committee Meeting we decided not to hold a Regatta next year, as there does not seem to be enough support to administer and control the event. Tomorrow evening we will hold the first meeting of the new Main Committee and the following week there will be a Sailing Sub-Committee meeting, during which we will decide upon an alternative to the Regatta. There has been certain concern about safety on the water and much time has been spent debating the subject. The annual visit by Rochester on Saturday and Sunday 8th and 9th June went quite well. Rochester won the individual and the overall team race. I am looking to Phil Gray, Peter Clayton and the Sailing Sub-Committee to redress this situation next year. The Barbecue was not blessed with fine weather. However, four hundred tickets were sold, thereby creating a good profit and marking the start of Cadet Week. Fifty Sea Cadets and their instructors joined us for Cadet Week. I hope this visit will be repeated next season. Derek Hall did a remarkable job teaching and entertaining the M.S.C. cadets during the week. Whilst on the subject of our cadets, we have now decided to allocate Garage No. 3 for their use. A new lawnmower has been purchased. I am sure that you are all pleased that the site now looks more inviting and well kept. Now to the problems and opportunities:- 1. Towards the end of Cadet Week, the engine of our Rescue Boat seized and is now beyond economical repair. The quotation is in excess of £1,300. We have contacted many other sailing clubs to talk about their choice of rescue boats and to seek their advice, et cetera. The concensus of opinion is that we should purchase 4 displacement type hull with inboard diesel, rather than a planing hull with outboard engine. 2. Sewage disposal. The worst problem we have, but I am pleaseé to report continued

-4- that Dick Papworth has taken this task on board and is making excellent progress. My concern is the cost, which could amount to many thousands of pounds. 3- We have agreed with M.A.S.C. that our contribution for this year will be £4,500. and for next year £5,000. We also have agreement with M.A.S.C. that they will finance the following items: 1. Sewerage; 2. Road resurfacing; 3 Site security; 4. Repairs to the hard; 5 Replacement rescue boat. Of course, we will endeavour to keep costs of all of the foregoing to a minimum and provide as much labour as possible. No doubt the N.A.S.C. Chairman, Mr Tony Mayhew, or Mr Wignall, the M.A.S.C. Club Manager, who are both here with us today, will comment later. We have given much thought to the succession and future leadership of M.S.C. We need dedicated persons who will adopt a professional attitude and feel that we must now change our rules to allow and encourage Associate Members to hold senior posts. Of course, any agreement will have to be ratified by M.A.S.C. Rules Committee. I will now table objectives for next season, irrespective of the constitution of the Committee:- 1. Encourage more dinghies on to the water. 2. Increase even further the utilisation of the Stansgate facilities. 3- Organise fund raising events in order that we can keep subscriptions at an acceptable level. 4. Help Maureen Ball, who has done a most marvellous job looking after the Galley, by finding some more volunteers to man the Galley each weekend. Maureen is resigning as soon as we have found a suitable replacement. Any offers of help will be very much appreciated. On that note, I thank you all for your support and apologise for not being able to spend more time in your company here at Stansgate this year. Pat and I hope for a better year in 1986, with fewer family problems. Lastly, my thanks to the wives of the Executive Members, who have been so understanding regarding the time we have spent on Club affairs, and a special thank you to Pat Black, our Secretary, and Neil Pembleton, our Treasurer, for keeping us on course. David Harper SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT - 1985 There were several developments affecting sailing before the season started. continued

- 5 - One of these was the demise of the Hornet fleet, which suffered a sudden and dramatic loss of boats at the end of last season. Another, more positive event resulted from the decision to advertise the Club at the London Dinghy Exhibition. The emphasis was placed on attracting more dinghy sailors and the venture proved to be successful in this end. A new format for the year's sailing programme was planned. This consisted of extending the Spring and Autumn Points Series and extracting points from the closed club races held during the summer to form a Summer Points Series. The weather during the spring and summer months was not conducive even to the more experienced helmsmen to compete, let alone the novices, and as a result the turnouts for the Spring Points Series were low, with the 420 fleet not managing to complete one race. The Solo fleet were an exception to this trend and maintained a steady attendance. The number of entrants to the Regatta returned back to its usual level this year and a successful sailing programme was organised. Strong winds during Cadet Week prevented the Cadet Series from being sailed and serious damage was incurred by the Rescue Boat engine at the end of the week. This disabled the Rescue Boat for the rest of the season and prevented some of the Club's longer distance races from being sailed. The new format for summer sailing enabled points series to be formed for all classes except Enterprises. The Cruiser Cup was well supported by M.S.C. boats, which is a strong indication that the Barnacle Points Series could be reinstated in the future. Wednesday evening racing was as popular as ever, the simple format being enjoyed by both race organisers and competitors. The autumn brought better weather, which encouraged many more sailors to participate in the racing, with the Solo and Mirror fleets in particular showing large increases in competitors. The growth of the Mirror fleet should be taken as an encouraging sign for the future, when a progression should be made up to a larger two man dinghy, thereby filling a gap which presently exists within the Club. The organisation and effort laid on for the Hornet Junior Nationals was extensive and the Championships were run very smoothly, but the entry was disappointingly low. The Solo and Dart Open Meetings were as well organised and the higher number of entrants made the events enjoyable for both competitors and organisers. a MARCONI SAILING CLUB, Stansgate. 28/10/85 Treasurer's Report. During 1985 the Club's finances have improved substantially over previous years. This is generally due to two factors. Firstly the substantial rise in subscription rates approved at the last A.G.M.; however if the membership had stayed at last year's level this would have only raised £16,000. As can be seen the rise in membership this year has raised a further £2,440 and is the second reason for the improvement. The actual membership figures are:- 1984 1985 Ordinary 202 209 Family 34 40 Associate 111 133 Honorary 2 10 Cadet 3 1 Student 5 3 TOTAL 307 396 This is a welcome and significant achievement as it allows the overhead costs of the Club to be spread amongst more people and hence hold down subscription rates. In general the individual Accounts show the level of spend and income as predicted in the budget for the year. It is in the area of Capital expenditure that the effect of the increase of membership had the greatest effect. Here it was possible to use some of the extra income for improvements around the site and the facilities, although the road has not been resurfaced. The reason for postponing this will be seen when looking at next year's expenditure. As a consequence of this the Club has achieved a modest surplus of £2000 to £2500 as opposed to the loss which was predicted at this time last year. Looking forward to 1986, there are a number of significant points. As was explained last year the expectation that 'Exceptional Items' of spend will ever end is false. Currently the Club is faced with funding a number of urgent capital projects. As you are aware the Rescue Boat engine has to be replaced before next season. In addition the actual hull will probably need replacement within the next 4-5 years. It has therefore been decided to examine a number of alternative combinations of engine and hull. While this may impose a greater requirement for funding at this moment, the longer term benefits should be a substantial reduction in running costs. There is also an urgent need, indeed Maldon Council are insisting, to improve our sewage facilities; the Hard needs reconstruction; the road needs resurfacing; and security on the site needs improving. The estimate for these items is:- Cont. 6:'3é

However it is also essential to avoid the trap of running a permanent deficit account (as most Nations do). This however requires that the Club is able to Budget for a number of years into the future and that the Club can raise the funds to pay the bills on some form of loan basis. It is for these reasons that the Committe has approached the M.A.S.C. for a short term loan. However the initial response appears to be that while they will fund the work it will not be on a loan basis but on an increase in contribution, which as we all know is never reduced when the ‘loan' is repaid. This raises the whole question of the basis on which the contribution is calculated. We as a Club have very little control over the level. The constitution of both Clubs does not permit us to run our own bank account; we have to use the M.A.S.C. as our bank. Therefore if we fail to agree on the contribution effectively the M.A.S.C. can simply withold the sum required in their opinion. During this year the Committee have been attempting to resolve two points with the M.A.S.C.. Firstly the current level of the contribution and secondly the basis for the future increase in its level. It is the second of these which is more important to allow future budgeting to be carried out effectively. Turning now to this year's proposals before the meeting and dealing first. with subscriptions. Last year I said that I hoped to hold the increase this year to the level of inflation. Due largely to the increase in membership the proposed increase has been held to an average of 6.2% approximately, which is in line with inflation during the year. The second and separate proposal relates to the level of contribution to the M.A.S.C.. The Committee feel that a mandate from the Club is necessary to help in the negotiations with the M.A.S.C.. If passed the motion will stengthen our position and should it be necessary we will ask for your further support during the year on this matter. Finally let us look at the longer term future of the Club financially. The Club now has a turnover of £30,000 per year which is the equivalent of some small businesses and therefore has to adopt a more business like approach to its financial dealings. It is not unreasonable to forsee a continuing Capital spend of 10-15% per year. It is also obvious that costs will continue to rise due to inflation. - 9 - MARCONI SAILING CLUB, Stansgate. 28/10/85 membership increase. This year we have been very successful in recruitment. It is considered that the Club can expand to 500 members with the present basic facilities and as can be seen from this year the improvement in financing would be dramatic. The other area which must be pursued is reduction of costs. Again this year some savings have been achieved; most notably in the area of Navigans and the Year Book. However the biggest single cost in any project is labour. The wiring of the Cruiser Park this year would have been two or three times as much if it had been all done on a contract basis. However it is not only the one off project where labour costs are important. We all like to enjoy the facilities offered by the Bar and Galley on sailing weekends. To supply thes services requires labour. Yes they could be subcontracted to an outside organisation; however the profit on them would probably not even pay the outsider, let alone give the Club any return. There are approximately 30 sailing weekends per year and, if it is assummed that the Bar requires 2 people and the Galley requires 2 people, to man this 2 days ever weekend requires 240 people on a One Day basis. In other words with a membership of 400 people it only requires each of us to give up ONE days sailing every YEAR AND A HALF. This is an area of the Club which can generate a very substantial level of income and profit for the Club. I would ask you all to consider giving up just the one day to help keep the Clubs costs down to a minimum. Neil Pembleton FREE! ENTERPRISE FLEET NEWS Well,as most of you will know by now, I shall not be sailing at the Club next year; Derek Webb and myself are moving to another club with an active racing fleet. It was a hard decision, as we have both been members of the Club and the fleet for about 8 years now. But, at the end of the day, we are both interested in competitive Enterprise racing and, after this year's racing, or lack of it, we have decided upon a move. Over the past 8 years we have tried hard to build up the fleet, but must conclude that, although we have some 13 boats, most are content to potter. In September of this year I sent out a questionaire to all fleet members, asking what sort of racing they wanted next year and whether anybody would take on the job of Fleet Captain. Apart from the "active three", I had two replies. Need I say more! I have therefore reccomended to the Sailing Sub-Committee that fleet status is withdrawn next year and that the Enterprise Fleet sail as part of the Handicap Fleet. If in future anyone wants to take on the job of building up the fleet again, they should contact a Sailing Sub-Committee member. I hope we shall see an Enterprise Fleet at the Club again. It's an excellent boat, and the Club has had a fleet for many, many years - it would be a shame if it disappeared forever. Good sailing. Steve Evans Ed.'s note: Steve, we'll miss you, June and Derek. Sheila Wade Social Secretary MIRROR FLEET NEWS The Mirror Fleet Meeting, which was held at my home on 11th November, was exceedingly well supported, especially by new members. All the items were discussed at length on a very informal basis, with all fleet members putting forward their own ideas and thoughts. For those fleet members who could not attend, you can still make your views heard if you would like to contact me (telephone [redacted]) or perhaps put an article into Navigans as Maggie Boreham did so well recently. (d's note: Hear, hear!) The main views of the meeting were as follows: 1. That we would like to re-introduce the Cadet Series and Ladies Race into the sailing calendar. 2. That we feel duty cover can still only be given to one complete weekend by the fleet. 3. We would like to hold a Mirror Open Meeting during 1986. 4. We would enter with 4 boats into several other Clubs' Open Meetings in our area. 5. The Mirror Association would be contacted with a view to 2 of our fleet members becoming Class Measurers. 6. Great concern was expressed about the efficiency of the Club's radio communication system, i.e. the number of times it seemed to be inoperable. 7» A “Mirror Fun Day" would be held, possibly on the first Saturday of Cadet Week, 8. A Fleet Winter Meeting would be held during February 1986; venue and time to be arranged (hopefully to follow from a Cadet Meeting). Finally, the meeting was interested to know why our dinghy park is full of ‘Mirrors which never seem to move from one sailing season to the next. Can anyone let me know if they would like to see anything introduced into the Club which would tempt them onto the water? On a more personal note, I would like to say that 1985 has definitely been one of the better years for our fleet (even if the weather hasn't). We have seen an increase in members and, more importantly, an increase in the number of Mirrors on the water. The friendliness and Willingness of the members to help one another and the Club in general has been very evident this year and I hope it will continue to grow and strengthen during 1986. COMMODORE'S REPORT My apologies for not reporting to you in the December issue but, as Sue informed you, I was abroad on business. First, I take this opportunity to wish you all a very happy 1986 - let's hope for a better summer than last year! We all enjoyed a very well attended Laying-Up Supper at the County Hotel, all tickets being sold well before the event. Sheila Wade has booked the same venue for this year. Charles Stock was our principal guest - I feel sure those who attended will remember his talk! MR.N.F.TOVEY, NAVAL DIVISION, M BLOCK, WRITTLE ROAD WORKS. continued ...

- 2 - Recently we had the Christmas Working Party, which was once again very well attended. Two of the scrubbing posts were replaced; a base plinth for the new winch was cemented in position; part of the sewerage herringbone system was excavated to establish the problem associated with the cesspit system; the ditch in the Cruiser park was cleaned; and Dick Papworth completed even more jobs in the Clubhouse. An Executive meeting was held just before Christmas to prepare a purchase specification for the new sailing support boat. This meeting was also attended by Geoff Josey (Ford Motor Co.) who is providing us with invaluable help and assistance a propos the engine and installation of same. The specification was finalised, agreed with M.A.S.C. and work has now been put in hand with the boatbuilder at Deal, Kent. Our eventual choice was for a "Sea Worker 22" which is a Colvic Marine hull, wheelhouse and foredeck et cetera by Brian Cory Boatbuilders and will include a Ford FSD 425 4 cylinder direct injection marinised engine, rated at 70 BHP at 4000 r.p.m. We hope to conduct sea trials during mid to late March and take delivery on Saturday 29th March. The total cost will be in the region of £8,500. We are in the process of arranging a loan from M.A.S.C. which will be repaid over the next 4 or 5 years. Murray Bates has suggested we run a competition for naming the new support boat - yes, we will give a prize and the winner can have the honour of breaking a bottle of champagne over the new boat (except it might have to be a cheap sparkling wine, due to our financial state!) As I mentioned briefly above, we are still making some progress with our sewerage problems. Dick Papworth will now be talking to a land drainage engineer and then with Maldon District Council for approval of our proposed rectification scheme. In parallel with the above, we have also been considering ideas for improving the appeal of the Satnsgate site, particularly for those members and friends "left on the shore". An initial suggestion is to build a veranda out from the North wall of the Clubhouse with access from the lounge. This would be a very attractive area for spectators and sun worshippers alike and provide a ready made area under which we can site the outside bar for the Barbecue and Open Meetings. A Sub-Committee has been formed under the Chairmanship of George Robinson, who presented his first report at the last Main Committee meeting. In this issue you will find an article from George which I hope you will find most interesting. Please answer his questionnaire so it will help us decide upon future developments at Stansgate. I hope to see you all at the Barn Dance on 25th January at M.A.S.C. COMMODORE'S REPORT It is with profound regret that I report the sad and sudden loss of our dear friend and colleague, Jack Bigden. Julian, Jack's eldest son, and his wife Jill visited Pat and I recently and I am sure you will all be pleased to learn of their intention to cement the family relationship with M.S.C. Julian and Jill live in the U.S.A., but even if they are only able to visit us once or twice each season I have promised them a warm welcome. Hopefully, Connie, Tim, Maureen and family will be regular visitors to the Club. I must remind you that the Sailing season is only seven weeks away at the time of writing - almost unbelievable, for the outside temperature is only just above zero as I write. The Fitting-Out Party at Stansgate will be on 5th April - let's hope for a massive attendance this year. On Saturday 25th January we held the Barn Dance at M.A.S.C. - once again, all tickets were sold before the event. The good news is that we are on target with respect to the programme for MR.N.F.TOVEY, NAVAL DIVISION, M BLOCK, WRITTLE ROAD WORKS. continued ...

- 2 - delivery of the new sailing support boat. Peter Clayton and I will be arranging to visit the boatbuilder for the first inspection towards the end of February. The bad news is that we are still making heavy weather in attempting to resolve our sewerage disposal problem. On February 14th a meeting has been arranged at Stansgate to be attended by representatives of Effluent Engineering (Maldon), Anglian Water Authority, M.S.C. (Murray Bates, Dick Papworth and myself) and possibly a representative from M.A.S.C. It is sincerely hoped that at least a decision will be made which will enable us to at last appoint a contractor to resolve the problem. On an unpleasant note, I was disturbed to be informed at the last Main Committee Meeting that last season we were embarrassed, by the Handicap Fleet in particular, in failing to cover Race Officer and Rescue duties. Such duties are very infrequent - if you have any problem regarding coverage, please inform your Fleet Captain and give him as much notice as possible. At the end of the day, it is down to the individual assigned to find an alternative person to cover for them. My last moan is that George Robinson has not received any replies to his questionnaire - see last month's issue. As I have previously stated, we do require your input in order to steer the future of the Club. Please spare half an hour to consider the questions raised and reply to George. Let's hope next month's report will be good news on every account. Good progress has been made by George Robinson and Ian Lindsay regarding the Veranda Project - an outline drawing is included in this issue to give you some idea of our proposals and any comments will be very much appreciated. Next we have to obtain outline planning permission and discuss the project with M.A.S.C. Pat and I look forward to seeing you at the Fitting-Out Party. David Harper Editor's note: In the unlikely event of you having mislaid last month's issue, there is a brief resume of George's Questionnaire later in this issue. Please take the time to reply. JACK BIGDEN I was very sad to hear of the death of Jack on 26th January. As most of you will know, he was a Vice-President of our Club and had a long and active influence in its development. COMMODORE'S REPORT During February we at last made considerable progress regarding the sewerage disposal problem. Two separate meetings were held at Stansgate attended by representatives of Effluent Engineering Contracts, our consultants, and the many local authorities involved in the exercise. It is now clear that we have no sensible economic alternative but to introduce a proper treatment system. The output of such a system would be to a standard such that it could go direct into the Blackwater. Obviously, before we depart upon such an expensive long term solution, we have to obtain planning permission and then clearance from all the appropriate authorities. This will also include satisfying ourselves with regard to all aspects of hygiene and safety. The planning approval, et cetera, will take until at least the end of May 1986; consequently, we are seeking approval for a pilot scheme which will form part of the final overall project. This initial scheme is to link the present and the old Clubhouse cesspits so as to increase our holding capacity. Until the overall scheme is completed, we will arrange for the tanks to be emptied by local contractor. I am pleased that we are now in a position where we can at least implement our sailing and camping calendar. During the abovementioned meetings, we also took the opportunity to arrange visits from British Telecom re the telephone and Lander Alarms re the magnetic gate and door locks. Progress on the sailing support boat is still reasonably on time. s -3- SOSOTTI - which in Japanese doesn't mean a lot (Because it's not a Japanese word as far as I know) By the time you read this article, 'the season' will probably have already started and those few hardy souls who worked on their boat during the recent ice-age will, no doubt, have taken part in the first rites of the Spring Points Series. As I sit here writing this in front of a roaring (gas) fire, all those house-hold jobs I put off last season seem a more attractive proposition than painting boats in cold garages. Those of you with long memories and time to read the whole of Navigans might remember a few seasons ago that I was allowed to use our front room to store the Mirrors over winter. Now Maggie has got this funny idea that the room ought to be put to some 'good use'. Consequently, Mirrors are ‘out! (or rather never 'in') and the room houses a (mini) snooker table, Maggie's sewing machine (courtesy of Japan) and a whole load of junk (mostly mine so I am told). However, it is not the purpose of this article to reveal all that goes on in the Boreham household. - you'll have to buy the unexpurgated paper-back to discover that. No - the purpose of the above rambling is~ just an excuse to ask those who race , and those who race officer, to perform a few simple tasks to make life easier all round. Helms - please ensure you sign on with your name. The boat number, ot simply "Fred, does not mean a lot to me. If you can't remember who you are, how do you expect me to know? Besides in the interests of safety both the Race Office and 0.0.0. must be certain who you are in case you run into trouble on the water. Apart from that you might qualify for a prize sometime. Crews - the same goes for you. Don't forget, it's not the helm who gets all the glory. You earn points in your own right towards the prize for winning crew, irrespective of whether you sail with the same helm all season or not. Race Officers - please, please, fill in all details on the Signing On sheet. It's not too difficult to discover what race it is supposed to be or the approximate wind strength; at the very least you ought to know what the course is - after all, you set it ! However, of more importance is the requirement to time-in all boats in all races - not just the handicap races. The information is wanted to try and work out some ‘personal handicap' numbers. Signing Off or Retiring - don't forget to ‘sign off' at the end of the race. If the Race Officer has forgotten to put out a Signing Off sheet, then get one out of the folder yourself. If you retire before the end of a race, apart from signing off please let the Race Officer know before you go off for your pleasure sail (or go home). If the R.O. doesn't know you have retired, he might think you are 'missing, feared drowned' even in the calmest weather. So what does SOSOTTI mean ? - I'm not sure, but I think it means: SO - Sign On (that means both helm and crew) SO - Sign Off (or you will automatically be disqualified) TTI - Time Them In (please Mr/Mrs/Ms Race Officer, time in all boats in all races, not just the handicap class). Best wishes for a good sailing season to one and all. hike Boreham sesults Secretary fOR SALE OKTFPER 14. Trolley. Sails. Oars. Anchor. Life jackets, £325.00 Contact R.
