KRKKKKKKKKK To which the time honoured answer is 'not a lot' (Paul Daniels has much to answer for). The alternative title offered for this article is more likely to be your reaction after you've read the article itself, even supposing you get beyond the first bit about ‘Revised Yardstick Numbers according to Mike'. It all started when I got a message to the effect that I was supposed to ‘analyse the '85 handicap race results and work out revised Portsmouth Yardstick Numbers ready for a BJRC management meeting: Never having met this request before, I didn't have a clue of where to start, so I did what I normally do when I pick up a good book I haven't time to read; that is, I glance at the lst page, ‘ read the last page, and skip the bit in the middle. In other words, I went straight for the solution, Revised Yardstick Numbers according to Mike (a) Races considered were: ed the 4 races in the 1985 August Bank Holiday Handicap Series - the 4 races in the 1985 Autumn Points Handicap Series. (b) Using Phil Gray as my 'base' for the Bank Holiday Series results and Derek Webb as my ‘base! for the Autumn Series results, I worked out for each race what handicap all the other boats would individually have needed to finish in the same covrected time as the 'base' boat. (c) the resulting 'revised' handicaps for the individual boats were then plotted for each class and, after eliminating very extreme results (ie. the very slow boats) a line was drawn through the plotted points to produce what appeared to be a reasonable 'mean' handicap number (no doubt, the more scientific readers will wince at my layman's ignorance of mathematical methods). (d) the results are recorded in the Table below as 'Mike's Revised PYN'. Revised Yardstick Numbers (RYA Method) (a) Races considered were the 4 races in the 1985 August Bank Holiday Handicap Series only. (mainly because’the fun was beginning to wear off a bit). (b) the revised PYNs were then calculated according to the RYA method - or at least to my interpretation of the RYA booklet (the fun was definitely wearing off). In effect, the method eliminates the ‘slow boats' by considering the top two-thirds of each race only. (c) the results are recorded in the Table as 'Revised PYN (RYA Method). Revised Yardstick Numbers (RYA Method - slightly fiddled). Same races, same basic RYA method but all boats considered (fed up; wish I hadn't started - but duty to MSC triumphs in the end). The results are recorded in the Table as 'Revised PYN (Fiddled)'. NB. ON THE ASSUMPTION THAT SUE WILL NOT WANT TO RE-TYPE ALL THIS, YOU'LL FIND THE TABLE ON THE NEXT PAGE. MSC-DOC-1986-03-moorings-guidance.pdf: MOORINGS 1986 The following is an attempt to overcome the problems associated with the laying moorings in 1985; mainly C row stretched out almost to Stone, buoys sinking etc. Dave Thomas undertook to do a survey at the end of 1985. This confirmed that C row has a fairly constant depth. A and B rows however get significantly deeper towards Stone. So to allow for this please note the changes to recomended bridle lengths etc. Below is a sketch using B1 and B2 as an example. For laying purposes the buoy will be lashed directly to the bridle. This will guarantee slack in the bridle and enable accurate positioning. Issue 4 7.1.86 Marconi Sailing Club Code of Practice for Launching and Recovery of Cruisers Large Boats - Boats above 27ft. length will not be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. Tractor - Only to be operated by authorised drivers. Winches - When dinghy events are in progress the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies. The O.O.D. will be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for the information of dinghy sailors At other times the following code should be observed: When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed. Avoid sharp bends in winch cables-shackles must be used for attachment to trolleys. DO NOT shackle winch wire back on itself. It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strong team of helpers. If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the boat owner must provide a rope or cable of suitable strength and sufficient length that the tractor may remain level and always clear of loose shingle. Boat Trolleys - If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to other boats. Authorised tractor drivers and winch supervisors. COMMODORE'S REPORT This month I am writing to you later than usual as the Easter Weekend caused us to delay the Main Committee Meeting to 8th April. I was hoping that by now we would at least have experienced some reasonable weather. However, on the brighter side, we have again made good progress with jobs at the Club, and I consider us to be in good shape for the sailing season. The Solo Party held on Saturday 22nd March was an outstanding success and I sincerely hope that we may see many more similar functions. The following day we held the Working Party which was well attended and achieved much progress despite the awful weather - Arthur Hodges and his team even started work on the base for the new diesel store. Murray Bates and I have visited the boat builder to inspect the sailing support boat and we are delighted with the quality of the workmanship - it should be finished within one week of the time of writing, undergo sea trials on Saturday 12th April and be delivered to Stansgate by Saturday 19th April. The only jobs for us will be to fit the radio, then antifoul and launch. Sheila Wade and helpers must be congratulated on what was a superb Fitting-Out Party on Saturday 5th April - most members entered into the spirit of the Fancy Dress. MR.N.F.TOVEY, NAVAL DIVISION, M BLOCK, WRITTLE ROAD WORKS. continued ...

I wish to take this opportunity to thank personally all the many members who have now responded to George Robinson's questionnaire. The replies were discussed at the last Main Committee Meeting and we are very pleased that the consensus of opinion is in favour of our endeavours with respect to the improvement of facilities at Stansgate. Many members have requested that we try to extend the camping period and in this direction we will once again contact the local authorities to see if this is possible. We have also decided to reinstate a Club/Fun Day and introduce something special for the forthcoming Royal Wedding which luckily falls within Camping Week. On 10th May we are holding a New Members' Evening, similar to that held last year. The members of all committees will be pleased to welcome all new members and those who joined throughout 1985. Membership renewal is very promising - we are hoping to keep levels at least in line with 1985. Hopefully, by next month I will be able to confirm to you that the proposed extended bar and snack service at the Club will be effective from Friday 27th June through to the end of August. The bar will be open on Friday and Saturday evenings up to 11.00 p.m. and Sunday evenings up to 8.00 p.m. Bar snacks will be available at all times. I hope that you will support Allan's efforts and bear with any initial problems that might occur. N.T. Pembleton Treasurer

SAILBOAT '86 The Club put on a stand at Sailboat '86 again this year. The exhibition at Crystal Palace attracted over 10,000 visitors and was opened by Prince Andrew, who toured round the show. CRUISING IN COMPANY There is no Sailing Regatta at the Club this year and our Fleet Captain had hoped to organise a cruise to St. Katherine's Yacht Haven, London, to cover the Spring Bank Holiday weekend. Unfortunately, there are no berths available over that period, so this idea will have to be put off for the time being. continued ...

However, there is no reason to abandon the idea and, if there is sufficient ‘ interest, the trip can be made later in the year. In the meantime, there could be some form of Cruiser Rally over the Spring Bank Holiday weekend, which can be continued into the following week for those members who have the available time. The suggestion is that Cruiser members and their crews meet at the Clubhouse at about 8.00 p.m. on Friday 23rd Ma , when a destination can be agreed. With at least three days available, this could be the River Swale, Medway or any of the Essex/Suffolk waterways. Subject, of course, to weather, the Walton Backwaters would make a good destination as there will be ample moor- ings available at the Titmarsh Marina or there is good free anchorage. The steward at the Walton and Frinton Sailing Club is prepared to make an evening meal for under £3.00 a head and these could be booked prior to leaving the Club. Once the decision as to destination has been made, details of the passage can be discussed for the benefit of members with limited experience and any mis-— givings hopefully resolved. One of the aims would be to encourage members new to cruising and draw on the vast experience of others within the Club. In practice, as we all know, boats would not be Sailing abreast or immediately behind or in front of one another, but there should always be a friendly vessel in sight throughout the passage. The actual cruise, rally or whatever we call it would commence on Saturday 2'th May, time depending on destination. I envisage that some members will have to be back for Monday evening, ready to start work the following day, whilst others may decide to extend the weekend. This can be talked through on the Fridey eve- ning and of course anyone who cannot make the evening meeting but would like to participate by arriving in time for the departure on the Saturday can telephone the Clubhouse for particulars during the evening, This form of activity is commonplace in many sailing clubs and it would be very nice if this cruise proves to be the first of many. There is such a large range of Cruisers at the Club and it would be nice to say that anyone would be welcome, but I do not think that this would be practical. I suggest for this particular weekend that the participating boats should be capable of maintaining at least 4 knots under power. If anyone would like to make any suggestions or raise any point in connection with the above, please contact me, either at the Club or at my home telephone number. “whilst it is not essential, I would at the same time apprecia to some indication of the response. Arthur Hodges Tel. C'ford [redacted] CRUISER MOORINGS Last year, as in previous years, a number of moorings dragged and the presence of barnacles on the anchor flukes indicated that the anchors had landed on the bottom with the flukes uppermost. The weight of the ground chain holds the boat and it is only in strong conditions that the problem is apparent. I have spoken to members of the Chelmsford Diving Club and they are prepare d to visit the Club to check individual moorings. It will require at least two divers for safety and one would swim down the scope to follow the ground chain continued

- 7 - to each of the two anchors. The points of the flukes would be correctly positioned and bedded as far as possible. The main thing is that the flukes would be the correct way. There are of course expenses and the charge would be £3.00 per complete mooring, irrespective of position. This is payable by the individual and I expect that the job will be done sometime towards the end of April. If you want your mooring checked, please let me know. I will then supply the Diving Club with a numbered list of the moorings to be checked and receive back a list when the job is done. Arthur Hodges Tel. C'ford [redacted] ... CRUISER FLEET NEWS By the time you read this, the season will have started and, hopefully, the winter forgotten. Words of warning. Last season we had a case of one member using another member's mooring. His boat broke loose and caused damage to other craft. His Insurance Company took action against the owner of the mooring for all damage done. This could have been quite nasty but for the expertise of another member of the Club, who saved this from succeeding. Moral. If you pick up someone else's mooring, you are responsible for all eventualities, not the owner of the mooring. The Marine Police are introducing a scheme for reducing thefts et cetera from boats. It is called Marine Watch and a copy will be attached to the back of this issue (Ed's note: I hope). Anyone interested should fill in the form and return it to me or the Marine Police. John Wade Fleet Captain [redacted] ... CRUISER RACING It seems as if, suddenly, the season is upon us again and, for those interested in racing cruisers - judging from reading David Harper's comments in last month's Navigans about his new Pandora - it will be a competitive one. I would like to encourage all cruiser owners either fancying racing competition on the odd occasion or as a regular thing, to join the B.J.R.C. this year. Their registration fee has risen in 1986 from £3.00 to £5.00 to cover increased printing and postage costs, but for this you get a Year Book which will include all details of the racing programme, plus details of each race result soon after the event. There are no extra entry fees and all the races are local, so therefore do not involve travelling problems. Six Marconi members registered with the B.J.R.C. last year and, if you are interested this year, I shall require the owner's name, address and telephone number, plus the boat name and class or make, together with your sail number and PY handicap if known. We have some good new sailors joining the fleet; Phil Gray is selling his Hornet and will look for a Solo; Malcolm Gandy had bought John Murphy's boat to return to the sailing scene; Colin Willsmore is a new face who we are pleased to welcome; George White has bought Bob Anderson's old boat; and the one-third owner of the red and white boat is Mr Weston. We had a pleasant evening at Marie and Dennis Dear's house in February, which made a nice break despite the snowy weather. In January, Bob Anderson arranged with Dick Batt to give a winter talk, which he did with great enthusiasm. Recently, Malcolm Stuart organised a fleet party at the Club. This was a ‘great success, due to much hard work by Malcolm. The Solo helms cooked the meal and, as for as I am aware, everybody is fit and well! The highlight of the evening was a Victorian melodrama featuring that dastardly fiend, Sir Mountifield Dickbatt! On the sailing scene, four Solos went to the first Open Meeting of the year at Chess Sailing Club. It was a very good turnout, but the Marconi results were not of the highest order. It must be said, however, that there were seven or eight helms present who had been in the top ten in the Nationals in the past two years. Ron Greygoose was the top Marconi helm, with his new Batt sail looking good for the new season. Happy sailing. In October last year I came to the conclusion that, unless I did something soon about the paint flaking off my boat, then by next season there would be none left at all! So, one cold October evening, I set to work in the garage with an electric paint stripper. It shouldn't take too long, I thought; after all, most of it is flaking off anyway. Some hope! later Several hours and with only a small indent made into the wood, I realised that I had under- taken a longer job than I had first anticipated. Why didn't I buy a G.R.P. Mirror? It was around Christmas when I finally had the hull filled, sanded and generally ready to paint. I decided that, as Spring was on its way, with bright flowers and sunshine, black was the colour to have. So TI returned to the garage with continued .....

- 10 - a new brush and a couple of cans of International's best black. Halfway through February and after four months of working in a freezing cold garage, (I think I've got frostbite!) I finally had it finished. Okay, so it has a couple of runs and it's a bit blotchy, but it's finished now and that's that! Having consulted the Mirror Year Book and fixed up a crew, I decided that it was time to hit the water and the Bough Beech Open would be the boat's proving ground. So, on March 23rd, I set off with Nigel and the dad to Kent. I'm beginning to think it wasn't such a good idea. After getting up at 6.15 a.m., we arrived only to find the gates locked and nobody about - the first start was an hour later than I had thought! Eventually someone showed up and let us in, only for us to find a howling gale sweeping across the reservoir. The three races turned out to be survival lessons and, in the first race, after a broad spinnaker reach, we came to a sticky end, upside down in a bit of a vicious squall. After two races spent freezing at the back of a quickly diminishing fleet (20 boats in 1st race, 9 in 2nd!), we had had enough and decided to retire for the day without any idea of whether the boat was going any better than last year - the peak of which was an amazing 41st at the Nationals! But don't let me put you off visiting the local Opens - how could I? It is a lot of fun and does your sailing a lot of good to get amongst larger fleets and harder competition. I intend to visit a number of Open Meetings this year and hope that some other (keen and adventurous - there must be some!) Mirror sailors will join me. 4 a SAILING INSTRUCTIONS RULES Races will be sailed under the rules of the |.Y.R.U., R.Y.A., and class associations, except as provided for by these sailing instructions. The R.Y.A. prescription to |.Y.R.U. Rule 57 (leaving boat) shall not apply. The 720° turns penalty as provided in Rule 72.4, Alternative Penalties, and Appendix 3 of the yacht racing rules shall apply, instead of disqualification, for infringement of a rule of Part IV. COURSE INSTRUCTIONS Details of courses will be available at the club house at least one hour before the start of the race, but may be varied as above. STARTING LINE The starting line is the continuation of a line between the triangle on the racebox and the mete on the foreshore. When starting, boats must sail a course which passes between the mark D, and the mete, unless the letter ‘L’ is displayed after the course sign, when the boats must sail a course which passes between the mark No. 1 and the mark D. FINISHING LINE The finishing line is the line between the triangle on the racebox and the mark D. (There is no long line finish) PERSONAL BUOYANCY Personal Buoyancy shall be taken and must be worn by the helmsman and crew when the red flag ‘B’ is flown from the Club House, Cadets (under 18) must wear buoyancy at all times afloat. SIGNING ON Starters must sign on, at the Club house, on their Class Declaration form not earlier than 1 hour and not later than 15 minutes before each scheduled start. If you do not intend to start, please indicate this before the start. SIGNALS Flags flown from racebox masthead refer to the whole racing programme. Flags flown from racebox yardarm refer to individual races. All racing signals will normally be made from the racebox in accordance with |.Y.R.U. Rule 4 but Postponement (Answering pennant) Abandonment,- (flag N) and Buoyancy to be worn (flag B) signals flown from the Clubhouse also apply to racing and will not necessarily be duplicated at the racebox. Flags to be used for each Class of dinghy will be displayed at the Clubhouse. For International and National Classes the Warning Signals will be as prescribed by the R.Y.A. RECALLS : Rule 8.2(b) will apply and no recall numbers will be displayed. If any part of a competing boat is over the starting line when the signal to start is made, another sound signal will be made and the class flag will be left flying at the dip, until the boats over the line have returned to the satisfaction of the Race Officer, or until such time as he sees fit. For a general recall the false start will be the 10 minute warning signal for the new start, unless other races are starting within 10 minutes, when the start of the last race will be the five minute preparatory signal for the new start. Rule 51.1(c) will apply after general recalls. 10. SHORTENED COURSE When the shortened course signal is displayed at the racebox. the race will end when the leading boat, continuing round the course, next crosses the finishing line. To inform the police or the liaison persons of any suspicious activity. 4. To make everyone more aware of local crime problems and more security conscious about their own boats. What's in it for me ? COMMODORE'S REPORT On behalf of the Committee I feel we must apologise to all our active racing dinghy members for the late delivery of the sailing support boat. As you will know, the building programme was virtually on schedule and we expected to conduct sea trials on Saturday 12th April. Since then, now four weeks ago at the time of writing, we have been plagued with petty excuses for non-completion. On Friday 2nd May, Murray Bates and Peter Clayton visited Deal - yet another abortive trip as the propeller was supplied with the wrong internal taper. On Saturday 10th May Peter and I arrived at Deal at 9.30 a.m. ready for the sea trials at 11.00 a.m. On entering Brian Corey's yard, the "Jack B" looked most impressive; the engine was running very quietly and with little vibration. Almost unbelievable, I thought. Then the bad news - it would only idle and not rev. The morning was spent fault-finding and on the telephone to Geoff Josey, our Ford diesel engine expert. Despite all efforts, we eventually gave up at 2.30 p.m. Geoff Josey will no doubt solve the problem. Sea trials will hopefully be midweek and delivery to Stansgate prior to the week-end of 17th May. On Saturday 10th May we held the New Members' Evening, which was well attended. I was very pleased to see so many new and very interested members - let's hope we can now re-establish some enthusiasm particularly in dinghy sailing activities. continued ... Maureen Ball SOLO NEWS Well done, folks. We were in to double figures (11) on Sunday 1st June, not only on the water but sailing the full course! Now the Open Meeting. We had a turnout of 21 boats, rather less than I expected, probably due to the rough weather on Sunday deterring some of the Fishers Green people and some of the new Soloists from Halfway and Upriver. The best thing about the weekend was the superb organisation by the Mirror Fleet with very limited resources. Galley, Rescue and race facilities all worked well. Thank you very much, all of you, especially the Battles and the Borehams. The weather was kind to us, giving a varied selection of conditions from the nearly sublime to the nearly ridiculous. The meeting was won by Tony Cook from Littleton S.C., although he lives on the South Coast near Hythe. The best Marconi boat was John Rutherford in 6th place - well done, John. Don't forget the Solo Fleet Barbecues (anybody and everybody welcome) on 22nd June and 13th July and the team racing on the latter. Other dates for your diary:- 5th/6th July is the Halfway Y.C. Open Meeting at Southend. The Solo Inland Nationals is at Former Reservoir near Oxford on 28th/29th June. The Nationals is a three day, six race event this year on 18th/19th/20th July at Lee-on-Solent. The secondhand boat market is looking good if you're selling; Dennis Dear sold his boat on the first day it was in Yachts and Yachting. Any readers wishing to sell, please contact me first as we have several people looking for boats. Also, we had a visit from an ex-Soloist from Dabchicks S.C. continued ...

- 4 - at West Mersea. He was looking for a boat and feels there could be a resurgence of interest in the class at Dabchicks. Barry Peters and a couple of colleagues from Halfway went to the Solo Teach-In week at the National Sailing Centre at Cowes. He thoroughly enjoyed the intensive week and would recommend it. Start saving for next year. Roger Smith MIRROR FLEET NEWS I understand that it is customary in many organisations to put new members through some from of initiation ceremony. Twelve months ago, as new members launching a new boat, we capsized in two feet of water. This year, as co-opted Fleet Captain, I had the dubious task of arranging the fleet's duties for the first Open Meeting! What next, I ask myself! Fortunately for me, the Mirror Fleet rose to the occasion for the Solo and Dart Open weekend. Thanks to many of the longer-serving members, my job was made easier. It would take a whole Navigans to thank everyone in person for their particular role, but I must mention a few. Mike Boreham, Robbie Simms and Mike Turner had the unenviable task of keeping two contrasting fleets happy in differing weather conditions. Ably assisted by the Fleet Captains, however, I think they were able to please the majority if not everybody, which I gather is par for the course. With nearly 40 boats on the water, Committee boats were necessary and it was good of John Hooper and Dave Stewart to give up their time over a Bank Holiday weekend. To all the ladies who kept both sailors and spectators fed and watered - many thanks for all your hard work. The Mirror Fleet has to rely heavily upon the younger-members-of-the-family sailors. Neil, Damian, Lucy, Richard and Alison did more than their fair share of work over the weekend and helped enormously in a multitude of activities. I said at the beginning of this article that I would not mention everyone and already it reads like the speech after an Oscar award, but I think it serves to show how much I, and probably many others, take for granted the work required to provide for a special weekend event. Enough of the commendations - what about the sailing? It was great to see so many boats on the water again at Stansgate and the Bank Holiday's weather certainly provided the thrills and spills to make it entertaining both on and off the water. The Mirror Fleet start to the season has been somewhat slow in terms of red sails on the water. The Spring Points have almost been and gone with Mirrors only racing in the final 4 or 5 races. I know that many Mirrors are still undergoing winter overhauls and that some of the newer members have yet to embark upon racing. The future promises a return to the regular 8 or 9 Mirrors racing each Sunday. Even "Battleship" hasn't seen much action yet - 4 reaches across the estuary and two dramatic capsizes do not amount to a great deal of sailing action! Finally, there is the call to ALL members of the Mirror Fleet to help with at least two duties throughout the year. Please ring me on Chelmsford [redacted] if you can help in any way. Mike Battle

- 5 - Excuse me Sir - your Personal PYN is showing or What your best friend will be too embarrassed to tell you. Now I know the meaning of being 'hoist by his own petard' ; just as I thought nobody, but nobody, was interested in Personal PYNs, some clown decides to ask me when the results are going to be published. I suppose some might say I'm the bigger clown for suggesting it in the first place and I guess they're right. Things are not helped very much by the fact that my own Personal PYN looks distinctly sick -- as I said , hoist by his own petard (or is it 'on' his own petard - what is a petard anyway ?). After juggling with the Personal PYN 'rules' and rehashing the 'method', a result of sorts has been achieved. So, for what it's worth, the table below sets out, for all to see, the horrible truth about the Solo fleet. Why the Solo fleet you ask ? Well, they seem to be the only fleet to sail regularly. Apart from that, I reckoned if they're hard enough to go 'frost-biting' then they're hard enough to suffer the ignominy of public exposure of their PYN. Now to the table - if we start out on the basis that virtually nobody sails to their PYN standard, then we're halfway to understanding the table. To make it easy, we assume that only one person (ie. the person who finishes 3rd on corrected time) actually sails up to the class PYN standard. That obviously means that the two who finished in front of him/her must have sailed better than the standard whilst those behind clearly did not achieve such excellence.(it gets worse as we proceed). Let the doubters consider - if we all sailed to the class standard, we'd finish in a gigantic dead-heat. For any one race, each elapsed time was compared to the corrected time of the person who came third and this produces a unique PYN for that race for each competitor. This is added to the aggregate of previous unique PYNs calculated , divided by the number of races (+1) considered and a new personal PYN is the result. In the table: Column 1 = standard class PYN attributed to all before they compete, or complete, a race Columns 2-5 = Easter Series Columns 6-14 = Spring points races (except 9 & 10 which were not timed) Columns 15-16 = 'Psuedo-races' based upon the combined Handicap, Mirror and Solo fleets who competed in Spring 13 & 14, having sailed the same course in the same conditions. The Table: Helm - R1 - R2 - R3 - R4 - R5 - R6 - R7 - R8 - R9 - R10 - R11 - R12 - R13 - R14 - R15 - R16 D.Nixson - 122 - 122 - 118 - 118 - 120 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 123 - 124 - 126 - 127 R.L.Smith - 122 - 121 - 121 - 118 - 116 - 116 - 116 - 116 - 117 - 116 - 116 - 116 - 116 - 116 - 117 - 117 M.Stuart - 122 - 132 - 132 - 132 - 132 - 131 - 129 - 128 - 128 - 128 - 128 - 128 - 129 - 129 - 130 - 131 R.Greygoose - 122 - 122 - 118 - 130 - 125 - 124 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 120 - 120 - 120 - 120 - 120 - 120 - 120 J.Walker - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 124 - 124 - 125 - 125 - 126 J.Salmon - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 125 - 125 - 125 - 124 - 125 - 124 - 125 - 124 - 124 - 124 - 125 R.Anderson - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 123 - 125 - 126 - 128 - 129 S.Rutherford - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 124 - 125 - 126 - 127 J.Rutherford - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 121 - 121 - 121 - 121 M.Gandy - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 123 - 124 - 124 - 125 - 126 - 127 C.Willsmore - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 - 122 NB. Where a helm has not taken part in, or completed, a race, it is assumed the unique PYN for that race is the same as his/her Personal PYN , and so the personal PYN doesn't change. This is fair enough since there is no evidence to show it has changed. EG. to date, Colin Willsmore hasn't completed a race

due to either not entering or due to retiring. Consequently, he retained the full class PYN of 122; this would obviously be a distinct disadvantage if the race results were calculated on the basis of the Personal PYN. The lesson is there to be seen - you must finish the races (ie be timed in) to get a more favourable personal PYN (unless you're the champion and you're then likely to find your PYN getting somewhat onerous as the season progresses). It is worth noting that a very good (or very bad) result has a more dramatic effect early in the season than it does later on in the year since those later in the year are masked by the aggregate PYNs of the past. A PYN which is rising with each subsequent race would suggest the person is sailing below (ie.worse) than the current personal PYN attributed to them. Conversely, a falling PYN indicates sailing better than the personal PYN. No prizes for guessing that a substantially unchanged PYN indicates you are sailing up to (your) standard compared to others in the list. Conclusion No conclusions . As with all handicapping systems, nobody is satisfied except the winner. One could argue the merits, or otherwise, of a particular handicap system for as long as it takes to find the QOD to put toilet paper in the ladies loo (I'm told it sometimes takes a very long time - or used ww to ). For those who think Gods smile on the virtuous, they can take comfort that they (the Gods) are falling about laughing as far as my personal PYN is concerned. From the sailing to date it appears that the Mirror fleet table looks like ; N.Salmon current personal PYN = 140 J.Rusbridge " ” "= 146 D.Dear 7 : "= 146 M.Battle " m "= 146 M.Boreham a m se (i5U D.Boreham " . "= 152 I reckon that's a bit hard seeing that I managed to come second to Neil Salmon in the only two races completed so far, and that Damian is the only other Mirror to have finished a race. The thing is, the personal PYN is not a measure of personal skill, only an indicator to past performance. Thus although Jack, Dennis and Mike did not finish a race, we continue to attribute the class PYN of 146 to them - because there is nothing to say it should be anything else.., Final comment. wy As an experiment, the Personal PYN had its interesting sidelights as I worked it out; however, should we use them for series racing ? Apart from the hassle, its not likely to win me many fiends (sorry) friends. After all, those with a low personal PYN will feel cheated whilst those with a high personal PYN will feel slighted. As I said before, only the winner will be happy. Mike Boreham Results Secretary

COMMODORE'S REPORT Unfortunately, due to situation still unexplained my last Navigans Report was not printed, despite writing it the evening before Pat and I departed for Spain! All is now calm so I will attempt to brief you on the main events since the May Navigans issue. The extended Bar and Galley service commenced on 30th May 1986, we have been very pleased with the general comments about the service and the interest shown by the membership. The Jack 'B' has been delivered and fitted out with Radio, VHF only at present as to date we have not been able to find a suitable C.B. system. My personal thanks to Murray, Peter, Robert, Geoff, Doug, Niel etc. for completing the task. I feel sure you will all be very pleased with the end result - I must admit the procurement did try our patience 'just a little'! MR.N.F.TOVEY, NAVAL DIVISION, M BLOCK, WRITTLE ROAD WORKS.

Mrs Connie Bigden has kindly agreed to formally launch the Jack B on Saturday 19th July at 12.00 noon at the Club and all Members are cordially invited to attend. The Solo/Catamaran Open Meeting was held during the Spring Bank Holiday weekend, 19 Solos and 15 Catamarans entered. In the main the event was organised by the Mirror Fleet who must be congratulated for the efficiency and smooth running of the event. I must take this opportunity to thank Mike and Janet Battle, Mike Boreham, The Simms Team at the race box and particularly all those involved with the Galley and with sailing support. The weather was very kind to us — we could not have ordered anything better. Now we must consider the format for next year and decide whether or not to revert back to our traditional Regatta. During the weekend a collection was organised for 'Sports Aid' - £50 was collected and paid in to National Westminster Bank, Great Baddow, The first draw of the 100 Club took place on Sunday lst June, the winners were Niel Pembleton £50 and Mike Boreham £5, The second draw was on Sunday 6th July and £5 was won by George Robinson. ed There are still plenty of tickets left so please complete your application form and send it to Alan Goss in order to qualify for next month's draw. (Ed's note: Form attached to April Navigans, and I'm told further forms available from the bar). Good progress to report regarding the sewerage scheme. Full details have been received from Effluent Engineering Contracts and approval should be forthcoming. The plans and estimate for the scheme have been passed to M.A.S.C. for approval and funding of the project, On Friday 25th July a team of sailors arrive from Qatar for the return challenge Sailing match. A series of races have been organised for Saturday 26th, Sunday 27th and Monday 28th July. Last year we lost the event so I am hoping to put matters to right this time, Looking forward to seeing you at the Barbecue, the Camping weeks, or during the Doha visit. David Harper * * * one Letter to: Marconi Sailing Club, Committee and Club Members. On behalf of my mother Connie, my brother Tim and his family, and myself and my family, I would like to thank everyone in the Marconi Sailing Club for their many good wishes and messages of condolence on the death of my father, Jack. We were particularly touched that so many of you could take the time to attend his funeral. Although she may not have been able to say it at the time, this meant a great deal to my mother and to the rest of us also, The Sailing Club meant a great deal to Jack, and I'm sure many of you have warm and sometimes humurous memories of him, Perhaps later you might wish to share some of them with Connie to add to her own. You all meant a great deal to Jack and we feel sure that he would appreciate your thoughtful gesture in naming the new rescue launch "The Jack B", Our thanks to Doug and Viv-(nee Hallam) Field for suggesting this. Although our family is now spread apart, we would like to feel we can continue with our association with the MSC, and Stansgate is the one place we like to visit on our visits home to England. Many thanks from all members of Jack's family. Sincerely, Julian Bigden, 2420 [redacted], Lancaster, PA 17601 May 28th 1986.

Roger Smith Saffron Walden [redacted] THE RIVER BLACKWATER If you've ever felt you'd like to know more about the River where you sail, I can recommend reading 'The Salty Shore' by John Leather. He writes of places so familiar to us by name such as Mersea, Bradwell, Tollesbury etc. A couple of years ago while visiting St Peter's Church by the sea wall at Bradwell we found a charming cottage nearby and wondered who it had once belonged to. It turns out that it was once lived in by a Walter Linnett, a professional wildfowler, and the last surviving one on the Blackwater by 1947. John Leather has also written an excellent book, '"Barges', about the sailing barges of South East England. We are still privileged with the frequent sight of these gracing our river and this book should be able to tell you all you'd want to know. In the Chelmsford library they can be found under the section 'Essex Books'., Maureen Ball

M.S.C. Spring Cruise On Friday 23rd May at 8pm several Cruiser members met in the Clubhouse to discuss 'Cruising in Company' as suggested by Arthur Hodges in the April edition of Navigans. Following a few drinks and a lot of chat, it was decided that we would head for Titmarsh Marina the next day. The wind came up in the night and it was none too comfortable on the moorings. We still had the high winds Saturday morning so a council was called ashore at llam and the decision made to sail down-river under head-sails, I was glad to be off; although I have not suffered the miseries of sea-sickness I was beginning to feel decidedly queasy, and some other crews felt the same way. Eight Cruisers left Stansgate between 12.15 and 12,30 and enjoyed a comfortable sail up the Wallet. Pye End is just one of the buoys we have trouble finding, but our boat, Veruna II, was saved from sailing into Harwich by the crew of Kellys Eye, 4.30 found us all at Titmarsh with Viridia aground in the entrance, but not long after there was enough water for all boats to enter, We were soon safely berthed, as crews helped each other with fending off and tying up. Everyone had a good night's rest, and Sunday morning was spent relaxing, pottering about on our boats. Ron decided to put his inflatable on the coach roof of Tekin Two, and the crews of Kellys Eye and Veruna II were engaged in the same task. Pete and Kelly were somewhat surprised to find a swordfish in their inflatable that they had been towing. I can't say I saw the fish, but can vouch they had not had a drink at that point in time. Unfortunately, Snoopy had a sick little boy on board which was rather worrying, but I am pleased to say he soon recovered. At 4pm the crews of Viridia, Kellys Bye, Tekin Two, Two Jays and Veruna II walked into Walton to be met at 6.30pm by the crews of Snoopy, Sandpiper, Olaf and ; Ebony Rose for dinner in the Walton and Frinton Sailing Club, We can all thoroughly recommend the cuisine at under £3 a head. After dinner, discussion was the laying of plans to sail to the Deben the following morning. Two Jays and Sandpiper could not stay any longer, so would be heading for home on the Momay morning. We bid them good night and safe journey, and I understand both crews had enjoyed cruising in company. 10am Monday mormming our flotilla of six were motoring out of the Marina, making for the Deben and the dreaded bar!! lpm found us at Felixtowe Ferry with every- one telling us that was the calmest they had ever known the entrance to the Deben,. I was pleasantly surprised, or more to the point relieved, after the tales I had heard. Tekin Two came on the radio, Ron and Joyce were enjoying their sail, and would meet us later, That later turned out to be the next morning! All the other vessels went on to anchor at the Rocks, but when the tide went out Veruna II was sitting high and dry on the shingle, so out came the bucket and brush for a scrub- down, It was a lovely, warm,calm evening so Arthur and Irene from Viridia, along with Pete, Kelly, Malcolm, Helen, their two children plus Malcolm and I, strolled down to the Ramsholt Arms. We managed a couple? of drinks and it was so pleasant getting to know one another. Coming back in the dark was good fun, Pete was telling me a creapy story which made me cry with laughter, not fright, sorry Pete! Arriving back at the Rocks we found Viridia with all her cabin lights on and it was suggested to Arthur that motoring up and down the river for 2 or 3 hours would charge the batteries, but I'm not sure he found this amusing, Sorry Arthur! Malcolm and I had to stay awake until 1.30 am until Veruna II came afloat so we could move her into deeper water. It was a dreadful night, every boat had a fair amount of anchor chain out but the wind was so strong the boats were swinging around and no-one managed to get much sleep. At the first light of day Viridia and Snoopy upped anchors and went on to Waldringfield. Veruna II had dragged her anchor, and was almost in mid-channel. Kellys Eye had anchored on the opposite shore and had spent a comfortable night. Here was a lesson to be learnt, Pete had experienced anchoring at the Rocks, so a

- 6 - knew what to expect. It had been such a calm evening we didn't listen to the voice of experience, but we will in future. Malcolm and Helen appeared on Olaf, they were heading back to Stansgate as they could stay no longer, but had told us the evening before how much they had enjoyed cruising in company and when would be the next event? We waved good-byp to Malcolm, Helen and their two little girls. At mid-day Kellys Eye and Veruna II left the Rocks to meet up with Tekin Two, Viridia and Snoopy at Waldringfield. Installation of Sewage Treatment Plant At long last we have obtained overall approval for the scheme. This involved the following clearances:- Maldon District Council Rivers & Waterways Committee - 12th April Maldon District Council - Building Regulation - 10th June Anglian Water Authority - Land Drainage Act - 26th June Maldon District Council - Town Planning Act - 1st July Anglian Water Authority - Control of Pollution Act - 20th August The approval under The Control of Pollution Act 1974 also grants the consent of the Ministry of Agriculture & Fisheries. A fixed price quotation of £11,899 excluding VAT has been accepted and I am now in possession of confirmation by Mr. G. Wignall, Club Manager M.A.S.C. that clearance by the M.A.S.C. General Committee should be obtained next week, and that work on the project will be started without delay. This problem has been very demanding of the Committees time. Moorings We now have approval from Maldon Distict Council for 12 additional moorings in the direction of Stone. These will cost approx £250.00 per annum. Herewith copy of report that appeared in the 'Daily Gulf Times' on August 23rd 1986. quote Marconi Sailing Club of Essex England won a recent racing competition for 420 and Laser class dinghies against Doha Sailing Association. The event was a return match as the Marconi Sailors had visited Doha in October 1985 when the visitors were defeated at West Bay. Marconi tactics were somewhat evident with a change of class in the single sailed dinghies from Laser to Solos. However DSA had ample chance to practise. With slack tide conditions for the first race, DSA were victorious in the 420 class but came second in the Solos. On the afternoon of the first day of the competition, strengthening wind and a rapidly rising tide created a new experience of the relatively "tide free" Gulf team, resulting in a defeat in both classes. Although two further races had been scheduled for the next day, the result of the first was in favour of Marconi who won the competition on aggregate points for the two classes. Sailing was concluded with a well organised but largely "rule free" fun race in which the DSA were winners. Prizes were presented by the club Commodores Mr. David Harper of Marconi and Sami Abu Shaikha of the DSA. Sami Abu Shaikha presented prizes to Marconi Sailing Club, provided by the Qatar Supreme Youth Welfare Council. A cup donated by TRAGS was also presented to David Harper. Sami Abu Shaikha then invited Marconi to return to Doha in 1987 for further team racing. Unquote I forgive the 'bias' of report and thank the Marconi team and all members associated with the event. I take this opportunity to personally thank Ron & Mary Greygoose who helped Pat and me with the planning and organisation and Malcolm Stuart who did a first class job as race officer and for organising the fun race. We now have a superb cup to add to our trophies. I have requested that the sailing Sub Committee decide upon an event to be associated with the trophy. 7. GENERAL I was disturbed to see one cruiser being taken from the water last weekend - lets hope for some reasonable weather to finish the sailing season. We have had some problems with regard to non attendance of an O.O.D. on two weekends. We appreciate the importance of this and have addressed the problem. John Weedon has highlighted some problems with regard to our dinghy racing acitivites. We are grateful for the comments and have organised action by our sailing sub committee. We now look forward to the Hornet/Dart open weekend and hopefully more Marconi sailing success. Hope to see you at the Club. David Harper Commodore

CRUISER NEWS It is quite a common sight to see cruisers anchored between Bradwell Power Station and the Baffle, and one of our new members decided to drop his hook there whilst he made a cup of tea, On leaving he found the anchor snagged and after a great deal’ of effort managed to get the anchor to the surface together with a very obvious Power Cable, He had no choice really but to pass a rope under the Cable whilst the anchor was released with a great sigh of relief, Yes! The Cable is live, I am told 415 volts, and there are notices on the land and on the Baffle, but thought I would mention the incident to prevent a recurrence, Cruiser Laying Up ‘I know it sounds early to think about laying up boats, but one boat is already out of the water and I expect others will soon follow, It is anticipated that extensive excavations will take place this Autumn and Winter when the new sewerage scheme starts and much of this will take place in the Cruiser Laying Up area. I mention this now as many members may not be able to park in their usual spot and some will even be outside the Cruiser Park, a There is a strong possibility that some places will be permanently lost,as the sewerage pipes may be near the surface and the ground in the vicinity will not stand the weight of a cruiser, If you do come out of the water before the plan is published then please do not jack up the trolley onto blocks — to permit movement of the unit if necessary. There is to be a drive to dispose of old trailers and boats with no record of membership which should help the space problem a little. Some members have purchased new boats during the season and the replaced boats are still in the park. If these boats are not removed by the end of the season please let me know early and I will endeavour to make some arrangements, Night Sailing I think most people who have sailed at night can recount some incident, and one gentleman from Brading Haven Yacht Club (I of W) reverted to verse, The following appeared in the Newsletter of the above club and I thought some of our members might appreciate it: When both lights you see ahead Port your helm and show your red, When to your starboard red appear ‘Tis your duty to keep clear But when upon your port is seen A steamer's starboard light of green, There ‘s not so much for you to do For green to port keeps clear of you, Green to green and red to red Perfect safety, go ahead, When in danger or in doubt Always keep a good look-out. When in danger with no room to turn, Ease her, Back her, GO ASTERN. —-000000-— Winter Meetings will be held in the Committee Rooms of the Main Club, Beehive Lane, Chelmsford, 7.30pm on the first Wednesday of each month, commencing WEDNESDAY 5th NOVEMBER 1986 Arthur Hodges Fleet Captain Chelmsford [redacted]

-3- CRUISER NEWS If this section of Navigans is to be interesting then I will require some assistance from members of the Fleet particularly in the supply of information, points of view and even what we are doing right or wrong. If there is something that you think the Section should be doing then let me know and if you do not want to go into print, then I will do it on your behalf. In the meantime, ever thought of writing a book or even an article? Well your chance has arrived. The idea is the continuing saga of the 'Travels of a Calor Gas Bottle'. Imagine the bottle travels on a boat to different parts of the world, making friends with other gas bottles, only eventually to run out of fuel. This could be anywhere, to be taken ashore, filled and shipped off in another boat or caravan. The potential for imagination is unlimited and could include the adventures of the boat or crew, seen through the context of this bottle. The ideas are yours. First installment by Dave Thomas of Marinero, to be followed by someone nominated by Dave (who must agree). So on and so forth. Why not be a little idiotic and use your imagination for the amusement of others? We may create a best-seller. One instalment each month with the contribution forwarded by the nominated writer to our Editor, Maureen Ball by the stated deadline. Thank you. -4- MOORINGS It was only a short time ago when the lifting of moorings on A, B and C rows was left to the discretion of the individual, until the number of boats going adrift in a season reached the unacceptable figure of fifteen. There was of course the resultant damage to innocent vessels and this year, due mainly to the mass lifting of the tackle, the number has been reduced to just two. The Moorings Committee members decided unanimously to once again lift all A, B and C row Moorings, and the dates for this are as follows: MOORING POSITION - LIFTING DATE - COMMENCING TIME A1 - A8 - 1 November - 2pm A9 - A16 - 2 November - 2pm C1 - C14 - 8 November - 7.30 am C15 - C26 - 9 November - 7.30 am – - 15 November, 16 November - To be used of problems encountered on previous dates. Commence 2pm. B1 - B10 - 22 November - 7am B11 - B20 - 23 November - 7am All Boat Owners with a Mooring on A, B or C rows please be at the Club at the Commencing Time to assist in lifting your mooring. HIGH PRESSURE WASHER This machine is working well and anyone requiring the use of it should obtain the permission of the O.O.D. There have been problems in the past due mainly to grit getting under the valves and this problem can be eliminated by connecting the water inlet pipe directly onto the supply hose. The Committee has asked me to emphasise that in no circumstances should the machine be operated with the inlet pipe sucking water from a reservoir, namely the large plastic tank on the hard. There were at least six abandoned trollies, some with broken steering, old lorry axles, punctured wheels and lots of other bits which some of us have had to move. 'Travels of a Calor Gas Bottle' Dave Thomas. What a holiday!! Two weeks in the Scottish Highlands sounded OK and the people looked nice but, oh dear, the weather was awful.. I was strapped to the front of a caravan and looked forward to some scintillating scenery, but beyond Watford Gap the heavens opened and remained that way. By the time we returned to Maldon I was exhausted and beginning to show signs of rust. Time for a re-charge and a general face-lift. I refer to myself as Dora - well Dumpy Dora actually, as my shape as a gas container has long been referred to as a 'Dumpy' by all the people I have worked for. Somehow I have been diverted since my recent service and now find myself highly charged and in company of other friends at a Yacht Chandler's in Bradwell. There is an atmosphere of anticipation and excitement but I am somewhat apprehensive at the prospect of what will be my first sailing trip. Indeed the thought of so much water brings on some painful memories, By Saturday however I have been exchanged and almost lovingly installed aboard the yacht 'Marinero'. I am impressed. The boat hardly rocks at all except when the elderly couple stumble aboard late at night singing some hit from the 1930s, From the final clinking of the Geneva bottle it seems no time before they are up and untying ropes. The engine has erupted and we are moving off into what looks like very deep water to me. After about an hour the engine stopned and I was disappointed that the journey was over so soon — but no, there is activity on deck and contrary to some of the rumours I had heard in Bradwell, sails were being hoisted. Three days later having touched down briefly in Ramsgate and Brighton we were in Cherbourg and the boat began to sink!! Well, it seemed like it to me as a constant procession of Frenchmen called out for Marinero and deposited box after box of what they referred to as ‘ship's stores' onto the deck and into the cockpit. Now I can tell you there was nothing edible in the whole consignment and either we were destined for a voyage well beyond my capacity or an army of guests were coming for a long stay. I was not aware at this stage of the drink problem called "Becketts" which emanated apparently from a travelling companion named 'Northerner'. In due course all stores were stowed reverently away and we sailed to Guernsey and thence to Lezardrieuy in northern Brittany. The river approach was magnificent scenery of steep rocky’ hills on both sides and without exception all the natives gave a friendly wave or call. My services were not called upon too much during the next few days as the owners were enjoying the gastronomic delights of true French cuisine ashore, About a week later we sailed north again in brilliant sunshine upwards but thick fog sideways and I for one was pleased to arrive in Jersey. 2 Although by now I was beginning to feel a little drained it was again a relaxing few days for me, Then we left for Cherbourg and I did not enjoy the conditions round the Cap de la Hague although I gather that 'those upstairs' judged it a good sail and celebrated in their normal manner. It was in Brighton that I had my first tummy rumble, that feeling of emptiness that signals the need for a re-charge. Before I could blink I was yanked roughly upwards and shaken and the adjudged to be fit for a bit longer, then dropped unceremoniously back in my box. contd...

5 There never is a convenient time for a gas bottle to run out apparently. Well, I won't be treated like that and I've learnt a trick or two over the years. That night the flag officers of alcoholics anonymous came over from 'Northener' and amidst the drinking there was obviously some attempt to cook dinner. I know because 2 gas rings, the grill and the oven plays havoc with my insides and ordinarily I would have quietly given in at this stage. Not this time though. I strained and sucked and held on until I could smell the pastry starting to rise and then I switched off. The singing eventually stopped and there was an awareness through the haze that all was not well in the galley - then came the language, totally unrepeatable, and from such nice ladies too. I chuckled then and I still do in my new paint, waiting at Dan Webb & Feezey for my next purchaser. Dumpy Dora. Ed. said: There have been several interesting sailing programmes on television during the past year, more than I can ever remember seeing in the past. At the time of preparing this Navigans is an interesting series on the forthcoming battle for the America's Cup in Australia. It is on Channel 4, 6.30pm Saturdays, and called the Great Australian Boat Race. There is some exciting filming of boats racing, and amusing reports of the razzamatazz on shore. B.B.C. Radio London, (1458kHz/206m 94.9MHz Stereo) is where you can find 'The Boat Show' - News from the water on the air, with John Murray. 6.30pm Fridays, 8.30am Saturdays. Featuring: Sailing Forecasts - Best Buys - Cross Channel News - Kit & Tackle Tips - Interviews - News & Reviews - Racing & Cruising.

COMMODORE'S REPORT - AGM 2nd November 1986 A year ago I was able to report that the MSC membership had been significantly increased during the 1985 season - I now have to inform you that despite all of our efforts, we have experienced a 4.2% decline. However it is with much pleasure that I am able to inform you that the majority of the problems previously highlighted to you have been addressed and resolved. Before talking about the events of this season, I must remind you that there is a national decline in dinghy sailing activities: in fact, some well established clubs have had no alternative but to close their dinghy sections. I feel sure that our success is based on maintaining varied interests and promoting a friendly and helpful atmosphere throughout the Club. We have achieved a better sense of belonging into the membership and made huge strides to unite our dinghy and cruiser sections. Incidentally, following the last AGM we wrote to the MASC confirming the two AGM proposals - Agenda Items 9.2 and 9.3 regarding: 1. Levy imposed upon MSC by MASC 2. The amendment to the rules to permit Associate Members to participate fully in the running of the Club, i.e. to become Flag Officers. Although no formal written answer was received, Gerry Wignall showed me copies of the MASC Committee Meeting minutes where discussion took place on this subject. The MASC ruling as interpreted by Gerry Wignall is that the Commodore, the Hon. Secretary and the Treasurer must be Ordinary members. This is now a subject to be steered and handled by your new Committee. From within our membership we again received requests for reduced subscription rates for retired members. This subject has been debated and agreed by your Main Committee and is tabled before you as a proposal today. You will also see proposals introduced to overcome certain other problems apropos Club operational management. The following comments relate to significant events in the 1986 season. I will avoid talking about the weather this of course, no doubt played a role with respect to the reduction in our membership levels. contd...

Sewerage I will not dwell on this topic as I have kept you informed through Navigans reports. We are pleased that at long last we have approval from the six authorities and that approval has been given by MASC, and work commences tomorrow, The project will be completed and working before the start of the 1987 season. The 1985 Laying-Up Supper at the County Hotel was a great success - all tickets being sold well before the event. Next followed the Christmas Working Party during which two of the scrubbing posts were replaced: a base was prepared for the new winch: part of the old sewerage herring—bone system was excavated; the Cruiser park was cleared and further Clubhouse decoration completed. We next addressed the problem of replacing the Sailing Support Boat. Although this was a tortuous exercise, we eventually took delivery and commissioned the boat in time for the more active part of our racing season, A competition was organised to name the new boat which was formally launched on Saturday 19th July 1986. Our next objective was to examine our position in order to maintain our membership level and establish our viability. We therefore debated ways of improving the appeal of the Stansgate site. A significant consideration was to those members and friends ‘left on the shore’, Initial suggestions were to build a verandah on the north wall of the Clubhouse and provide a 'play area’ for children. We also decided to consider catering and manning the bar on certain Friday, Saturday and early Sunday evenings. The play area was completed but the verandah project hit a snag when we were informed that due to the Thames Barrier Scheme it is planned to increase the height of the sea wall on the south bank of the River Blackwater by three feet. Our planning approval has been held up but the retiring Committee envisages that this is only a temporary hold and that approval and implementation of the project should be achieved in 1987, or 1988 at the latest. The Barn Dance held at the MASC on Saturday 25th January 1986 was another total sell-out and a very enjoyable event. Unfortunately we then had bad news with the sad and sudden loss of our dear friend and colleague, Jack Bigden a former Commodore, A new telephone was installed at Stansgate and a '100 Club' introduced. My thanks to Alan Goss for organising the Club. I will leave it to Niel to report on the Club —- if he has the courage! Personally I feel that the '100 Club‘ has been the best scheme I have ever joined! The Solo Fleet party was held on Saturday 22nd May 1986 - a super event. Pat and I feel all sections should consider a party. Maybe Malcolm Stuart could take on yet another job and become Party Manager. We are sure you would all enjoy them. The winter series of lectures were all very well attended despite the weather. Murray and I offer our sincere thanks to all the organisers, The Fitting Out Party on 5th April 1986 was exceptional with most members joining in the spirit of the fancy dress, Another success down to Sheila Wade and her team. Let us hope that we find another energetic replacement to follow Sheila's excellent term of office, On 10th May we held the New Members' Evening. This must now surely become an annual event. This year we had a cabaret provided by a flock of sheep! The stage was the dinghy park and there was quite a remarkable performance by a number of animals on Malcolm Stuart's Solo. This was to the delight and amazement of our new members and Committee members alike — Malcolm was not so delighted!

Our extended bar and snack service commenced on Friday 30th May 1986, and on balance is considered by the retiring Committee to have been an overwhelming success. I feel sure that the membership will all join me in thanking June and Robert for the excellent and much appreciated service. Unfortunately, June and Robert will not be able to help us next year, so I appeal to you all for volunteers. Bank Holiday Weekend 25th - 26th May brought the Catamaran/Solo Open Meeting, an alternative to our normal Regatta, Fifteen Catamarans and nineteen Solos entered, the event being very well run, mainly by the Mirror Fleet. During the weekend we collected £50 for the Sport Aid Fund, The next Committee will have to decide upon the formula for next year. I feel that our active dinghy members will plan fora Regatta revival, probably in 1988. Mrs Connie Bigden formally launched the'"Jack B." - Doug Field won the prize for naming the boat. His suggestion was supported unanimously by the Main Committee. On 14th June the team from Rochester visited us - at least MSC won, if only by a narrow margin, It is unfortunate that Jack Pateman will not be able to attend our forthcoming Laying-Up Supper .... something about "he who laughs last..." remembering his comment to me when Rochester won the previous year, The Cadet Week followed by the Camping Week, 18th - 26th July was again very popular this season - my particular thanks to Derek Hall, our Cadet Skipper, for all of his efforts, energy and enthusiasm, On 19th July of that week we had the Barbecue —- an excellent evening, a record attendance and thoroughly enjoyed by all concerned, Let us hope that the verandah project is completed without too much delay as this should also reduce the burden of setting up the Barbecue bar. On Friday 25th July 1986, the Doha team arrived and, as I have recently reported fully in the September issue of Navigans, I will only remind everyone here that MARCONI WON and that we have been invited back to Doha next year for another return match. Our future Projects are: 1. Road resurfacing. 2. Repairs to the Hard. 3. Implementation of the verandah project. 4. Improvements to the catering facilities. 5. Re-examination of all aspects of site security. To complete my report, I must inform you that Murray Bates has declined the nomi- nation of Commodore. I confess that I was deeply disappointed and concerned when ke informed me of his decision only a few weeks ago. Murray and I and the Executive Committee had formed a very good working relationship and at last were realising the rewards of our efforts. We felt that most of our problems were over and that the way ahead had been paved for a good future of the MSC and a sensible term of office for Murray. I respect Murray's reasons for not continuing and am delighted that he has agreed to accept nomination for Vice-President. At least we can now rely upon his continuing. interest albeit not as active as in the past, Peter Clayton had previously agreed with me to complete this year's term of office and then retire from the Executive Team, As usual, Peter has very kindly helped us out by agreeing to stand as Vice-Commodore for one year, with George Robinson acting as his assistant. George is very capable and has been a most active member of Committee. I hope to see him as Vice-—Commodore in the not too distant future, Our main problem was to find a new Commodore. Murray, Peter, Pat Black, Neil and I are indebted to Robbie Sims for agreeing to accept nomination. Robbie is a well established member of the Club am was Vice-—Commodore in 1962 when the Club was at Heybridge. Also he was instrumental in the procurement of our present site. We have had to introduce a rule change to allow Robbie to become Commodore - this is included in your AGM notice. CONTD...0.0:0:6

A final note is to thank everyone for supporting me during my two years as your Commodore. My thanks are extended to the MASC, particularly Tony Mayhew and Gerry Wignall, who unfortunately are not present today. ---- And a very special "Thank You" to Pat (my wife) for her tireless support, encouragement and understanding. However we have failed to achieve the budgetted surplus for the year of £4000.00. In practice it appears at present that the surplus will only be £2300.00 approx.. Looking at the individual accounts, the noticeable failures to achieve budget were:- CLUBHOUSE This was due to the heavy expenditure on sewage disposal, approx £750.00 during the year. However the new phone must have been working better as the income has more than doubled. SAILING The expenditure includes the first purchase of diesel and the fitting out of the JACK B. The income has mainly come from the fees charged during the Camping Fortnight. The Sailing Sub Committee have done well to contain the expenses in view of the late delivery of the JACK B. SOCIAL An excellent result with an increased profit due to the efforts of Sheila and the support of the membership at the events. NAVIGANS The increased expenditure has largely been due to higher printing and postage costs. OPEN MEETINGS Again an increased profit due both to the organisers and the support by people attending. SUBSCRIPTIONS This has been slightly disappointing. The failure to increase the income

13 results from a slight drop instead of an increase in the membership. Hopefully the proposed increases in next years rates will not deter members and we can continue our efforts to expand the numbers. RATES As you are aware the block mooring fee was renegotiated during the year and an increase of 33% is likely. This increase relates to the figure at the commencement of the last five year period. GALLEY and BAR The analysis of these figures is particularly hard. This is caused by a number of factors. Firstly there is the lost income of the Regatta Weekend to consider which is estimated to have cost about £1800.00 in profit. Secondly the experiment of the Galley opening has cost Galley profit, however the better use of the Club on Fridays and Saturdays has contributed to the Bar profit. RESERVE ACCOUNT MOVEMENT The original budget for the year anticipated a Capital spend of £2500.00 approx. This was overspent by £1500.00 mainly on the opportunity to purchase the farm equipment from Osea, the necessity to put Roll over cages on the tractors and the Scrubbing posts platform. In addition we failed to budget for the trailer for the JACK B. Generally I believe that we contiue to have a healthy situation and that the Reserve will increase during next year. Looking forward to next year, the M.A.S.C wrote to us in April and asked us to budget for a contribution of £5250.00 compared with £5000.00 this year. The Committee accepted this figure. However the basis of the contribution is still the subject of negotiation to determine the ground rules for the years after next. During next year there are a number of projects which may be able to proceed if the budget allows. These may include the provision of a CB radio system with a semi portable unit, the construction of the veranda, etc.. In addition both the Road and Hard are in need of repair, however the expenditure on these last two items is part of the discussion on the contribution to the M.A.S.C.. The ONE HUNDRED CLUB at present has a membership of 17 and needs at least 25 to break even. It will therefore be necessary to subsidise the prizes from the general club funds unless there is a sudden increase in membership.

Solo News The Fleet AGM was held on 14th November with 11 members attending. Roger Smith resigned his fleet captaincy because of his new appointment as Sailing Secretary of the Club. During Roger's term of office the fleet activity has increased as has the membership and he deserves most of the credit for this happy state of affairs. His energy, enthusiasm and constant good humour has been an example to all, and deserves our sincere thanks. I was elected as the new Fleet Captain and have resigned from the Main Committee as a result. This meant that a new Committee member was needed to represent Associate Membership and the dinghy sailing activity. John Rutherford has agreed to do this so Solo interests will be well represented on the Main Committee. Associate Members should channel their concerns through hin. A few of the other key points from the AGM are as follows: It was agreed to count finishing order in local open meetings towards our 1987 Summer and Autumn points series (Results Secretary please note). We have done this for several years now in order to actively encourage our Fleet to support these meetings as this tends to stimulate the growth of the class in this area. I believe this adds variety and enjoyment to the sailing season whatever your standard of performance. I will publish meeting dates as soon as they are confirmed and recommend you note them and give it a try. In 1986 the meetings concerned .were: Halfway Y.C. and Fishers Green but in 1987 it is possible that: Dabchicks, Up River and Berwl Valley may be added. 8. A WINTER'S TALE (continuing the tale of Dumpy Dora). Dumpy Dora was glad to be spending the winter in the chandler's - it was very cold with thick snow made crunchy by a daily coating of ice and a biting wind that stirred the gas bottle from her hibernation each time the chandler's door opened, as it had just then. A customer was asking for gas and the chandler obligingly lifted Dora from his stock rudely awakening her from her dormant state. The customer carried Dora out into the cold air and into his car. In the car was a pile of clothes and blankets, but as the man drove away he started to talk to the pile. 'Now, you know the plan, you will work on the outside of the boat, while I concentrate on the cabin interior.' The pile answered in a strange language but the man seemed to understand: 'No, my dear, you can't do inside the cabin, you're not experienced, and no you have not got frost bite, you haven't got out of the car yet.' After a short journey the car stopped and the man got out saying: 'Right I'll get the cover off the boat and this gas bottle hitched up, then every so often we can have a hot drink.' Dumpy Dora blinked to see a woman appear from the pile wrapped up like an eskimo and sniffing in a most unbecoming manner. The man set to work cheerfully while the woman sniffed louder and staggered from car to boat with armfuls of tools. 'We want all this old paint and varnish off, here's a new Skarsten scraper for you and I'll get cracking inside.' With that the man disappeared into the cabin with the gas bottle, calling out: 'Don't put any nicks in the wood, my love.' The woman eyed the scruffy little boat balefully then, wrestling with a ladder in the wind, eventually managed to bash it onto the boat, climbed up and started to scrape and sniff. So the winter wore on, all week Dora and the little boat lay warm beneath the heavy cover, but come the weekends, the couple arrived to rub and scrape. 'They are wearing me out,' Dora told the boat. 'Every hour 'er out there knocking to come in for a hot drink and moan about her cold and chillblains. Did you hear it this week?' ('How's your cold?' asked the man. 'Gone to my chest,' she said 'That's why it's best you work outside, the fresh air will do your lungs good. Are your chillblains any better?' he enquired. 'I've made medical history with them,' was the doleful answer. 'The doctor said he's never seen them in places where I've got them." 'All that rubbing and scraping should help your circulation,' the man told her.) 'He's a decent chap,' Dora told the boat another time. 'Do you know, this week he bought her a new blade for her scraper and a tin of Nitromors, and she never even smiled.' As spring approached the smell of paint and varnish enveloped the little boat and Dora hoped the better weather would cheer the woman up, but, as yet another cup of tea was being made, her hopes were dashed when she heard the reply to the man's conversational question: 'Did you have a good week at work, dear?' 'No, the manager called me into his office and said that punk-rock may be in style for the younger generation, but he expected a woman of my age to have a little "taste". I explained my hair was red and blue from anti-fouling, but all he said was "I suggest you change your hairdresser."' contd...

9 ‘Well, I told you to wear something on your head,’ said the man. Then more kindly: ‘Here, borrow my balaclava, it was issued to me in my RAF days, it should help while you paint between the keels.’ The weather improved and the little boat took on a new look with coats of paint and warnish. At long last launching day arrived and the boat slipped gratefully into her natural home. "Summer's here, and we're afloat. Surely that woman will smile now,’ mused Dora to herself, feeling a bit empty and sleepy with the rocking motion, ‘I"ve never sailed before, will I be sick?" she heard the woman ask. ‘No, of course not,’ said the man. ‘We'll take it nice and easy. Tonight we will have a few drinks in the pub, and tomorrow,a run to Bradwell. Weather forecast is good, you'll enjoy it - I know you will.’ So the little boat was left rocking gently on her mooring but as the sun went down the tide went out leaving her aground on soft mud. Much later the plop, plop, of oars announced the couple's return and Dora woke to the sound of the man's voice: ‘We're aground, Hop out, my love, and give me a hand to pull up the dinghy.' * "Oooh! ‘What's the matter?" "My leg has sunk.’ "Put your other leg out, even up the weight.’ * ‘Aaagh! "Now what?! ‘That's sunk as well.’ The gas bottle heard the note of annoyance creep into the man's voice: ‘Why aren't you wearing wellies?' Giggle - 'I am.' "Right, let go of the dinghy, get your legs out of the mud and be quiet. Other people are asleep on their boats.’ Giggle - giggle, came the reply tothe astonishment of Dora and the boat. "Are you drunk?’ whispered the man angrily. ‘NO, DON'T SIT DOWN!’ Too late - Dora heard a splosh then the giggle turned to laughter. "You look so angry,’ howled the woman, "You're not coming on board in that state,’ thundered the man. ‘Get your clothes off. ‘What, now? Someone might see me.' gasped the woman. ‘I don't care,’ replied the man, and it was clear he was not amused. ‘Stand still while I throw sea water over you.’ The lady's language-during the sea water bath was unprintable, and again while she struggled on board dripping and shivering, we leave to your imagination, ‘I'm putting the oven on to warm myself up,’ called out the wet woman. "Oh no, I'm nearly empty,’ gasped Dora as all the taps were turned on. ‘This will be the end of me.* A few minutes later it was: ‘I'm drained,’ sighed Dora, So it was the next day a little boat sailed into Bradwell and Dumpy Dora was left without ceremony, to be replenished and await her fate. Margaret Yeoman.
