SOLO NEWS Well, the festive season is behind us once again, 1987 has arrived as promised, and our thoughts can begin to turn once more to plans for the coming sailing season, The prospects for our Solo fleet look particularly bright, with 23 people on the active membership list which Roger Smith passed over to me, and some big fleet turnouts for points racing toward the end of last season, An improvement in overall performance standard was also noticeable last season which was to be expected considering the large number of relatively new fleet members who are still learning the boat. So, given the close competitive racing which our fleet now offers, we can look forward to further improvements both numerically and in standard during 87. Very often the early season racing offers some of the best sailing conditions of the year (given the right clothing), so why not get the jump on the competition and be there for Spring Points 1& 2. The date to aim for is 29th March, but to achieve that your preparation of boat and equipment really needs to start now! A brief word now, about the National Solo Class Association. The NSCA is very active in promoting the interests of the class at both National and Area levels and as such deserves your support. Besides organising the championships and various other events it issues newsletters and offers a boat insurance scheme which I have personally found to be very competitive on price, and straightforward on compensation. Membership is a prerequisite for entering championships or open meetings. Anyone wishing to join should write to the Secretary, Tony Hanan, [redacted], Shrewsbury, or talk to someone on the NSCA stand at Sailboat 87 which will be at Crystal Palace National Recreation Centre on the 7th & 8th March. Those of you in the ‘have trailer, will travel’ category may like to note the following dates: June 27/28 Solo Inland Nationals Bala, N. Wales, July 11/12 Sole Open Meeting Halfway Y.C., Southend. Aug. 23=28 Solo World Championships Mumbles, Swansea. Oct. 4 Solo Open Meeting Fishers Green S.C., Waltham Cross. In my new capacity as Fleet Captain I am anxious to serve the Fleet in the best way I can, but that requires an understanding of each individual's hopes and expectations for their future sailing and social activities - including you. Please feel free therefore to phone, write or collar me at any time with any suggestions or queries which you may have, It remains only for me on behalf of the Solo Fleet to wish all club members a Happy New Year and successful 1987 Sailing Season. John Salmon, [redacted], Billericay Tel. [redacted] FURTHER SOLO NEWS from Bob Anderson Maylandsea Bay Y.C. Winter Series - November 16th to December 14th. When asked to write a brief report on the series, it will become obvious that it is not due to my literary talents but simply as an attender. Three Solo helms from the club took part in the series, Roger Smith, John Walker and yours truly. All three of us thoroughly enjoyed ourselves taking part ina well organised event run by very friendly people. Sailing took place in wind conditions varying from 30 mph to sore: although we started with the slow handicap fleet, in the final results we were given fleet contd...

be status: Roger winning the series, with Peter Harris from the home club taking second place, Despite John and myself not getting into the prize-winning frame, we each had our own individual successes, John demonstrated his prowess as a light airs ‘expert’ by sailing into first place in the penultimate race and with a similar rush of blood, sailed into second place in the final race, My own success was somewhat rather more short lived. Having all sailed out of the creek on what can only be described as screaming reaches (me screaming), tortuous Yuns and horrific gybes we rounded the Doctor now to be faced with the long beat back to the finish. Having trailed behind Roger for most of the beat I managed to sail under him, called starboard, and in my excitement held the starboard tack too long and blew it. I did say it was short lived. As I was only asked to give a brief report I will not tell you about how we never got the starts right or the adrenalin pumping survival sailing reaches, sailed in some of the highest waves seen in the Blackwater, What I will say is that I can highly recommend that whatever class of dinghy sailed, you seriously consider taking part in 1987. A number of classes were well represented ranging from Flying Dutchmen to Fleetwinds. I know of three helms that are intending to take part. SAILING SECRETARY'S NOTE The Club will be having a stand at the Crystal Palace Dinghy Exhibition "SAILBOAT 87! again this year. It will be held on 7th and 8th of March and we will need a rota of Club Members to spend a couple of hours over the weekend to look after the stand and help to recruit new members, Please let your Fleet Captain know the time and day (Saturday or Sunday) you would prefer, Roger Smith, Tel. 0799 [redacted] A FAMOUS VICTORY This is a story of courage; a story of achievement; of men against the elements in intense competition against the best helms in the Blackwater. Dawn breaks. Some hours later the Solo team from Marconi Sailing Club make the final adjustments to their highly tuned machinery on the hard at Stansgate. In a fresh Force 4 the intrepid team sail to the distant shores of Osea Island where the teams gather for the start of the Maylandsea Bay Y.C. Challenge Cup. At the start the Marconi team of Solos helmed by Malcolm Stuart, Dave Nixson and Roger Smith put into action the well honed plan, rehearsed over weeks of secret practice, The plan was to go round Northey, then Osea and avoid going up Lawling Creek (sorry, Phil) as fast as possible! The race was finished in a decreasing wind after a pleasant sail in pleasant company. Only later were we to learn that for the first time for many years Marconi had won the Challenge Cup. CATAMARAN FLEET BRAVE THE ELEMENTS TO BE THE FIRST ON THE WATER IN 1987 Report from Gur On The Spot Correspondent In conditions far beyond those normally endured by other members of the Club, (S.1s), the Cat. fleet dipped their paws on the first Sunday of the New Year. Force 6 - 7 winds over a strong tide, whipped up to a steep chop, which together with horizontal rain provided the ideal sailing weather. The race course was set from the slipway, up-river to Osea Pier (no extra points for sailing through the gap in the pier!), down to Fisheries mark and back to the slip. Three boats turned out for the event, two Darts sailed by Mike and Tom Duckmanton, Andy Rimmer and Anthony Prior, and the Stampede with Trevor Milton, John Nickalls and Morris Brill. The Duckmantons got away first but half way up the beat, Tom was involved ina dramatic incident, As conditions deteriorated Tom decided 30 knots was a bit fast for Mike's Dart. He bravely sacrificed his personal comfort by breaking his trapeze wire and plunged into high seas to provide a sea anchor in an attempt to help his helm control the boat. He clung, white knuckles straining to the jib sheet for a full two minutes, The boat slowed down and his helm, not wishing to lose such a valiant crew to hypothermia, insisted Tom came back on board the boat, Meanwhile the other two boats were sailing hard behind them, Andy Rimmer, well known for his autocratic streak, had wrested his crew from his sick bed for one of the most demanding events of the season. Anthony was later heard asking if water-proof paper-hankies were available, Trevor turned out a strong team on the Stampede, using the weight gained over Christmas to best effect, After the first half he made a quick pitstop for technical adjustments and a replacement crew as Sarah Brill became the first lady on the water in 1987. The race result left little to question —- Mike and Tom had to retire as, despite Tom's valiant efforts in slowing the boat, he was in breach of Dart Class Rule No. 7(a) which states that the person using the trapeze shall have at least one foot in contact with the boat. Andy Rimmer was disqualified under RYA . Rule on fair sailing for dragging his crew out of bed whilst suffering from flu, a sore throat and a cough. This left Trevor and his crews to take line honours with the Stampede, So with sacrificial sons, the risen dead and adjustable crews, the Fleet is ready for 1987 to be - The Year Of The Cat, He 4 HH HH He He BE THE FIRST HH HH H %

8. Adventures Of A Gas Bottle It was late in the season when George and myself, carrying enough supplies for a fortnight's sailing holiday, got on board 'Sagtob', George's Warsash One Design. We purchased two bottles of gas, one of which was brightly painted. Once on board we stowed the maps, food and drink. We connected the painted gas bottle to the cooker, lashing the other one in a locker. The easterly wind was fresh and, as we had arrived at Bradwell Marina early, we left almost immediately. The sun was brilliant and we made a good fast passage to Ostend, needing to make only two tacks. The next day's offshore trip to Flushing was an easy one and prior to entering the Walcheren canal we stayed overnight in the small yacht harbour and purchased duty free drink. George liked gin. Every day of the holiday started with a breakfast of boiled eggs and toast and the highlight of the day was 'opening time' at twelve noon. Drinks but little food! No wonder we were hungry come the evenings. Our journey through the canals was therefore enriched by good restaurant food. We ate well in Were, where we had moored, nestled in the fisherman's harbour right in the centre of the town. Kortgene marina in the Versemeer also had a good restaurant as well as showers. Willemstad will be remembered for its Victorian hotel and marvellous a la carte. We had sunny weather as we sailed (and motored) through the canals and had only two minor mishaps. After coming through the enormous lock gates into the Maas we kept inshore to avoid the many large ships and barges. At a bend in the river we went aground on a submerged slipway. Luckily we were quickly pulled off by a motorboat. The other fright was an engine stoppage coming up the river to Rotterdam. The Warsash OD had a Vire engine and, as is usual, the plug oiled up at the most inconvenient time. Until we reached the Yacht Club in Rotterdam I sat ready with a fresh plug in my hand in case of further breakdown, as the river was as busy as Piccadilly Circus. We had an expensive meal in a small exclusive restaurant before I flew back to England - penniless! George's wife was joining him for the second week. A week later I had a telephone call from George. He had returned to Burnham slightly slightly early and was doing some painting and varnishing inside the boat but would I join him for a weekend sail. So on the Friday afternoon I joined him aboard 'Sagtob' to clear the holiday gear. We changed gas bottles and, before going ashore for a few minutes, George lit a small gas heater to help dry the paint. We had nearly reached the slipway in the Club launch when there was an explosion and we could see that 'Sagtob' was ablaze and sinking. There must have been a small leak of gas from the new cylinder. We were lucky that no lives were lost. Broken-hearted we cleared away and went home after leaving the empty gas bottle at the Burnham chandlery. George bought an identical boat with the insurance money, and gave it the same name. I wish this story were fictional, but unfortunately it is not. George has never had gas on board since that time and neither have I. Geoffrey Bond

COMMODORE'S NOTES Your Navigans has been bereft of these notes for several issues now. This was a deliberate ploy on my part because I felt that until I had given myself a chance to work myself into my unexpected role I would be guilty of being a trifle presump- tuous if I launched forth my opinions on some subject or other. Oh, very well then, perhaps I can also plead guilty to being a little lazy also — but only a very little. Since the A.G.M. we have had two full Committee Meetings and three Executive Meetings at which I have been very much the new boy learning the business and I now feel I am beginning to glimpse the shape of our coming seasons. Coming in fresh as I do to the running of the Club I can appreciate that we have some quite difficult situations with which to deal - all, of course, revolving around money. It is the usual dilemma, we want to expand and improve our facilities but we want to do it without over-—burdening our costs. As some of you will know we now have a new sewage system which should make life much sweeter in future seasons. We are hoping that the veranda scheme will also stil] be possible despite the raising of the height of the sea wall necessitated by the advent of the Thames Barrier. There will, however, be a delay and negotiations/investiga- tions continue, The security system at the Club is ageing and we are actively seeking to replace it. Hopefully, at the the fitting out WORKING PARTY we will be providing only those who attend with means of future entry. Please do not think that we are TM doing it just to encourage you to attend —- because we ARH! These parties can be fun and fulfilling, for those actively participating are putting part of themselves into the Club. Something very close to my heart, for reasons which many of you will appreciate, is the Marconi Regatta, and I was particularly saddened when it had to be cancelled last year. Because of time and other reasons we are not able to have one again this year. I feel very strongly that we owe it to ourselves and to the rest of the Blackwater as the occupiers of the most prestigious site on the river to hold a Regatta — BUT it can only bappen if there is sufficient positive response from you for such an event. Hence it was at a recent Executive Meeting that we decided to recommend, in principle only, a Regatta for 1988 (but only after very lengthy discussion) to the Main Committee. To turn principle into fact, 1988 will require commitment from many more of our members. Therefore, whatever your views, please write and tell me your feelings. No response means no Regatta for that will be your will. Robbie Sims, Commodore, RESCUE BOAT DRIVERS REQUIRED Any member interested, please contact Doug Brown on Chelmsford [redacted] after 7pm. Boat—handling and sailing dinghy experience would be an advantage, but those interested must be prepared to go out with the regular Drivers to famaliarise themselves with the four boats at our disposal, We operate a Rota, and usually are required to drive only one Sunday each month. Doug Brown, Coxswain.

To DUMPY DORA HOMEWARD VOYAGE The morning of the third day was as calm and windless as the past two days during which we had motor sailed the entire distance from Poole to Dover, Naturally such conditions are not acceptable to any yachtsman, let alone one schooled in the tradi- tions of the East Coast, where the wind blows with exuberance and periods of calm are considered monstrous, offensive and even unholy. This persistent lack of wind and the prospect of yet another full day of motor sailing was, not surprisingly, regarded by the crew with distaste which manifested itself in slow, sullen and dispirited activity as the boat was prepared for sea, When the tide served we slipped through the Western entrance and set a course for the Downs. It was dawn. Movement through the water was reluctant, deliberate and sluggish, Now and again the helmsman would glance in at the cabin clock, not with anxiety, but merely to please himself with the thought that each minute gone by made it nearer the time when this ordeal would come to an end. So it was,in an atmosphere of gloom and despondency which hovered over the boat like a sea fog, we came, some two hours later, to Ramsgate. In Ramsgate we refuelled, collected vital stores and within the hour had once more put to sea. But now there was a change for during that hour the accursed calm had ended. At first we stared stupefied, unable to comprehend the scene which now confronted us. Then quite softly someone said, "It's wind," and someone else, as if this observation needed confirmation shouted, "It's wind, it's wind, a westerly wind!" A passion of intense physical activity now afflicted the crew so that before we had reached the Quern buoy, which marks the deep water channel to Ramsgate, the big genoa was up and sheeted in, the engine was off and we were SAILING! At the Quern buoy, where there was more sea room, we headed up into the wind and jubilantly raised the full mainsail. We bore away on to a broad reach,and with the boat moving at near Ats maximum speed, headed toward the Longnose and N.E. Spit buoys in the Thames estuary. The hiss of disturbed water as the wake streamed astern, the exciting sensuous rhythm as the boat plunged forward into a sunlight sea, heeling to the wind, combined to produce an assured complacent air of deep satisfaction which rapidly erased all memory of the tortuous movement of the past two days. The Westerly wind posed a problem because a course following any of the principal channels of the Thames estuary would have involved sailing to windward adding many extra miles. To avoid this a course was plotted which would bring the wind fair, but in so doing involve a passage across the notorious sands that encumber these waters. It was a bold plan for no one except fishermen,who are accepted to be foolish, crossed the sands. It was a plan which depended upon exact timing and to have any chance of success our first objective, the North Edinburgh channel, needed to be entered just as the flood tide commenced, Sailing is an activity which is both repulsive and attractive. Repulsive because it is dangerous, mostly frustrating, wet, cold and uncomfortable. It is attractive because it brings adventure and exciting rewards at any moment, and because there are moments which elevate the spirit to peaks of supreme ecstasy. As we sailed in a silvery sea, under cloudless skies with a fair and constant wind we experienced one of these peaks. Very soon the Longnose and the N.E. Spit were astern and just ahead,at the time we wanted, was the Tongue Sand Tower and the Edinburgh channel. The first part of this channel is quite short and in less than forty minutes we were heading out into shoal water towards the Knock John. A dramatic change of depth from 40m to 2.5m was recorded just beyond the buoys marking the northern edge of this channel. The surface of the water which had all the characteristics of shoal water running off a sand bar caused some anxious moments, but the depth was adequate for our moderate draught. The Knock John was the first of the drying sands, reported to be .6m in 1973, but no sand showed now. About two cables to seaward of this drying area a shallow rill with

8. a minimum depth of 1.2m was shown. We estimated that as the tides were half springs, and the flood tide had been making for an hour, there would be sufficient water for us to pass safely. We stood on towards the sands. The colour of the water changed from deep blue to sandy yellow which streaked out East to West along the length of the sands. Ahead, only a hundred metres away, we could see the Barrow Deep with its usual traffic of commercial craft plying to and from London. Slowly the depth decreased until it was almost 1.2m, the draught of the boat. It remained at this figure fully five minutes as we skimmed across the bank, then quite suddenly in deep water again. When we looked back a plume of disturbed sand could be seen drifting across our wake. The keel had ‘smelt the bottom’ as the bargemen would say. Hazards of sailing in shallow water were now temporarily replaced by the problems of navigation in restricted waters. At least three ships were close enough to require a constant check on their progress towards us. A tanker and a container ship were approaching from the starboard and a Swedish timber boat from the port side. We took bearings every few minutes, with the hand bearing compass, on their respective bridge decks and in seamanlike fashion passed safely between them. The last of the ships had barely crossed our stern before once more we were confronting the shallow waters at the edge of the channel. Before us now were the East and West Barrow Sands. We cleared the West Barrow easily but we touched on the East Barrow close beside the Barrow Beacon. Undaunted, in the Swin now, we maintained our course toward the Maplins and found the edge of these sands halfway between the N.&. Maplin and S.W. Middle, We now faced the most critical part of the voyage and once more depth was the principal - concern, Those calculations, so carefully checked and recheched and upon which the decision to cross the sands had been made, were about to be tested. We were fast approaching the Ridge,a great hump of sand raised by the ebb and flow of the Crouch as it scours its course between.the Foulness Sands and the Buxey. Depths here are unreliable because with every gale the sands change, so with trepidation, tinged with no small amount of panic, we drew closer to this final barrier. Failure to cross would entail a long detour, also if we grounded the taunts and smirks of other yachts— men would be intolerable. The belief this sand bar could be crossed was encouraged by a certain familiarity,that is, I was acquainted with these waters as I had sailed in the Crouch for many seasons and often sailed past the Ridge, but I had not tried to cross it before. As we drew near I could see,two cables distant on the port side, the surface of the water dancing in Pyramidical confusion suggesting a concealed underwater obstruction. To starboard the sea was green, the surface untroubled and smooth like a pond. I chose this way Ww and freeing the headsail to slow the boat,steered purposefully towards it, The Gods were benign for there was no sudden shock, no bump or brating sound as sand and shingle ground beneath the keel. Instead we found a fathom, two whole metres, and swept across the fearsome barrier into the Crouch. I offered silentprayers to those Gods whose whims and fancies determine the success (or otherwise) of our more desperate schemes, With deep sighs of relief we sailed on congratulating ourselves on our audacity. Without further anxiety we reached the Blackwater and somewhere near the Nass beacon made our first tack in forty miles. As we passed Bradwell there was barely thirty minutes of favourable tide remaining, but the wind held and we beat up river to pick up our mooring just twelve hours after we had left Dover, Then,as if satisfied all was well, the wind fell away and a tranquil evening peace suffused both boat and crew, Never had here been such a day, and as we swung to our mooring we drank a toast to all the Gods who command the elements upon which our sailing is dependent. "And me — Dumpy Dora — how do I fit into all this? I was taken aboard at Ramsgate and stowed in the cockpit locker where I shared all these anxieties and excitements of the crew. During the following winter the owner sold the boat and me with it. The new owner, I have to say, is less adventurous - or should it be foolhardy?" Bill Chrystie

MARCONI SAILING CLUB CODE OF PRACTICE FOR LAUNCHING AND RECOVERY OF CRUISERS Large Boats — Boats above 27ft. length will not be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. Tractor — Only to be operated by authorised drivers. Winches — When dinghy events are in progress the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies. The O.O.D. will be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for the information of dinghy sailors. At other times the following code should be observed: When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed. Avoid sharp bends in winch cables-shackles must be used for attachment to trolleys. DO NOT shackle winch wire back on itself. It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strong team of helpers. Leave winches tidy, return shackles, strops, etc. to garage after use, rewind cable tidily riding turns can damage the cable. Report any damage or wear of any equipment to an authorised tractor driver. REMEMBER it is your responsibility to check for safety any equipment in use, if in doubt DO NOT USE. If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the boat owner must provide a rope or cable of suitable strength and sufficient length that the tractor may remain level and always clear of loose shingle. Boat Trolleys — If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to other boats. Handicap Fleet News The February Fleet Meeting at the Hurdlemakers Arms was very well supported with plenty of members both old and new turning out on a dark and damp night to ease the locals out of their corner of the pub. Perhaps next time we shall pick a bigger pub. A pleasant evening was had by everyone, meeting new people and chatting about sailing. I would like to thank everyone for turning up and to announce an intention to hold some further social evenings later on in the year, probably at the Sailing Club. As they say, watch this space for further news. By the time you read this the Season will just be beginning, Those of you who intend to make an early start, and I hope a few will, please see that you have sensible clothing as the water will still be very cold, especially as it is snowing as I write this, The first two fleet duties for our fleet this year are on Sunday 29th March (the first meeting) and Easter Monday, 20th April. I hope to have expert Race Officers manning the Race Box on these days, so that anyone who has not done any race ow controlling before can come along and learn how it is done. ** Please feel free to do so, it is not difficult and the Race Box is the best vnlace to be on a wet day, The Handicap Fleet this year will comprise of the following boats: seven 420s, seven GPlds, five Enterprises, four Lasers, three Hornets, two Embassys, and one each of the following: Albacore, Cherub, Express, Fireball, Fleetwind, Gull, Miracle, Mirror 14, Scorpion, Torch, Wayfarer, This list is only approximate as I have yet to have all the registration forms for this year, and also not all of the above boats will be racing. If anyone is thinking of changing to, or getting one of the above boats, let me know and I will try to put you in touch with an owner so that you can get all the gen and any useful tips. Chelmsford [redacted] MARCONI SAILING CLUB BOAT JUMBLE MONDAY MAY 4TH 12.00 Following the success of the initial M.S.C. Boat Jumble held in September 1986, it is proposed to make this an annual event to be held on the May Bank Holiday each year. This year's sale will take place at the Club (indoors if wet) on 4th May commencing at 12.00. This type of event can only be successful if adequately supported so dig out all those old bits of equipment or clothing you would like to get rid of. TREATMENT OF HYPOTHERMIA - Reprint from Navigans, June 1981 Just a few minutes in the Blackwater doesn't do some people much good, so imagine what half-an-hour would do to a sailor (not properly protected) after Capsizing - the rescue boat could be unaware of your trouble because he is helping another sailor elsewhere on the river. If you are called to a hypothermic casualty, this is what you are likely to find: The Patient Will Be: Blue with the cold. FPWwWNrF Stiff with the cold. Immobilised with the cold. Unconscious or semi-conscious with the cold. Possibly able to nod his head weakly in the affirmative to the question 'Can you understand what I am saying to you?" He is likely to be irrational. His respirations will be shallow, AN U slow and irregular, His pulse will be weak, slow and difficult to feel. His rectal temperature is likely to be below 31 “6. 8 His blood pressure, if you could record it, would be very low. 9 Since he is exposed to the cold and long boat the stage of shivering his deep core temperature is likely to be below 31 °c. I am not suggesting that you should stick a thermometer up his anus to find out! In any event, unless you take immediate action his temperature will accelerate downwards to death by heart failure, What You Should Do: 1 Treat him very gently. Rough handling may precipitate heart failure in a dangerously cold person. 2 Get him into the warm, out of the cold and away from the wind. 3 Keep him horizontal. His heart is weak and his blood pressure is low. Blood supply to the brain must be maintained at all costs to avoid irreversible brain damage. 4 If local conditions permit, get him to the nearest shelter and stop his heat loss. Remove his wet clothes — dry him — put on warm clothes - wrap him up in warm blankets with a‘warm human being beside him. 5 Do not waste time giving him hot drinks unless you are sure he can swallow. If he cannot swallow you may drown him, Unless he is getting warm and beginning to shiver do not give him alcohol. Alcohol dilates surface blood vessels and increases heat loss. 6 Trained mountain rescue teams carry special breathing apparatus capable of admini- storing heated, oxygen enriched, air. 7 Take him to the nearest available HOT BATH. 8 The water should be at Test it by putting in your elbow, if your elbow will accept it - so will the patient. 9 Lower the patient gently in. If sufficient help is available attempt to keep his upper and lower limbs out of the water. It is his trunk that needs reheating. The limbs have a larger surface area in relation to their mass than does the trunk. If immersed it is possible to reduce markedly an already low blood pressure by inducing vasodilatation over the skin of the limbs and, to make matters worse, excite the return to the heart of a pool of very cold blood in the extremities. This could prove to be the last straw that broke the camel's back and arrest cardiac function by lowering still further Deep Core temperature, 10 Do not forget to top the bath up with hot water to maintain the temperature at 42-44 "6, ll The first sign of positive recovery to look for is the onset of shivering. At that moment the patient will start dynamically to re-heat his own body. Continue to re-heat him passively with the bath treatment. His bodily functions will begin to nant

return, When you are sure he can swallow in spite of severe shivering, this is the time to give him hot grog. Alcohol is good fuel and quickly absorbed from the stomach, L2 You have now saved someone's life. Hopefully by this stage the patient is in hospital or medical help has arrived. Hand over, for the patient is not out of the wood yet. Lots of complications could occur - for instance a common one is pneumonia, Your patient is going to need expert medical care and devoted nursing. The practical aspects of survival training will now be considered under the following headings in decreasing order of importance: 1) Protection 2) Location 3) Water 4) Food. Contributor Unknown! SAILORS! IF YOU CAN AFFORD TO BUY A DINGHY OF ANY KIND — YOU CAN AFFORD TO BUY A WET-SUIT DUMPY DORA Dumpy Dora was fed up since her last trip at sea. She had been returned to the greatw dumping depot where all gas bottles are eventually sent when they are beginning to show wear and tear. Here they were either thrown on the scrap heap or smartened up to live another day. Dora was right at the back of the shelf looking forlorn. Her paint was chipped and she looked dejected. She was worried. From her position on the shelf she could see a large pile of gas bottles destined to be melted down, They were crying and groaning. A man was sorting out the shelves and throwing bottles on the heap with a crash, Nearer and nearer he came putting some bottles in a neat row on the floor and others on the ever growing scrap heap. Dora felt sick, all the sea air had got to her paint - it was peeling and she felt so drab, She could see her reflection in an old piece of broken mirror standing on the shelf. She looked awful and a tear rolled down her face, Suddenly a large brown hand came down on top of her and heaved her up in the air. Two large grey eyes stared at her. She trembled and tried to smile puffing out her chest and fluttering her eyelashes. The old man gazed at her. "You look a sorry old thing,' he said. Oh dear, she thought. ‘Still there might be life in you yet. Your body's not too bad.' Dora swelled a little, 'A might rusty though.' She felt sick again. ‘I guess with a new coat of paint you'll do, there are no holes in you.' Withy a big sigh of relief she found herself in a neat line of bottles waiting to be renovated. She was left like this for two days. It was cold and draughty on the floor and what was worse she would occasionally get kicked by people passing. I hope they don't have a dog here, she thought. She didn't fancy a hot shower, After two days she was heaved up and taken into the paint shop. Dumpy Dora felt quite embarrassed as wire brushes were vigorously rubbed up and down her until she was completely bare of blue paint. Then she was lightly rubbed over with sand paper, this tickled and she laughed. Then a man with a mask over his face sprayed her with a light grey flat paint. Dora was left for four hours to dry. She felt better with her underwear on and waited excitedly for her final coat of paint. When the paint sprayer came again she closed her eyes and mouth and sat very still while she was sprayed a nice blue. When she was dry her inside was refilled with gas and she was put back on the shelf, at the front this time. She felt wonderful, she swelled with pride and smiled at everyone who came near her, She knew it would not be long before someone bought her and she would be off on her travels again. She might even meet a nice Dumpy Daniel, after all those little Gaz bottles must come from somewhere. She smiled - suddenly the future looked very rosy, Julie Bloomfield. ‘Juliet '

7. DUMPY DORA Christina's Tale The snow swirled around as Dora dozed in her snug locker on board 'Moontide'. Although comfortable and well insulated from the elements, she was irritable and bored and wished that the winter would end so that she could be afloat once more. Then suddenly she was wide awake, disturbed by the regular crunching sound of approaching footsteps. A great fear spread through her liquid and left a lump in her valve, for she knew that the locker door was broken and she was therefore easy prey for a robber. She turned for help to Clive, her key, hanging on his usual clip, but he slept on, snoring contentedly, unaware of the drama. The crunching stopped outside and was followed by the banging of a ladder against the hull and the sound of boots climbing the rungs. Something dropped into the cockpit and the boots returned down the ladder and crunched their way back into the gloom. Dora waited a few minutes and then nervously opened her locker to see what had been delivered in such a disturbing way. Dora's fluid gurgled with glee as she saw the envelope with a Greek stamp and recognised the strange hand of Christina Calabottapopoulos, her pen friend. Her sudden cry woke Clive and with his help the envelope was soon opened. Dora started to read and as she did so, the cockpit seemed to become sunny and the sound of swirling snow was replaced by the gentle lapping of warm sea against the hull. "Dear Dora, I just had to write and tell you what a terrible season I have had serving on a charter boat this year. There I was, minding my own business on a shelf in George the chandler's in Nidri, Lefkas, which is an island in the Ionian sea, when Captain Birdseye comes in with a very sorry looking bottle. Her body was all dented, the paintwork chipped, and she was covered in various dead creatures: the smell was unbearable. This was a premonition of my fate. I was exchanged for this poor wretch and rudely swung through the streets of the town on the way to the quay. New 'Alkadi' is a trim Aloa 27 and I was pleased to be installed in the vast port locker, especially as I was the sole occupant - luxury indeed! Birdseye stomped off muttering that he intended to "get yamassed at Nicks" and I settled down to a quiet snooze in the warm sun. Suddenly all hell broke loose. The boat lurched and Alkadi reverberated to the stomping feet and shrill voices of Birdseye, Boozy Suzy, Krystos and Julie, my companions for two terrible weeks. To my dismay, the locker was thrown open and I was showered with a bucket, warps, boat hook, flippers snorkles, deck shoes, frisbee, fishing lines and a vicious octopus worrier. The next half hour was chaotic, as supplies were stowed aboard. Anything which could not be placed in the cabin lockers was heaved in on top of me, particularly Retsina bottles and containers of draught Metaxa. Eventually the engine, called Donka for some strange reason, was started and we eased our way astern, helped by Birdseye hauling in a line which led down deep into the clear water. Suddenly Birdseye fell back into the cockpit, followed by sodden rope and chain and the liberated kedge anchor, a performance to be repeated many times during the next two weeks. Then, horror of horrors, the anchor, chain and warp were thrown in on top of me, closely followed by the fenders - oh misery. There follows a precis of my two weeks as often described by Birdseye: 'The shakedown cruise to Paleros on the mainland passed without incident, except that Suzy's first rule of sailing was established, i.e. the angle of heel allowed is directly proportional to the amount of Retsina consumed. contd....

Dumpy Dora contd. 8. Paleros will be remembered for the destruction testing of Ouzo and the enterprising Greek taverna owner who flushed his toilet with this spirit because of a water shortage. The voyage from Paleros via Kalamos to Astakos was noteworthy, as a sudden squall off Mitakos blew a hole in the mainsail and put Suzy's first fule to the test - she slept the rest of the way. Astakos is not one of the flotilla calls and is a bustling, lively ferry port. After much searching, the worst tailor in the world was soon found and he agreed to haul out his ancient machine into the main street and repair the sail. We couldn't bear to watch the appalling artisan at work: we thought he had a limp until we learnt that he was wearing one of his own suits, so we explored the town. A dingy bar was soon discovered which we christened "The Last of The Summer Retsina". The wine was served in copper jugs from vast barrels packed floor to ceiling. All four of us managed to become seriously yamassed for 50p. Many adventures were to follow in places with names straight from the pages of Homer: Sami, Fiskardo, Assos and Argostoli on Cephalonia, Frikes, Kioni and Port Vathi on Ithaca. Ah, the joys of bare boat charter! The time swept past and soon we were making a late evening run up the Meganissi channel, past Christina Onassis's island of Skorpios towards the lights of Nidri and the welcoming party at Nicks.' Christina continued - They may have had a good time, but my life was a misery, having all sorts of debris hurled into my locker. And as for that kedge anchor, no manners at all. Anyway in true bottle tradition, I gave my all and helped produce many delightful meals and I now await my fate in George's chandlery for next year: I pray for a gin palace to be my next berth and I hope you never have to serve Birdseye and his appalling friends. Hope you are well, Christina" Dora read the letter over and over again and each time she became more embarrassed. She was thankful that her locker was only large enough to accommodate Clive, herself and a few cans of beer during the season and that the kedge anchor on 'Moontide' was stowed in the starboard locker. However, how could she face Birdseye when he fondled her tap at the beginning of the season, knowing that he had upset her penfriend in Greece? Birdseye, 'Moontide'

3 COMMODORE'S NOTES Midsummer is almost upon us and your Commodore still has not managed to move his boat from the back garden. Heigh-ho for the camping fortnight by which time, hopefully, I can look forward to being waterbound, along with a really strong support from our Members at large. I consider events such as this as crucial to the development of the Sailing Club by its Members, because most of us have to rush down to Stansgate to do something specific with little opportunity to stand and stare. With a week or a fortnight, however, we can take time to appreciate and understand our good fortune at having a Club with togetherness which will help to keep us the best CLUB in the area. So make the effort and join us. As most of you will know by now the new security system is almost fully implemented - in fact when you read this it should be! - and you will all be adept at wielding your bit of magic plastic. It has taken longer than we imagined but I am sure we will come to be grateful for it in the future. Despite my previous pleas some members persist in allowing their pets to roam unrestrained. This is anti-social. We have already had a youngster bitten and badly frightened this year. Please remember that the most docile of pets can unwittingly startle someone and thus initiate an unfortunate train of events. Roaming farm dogs are almost beyond our control but yours need not be. The one does not excuse the other either way. The Spring Bank Holiday Open went very well - despite the Saturday rain and I would like to express my grateful thanks for the enormous commitment to it made by Malcolm Stuart, Mike Battle and Mike Boreham & family to ensuring the weekend's success. It augers well for next year. I was particularly heartened by very strong M.S.C. entry to the event. Keep it up. As for the Galley - The Jessops did us proud - thanks from all of us who savoured their sustenance - More Please! See you at Camp. Robbie Sims Commodore I called on Irene Hodges to gather in Lifeboat Boxes she had kindly taken to make collections for the R.N.L.I. and learnt for the first time that Arthur had been in hospital recently. He is home now and recovering well, but on medical advice, is to give up actively sailing, which means Viridia will be for sale. Arthur assures me he intends to continue his connections and activities unabated with the Club, albeit as a landlubber, so I'm sure Arthur we all wish you continued recovery, and look forward to seeing you and Irene at Stansgate as much as - or more than? - ever. Ed.

Sailors from seven Clubs joined ten 'home' Soloists, making a total of twenty-one entrants during the Spring Bank Holiday Weekend at Stansgate. Four races were sailed over the two days, and the results qualify for the re-established Eastern Area Travellers' Trophy. Malcolm Stuart, Rear Commodore, Chelmsford [redacted] CLUB DINGHY, 'IDLE VICE' The Club's Challenger dinghy 'Idle Vice' has now been fitted out for the season and has been allocated a space in the Handicap Fleet dinghy area. As she was leaking badly last season, the opportunity has been taken to give hull and rigging an overhaul. As well as the obvious work, such as revarnishing, a lot of effort has been put into resealing hull fittings, providing new aluminium keel bands and filling holes and damaged areas. Some running rigging has been replaced and a sailbag donated so that all Idle Vice's gear can be kept together and stored in one of the garages when not in use. To make this work (and the expense to the Club) worthwhile, I hope that maximum use will be made of the boat. Item 5 on Page 13 of the Year Book refers to use of Club Dinghies. Idle Vice is simple to rig but like all boats has a few 'quirks'. When the boat is 'parked' the gaff is stored in the boat, projecting into the forward buoyance tank. Remember to replace the forward hatch cover before sailing and also check that the aft tank cover is in situ. To slot the gaff onto the mast, loosen the gooseneck fitting and remove the boom, slide the plastic 'slug' into the track and replace the boom (pushing it fairly high up the track). Hoist the sail until the gaff fitting is close up to the mast, secure the main halliard, pull the gooseneck fitting down the track to tension the luff, then tighten the gooseneck locking nut. I hope that considerably less work will be required on Idle Vice next year and she should be available for sailing earlier in the season. The assistance of users is requested to help keep her in good trim by observing a few simple rules. PLEASE: Do not allow the hull or rudder to be scraped or bumped on the hard or beach. Ensure that the boat is placed centrally on the trolley so that weight is taken on the chine and bilge keels (a look underneath will make it clear what I mean.) Do not cut or alter the rigging in any way. If you have trouble rigging the boat, ask an experienced club member. When you have finished sailing, wash the boat and gear, return the boat to the dinghy park, tie down to stakes provided and cover up. Put sails and loose gear in sail bag and return to garage. (Consult O.O.D. if in doubt) contd......

10 MIRROR FLEET NEWS Here is my first News as ‘official scribe' to the Mirror Fleet. Readers may remember I have been 'self-appointed'scribe' in the past but now it is OFFICIAL ! What have I done to deserve this ? It must be punishment for my non-attendance at the Mirror Fleet AGM (unfortunately, I really did have a prior engagement). The sailing season has started and although no Mirrors sailed in the first few Spring points races, three did race in the Easter Series - all with Cadet helms and crew. However, if there was a prize for the first Mirror on the water then it would go to Debbie Yorston and Helen Bates who had a short sail the weekend before Easter. Easter Sunday was cold and windy - such a contrast from the previous Friday and Saturday, but the Sunday morning race was sailed in a good breeze and the three Mirrors (Debbie & Helen, Jon Yorston & Jenny Ball and Damian & Lucy Boreham) all completed the course and were eager to try again after lunch despite the worsening conditions. I think they were very brave because Mike and I retired immediately- after the start of the afternoon race whilst sailing our other boat (can't mention the class in this news letter). Personally I was TERRIFIED and Mike was none tookeen to carry on still, we were glad we did retire because all the boats left in the race capsized around ‘E' mark except for Malcolm Stuart in his Solo and Damian & Lucy in the Mirror. Unfortunately Jon and Jenny capsized only yards from the finish line and earned the accolade of being the unluckiest cadets. Malcolm Stuart was the winner with Ron Greygoose (Solo) finishing second despite a capsize, Damian & Lucy 3rd and Carén Stuart 4th (420) also after a capsize. Only these finished out of 18 starters - not unlike some Grand Nationals! ww The next weekend, the same 3 Mirrors raced in Spring Points 7 & 8 in very quiet conditions with slight crew changes. Katy Rutherford crewed for Damian whilst Lucy crewed for Jon. Despite bad starts (Dad moaned inwardly and outwardly) Damian & Katy won both races. They were the only Mirror with a spinnaker and it probably made quite a difference - they will have to watch out when Jon and Debbie each get a spinnaker for their boats. Spring Points 11,12,13 and 14 have also been sailed, with Peter Collis arriving in time to win Spring Points14 single-handed just a few seconds in front of Damian (this time with yours truly as his crew - too heavy says D.). If 13 is unlucky for some, then Spring Points 13 was aptly numbered. Three Mirrors started in a strong breeze but, close to 'E' mark, Damian's boom broke near Osea island and he had to be towed back to the club. In the meantime Jon and Debbie continued on to have a close race but both missed out 'A' mark and so were both disqualified. Its good to see the cadets racing so early in the season - it augurs well for the rest of the year. 11 PYN-man returneth - repent ye sailors before 'tis too late. Those sinners/sailors (delete as you feel appropriate) who can remember back as far as March and June, 1986, might recall the articles on the Portsmouth Yardstick Numbers (PYN) which appeared in Navigans. Although written with a certain amount of, hopefully, obvious light-heartedness it was still the intention to test the reaction to the idea of the Personal PYN. In all, I received four responses to the articles; one indirectly from Eleanor Witter who seemed to have been enthusiastic (unfortunately Eleanor no longer sailed at MSC), a second from Maggie (who hinted I ought to do something useful - like slaughter the weeds in the garden), another from an MSC member who wasn't, however, included in the list (he thought it a good idea) whilst the last response was torn from a rather reluctant sailor who was included in the PYN list and who seemed to suggest the whole thing should be dropped - preferably on my head (not really that bad - just author's licence). The point is, no positive response was received from anyone involved so the whole thing was dropped . I was therefore somewhat surprized (and rather pleased) when one of our leading Solo sailors asked what had happened to the personal PYN, said he personally found it interesting and would be pleased to see it revived. Thus flushed with renewed enthusiasm, I have revived PYN-man. My idea is to post on the notice boards a list of race-by-race 'Performance' PYNs, together with a 'Personal' PYN calculated for every 4 races you complete. With luck, by the time you read this article, the notices will be on the board and I might also be able to publish some 'unofficial' race results based upon the Personal PYNs. Don't worry, the 'official' results (and prizes) will still be calculated using the standard class PYN. Performance PYN - this is calculated for each competitor in each race by taking the Average Corrected Time (ACT) of the top two-thirds of the placed yachts in the race, then multiplying the ACT by 1.05. Let's call this the New ACT (NACT). We now take the NACT figure and eliminate (from the calculation) those yachts in the top two-thirds whose Corrected Time is greater than the NACT. The Corrected Times of those yachts still left are now averaged to produce the Standard Corrected Time (S ) and it is this S which is divided into the Elapsed Time for each yacht in turn to produce the 'Performance' PYN for each yacht placed in the race . All this supposes that the Race Officer has remembered to time in all boats (SOSOTTI !). It also supposes that I have read the instructions correctly. Personal PYN - after the first four Performance PYNs obtained for any particular helm, the personal PYN is obtained by taking the average of the four Performance PYNs and then using this (new) Personal PYN for calculating the helm's Corrected times for his/her next four races ; we then repeat the calculation of yet another new personal PYN and so on . Will it work ? - I haven't the foggiest notion; all I can say is that if you understand the above then you're a good deal cleverer than me - and I wrote it ! 2 THE SECRET DIARY OF AN M.S.C. CADET NOW MADE PUBLIC! Cadet Week SUNDAY We went over all the parts of the boat we could think of. One group came up with 110 parts! (See if you can beat that!). MONDAY Howling winds varying from forces 6 - 8 prevented the beginners from sailing, but, not to be deterred, the more advanced group were dragged out onto the Mooring Raft to do a single-handed capsize and recovery drill. The capsize bit was easy, but the recovery was a different matter. TUESDAY Calmer winds but still quite gusty. The Mini-sails were tried out. I was given one - I knew I couldn't sail it - but it took two capsizes in it for me to convince Mike Turner! WEDNESDAY Sixteen cadets had a good sail down to Blackwater Sailing Club where we had been invited to race. It was flat calm. Until, that is, a storm blew up blowing Melanie and me onto Northey Island where Sea Scouts provided us with a cup of tea! Because of the wind conditions the race was cancelled. Out of the M.S.C. cadets it was Damian Boreham who drew as joint leader with Jonathan Bigden. I put it down to Damian's English skill and Jonathan's American style! THURSDAY Listened with horror as Derek said that five of us were to be handed over to the Sea Cadets next day to be tested for Seamanship One. Went to Osea for lunch. Most of the older cadets ended up having an involuntary swim! We were told to sail round a barge and then back to the club. Unfortunately the wind dropped so everyone had to paddle back. FRIDAY The fateful day! About twelve cadets walking around as white as a sheet and biting their nails. The N.D.S.C. people were tested by Derek and the five Seamanship One people sailed off. We sailed near each other, tried to cut each other up. Several official sailing terms were used, i.e. 'Starboard' 'Mast Abeam' etc. However, many more unofficial terms were used in reply: i.e. 'Le Port' 'Clear off' 'You must be Joking!' When 'Starboard' was called on Sea Cadets, we heard an even more well-used reply which I cannot repeat. Prize-giving at 9.15 pm (Derek was quarter of an hour late). Derek called out the names of people and their progress. The lucky girls were forced to kiss him! (Yuk) Altogether it was a successful week. Jenny Ball P.S. I and the Cadets would like to thank the people responsible for organising the activities laid on for us. We are grateful to the Boreham's, the Boustred's the rescue team, Mike Turner, and most of all Derek Hall - M.S.C.s 'PLONKA AWARD' Winner! Ed's note: I wonder if the PLONKA AWARD could become an annual award - that is, if any member is brave enough to own up to the fact that he/she has earned it - Derek might feel less lonely with a few other names on the records. Ray Ball thinks he might have qualified by breaking his cruiser's rudder during launching and letting his tender drift away from him on the mooring - all in one weekend. Just a thought!

Chelmsford [redacted] CASUAL SAILING I recently witnessed a disturbing but not unusual incident when two dinghies were launched in a Force 5 wind with a strong ebb tide. Neither dinghy was properly rigged and three of the four sailors were inadequately dressed for the weather conditions. Being midweek, no OOD was present to give advice and it was fortunate that both boats eventually got back to the hard without harm, one full of water and the other dragged in from Ramsey Marsh bay. If you are inexperienced, please admit it and seek help and advice before you venture out. Do remember that you need adequate clothing for sailing even in summer and particularly in a summer like this. It is a fine line between staggering back blue with cold and not getting back at all. To enjoy sailing you need a well-found boat and you need to be properly kitted out. The last thing we want is to lose members through disillusionment - or worse. This year's Cadet Week saw an increasing number of adults joining in and learning how to sail properly. For next year we will consider setting up in parallel with Cadet Week a special course for those adults who would like to learn how to sail but are not necessarily interested in going through the full RYA training scheme. 6 SOLO TEAM RACE - Saturday 1st August Which could be retitled 'Nine brave fools get blown into oblivion' Team racing takes place between teams of three boats where the winner is decided on the TOTAL score of all three boats. The scoring is the standard ¾ pts for 1st , 2 pts for 2nd , 3 pts for 3rd, etc with 7 pts for retired and 10 pts for disqualified boats. The basic principle of team racing is to prevent members of the opposing team overtaking any of your team members, or to enable a member of your team to overtake a member of the opposing team, without losing a place yourself. By a wonderful piece of luck the Solo team race took place on the first really windy sailing-day of the summer. Starting with a modest force four the wind gusted up to a steady five by the mid-afternoon. Out of nine enthusiastic entrants three team captains were picked ; Roger Smith, Dave Nixon and myself. The other two members of each team were placed by the team captains picking their names from a hat. This gave teams comprising ; Roger Smith - Dave Nixon - Stephen Rutherford Dave Payne - Colin Willsmore - Steve Keeble Bob Anderson - Malcolm Stuart - Dennis Dear The COURSE for all three races was : E.st , No1.st , F.st , Finish with D.st First Race - Dave/Colin/Malcolm against Stephen/Steve/Dennis A very scattered start left Dennis and Dave with a good lead ahead of the rest of us. With the wind blowing against the tide the beat proved slow and bumpy, producing little opportunity for team tactics . The following reach was little better, where boat-speed and control (or lack of it!) were most important. No 1 was the gybe mark which everyone completed without incident. The following run was a good test of tactics and I got myself in a diabolical position, stuck on the outside of Malcolm with Colin approaching fast from behind. At F Colin slipped round the mark right behind Malcolm and overtook me before I reached the line. Up ahead Dave had already managed to beat Dennis for first place. Second Race - Roger/Dave/Bob against Dave/Colin/Malcolm This race began with a very keen start that left three boats ahead of the line at the gun; Dave Payne, Colin and Bob. Although Colin turned back toward the line he was still a good twenty feet away from it when he decided to rejoin the race. It didn't take long for the two teams to split into three fiercely competing pairs . Once on the reach the solos screemed across the river, all keeping surprisingly close. Because of a slight change in wind direction it was now

7 possible to gybe anywhere between 1 and F. Gybeing however, proved easier said than done, with the lumpy seas and gusty winds. The resulting capsizes where as spectacular as they were frequent. Due to either his enormous talent or good luck Malcolm avoided capsizing, but wasn't quite fast enough to beat Roger to the line. Once everyone had returned to the hard, it was agreed to take a long lunch. Third Race - Stephen/Steve/Dennis against Roger/Dave/Bob By this time the wind was blowing at a constant force-five. After missing our first start due to lack of upright boats we managed a second, reasonable start. With the tide coming in, the beat was hard-going but fast with Steve Keeble going particularly well. Once on the reach Steve was just ahead of me, with Dennis and Roger both well ahead. Once out of the cover of Osea Island the boats really howled along. At No.1, I thought it best to tack around, allowing Dave and Bob to catch up with me. On the run to F Dave capsized and I nosedived, leaving us both in the middle of the river with a boats full of water. Steve managed to gybe at the mark, then almost sailed over Bob's boat as it capsized in front of him. The result of all this was Steve getting a third, Bob a fourth and myself (after plenty of messing about) a fifth. Dave capsized again at F and had to be towed back to the hard. Conclusion Judging from the response of those taking part, the day was a success despite the weather. It also seems that when approached in an unhurried manner team racing is a lot simpler and less ruthless than most people expect. Another point to be noted is that to be a success any team competition needs a whole day allocated to it. I personally hope the Solo team race becomes an annual event (possibly with its own trophy) and that other fleets in the club try a team racing event themselves. - From Stephen Rutherford, our mobile correspondent. 8 LADIES RACE SERIES, 1987 A few years ago, the lady helms at MSC had their own series of races, usually held at the same time as the Cadet Series. However, with declining numbers and a change of the Cadet Series format, the Ladies Series races have not been sailed since 1982. This year, we persuaded the 'powers-that-be' to put on the series again and it was decided to run a series of three races on 2nd August, that is, the middle Sunday of the two camping weeks. The 'Rools' were posted at the Club some weeks before and although male crews were permitted they had to be 'suitably' dressed. Sunday 2nd August dawned bright with a light breeze much to the relief of most of the ladies (although I did hear one say she would have preferred a stronger wind). With what must have been a record turn-out for any club race for ladies in recent years, some 9 helms signed on for Race 1 at 11.30 and most of the male crew members complied with the 'Rools'. Peter Brown was most fetching with a wig and coconuts suitably placed ( or nearly so, unless, of course, it's the place you like them), Willy Pitcairn sported wonderfully long blond plaits which had the photographers gathering round whilst Damian Boreham displayed very nice white frilly suspenders to support leg-warmers that looked more like football socks ; I'm still curious about from whom he obtained the suspenders but he isn't saying and his lips are sealed. Ian Fletcher managed to wear his hair in bunches and , all-in-all, the men 'minders' really entered into the spirit of the thing. However, you should not think that the series was put on as a knock-about farce; the Ladies Cup is worth sailing for in its own right and if this year's preliminaries were light-hearted, then the racing was serious. Race 1 was won by Debbie Yorston in her Mirror, with Lucy Boreham acting as her crew. Maggie Boreham had a superb start - or thought so until the race officer signalled an 'early starter' and Maggie had to sail some fair way back to start again. Even so, she rapidly clawed back the deficit on the beats, but Debbie handled her spinnaker well on the run and held on to the lead and was the winner of Race 1. Charlotte Burck (a very recent new member) sailed her Wayfarer into 2nd place and Maggie was 3rd. Race 2 saw two more lady helms signing on, giving us a new record of 11 starters. In addition, two very 'odd' sailore indeed placed their names on the Signing On sheet; one was called Lily White whilst the other rejoiced in the name of Norma Stits. Suspicions aroused, the 'regular' lady helms demanded an investigation and both Lily and Norma failed the sex test, conducted, we understand, by Malcolm Stuart. Race 2 was won by Charlotte Burck by over 3 minutes on corrected time - a very convincing win by a helm who is quite clearly not new to helming even though, we understand, she has not done much racing. Race 3 was proceeded by lemonade served on the hard (but not on the rocks). I bet the men would have had beer but I guess we have to be thankful for small mercies. Still, I have my suspicions about the 'lemonade' because at the start of Race 3 there were so many boats over the line that the Race Officer signalled a General Recall - something that I cannot recall in a club race over the last 10-12 years. Charlotte Burck again crossed the finish line first, being over 5 minutes ahead on corrected time but perhaps there was 'something' in that lemonade after all (or perhaps Charlotte had two glasses) because she was disqualified for again being over the start. This left Maggie Boreham the winner, with Debbie Yorston 2nd in this race. With two out of three races to count, Charlotte, Debbie and Maggie each had one win and one second, so the series was settled on the 'discarded' race. This left Debbie and Maggie to share the Ladies Cup for 1987 and a rather unfortunate, but very cheerful, Charlotte in 3rd place overall. Thanks to all the ladies who took part in the series; let us hope we can continue to make the series rather more than just a 'fun thing' in 1988 - but still with a sense of humour to make it enjoyable. Little Annie Fanny Ladies Series Reporter NB. Full results can be found towards the rear of this Navigans.

9 MIRROR NEWS This is being written at the end of the Cadet Week which was a great success despite poor weather most days. It was great to see all the dinghies on the water particularly the red of the Mirror sails which were outstanding for their number as well as their colour. Let's hope all those dinghies will continue to sail during the rest of the season, both in the ordinary Points Series as well as the Cadet Series. On the Wednesday of Cadet Week, 16 cadets sailed up the river (in 8 Mirrors) to the Blackwater Sailing Club to take part in their Cadet Week Wednesday afternoon race. I'm not sure how many Mirrors were racing but there must have been around 20 of them and it looked like a Mirror Open meeting. Add the toppers, Lasers, Fireballs, etc that the Blackwater cadets were also sailing and it was quite a fleet which set out on the race in almost windless conditions. A somewhat extended start sequence found 'our mob' too far up the line and in slack water whilst 'the locals' stayed at ' other end and took advantage of a stronger favourable tide and what little wind was available. However, not too long after the start, with the leaders on a run back from the windward mark, a thunder storm struck us, bringing with it a very fierce squall and very heavy rain. For those of us in the work-boat we could neither see the boats nor make any headway against the onslaught for several minutes but eventually we were able to go in search of 'casualties'. Many of the dinghies capsized but we're proud to say that all of the Marconi boats stayed upright. Jenny Ball sought the shelter of the causeway to Northey Island and we found her bright and cheerful, tidying the sails away before she and crew Melanie Keeble went off to be entertained to tea by some sea cadets camping on Northey . It seemed a shame to break up the party so we left them there whilst we went in search of other boats needing assistance. As already mentioned, all our boats stayed upright and sailed back under their own control to the Blackwater S.C, the race having been abandoned. When you consider that on the previous Monday, few of our cadets had any real experience of sailing in normal conditions, let alone racing in bad conditions, then it is a tribute to Derek Hall's teaching of seamanship that they all handled the situation with no apparent difficulty. No doubt others will offer their thanks to the Blackwater SC for the very warm and generous welcome they gave to our members; it would be nice to keep the link thus established between the two clubs, perhaps by organising a 'Mirror Match' next year. Anyway, thank you Blackwater Sailing Club - we enjoyed our visit and were very impressed by your hospitality. Four out of six Summer Points races have been sailed, with Peter Collis winning three and Dammian Boreham one. Summer Points 6 provided one of the closest finishes for some time. Peter and Damian swopped the lead between them all the way round, each having their moments of triumph and 'disaster' but Peter eventually crossed the finish just inches ahead of Damian to be credited with a win by just 1 second. Two new names to add to the list of 'Mirror Racers'; they are Roy Wood and Greg Hall. Greg is one of our younger cadets and has taken part in his first Mirror Series race. Other new members to the Mirror Fleet (even if not yet actually racing with us) are Martin and Alison Edwards and the Davies family with 'Red Dwarf'. Graham Baker and Dave Onyons (new members last year) have also made a racing start this season. 11 AMENDMENTS TO THE M.S.C. SAILING INSTRUCTIONS (S.I.). Rule 6 - Signing On. The Sailing Sub-Committee has decided that, with effect from the commencement of the 1987 Autumn Points Series for all classes , scheduled races will be held if only one starter signs on. The previous Rule 6 which required three starters to sign on will no longer be in operation from 13 August 1987. Previous publication of SI Rule 6 has included the sentence 'If less than three starters sign on the race will not be sailed'. The reasons for the original adoption of this sentence are probably lost in the club archives but it seems logical to assume that our predecessors wished to establish a measurable minimum level of competitive sailing before awarding the club's major trophies. The last publication of Rule 6 in this form was in the 1984 Year Book, the shortened versions of the Year Book '85 and '86 did not include the publication of the Sailing Instructions. The traditional version of the Year Book'87 once again included publication of Rule 6 but omitted the sentence 'If less than three starters sign on the race will not be sailed'. It is not clear whether the omission was accidental or intended, but the Sailing Sub-Committee, after some considerable debate, has decided to let the 1987 version of Rule 6 stand as published. For a number of seasons, the Handicap Fleet was allowed to sail races with only one starter; this was done to encourage/reward those very few helms who regularly turned up to sail handicap races only to find less than three starters signing on. The change of Rule 6 brings all classes onto the same basis as far as the award of the club's major prizes is concerned. IYRU Rule 50 defines 'Ranking as a starter' as;- (a) a yacht whose entry has been accepted (presumably by the action of 'signing on' as far as MSC is concerned) and (b) that sails about in the vicinity of the starting line between her preparatory and starting signals. whether she starts or not. Clearly therefore, Rule 6 can never be correctly interpreted as meaning that the action of 'signing on' is, itself, sufficient to rank as a starter. Therefore a single helmsman cannot claim a win in a Points Series race by merely 'signing on' but not sailing. To rank as a 'Starter' a single helmsman must show a willingness/intention to sail the course by sailing 'in the vicinity of the start line etc...' but need not necessarily actually start. To claim a 'win' in a single-boat race, the helm concerned will presumably be required to complete the course set within the meaning and intent of the MSC Sailing Instructions (which includes the IYRU Rules). A helm who does not start cannot 'retire'; they rank as 'Did not Start'. Handicap Fleet - Prizes for winning Page 2 of the 1987 Year Book shows an asterisk against the Handicap Points Series races and states '* Dinghies eligible for class points may enter but are not eligible for prizes'. The Sailing Sub-Committee have confirmed that this refers to the Major Club Racing Awards for the Spring, Summer and Autumn Points Series only (eg. the award of the Edwards Cup). Any boat winning a Handicap Points Series Race will receive a prize for winning the individual race; this is, in fact, the policy adopted in previous years and the Sailing Sub-Committee merely re-state the policy in view of some recent confusion as to the intent of the statement. The 1988 Year Book may be amended to make the intention clearer. Continued next page .

12 Major Awards for the 420 Dinghy The Sailing Sub-Committee advise that none of the three major awards for the 420 dinghy class will be awarded for 1987. This is because the 420 dinghy helms lost their 'Fleet status' when they agreed to start with the Handicap Fleet rather than have a separate start time. The trophies affected are:- Spring Points Series - Jumbly Trophy Summer Points Series - Blackbird Trophy Autumn Points Series - Seaweed Trophy On the basis of the 'old' Rule 6 (ie. 'three starters'), there has only been one race this season when it was possible to extract from a Handicap Race an effective 3-boat 420 race, and this was Summer Points 3. The affect of 'extracting' this 420 result from the Handicap Fleet race was, of course, to eliminate the 420 boats from the Handicap Summer Points Series. However, now that the Sailing Sub-Committee have decided that the 420 awards cannot be made in 1987, all 420s are again eligible for the Handicap Summer Points Series award(Edwards Trophy). Logical illogicalities - or 'who wins what, when and how ?' One hopes that the following will be read with a certain amount of good humour. Now that the club has accepted the universal principle of the validity of 'the one horse race', Race Officers must obviously make sure that 'starters' are, indeed, starters according to IYRU Rule 50 and sail 'in the vicinity of the starting line between...etc.,etc.'. The R.O. should also only accept as a 'starter' a helm who has 'signed on' before his/her class 10-minute signal. A (Billericay) 420 late-comer, having overslept by 1½ hours, could arrive at the club to find that no other 420s were racing; therefore he sends his crew to chat up the R.O who, being a kindly soul, allows said 420 to sail the course set some (say) 47 minutes 23 seconds after the official time of the 'start' for the 420. Said 420 then claims a 'win'. Assuming the reader has now recovered his/her composure following the exclamation of indignation at such a dastardly deed, is there any real difference in a 'one horse race' if the lone sailor starts at the 'official' start time, or a later start time agreed between the R.O and the helm ? The logic of the 'one horse race' principle is to reward those who turn up to support the club's racing programme; it makes no difference to the 'result' of a one horse race whether said lone helm starts at 11.40 (for the Solo Lone Helmer) or at 12.40 for the self-same lone helmer (all 'tother Solo sailors probably went off to Fishers Green). Now that the Autumn Points Series are to be decided on the one horse race principle rather than 'the best of three helms' for each race, there seems no reason why the Enterprise and 420 Autumn Points major prizes should not be awarded even though neither have 'Fleet status'; similarly for the Hornet trophies and, no doubt, for other trophies which lie in the back of someone's cupboard for a former MSC class now defunct. These 'defunct' classes can all start with the Handicap Fleet and the pre-ordained win of the lone helmsman extracted. Who knows, perhaps I'll buy back my old Firefly, present a cup to the club and be the happy recipient of it for the next 6 years. It might not mean much in terms of sailing achievement but it sure looks good on the sideboard. As I said, to be read with a sense of humour - but also food for thought. I support the one horse race principle because the alternative leads to the discouragement of the 'lone sailor' from supporting the racing programme. Sorry about the typing - I'm using a 1930 petrol-driven portable and my left big toe is too big for the keys. Mike Boreham Result Secretary

2 CADET AND CAMPING FORTNIGHT JULY 24th to AUGUST 9th CAMPING CLUB BOATING GROUP This was the 4th year that the Camping Club Boating Group was invited to camp with the MSC at Stansgate. All those members of the CCBG who attended thoroughly enjoyed the camp, and would like me to thank the Committee and Members of the MSC for their hospitality and helpfulness. Some names were suggested for particular thanks, but I feel that to mention those would be unfair to all the others who also contributed to making this such an enjoyable holiday. The Camping Club Boating Group is a special interest group of The Camping and Caravanning Club (formerly The Camping Club of Great Britain and Ireland), and it is of particular credit to the MSC that several members of the CCBG have attended all 4 invitation camps, and some come from as far afield as Leicestershire and Lancashire. Nineteen CCBG units attended this year, with eleven camping for the full 2 weeks, and we hope that next year we can match these numbers to the mutual benefits of both the MSC and the CCBG Graham Boustred CADET WEEK 1987 I would like to thank all those who attended and, whether press-ganged or otherwise, helped to run the event. I feel that there was so much willing help given that it would be wrong to single out any individual names. It is intended to organise a similar week next year, but it is apparent that the Cadet Skipper will require even more assistance on the water with the ever-increasing number of Cadets. Could I ask you now to consider how you could help, perhaps? Again, many thanks to all concerned and I hope we will see you next year. N.T. COMMODORE 'S NOTES Here we are in September; the season is nearly over and the period of mellow fruitfulness is upon us. Was anyone quick enough to catch our summer? Let us away with frivolity and think only of such jollifications as 'working parties' and ‘laying up’ and next summer. The first of the new season's working parties has already taken place and I offer our congratulations and thanks to the environs party for their splendid efforts in the Cruiser Park which is now free of all extraneous lumps of iron and material and is quite ready for its quota of winter custamers. I am assured that every boat has been allocated a place and we require owners to use those spots only. If there are any difficulties, please refer to Arthur Hodges who will be happy to resolve them for you. We have had one or two unfortunate incidents this year which make it necessary for me to bring to your attention our rules and bye-laws of which every member is expected to be aware. These regulations are the result of thirty-five years worth of experience and have evolved from this accumulated wealth. They are there to allow us all to live in harmony and SAFETY with one another. In this connection I must remind members that they must have insurance for themselves and any guests using their equipment. In an effort to to emphasise this need, members will be asked to identify their insurance company and policy number at subscription time. One further safety point I must make is to tell you that children must NEVER be allowed to ride on the tractors. A child was doing so recently, fell off and was nearly run over - such an event must never happen. Another lot of unsung heroes of whom I must make mention are the crews who man our rescue facilities. They do a splendid job involving very long days and all that I would ask is that those who go sailing just as a long day is caming to a close should do so with due regard to their own safety and not stray so far as to require the further services of our hard-pressed rescue crews. Finally, on a happier note, I am sure you would like me to offer our thanks and appreciation to the Jessops for their imaginative menus of nutritious grub on offer to us these past few weeks. Thank you, we needed that. Robbie Sims, 13th September 1987
