Tales from Stansgate (1) THE TAIL OF TERRY LINN There was once a field mouse named Terry Linn who lived in the farmer's field near to the Big River. Also by this river was a sailing club named after the famous inventor Guglielmo Marconi. Terry Linn would often sit and watch the sailors having a wonderful time sailing in, and falling out of, their boats and he resolved to build one for himself. He searched for materials fran which to build his boat, and had no trouble at all finding same scrap wood. Being a rodent with big strong teeth he soon gnawed a perfect little Mirror Dinghy complete with a little mast, gaff and boon. He found same discarded whipping for sheets, halliards and painter, but he could not find any suitable material from which to make his sails, until one day in July, same Camping Club Boating Group members set up canp in the field next to that in which he lived. One of these campers, after a particularly wet day sailing, left his Mirror Dinghy sail spread out to dry on the ground in his caravan awning. In the middle of the night Terry Linn crept in and carefully nibbled out a piece just the right size to make a sail for his little boat. So now if you look carefully when the MSC Mirror fleet is out racing you will often see, right at the back, Terry Linn in his little boat - Sail No. Mouse 1 - and if Terry's friends can find enough sails left where they can borrow same pieces, then maybe next year Marconi's will have a Mouse Class fleet. THE END TERRY LINN

7 NOTES FROM THE SOLO A.G.M. - 27th AUGUST 1987 1. The AGM for the Solo Class Association was held during the World Championships at Mumbles Yacht Club. 2. The subscription is to go up to £10 next year with a view to holding it for two years after that. 3. The National Championships will be held at Whitstable next year, presumably on the long weekend formula. 4. The Meeting was chaired by Nick Yeomans in a brisk, constructive way. He was eventually elected President as Paul Hemsley resigned. 5. Most of the meeting was taken up by discussion of proposed rule changes, notified to members in advance. These had been proposed to update the rules to reflect modern construction practices and remove ambiguities. 6. No-one wanted the Solo to become a class where the ability to buy the most expensive equipment was the key to success. 7. The official situation is that where the AGM gave approval in principle to the rule changes, the Class Association will now get RYA lawyers to draft the changes in legalese before applying to the RYA for formal ratification of the changes. The basic information is as set out in the pack sent to members, I shall comment on amendments, etc. 8. - Transom flaps may be side hinged. - Instead of measuring mast weight plus C of G, the tip weight will now be specified. (Like Enterprises, apparently). - Internal (T-piece) fittings for shrouds were ruled out. It was felt they could be dangerous in a boat like the Solo with a slack rig. - It was stressed that shrouds must be removable; Jim Gates said that he would rule out shrouds connected directly to the hounds. - Wooden side tanks would be allowed on composite boats, they would have three buoyancy compartments like a wooden boat. - Centreboards and rudders may be glass sheathed in future. Most discussion on this point - many people thought it could lead to very expensive construction, but it was thought this could be overcome by a minimum weight limit. 9. Bill Loy and Michael Barnes were elected on to the Committee. There was one space left unfilled. Nick Yeomans thought this could be filled by someone to represent the Eastern Area. Meetings are in London on Friday evenings, about once every six weeks or so - Any offers? Roger Smith FOR SALE Road Trailer, 4-wheel, suit up to 27' fin. 8 AUTUMN BANK HOLIDAY HANDICAP SERIES 1987 To be honest, at the time of typing this article, I do not actually know for certain who has won the Autumn Bank Holiday Handicap Series; it's a job for the Sailing SubCommittee to adjudicate upon. Hopefully, by the time I reach the bottom of the page, the Sailing Sub will have decided in their wisdom what is to be done, and then I'll be able to fill in the gaps I left on the page. Just think, if I hadn't mentioned it, you'd never have known of the drama I've experienced in preparing this report. Race 1 was 'sailed' in little or no wind; an occasional puff helped those fortunate enough to be in the right position at the right time but 13 out of 18 didn't manage to finish, mainly due to lack of wind. Several of us spent a very frustrating 15 20 minutes only a few feet from the finish but the adverse tide thwarted our efforts. Dave Nixson, however, persisted with his characteristic single-mindedness, as did Colin Willsmore, and they both finished some 15 - 20 minutes after the winner, Ron Greygoose. When you consider that Ron was only about 50 yards ahead of them, you can understand the situation. Race 2 did at least have some wind, even if not a lot. The course was good in that it gave a true beat from Goldhanger to Breezy and this provided an interesting choice of route. As usual, I chose the wrong one and lost out badly, as did Peter Collis and Damian Boreham in the Mirrors. Mike Taylor, however, chose the right course and won the race; the point of this tale is that both Peter and Damian had a good lead over Mike at the time they chose the wrong way so, who knows, the Mirrors might have had 1, 2 and 3 in this race had they been as wise as Mike. 'Ah! if only....' ought to be emblazoned in bottle tops over the club bar, for such are the tales of woe to be heard every week in the changing room and what would be the 19th hole if we were a Golf Club. Race 3 saw not only a much better wind, but also the first appearance of the catamarans. Trevor Milton won it in his Stampede, Joan Hardie was second in her 420 and Dave Nixson sailed a canny race to just beat fellow Soloist Malcolm Gandy by 31 seconds on elapsed time. Again, the beat from 'E' mark to 'D' mark provided a choice of route - and again I chose the wrong one; it's getting to be a habit with me. Race 4 was sailed in the best wind yet and the catamarans won easily over the monohulls, filling the first three places with Mike Duckmanton providing his son, Tom, with another win towards his 'Mug's Mug' tally. A rush to pack up tents and caravans saw little time for frivolity, ending a weekend's sailing which saw varying fortunes as well as extremes of wind strength, a multitude of hard luck stories as well as a whole host of 'might-have-beens'; by the time you read this it will have all faded into the Club's history. I heard someone joke that maybe ‘over 40' referred to the waistline - in which case a girth certificate might have been more appropriate. Don't ask me why it's done this way - perhaps the first Jackpot race so exhausted the club's ancient mariners that, ever after, they insisted on a rest half way around. By happy chance, the half way point coincided with the J.S. Again, as a matter of interest, I've also produced an unofficial result based on each leg being treated as a separate race. Just because 'your' helm wins a Points Series, it doesn't mean you automatically get the crew's prize. It pays to turn out regularly (within the particular class) - even if you do not crew for the same helm each week. Similarly, a crew can win a Points Series prize even if their 'normal' helmsman doesn't receive one; take a look at who receives the 1st place 'crew's prize' for the Summer Mirror Points and you'll see what I mean (helm-husband Jack came 3rd). ********** ANY OLD NAVIGANS ? 2 CRUISER MEMBERS Firstly, apologies for not expending very much time with the Fleet this year, but as most know, I had an illness early in the Season. I was advised to stop sailing for some time and as a result made a calculated decision to sell Viridia. Initially I thought I could carry on as Fleet Captain but found it very difficult without a floating base and particularly when "Cruising in Company" needs the organiser to go along. I am therefore relinquishing the position as from the A.G.M. To date a successor has not bee found, although Malcolm Yeoman has kindly agreed to arrange the Winter Meeting programme. He has also offered to organise the Discount Paint Order, and you will be hearing from him about the details. The Laying-Up plan for this Winter is desplayed on the Club Notice Board and this should be 99% correct. Slight inaccuracy has arisen through two boats remaining at the Club after initially giving notice of leaving, but if any member has a problem please give me a telephone call. That takes care of everything except the trip to the Boat Show in January - so I am asking for a volunteer to make the necessary arrangements. Not a difficult task but preferably requires someone who will be going along. Next Season we should have a new Fleet Captain to take over the tasks and hopefully the "Cruising in Company" which has sadly been hit by the weather this year. Thank you for your help and support, particularly during my illness and the offers of a sail which I will be taking up next year. I am not leaving the Club, and from the date of the A.G.M. will probably be taking over a job on the shore where I can keep in touch albeit without a boat. 7 * * * MIRROR NEWS The Summer (what summer ??) Points Series has now finished and the Autumn Series has begun; results for the Summer Series are to be found elsewhere in this Navigans (I hope!). Whatever the results, it was nice to see Mike Taylor and his daughter, Helen, sailing again in the Autumn Bank Holiday Series in which they proved themselves the leading Mirror - and won one of the races. The weekend of 19/20 September was the club's Mirror Open Meeting and I'm happy to report that 5 MSC Mirrors took part, along with 6 visiting boats. The club helms were Debbie Yorston, Jon Yorston, Mike Battle, Damian Boreham and Mike Boreham . The winner was Michael Wright (from our near neighbours, Maylandsea Bay Sailing Club) who not only won overall, but also won the first three races (he didn't sail the last race). However, he didn't have it all his own way all the time and some good racing was enjoyed throughout the fleet. The best MSC boat was Damian, crewed by Katy Rutherford, who finished 3rd overall.and the full results are set out below. Our thanks to the Catamaran Fleet who organised this open meeting so well (and, as always, with good humour and friendliness) . Our thanks also to the Jessop family - no, not just for doing the catering, but for providing Mike Boreham with a crew for races 3 and 4 (he went single-handed for 1 and 2); Susan Jessop had her first taste of sailing in the Mirror image and apparently thoroughly enjoyed it. Rumour has it that Susan is now trying to persuade her Dad to buy her a Mirror - let's hope she is successful and that she is able to join the Mirror Fleet in 1988. Autumn Points 3 saw 7 Mirrors racing whilst, in the afternoon, race 4 had 8 Mirrors sailing (and we could have had 10 sailing !). There's no doubt about it, we're growing in strength and slowly but surely catching up the Solo Fleet with our numbers. ** Vic Braybrook returned to the fold on the morning of 27 September with 'Flaming Pest', complete with his crew-daughter Kim, and they proved that a long break hadn't affected their sailing skill - except for Vic's timing ! He was a long way over the line at the start of Autumn 4 but by the 2nd mark had overtaken all but Damian, Roy Woods and Dave Onyons. The lead then changed between these 4 boats until the final leg when Damian crossed the line 1st, Vic 2nd, Dave 3rd and Roy 4th. However, an eerie silence greeted Damian from the Race Box as he optimistically waited for 'the hoot'; what a pity he'd forgotten to sign on ! Thus, Vic was the well deserved winner after all, everyone moved up a place and Damian discovered he'd literally never been in the race in the first place; I bet that's something he won't do again, at least for a while. By the time you read this, the sailing will be over for another year, so let's hope all the Mirror people who sailed in 1987 will continue to do so in 1988; perhaps some others will join us on the waters in what must be one of the most pleasant of sailing areas. ** STOP-PRESS: There were 12 Mirrors in Autumn Points Race 6, and we could have had 14. We have just had our 1987 A.G.M. and the Commodore's and Sailing Secretary's reports are in this Navigans and will make interesting and informative reading if you weren't able to get to the A.G.M. * The Cadet Winter Meetings are due to begin in January, more details to appear in next Navigans. (Note that Year-Book dates do not tie in with Saturdays - hence question mark.) Congratulations to Helen (Bates) who was awarded the Garrett Trophy, taking over from Richard Battle who held it last year. It is awarded to the Cadet considered to have contributed most to the good of the Club - not necessarily on the water. Finally, I do hope the Navigans doesn't arrive too late as I am typing it over a week after the deadline. Luckily our schedule of Diary Dates are much less hectic at this time of year.

COMMODORE'S REPORT - A.G.M. 8th November 1987 When I came to write this report for you I was at first under the impression that in many ways the year has been a non-Year. Principally I think this has been the result of the non-summer of wet and not particularly warn weather we have ‘enjoyed' culminating in a hurricane the likes of which we have not had in the past century, or two, or three! Some serious losses have resulted from the hurricane to some members while others have had lucky escapes. I should like to express our sympathy to those who have suffered losses and offer felicitations to those who were lucky. There, but for the Grace of God, go any of us. I do not propose in my report to deal with a load of statistics of our events as I am assuming that these will be the basis of the secretarial reports which follow mine. My task as I see it is to deal with policy and to try to make myself sensitive to the wishes of the membership as a whole. In this connection T have found it to be an extremely difficult year since I found myself precipitated into M.S.C. politics after a break of 24 years. So I have had a lot of catching up, learning and re-organising of my thoughts to do before being in a position to offer the lead you could expect from my predecessors. ww My first impression of the Club was that it was well run by a core of able, well motivated, active members operating a well-established routine, developed over many years. This impression I have discovered to be well-founded. You do have such a core of enthusiasts to whom we owe a great debt of gratitude for their work and dedication and without whom we would not have survived so long. Thank you from us all. I refer, of course, to all those members of committees, sub- committees, project groups etc., both official and unofficial who have for so long dedicated their lives (not too strong a term) to our better enjoyment of our chosen sport/pastime, call it what you will. What is worrying though, to me aS a new boy is the impression that we need far more active involvement from our younger members. SO come on you younger ambitious ones, help us to identify you and so harness your energies and ideas to the greater good! I should like now to turn to our ongoing sore which we are still truing to resolve and that is the question of our contribution to the MASC for the facilities which we enjoy here. We have so far signally failed ever to achieve a sensible dialogue with the General Committee of the MASC with whose philosophy and approach in this matter we disagree profoundly. To this end we have invoked the aid of the Trustees to see if they can offer some acceptable arbitration. Your committee does notTM object to making a contribution, or even its magnitude,Wthe MASC for our facilities which we think is only fair - but only to the manner in which the MASC wants to assess this hurden and with which we disagree fundamentally as being wrong. There is a resolution for you to consider later which, with your support, may help us to precipitate a solution to our difficulty. A solution to this difficulty is fundamental to our future development since we are coming to size and activity level when our tradition of self-help may no longer be possihle or even relevant. This will give rise to a great deal of serious thinking on how to go forward as additional substantial funding may be necessary and if we cannot have an acceptable, fair and predictable arrangement with our parent how can we expect to plan ahead? Your committee is nothing if not optimistic though, and I am very pleased to announce that 1988 will see us once again holding a Regatta at the end of May. This result is due in no small way to the dedication and imagination of Malcolm Stuart who has driven this project forward overcoming all the difficulties to produce a package which will make it work in practice. So I hope we can now unite 100% behind him to help the project exceed our expectations. As a spin-off we will be trying

3 certain re-organisation of the garage areas and from this experience we hope to learn and then promulgate a 5-Year Plan of development where it will be possible to correlate funding and spend in a way which will do most good. It is terribly easy to blue a lot of money on eating out at the best restaurants when, perhaps by planned restraint, we should be planning to buy the restaurant. Another aspect of our Club which your Committee has recognised as a growth area is that relating to Winter Storage of boats which I can only see increasing both for Cruisers and Dinghies. This means improved storage facilities will be a must if we are not all to sink into a quagmire. This will need funding, and we have taken the initial step of proposing differential storage fees for Cruisers based on length - for want of a better yard stick! We hope you can support this important measure because the Cruiser fleet is growing in size and influence and, by definition needs additional facilities like hard standings, power, space etc. which we will try to provide as fast as funds will allow. One area which has become a bit of a minefield is our Rules where certain changes, particularly over the past few years have not (perhaps?) been properly ratified by the MASC. This is my fault because I did not really appreciate the extent of the situation early enough. (Sorry, Malcolm, you did kick hard enough - but I was too thick!) However, I have now had discussion with Gerry Wignall, and Pat is preparing a new corrected full set of rules which we will then submit to the General Committee of the MASC formally. I do not expect more than one or two changes will be necessary. Implicit in a lot I have been saying is the underlying need to increase our membership substantially and I would like to take this opportunity to promote the idea in each of your minds the resolve to say out loud on January 1st 1988 "This year I will find and introduce a new member to the Club." To succeed in this resolve would, at a stroke, dissolve many of our financial and funding worries and we could then do most of what we need to without having to raise any additional funds. Before I conclude I am pleased to announce that Eastern Electricity has undertaken to divert our power lines underground (somebody must have worked hard on them) and because one of the new stays comes on our ground they will be paying us rent of £1.19 p.a. for the privilege. In conclusion I would like to say what an honour and a privilege I have regarded being your Commodore this past year. We are the best Sailing Club around and we can all take pride in being members and for my part - I thank you. SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT A.G.M The main events over the year were as follows: 1. Thanks to the assistance of Mike Battle we have been able to return to the 'book' type of Year Book; I hope this is satisfactory to members. 2. John Nickalls organised a stand at the SAILBOAT 87 Exhibition at Crystal Palace again this year. It was a good stand which did the Club credit and attracted much interest. We plan to put on a stand in 1988. 3. Although we experimented with sub-committee meetings at Stansgate on Sundays in the summer, we could not get people out of the bar or off the water (no names, no pack drill), so we reverted to MASC. 4. 1987 has once again seen an increase in the number of dinghies sailed at the Club from 179 in 1986 to 311 in 1987. Racing in the points series has also seen an increase in participation. contd....

4 5. There has been plenty of activity in the Cruiser fleet with many individual cruises and cruises-in-company being organised under the leadership of Arthur Hodges. It was rather disappointing that the Barnacle points series did not receive better support. 6. Results of major events: Helmsman of Year - Trevor Milton (Cat Fleet) Marconi Dinghy Challenge Cup - John Weedon (H/c) Marconi Cruiser Cup - A. Moncrieff (MLSC) Rum Tub & Bung - Joan & Jack Hardie (MSC) Barnacle Points - Mike Turner & Ian Lindsay Ladies Cup - Maggie Boreham & Debbie Yorston Cadet Cup - Damian Boreham The Cadet Week had again been a great success due in no small measure to the efforts of the Cadet Captain, Derek Hall. It was good to see the Ladies Cup sailed for once again, despite the attentions of some drag competitors (sex tests next year?) 7. Three open meetings had been held at the Club: Cat/Solo/Enterprise at the Spring bank holiday organised by the Mirror Fleet; in September a Cat/Hornet meeting run by the Solo fleet; and a Solo/Mirror open organised by the Caramaran fleet. All the meetings had been well run, attracting favourable comment from visitors. Attendance had been similar to last year with a slight upturn in the Mirror fleet. These meetings provide enjoyment to club members and visitors as well as a useful contribution to club funds. 8. Team sailing must be improved in 1988. We failed to win the Rochester Visit, Boothby Cup or the MBYC Challenge. 9. Sailboarding at the Club has steadily increased and whilst they do not yet participate in racing they have made a good contribution to the running of the Club. 10. Rescue facilities at the Club were in good shape thanks to the efforts of the Coxswain, Doug Brown and his team of drivers. Radio communications have not been without problems, but these had now been solved. Arthur Hodges would run a radio users course in the winter. 11. Finally, thanks go to the Fleet Captains for their support throughout the season in organising duties etc. Also to other volunteers such as Ray Ball, Bosun; John Walker, Race Equipment Officer; Mike Boreham, Results Secretary; Andy Rimmer, (radios) etc. Roger Smith, Sailing Secretary. SOLO NEWS Helmsman of the Year Final - our man Malcolm Gandy battled valiantly throughout but had to give best finally to Trevor Milton in the demanding conditions. The Solo Fleet would like to add our contratulations to Trevor for a fine performance. Now that the sailing season is over, the Fleet would like to express appreciation to the Rescue Boat Coxswain and Drivers for sustaining that essential service throughout the season. The Fleet AGM was held on October 7th with eleven Solo helms in attendance. I will not attempt to repeat the minutes here, but only to pick out a few of the decisions made, as follows:

5 1. A marginal decision on a split vote to support continuation of the Sailing Programme for 1988 generally in line with this year, although some were unhappy with the pursuit race format on a Sunday. 2. The Club will send a team or teams to the NSCA Team Racing Championships in 1988. 3. John Salmon agreed to continue as Fleet Captain for another year. He requested that an Assistant be appointed. Dave Nixson agreed to fulfill that function. 4. Three main Solo Class Social Events for the winter were agreed as follows: a) Solo Supper - Friday 15th January. b) Meeting/Party at John Rutherford's - early March. (This will be a 'bring your own food' job - details later.) c) Solo Dinner Party at Stansgate - Sat 9th April. 5. The possibility of a training day at Stansgate on a Saturday, with RYA personnel providing instruction, to be investigated. 6. The Club should attempt to provide more beats in the courses set for 1988. The Sailing Sub Committee was requested to consider using additional inflatable marks in order to achieve this. Since the AGM the details of our first social event have been finalised. The Supper will be at the Cross Keys pub in Roxwell on Friday 15th January commencing at 8.15pm. They offer quite a good choice of menu, with an average three course meal costing about £7.50. A private room will be provided which we can use for the evening so it promises to be a first class event, in a geographic location which minimises travel time. A good turn-out is needed in order to make it a success, so please note the date now and try to support it. An indication of numbers attending is required, so if you intend to go, please inform Pat Stuart or myself. John Salmon, 0277 [redacted] THANK YOU.... May we, through Navigans, express our thanks to Peter Clayton, Dave Thomas, Murray Bates and all those many people who helped to recover 'Juliet' which capsized during the recent storms. Sincerely, Julie and Peter Bloomfield. B) Mr & Mrs Apthorpe would like to thank the unknown member/s who secured the hatch on 'Bella' after the storm. C) Thank You I would like to say a public thank-you to all those who gave or offered help in the recovery of the battered remains of the unfortunate MEG after she capsized on her mooring during the night of the great storm. In particular, I would mention the prompt action of club officials in righting her which meant that she only dried out twice in the inverted state. To someone living 75 miles away from Stansgate, this kind of immediate action is especially welcome. I hope that the two volunteers who helped carry the mast and spars with trailing halyards and shrouds across what seemed like a hundred yards of Blackwater mud and then over the sea wall didn't suffer any permanent damage to their clothing from that same mud. As the hull is intact, my own view is that repair should be an economic proposition contd....

4 A NOTE FROM THE SAILING SECRETARY 1987 Prizes First a note from the 1987 season. Several people were either unable to attend the prizegiving on 8th November and/or were perhaps unaware that they won a prize. I have still got some prizes that I have not been able to distribute so could the following people get in touch with me to arrange for your prize to be collected. Charlotte Burck Phil May Mike Taylor Dave Onyons Janet Keeble Howard Knott My telephone number is 0799 [redacted] (home) 01-936-2211 (work) MAMGU On my mantlepiece stands the magnificent model of the barge yacht Mamgu. I am rather embarrassed about it since I have done nothing to win it. However, since John Wade returned it to me this season, it seems far too good to put away in a cupboard. One of the perks of the Hon. Sailing Secretary? So what about it, folks, who is going to wrest it from my grasp at the Laying Up Supper next year? The period to be covered is from August 1st 1987 (so there is still time to write up this year's cruise in those lazy winter evenings) and the cruise should normally be of more than three days' duration. It is not confined to cruisers, dinghy cruises count and you don't have to be the owner or helmsman of the yacht, as long as you contributed to the voyage. How about it kids? It might double up as a homework project! What I should say at this stage is that the trophy is awarded to the best account or log of a cruise voyage in a sailing or auxillary yacht or dinghy. On a rather sombre note "a colourful account of escapades arising out of gross ignorance or neglect of seamanlike prudence or out of sheer foolhardiness, may be placed lower than a cruise in which hazardous conditions were avoided by good planning." (That lets the Cat Fleet out!) Other Prizes Whilst I'm on the subject of cruising prizes you may notice that the yearbook mentions that prizes will be given for various cruises as follows: a) For a cruise to a neighbouring estuary (the Colne doesn't count). b) For a week's cruise away from home waters c) For going foreign! These prizes are for members' first cruise in each category. So! tell the Cruiser Fleet Captain about your achievements and we will try to wind it up next year. Roger Smith THE HANDICAP FLEET CHRISTMAS CARD As we come to the end of the year I would like to thank everyone who helped me with Fleet Duties during the past year, especially those who stepped in at short notice. Without your help we would not be able to race as often as we do. Thanks also, on behalf of the handicap fleet, to the drivers and crews of the Jack B for pulling us out of the water, I will try not to make as much use of your services next year. It is nice to see that the numbers of people who raced are up on last year's figures, let us see if we can make it even more next year. Congratulations to everyone who took part in the racing and did not win (the winners have already been rightly congratulated.) I hope you, like me, still got lots of enjoyment out of your sailing, and just think without us there could not be any winners. Irene and myself would like to wish every Handicap Member, their crews, wives etc. a very happy Christmas, together with Best Wishes for good sailing in the New Year. We look forward to meeting you on the water next year. Mike Hellewell

5 SOLO NEWS One important decision from the Solo Fleet AGM which I omitted to mention last month was that positions in selected Eastern Area open meetings would not in 1988 count toward points for the relevant MSC series. This is a deviation from our fleet practice in recent seasons. Would the Results Secretary kindly take note. In case anyone missed the information in last month's Navigans I will repeat here the details of arrangements for the Solo Fleet Supper: Date: Friday 15th January 1988 Time: 8.15pm Cost of meal: Approx £7.50 (depending on what you order from quite a broad-choiced menu.) Location: Cross Keys pub - Roxwell Leaving Chelmsford, travelling west on the A414 toward Hertford, the pub is on your left. Since a private room has been booked for there event, I really would like to know who is going to attend - the more the merrier, so please give me a call if you are intending to go. There have been some enquiries from Club Members interested in sailing Solo next season, for obvious reasons. I would welcome hearing from any others who are similarly inclined, as I am planning to provide opportunities to sail the boat early next season, under racing or non-racing conditions as preferred. In this respect I would also like to compile a list of Solo owners who would be prepared to let others sail their boat on occasions when they are tied up with Fleet Duties, OOD Duties, etc. Would any such willing souls please let me know. For most of us the season is now over, although one or two brave men can even now be seen of a Sunday up the darkest crevices of Mayland Creek challenging the elements and carrying the banner of the MSC. I am anticipating a report from this field of conflict in the February edition. Looking back over the year should give us all a great deal of satisfaction since we have seen significant increases both numerically and in competitive standard of our fleet without, I feel, losing any of the good sportsmanship and camaraderie which is an essential part of our enjoyment of sailing. Everyone who has participated in the fleet's activities, at whatever level, should take some pride and satisfaction in that achievement. It has certainly made the Fleet Captain's job an easy and a pleasurable one - thank you. I'm sure the Solo Fleet would like to join me in wishing all Club Members a very Happy Christmas*. Hope to see you all on the 28th December working party. John Salmon, [redacted] *On behalf of the other Members Ed. returns your good wishes! 6 CADET NEWS 1988 Looms For those of you who are wanting to start at the beginning or who want to move up a rung on the ladder, the winter talks are beginning on Saturday evenings, 6-7pm in the Board Room as follows: Jan 9th Jan 23rd Feb 6th Feb 20th March 5th March 19th We aim to get you sailing safely and competently and have a lot of fun at the same time. All who obtained or upgraded their RYA qualifications this summer and haven't got a certificate, please return their log books to me with 35p for updating. Keep logging your sailing time and you will soon be qualified to take over my sailing job. Derek Hall LAYING UP SUPPER Conrad passes on his thanks to all who came along to the Laying Up Supper which, was much enjoyed by those who attended. Robbies's speech went down well; and the excellent band & cabaret will be booked again for next year's event. Personal thanks go to Mr & Mrs John Rutherford for their donation of some of the Raffle Prizes which added to the enjoyment of the evening. The next social function will be the Barn Dance on Saturday 13th February. Mr Claud Emerson Retirement Mr Claud Emerson, our caretaker for the past 18 years, retired recently. During his stay with us Claud distinguished himself by his friendly demeanour and general helpfulness to all who were fortunate enough to meet him. At a reception held at the Star Public House in Steeple on Wednesday 25th November, Claud was presented with a mounted ship's clock and barometer in thanks for his service to the Club. We all wish Claud and his wife Ivy a long and happy retirement. Pat Black Many of our club members may not know Claud by sight, even after 18 years, as Claud's work was done mainly when those of us who only frequented the club at weekends were not there. Claud told me that one day when he was unsuccessfully trying to get into the Clubhouse (the lock wouldn't work), a member came over to try and help but without result. "We'll have to call out the chap who looks after the place," the member said. Claud had to reply "I am the chap who looks after the place!" Claud and Ivy have now moved to Berkshire to be nearer to their family, but they will continue to receive Navigans and expect to visit the Club when they visit the area in the future. Ed. COMMODORE 'S NOTES Christmas has come and gone and here we are at the start of a bright new Leap Year and may I wish you all a very Happy and Prosperous Year. In many respects the Sailing Club is facing a year in which I foresee not a few pitfalls and difficulties which we will have to address and overcome. As I said at the AGM your Committee would like to take time to discuss and draw up a plan which looks at the development of the Sailing Club on a longer term basis so that we have a chance to arrange priorities and finance in a controlled manner including having discussions and obtaining the full backing of all the Members. The way forward, however, is being frustrated right from the outset because we do not have enough volunteers to fill the vacancies on the Main Committee, particularly from Marconi employee Members. Being a member of the Main Committee need not take up much of your time, only as much as you want to give. Your views, however, in that forum are vital to the future of sailing as we know it. If you are interested then phone me NOW at [redacted] Ext 437, or at home on [redacted] - or contact any Committee Member. Your Club Needs YOU. We have had our post-Christmas Working Party on what was a mild and pleasant day which, speaking for myself, helped to blow away many a cobweb. It was well attended, much valuable work was accomplished and it gives me much pleasure to thank everyone who came for their efforts, which are much appreciated. I have always been very proud of our Club and one ofthe principal factors which has sustained that view over the years has been the spirit of independence demonstrated by the degree of self-help shown by the Membership. We are a self-help Club and we get things done because WE do them. I recognise that as the Club activities expand the work-load becomes more onerous and a time will come when we will need to consider some full-time assistance. With the departure of Claude into well-earned retirement, perhaps now is the time. Do you have any views? If so, please talk to me or any Committee Member urgently. THE ANNUAL RNLI ROWING RACE MALDON LITTLE SHIP CLUB (Sunday 3rd January 1988) Never leave a meeting even for the most urgent reasons, because those that remain have a nasty habit of volunteering you for something. It happened to me at the Sailing Sub-Committee Meeting when I returned from a short walk down the MASC corridor to find that I had volunteered to join the M.S.C. crew in the Annual Rowing Race to be held on January 3rd. As I have a cruiser, (they said) I must be good at rowing. (Have they never heard of outboard motors?) The final crew line-up was Malcolm Stuart (team leader), Roger Smith, Ian Lindsay and yours truly. Malcolm decreed that we needed a practice, so the date was set for Sunday 20th December. So rapidly did our fame spread that my sister and brother-in-law flew in from Virginia, U.S.A. to witness the practice session. (They did stay for Christmas as well, but I am sure the initial attraction was the rowing race practice.) Ian could not make the practice session (he must have known a thing or two!) so David Ball substituted as helmsman. The Fisherman was launched and we managed to row it up to No.2 Buoy against the ebb tide and a fresh westerly breeze. I enjoyed the trip back resting on the oars. All this time brother-in-laww (like a true American) was clicking away with his camera ("Hey, you guys are crazy!") The practice session showed that fine tuning of the Fisherman was required. Some new '‘'go-faster' rowlocks were required, a pair of oars had to be shortened and new grips fashioned (technical stuff). Christmas was spent gathering sponsorship and manufacturing the obligatory Viking helmet. Sunday January 3rd dawned after a very wet and windy night. "Tt's a waste of time driving to Maldon this morning, it's too windy, they'll surely postpone the event," I told myself, turning over for my second sleep. However a sense of duty overcame my inertia and complete with family (for moral, and possibly later, physical support) I arrived at Hythe Quay roughly on time. The rest of the crew were already there sporting a variety of Viking helmets. The Fisherman was equipped with mast and M.S.C. Flag, lowered by crane into the water and secured on the pontoon ready for the start. The race plan was to down a drink at Maldon Little Ship Club, run to the boats and row to Maldon Yacht Club, run to the clubhouse, down another drink andTM@ collect a balloon. Then it was a run back to the boat and the long row up to the Fullbridge for another drink and balloon. Here we had a problem as the pub was upstream of the bridge and our boat had a mast..... The final leg was back to the M.L.S.C. and a run into the clubhouse to sign-off. (No-one said anything about this running). There was a good turn-out of boats and crews for the event, many in fancy dress and a lot of fun was had by all. The West Mersea Lifeboat and Dick Townshend in his Mobile Coastguard Vehicle and quite a few spectators turned up to provide a bit of extra support. We achieved 3rd place in some class or other and over £100 of sponsorship. Many thanks to all of you who donated to this worthy cause. RAY BALL, Usually Bosun. 6 Cadet Skipper Derek Hall has contributed notes from his sailing trip last year in the hope that it will be of interest to other members. It will appear in 2 or 3 instalments of Navigans and may well help to while away the winter while the keen ones among us are waiting to get onto the water again.... LISBON TO ST HELIER THOUGHTS AND FACTS RECORDED ALONG THE WAY ON "OCEAN CHALLENGER" SATURDAY 2nd MAY 1987 Martin and I flew from Heathrow on the 18.25 T.A.P. flight to Lisbon. The food was good and the drinks were free, and as I had never visited the capital of Portugal, I was looking forward to the trip. The boat, a Trident Challenger 35' long-keel sloop, had left Palma Mallorca two weeks previously and had last been heard from in Gibraltar. We were met at the airport by a tired looking skipper and crew. Spirits revived after a good seafood meal and a visit to a cafe in gardens right in the centre of Lisbon. The four of us sat drinking beer and watched the world go by, still in our shirt sleeves until 2.30am. This was a real transformation having left England enjoying a rainy Saturday in one of the coldest springs I can remember. We took a taxi out to the marina, and rowed out to the boat. We were moored next to a Swan which was bristling with winches. SUNDAY 3rd MAY This was a make and mend day. We worked on the engine and prepared for sea in the morning. Weather was glorious and sunny. In the afternoon we walked a way along the banks of the River Tagus. My camera seized up at the top of an eight storey sun dial monument. We then caught a 1930's vintage tram (all cast iron and wood) to the city centre where we took in the sights of Lisbon - the architecture and the senoritas. There being no food shops open anywhere, we boarded a trolley bus back to the boat for afternoon tea in the cockpit beneath the awning. A taxi was ordered in the evening for another hit at the seafood, which is plentiful and good everywhere in Lisbon. We still had to water and provision for the first leg of 150 miles north to Porto. MONDAY 4th MAY We shopped at the Co-Op first thing - fresh food for three days. Bought stamps but could not find postcards. Breakfasted and filled up with water. It was 10.30am when we slipped our berth and moved out into the river. We set our number two jib and were soon doing 6 - 7 knots with the wind behind us. The sun was scorching hot. Rubbing my factor 5 suntan oil in, we were fighting for the best positions in the cockpit - look out Atlantic, here we come! As we passed Estoril in the flat calm river I could see a line of white along the shore beneath the cliffs ahead. Could they be breakers? They were! Lunch-time and we turned northwards and the wind was now on the nose, and we encountered the Atlantic for the first time. The engine was turned on and we were doing 5 knots in a long swell of 20 feet top to bottom. As one who had never been physically seasick before, I scoffed my lunch of tinned salmon with asparagus and salad, feeling slightly uneasy. At 14.30 I could not navigate any more, and had a total paralysis in putting my head down into the locker to get my oilskins and seaboots out. The wind and the seas head risen and so was my lunch about to. Once oilskinned and harnessed up, I practised the mariner's ancient call to "Hughiee!!! The swell had grown in size to something I had never encountered before. We sailed up and up and up the side of each swell, and then down and down. They were very long and we collectively estimated them to be 30 - 40 feet from top to bottom. All I could do was steer the boat with the spray coming over the bow, over the boat, over the sprayhood and then over me. I was still heaving my heart out regularly, but eating the odd Ryvita. The night wore on and I finally went below at 0400, wet, tired and still very ill. Martin had also been sick since teatime and many plastic bags had come up and over the side from my berth where he lay prostrate. My relief at 0400 was very perky with a cheery "Good Morning!" - I won't repeat my reply! TUESDAY 5th MAY 0800 I was fast asleep in the pilot berth when I was awakenend as the engine was shut off with clouds of smoke. The engine water inlet seacock had broken off and overheated the engine. The top of a mastic tube cured the problem. We sailed for four hours to cool off the engine. The winds were still strong and the seas still rough. 1000 There was a loud crash as our radar reflector crashed down on deck and then over the side. The rivets on the crosstrees had pulled out. We had eight attempts to get alongside it and it took all four of us to get it on board. I think we were all thinking how difficult it would be if it was one

7 of us, but no-one said anything. I was cold, wet and sick, and my gear below had got wet. Oh what had I let myself in for? 2100 Nearing Oporto, the evening meal was served up and I tried my first meal for a day and a half. Cannelloni on Ryvita. The seas were flattening out and I felt a lot better. 2300 Secured in Oporto after having a devil of a job finding the entrance. We were now pumping the bilge every half an hour. 167 miles logged so far. I didn't think much of the first leg! WEDNESDAY 6th MAY The morning was spent finding the leak and curing it. We also had to change the alternator which was putting too much charge into the batteries and boiling them up. The boat was also in quite a mess after the heavy weather. Brunch and went shopping. Tasted a super crab salad in a local restaurant. We were so tired after brunch a sleep was called for. Late afternoon, provisions were bought in the port area where the ladies kept smiling at us? The Oporto Yacht Club visitors' books made fascinating reading of all the worldwide ocean voyagers who had called there. In the evening we caught a bus to take us the 14 kilometres into town. We were directed to a tourist restaurant by a policeman, but we decided not to eat after one beer. They wanted 350 escudos for the beer and 1800 escudos cover charge. It was a total rip-off and after a near punch-up we left and paid for beer only. I sent postcards from a hotel and had a meal on good old Barclaycard because I had spent all my escudos. We pooled our last money and had to run for the last bus at 2330. My, what jet setters! I slept the sleep of the dead again that night. THURSDAY 7th MAY To sea again. 175 miles for the next leg. I silently hoped it was not going to be like the last one. 0600 We slipped, hoping to get the local easterly winds which blow in the mornings only. Weather was superb. Six hours of great sailing, but by mid-day the winds had become northerly again. Engine on, we fought for the best in the cockpit. The sun was great. I was determined to get a sun tan before we got too far north. The day passed slowly by as we sailed a couple of miles offshore in 50 metres of water, watching the mountains through binoculars and keeping station with a Spanish yacht further inshore. PM We were suddenly surrounded by dolphins playing all around us. They were fantastic. They took it in turns to get right under our bows and keep station there. We were travelling at 5 - 6 knots while another dozen or so ducked and dived and rolled on their backs - a truly magnificent sight. Late afternoon a large cruise liner was seen ahead coming out of Vigo. We later found it was the 'Canberra'. The night passed by under a blaze of stars, and we could see many lights of the large fishing fleets all along the coast, which we managed not to get involved with. There were also many friendly lighthouses, some of which were 150 metres up the side of the cliffs and mountains. The Admiralty pilots disapprove of them being so high, because any mist or fog and they are obscured above the mist which is not uncommon on this coast. TO BE CONTINUED.......

2 CRUISER NEWS For the March Cruiser Meeting I have arranged a talk and video film covering an event of a slightly different flavour. The subject is 'The Three Peaks Yacht Race' and the speaker will be Duncan Phillips. As an introduction to this event I have included Duncan's comments providing some background to the race: "The Barmouth to Fort William Three Peaks Yacht Race was the brainchild of the famous explorer and venturer, Major H.W. Tilman. At the time, 1977, he was living in Barmouth in West Wales, and two local doctors conceived the actual details of the Race. The Race has been competed each year since then and has grown in number of entrants and is now a fiercely contested sailing and running race. An outline of the race is: Yachts of any size or type may compete with no handicapping. Crews to number 5 in all, with any 2 to run and climb each mountain. The overall sailing distance is about 400 miles, and running about 74 miles, with mountain ascents totalling 11,176 feet. Boats have to sail from Barmouth to Caernarfon - runners ascend Snowdon, 3,560 feet and distance of 24 miles, returning to boat totally unassisted. From Caernarfon to Ravenglass on Cumbria Coast by any route; runners scale Scafell Pike, 3,210 feet and 32 miles. Then to Fort William (Corpach) by Mull of Kintyre to climb Ben Nevis, 4,406 feet and 18 miles. The Race finishing when runners return to boat. Total number of boats restricted to 35 because of berthing problems in the harbours. Boats must comply with D.O.T. and Yacht Racing Standards for Category 3 Offshore Races. Runners' equipment must contain minimum for mountain survival. The race is run in June - usually the nearest Saturday to mid-summer with a convenient late afternoon high tide. I have personally competed some 6 years now, skippering a boat for 5 of these and taking part in the running. We have had various results from finishing 10th to not finishing at all. The important point is that anyone can enter. The purpose of the Race is to prove endurance; capability of finishing at whatever place is a tremendous achievement for those taking part." DUNCAN PHILLIPS. Look forward to seeing you all at the M.A.S.C. on 9th March, about 7.30pm. Malcolm Yeoman Varuna II Tel. 4 MIRROR NEWS Happy New Year to all the Mirror Fleet. Now is the time to start thinking about the coming season and preparing your boat. We are not much further than the thinking stage ourselves. Damian ventured out to the garage one day where Bumble is in residence awaiting attention but soon returned requesting a heater. My reply was unhelpful and Bumble is still waiting! Lars Tinn is up on a rack above Bumble so will probably have an even longer wait for attention. ("Thank goodness for fibre glass boats," I can hear some people saying!) The season starts early this year - March 27th - but it would be nice to see some red sails out with the Solo Fleet. Their Fleet Captain, by tradition, buys all the intrepid Solo helmsmen a pint on that first day. Perhaps we need that sort of incentive - how about it, Mike? A mug of soup would do and probably be more appropriate! The Dinghy Park is being laid out in a slightly different way this year; the Club will be providing stakes for your boat. If the positions are wrong then blame Malcolm Stuart who organised a few of us at the Christmas Working Party to measure out the area and put in posts and string to his measurements! This was done so that John Rutherford can easily place the stakes. I believe that it will be "first come, first served" as to where you actually park your boat; another reason to sail the first Spring Points races. The Cadet series is longer this year, 8 or 9 races instead of the usual 6, and some of these are being held on a Saturday. I hope the Cadets will be able to manage a Saturday as well as a Sunday. I don't know if we can but we'll try! I mention this here because a lot of Mirrors are sailed by Cadets and I hope you read this article. (...as well as my other reader!) 5 The second of three instalments of Cadet Skipper Derek Hall's account of his sailing trip last year from Lisbon to St Helier.... FRIDAY 8th MAY 0400 My watch began. We had been dodging the inshore fishing fleets all night and we had now rounded Cape Finisterre (I had always wondered where it was) with our diesel running low. At Cape Villano lighthouse we altered course eastwards. We were now round the tip of northern Spain and entering the Bay of Biscay. A decision had been made to pull in somewhere for diesel although none of our charts had any details of approach. We had large scale charts of only the places we were to visit. Our present charts covered Gibraltar to the Bay of Biscay, some 500 miles. After a day's run at 5½ knots average, we moved only several inches on the charts! Not like navigating on Thames estuary charts. On our approach to the most beautiful bay in which the town of Corme is situated we were directed across the bay to the village of Laxe where a fuel pump had been seen on the end of the jetty by a passing Moody. 1030 No one could be found to sell us diesel, until, with a lot of sign language, we ascertained that it was tokens only for the local fishing fleet. The sun was very hot by now after being at sea. I had drawn the short straw and, armed with a five gallon can, I climbed aboard the fish collection lorry on a one way trip inland. The driver spoke no English and me no Spanish. He was taking me some 16 kilometres to a service station at Cabanas. I had my piece of paper with the name of the village where I started from firmly in my pocket. It seemed to me as if he were taking me to Madrid. My head was spinning from lack of sleep and no food, but the scenery was beautiful and lush. I was dropped off at a garage where I bought 25 litres of gas oil at a cost of 1300 pesetas. I then started thumbing a lift, much to the amusement of the garage staff. Thirty minutes later the lady in the garage fixed me up with a lift with a lady and child in a Renault 5, again I had a language barrier, but, with lots of smiles, off we went. I was dropped off 3 kilometres from Laxe and the boat, and started walking the last two miles carrying the five gallons of diesel. There were no cars around as it was lunch time. The sounds and smell of the countryside in summer were breathtaking, the vegetation was green and lush and the scenery was beautiful. At last I got a lift from a Spaniard who spoke English. He got me back to the boat and my breakfast at 12.30. The others had been shopping and had sampled the local hostelry. I had been up since 0345 and was now somewhat cream crackered. 1300 To sea again. Lunch was fresh grilled sardines, with the grill pan tied into the cooker as we met the Atlantic swell again. Delicious! - followed by fresh strawberries and yoghurt. I slept the afternoon away happily. I was third in line to shower at teatime as we approached La Carona. I was all soaped and lathered up when the water ran out - oh bother! 1930 Secured at a pontoon for the first time this trip, we then went ashore and re-showered and telephoned home. La Carona was a very lively place as we ate a hearty evening meal ashore. Everyone was out promenading or sitting in the many cafes. The atmosphere was very friendly. SATURDAY 9th MAY After a good night's sleep we spent all morning working on "Ocean Challenger", cleaning, repairing, checking, refuelling and watering. We all went into town for brunch of Paella and beers followed by a walk around town. The shops were closed in the afternoon, but they were impressive and expensive for Spain. We found a supermarket open and spent £45 on food, and then lumped the six-bags-full back to the boat. Talked to three people who had just arrived from Falmouth in a Westerly Corsair. They'd had a force 9 wind up the backside all across Biscay, it didn't sound too good. We met many other voyagers, some going north like us, but most going south. We had a good yarn with all of them, swapping experiences. You do meet interesting people who cruise - three of them had arrived just behind us in a traditional thirty footer called "Mrs Muir" en route for Southampton. She was crewed by two guys from Liverpool, and skippered by a chap from Chester. It was their first delivery job. Saturday evening was spent in the company of "Mrs Muir's" crew. We had a most disjointed meal with large helpings of wine followed by a tour of the town ending in the waterfront cafes with local brandy and cigars. The is something special about the Liverpudlian humour. SUNDAY 10th MAY Today's The Day! 0700 Awoke after a sound night's sleep. A thunder storm was in progress and nobody wanted to get up.

6 1000 Preparations in progress, but it was still raining heavily. 1100 Slipped La Carona after eating our first meal all sitting round the saloon table. The rain had stopped and we were all full of hope as well as breakfast. We headed north with a bit of west across the Bay of Biscay. 1300 Two hours out and what little wind there was, was on the nose. The sea was calm,only 300 miles to go before we get to land again. I slept the afternoon away - the calm weather was a real treat. 1800 It was my watch now. The sea was still flat, but the day had become more and more overcast. It looked as if there was a lot of rain about. No more lying on deck sunbathing. Everyone now in hats, jumpers and oilskins. We were now 42 miles out and the wind was just picking up from - guess where - northerly! We were in radio contact with "Mrs Muir" who had left several hours after us. They were steering 018 degrees true, more directly across the bay than we were. We intended altering to a north-easterly course the next day, when we were expecting to pick up a NW 3 - 4 wind. Not a thing in sight as I looked forward to my dinner of corned beef hash. 2200 All alone on Deck. No.1 genoa still was up, but with the engine still ticking over. Darkness fell with overcast cold clear weather. Wind was still on the nose. 2400 Off watch, I wedged myself into the forecabin and slept peacefully. MONDAY 11th MAY 0400 Not much shipping around, although we had encountered a giant floating crane lit up like a Christmas tree. I understand we were slow at altering course, our helmsman of the hour was mesmerised, thought it was a block of flats! Whilst on my own I looked at the chart and saw that we were in a position where we had 5,000 metres of water beneath us. That's over 3 miles deep! Not at all the Thames estuary. 0500 Three ships had come up and gone down my starboard side but the fourth came slowly on. Would you believe it, I had to go about and pass under her stern, all this sea and I had to do that! It was now bitterly cold and four of us were sharing two pairs of gloves. 0615 Spoke to a Russian Cruise Liner, the "Leonard Bresnichoff" who was very helpful and gave us our latitude and longitude, as our Satellite navigator had long since given up the ghost. Our dead reckoning was about 3 miles out, which wasn't bad after a run of 102 miles. 0700 I dropped the genoa and headed 037°, more into the bay. Everyone was rested after we had introduced a new watch-keeping system. The day was fine but overcast, wind still N.E. I was fed up with the sound of the engine. I cooked breakfast - fresh orange juice, boiled eggs with french bread and coffee. A whale was seen in the distance as 50 - 100 dolphins descended on us well spread out. They were a truly fantastic sight. Lunched on lasagne, good old Marks & Sparks their food is very good. We were getting silly with the boat's standing jokes, the skipper hid the foot away whilst Martin and I were always hungry. Don, the other crew member, was permanently asleep when not on watch. 1600 - 1800 My watch again. The wind had finally arrived, we were tramping along at 7 knots. 2000 We now had five rolls in the mainsail and a full genoa, and were doing eight knots. We all sat and discussed the sky and cloud formation and thumbed our weather books, all agreeing it to be a warm front coming through. Final instalment in next Navigans.

CODE OF PRACTICE FOR LAUNCHING AND RECOVERY OF CRUISERS The O.O.D to be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for the information of dinghy sailors. Large Boats - Boats above 27ft. length will not be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. Tractors - Only to be used by authorised drivers. Winches - When dinghy events are in progress, the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies. At ALL times the following code should be observed: • When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the winch handle(s) removed. • Avoid sharp bends in the winch cables. • DO NOT shackle the winch wire back onto itself. USE THE CHAIN PROVIDED. • It is the responsibility of the BOAT OWNER to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing an adequate trailer and a sufficiently strong team of helpers. • Leave winches tidy, return shackles, strops etc. to the garage after use, rewind cable tidily as riding turns can damage the cable. • Report any damage or wear of any equipment to an authorised tractor driver. • REMEMBER, it is your responsibility to check for the safety of any equipment in use, if in doubt - DO NOT USE! • If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the WIRE STROP MUST BE USED to allow the tractor to remain on the level and always clear of loose shingle. Boat Trolleys - If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to other boats. MOORINGS INFORMATION 1988 The system we adopted in 1986, which is outlined again below for reference, was largely successful. We again did not receive any criticism from the River Bailiff for being too far out in the fairway. C row was marginally too far inshore but this will be rectified this year. One boat went adrift in 1987 due to a scope failure, so check your mooring tackle in plenty of time. Replace anything which is worn or suspect, IF IN DOUBT - RENEW. New gear is a small price to pay for peace of mind or against the real cost of damage to your own or other boats. Make sure your mooring buoy is of adequate size to support the additional weight of scope and bridle. During 1987, dinghies have been damaged by striking submerged trailers whilst approaching the hard. Trailers must not be left submerged. It is the responsibility of the owner to ensure the trailer is recovered immediately the boat is launched. Dave Thomas undertook a survey at the end of 1985 which confirmed that C row has a fairly constant depth but that A and B rows get significantly deeper towards Stone. So to allow for this please note the changes to recommended bridle lengths etc. Below is a sketch using B1 and B2 as an example. For laying purposes the buoy will be lashed directly to the bridle. This will guarantee slack in the bridle and enable accurate positioning. CRUISER DOES & DON’TS Over the last twenty years the Cruiser Fleet has developed from one of just a handfull of 18’ to 20’ cruisers to the present 120 plus fleet of boats up to 45’ in length. During this time a code of practice, based on practical experience, has been evolved, some parts of which are now Club Bye-Laws others are custom and practice. The purpose of this booklet is to acquaint new members, and remind existing members on how the Club operates with respect to cruisers, what equipment is available to you and how to get access to it. Moorings The Club leases the moorings area from Maldon District Council. The moorings are laid in six rows, three are deep water (rows A, B &C) and three drying (rows D, E &F). Rows A, B and C are laid in the spring and lifted in the autumn each year to ensure that they can be properly inspected and maintained. This is done in teams over a number of weekends, the dates of which are published in Navigans and in these notes which accompany the Year Book. Members will also be notified by their Team Leaders, see page 2, and they or their representative MUST be present on these occasions. Mooring buoys must be of an adequate size to be afloat at all states of the tide and be marked with the mooring number. Mooring strops, if made of rope, should be protected against chaffe by polythene tubing. Anchors in A, B and C rows should preferably be of the CQR or Danforth type, but if Fisherman types are used then provision must be made for lowering themin the correct plane. Chain sizes and lengths are given on page 3. It should be noted that 9/4 inch chainis the maximum size that can be laid at the Club. Shackles should be wired, and shackles and swivels should be of the largest practical size as they are THE WEAK LINK in any mooring. Tenders All tenders should have some form of identification on them. Tenders must NOT be parked on the sea wall (Anglia Water Authority Rule), or on the foreshore by the White Hut (Obstruction of a Right of Way). During the winter, tenders are to be stored with the cruiser, only one rigid tender per member. Cruiser Park It is the resposibility of each member to keep their allocated area tidy-PLEASE put any rubbishin the bins provided. DO NOT park your car in the cruiser park if you are going out sailing, it may obstruct the movement of boats or tractor. If you need electric power, this is availablein the park from the standpoints and you must use the correct 15amp waterproof plug - LEWDEN Part No PD 160/3. DO NOT ATTEMPT TO USE THE OLD DOMESTIC ROUND PIN TYPE. High The high pressure hose is available via the 0.0.D at weekends and by prior arrangement Pressure with the Cruiser Fleet Captain during the week. Please read the operating instructions Hose carefully and always ensure that there is oil in the reservoir. Scrubbing At present there is no booking system to use the posts, this may have to be reviewed in Posts the light of the current Anti-Fauling legislation. Drinking water is available at the posts, the stop cock being situated by the green Bio-Pack. Jack There is a 15 tonne toe jack in garage No. 5. Key available from the O.0.D or any tractor driver. Trailers It is the responsibility of each member to ensure that the trailer used for launching and recovery of his boat is suitable, not only for the boat but also for the conditions at the Club. e Axles must be big enough to take the weight of the cruiser. e Uprights must be strong enough to cope with the effects of the tide. Pea sticks and string will not do! e Wheels must be suitable for the hard and the field. Small solid wheels will not do! e Good steering is needed. With the increasing number of boats laying up at the Club it is important that trailers have reasonable steering as space is becoming limited. IF IN DOUBT - ASK! Page 6

2. The third and last instalment of Cadet Skipper Derek Hall's log from his sailing trip last year from Lisbon to St Helier. TUESDAY 12th MAY Midnight + 5 minutes, my watch again. It had taken me 20 minutes to get out of my sleeping bag, dress into full oilskins and harness up. We were being thrown about something awful. I decided the genoa must come down. We put the working jib up, not an easy job in the dark with the seas building up, and every third wave coming on board. We all now knew we were in for a a blow! 0630 Called up on deck again, I had not been able to sleep. We landed the mainsail, the seas were getting bigger by the hour. We were doing 6 knots under the working jib only, the wind was up to a NW 7, they had said it would be a NW 3 - 4, oh hell! The seas were getting bigger but were much shorter between waves, very uncomfortable. 1030 Skipper managed to do beans on toast, followed by yoghurt and biscuits with hot coffee. 1130 It was now up to a full Force 8 and the boat is being flung around everywhere. "Sea Scout", a large bulk carrier, altered course for us, but didn't answer our VHF call. Our position was now very approximate. "Mrs Muir" had caught us up, we met up in the middle of Biscay and were now three miles astern after a photo call. My writing in my notes at this point is almost illegible due to the rough seas. Biscay was really getting its revenge now. Very cold and wet on deck now and we were two to a watch, both on deck. We are hand steering as our Autohelm 3000 cannot cope. WEDNESDAY 13th MAY There is nothing worse than getting out of a warm sleeping bag, putting on damp clothes and wet oilskins to face a continuous Force 7 and 20-foot waves with someone throwing cold water at you for four hours at a stretch. Night watches were now very cold. The other three were now all sharing my gloves. Mostly we went over the beam waves which were now huge, although every now and then the damn things broke as we reached the top and and were sent crashing down, which shook every filling in my head. Sometimes when we were at the bottom, the force of the wind blew the crest off and down onto us. It is great fun trying to fix our position as we are now approaching Ushant. We sighted land after breakfast. I had never seen so many evil rocks and as many lighthouses in one area. Ushant is certainly a treacherous place. After a lot of time and effort we finally identified the correct approach to Brest (no room for mistakes here). 1430 We entered the Port of Camaret in France, very glad to be there too. Our log had recorded 388 miles. I stayed awake during the afternoon to have an early evening meal at a local hotel with our friends off "Mrs Muir". For 95 francs I started with half a dozen oysters which were scrumptious - although I had trouble opening my throat to let them slide down - followed by Cordon Bleu chicken with cheese, coffee and brandy. This was followed by one of the best night's sleep I had ever had. THURSDAY 14th MAY Up at 0800 ready for the off again as we were on a tight schedule. The weather was awful, blowing a hooli, with poor visibility. We poked our nose out and ran down-channel to find the entrance to the Dufore channel, "Mrs Muir" had decided to stay put. 1130 We were back again having had the only dissent of the trip over the decision on whether to continue or return. My decision was to return, which was what we did. The rain was coming down in sheets and the visibility very low as we were cleared by the Port Authorities and the Customs after we had secured alongside and had dropped off to sleep. The day was spent reading and sleeping and exploring the village of Camaret which was picturesque and still very sleepy even in mid-May. Our evening meal was cooked on board followed by drinks ashore. FRIDAY 15th MAY 0800 We were ready to try again, our forecast was Northerly 4 - 5, visibility good. 1000 Slipped Camaret after paying mooring fees and a further visit from a Coastguard boat. We were followed out by "Mrs Muir" and a Swedish boat who was heading for Brighton en route to Gothenburg. The narrow channel Dufore is not so bad in good visibility. 1400 After tacking for two hours we were into the English Channel. Wind was still on the nose after thirty miles logged, only one hundred and ten to go to St Helier. 1500 Amazing, we had freed off the wind and were sailing well.

3. 2000 Off watch and was not on again until 0200 to 0400. Still creaming along at 7 knots off the Brittany coast, really fantastic sailing and we were knocking off the miles with a strong tide with us. Oh no, it was lasagne again for dinner. Tonight was to be our last night at sea and we were allowed an extra tot after the weather forecast and evening news. The forecast was good and we were just beginning to pick up lighthouses. It was more demanding again allowing for tides and strong ones at that. SATURDAY 16th MAY 0145 Up to relieve the skipper. It was very cold. To think I was due home that day, it seemed impossible I could make it. We were still sailing well, logging 6 knots, but we were now against a foul tide. 0400 A good watch with brilliant sailing on a very cold but clear night, although I had been unable to get a good fix on the small scale chart. Had to get my sleep now to be fit for Jersey later in the day. 0830 I was up again. The engine had been started at 0545 when the wind died. We were approaching Jersey which looked good in the clear visibility. We entered through the Middle Passage, passing a type 42 Destroyer anchored in the bay. 1100 Secured in the marina at St Helier, just scraping over the ledge. I was looking forward to a good shower, several pints of Jersey's cheap beer, a slap-up lunch followed by an afternoon's kip and Saturday evening on the town. As it turned out I got the shower and lunch time pints, ate lunch in the Wimpy bar as everything had closed after our drinks. I went shopping in the afternoon for gifts and caught the evening flight back to Southend. There were no flights left Sunday or even Monday to either Southend, Stansted, Gatwick or Heathrow. ... In two weeks we logged 885 miles spending six nights at sea. An enjoyable experience although hard work at times keeping up a tight schedule. Cruising is my thing, I would go again tomorrow if I could. Don't rely too much on electronics though, our Sat. Nav. never worked; our VHF gave trouble, and our Autohelm gave up on the last two days. Well done everyone who played a part in the preparation or manning of the stand, particularly Mike Battle for the really excellent printed material he was able to provide for us this year. Let's hope we are rewarded with some active new membership as a result. Thanks again, John Salmon.
