INBOARD PROPELLERS available from Steel Developments EQUIPOISE TYPE Equipoise type propellers are designed for high speed and hard chine hulls such as speedboats and fast motor cruisers. They have a slightly greater blade area than the Turbine type, approximately 0.6 D.A.R. and have their maximum blade width near the tip of the blade. Equipoise propellers can be supplied with two or three blades. TURBINE TYPE Turbine type propellers are suitable for all normal types of craft from tugs and heavy work boats to cabin cruisers and small runabouts. These propellers are of the constant pitch type and have a blade area of approximately 0.5 D.A.R. The Turbine blade shape has proved, during the years, to be most efficient over a wide range of engine speeds. Turbine propellers can be supplied with two, three or four blades. SAILING TYPE Sailing type propellers are designed for use with Sailing craft fitted with an auxilliary engine. This is a two bladed propeller with special shaped blades which line up behind the deadwood when the engine is not in use and so offer tbe minimum resistance to the flow of water when sailing. contd.....

6. CAVITATION & VENTILATION are commonly confused with rubber bush damage but it is entirely different and costs consideraby less to rectify. Cavitation could be the result of poor propeller design, wrong blade area, or pitch for the application for which the propeller is being used. Usually the result of cavitation can be seen by metal "eaten" or "burned" off the propeller surface or gearcase. These "burned" areas are the result of vapour bubbles which have been formed by the water's inability to flow over or around poorly developed areas, such as damaged propeller blades, which impede the natural water flow. These bubbles attach themselves to a surface of higher pressure, such as the propeller blade face, and cause minute but high pressure impacts which erode the surface where they collapse. Ventilation is the effect of external air or exhaust gases being made available to the propellers. The propeller blades, during their operation, have a pressure- and a suction- side. When air is induced into the propeller's working area, the suction, or back side, of the blade will accept any migrant air, thus causing loss of thrust, increase in motor rpm and poor performance. Causes of Cavitation and Ventilation are: Too high a transom setting Severe turn when in use Wrong motor angle Damaged and out-of-balance propellers Fouled boat bottom or lower unit Loss of converging ring from a thru-hub exhaust propeller In general, incorrect boat 'set up' Although it is not possible to repair cavitation burns it is possible to reduce cavitation and therefore reduce the production of cavitation burns. This is done by cupping the propeller. Cupping is a slight turn on the trailing edge of the propeller. This reduces cavitation, increases acceleration and reduces vibration. Cupping is also the equivalent of increasing the pitch of the propeller by one inch and this should therefore be taken into consideration when thinking of cupping a propeller. Cavitation can also be reduced by having the propeller blade thinned down as this reduces the high pressure build up. ELECTROLYSIS .....Why is a propeller beyond repair when it has electrolysis? Because the metal structure of the propeller becomes so weak with fatigue that it would be dangerous to use it on a boat because considerable damage could be caused to the vessel, namely by a whole blade being "thrown off". It is also impossible to weld onto a propeller when it has electrolysis because the zinc, which would normally be present in the metal of the propeller, is drawn out and this zinc is needed to weld. .....How is electrolysis caused? Water, even fresh water, can act like acid in a battery. Two dissimilar metals immersed in water may form an active "battery" actually generating a small current and eating away one of the metals. This is called galvanic corrosion which is a wasting process that can go on all the time the craft is afloat and can attack all metal components immersed in water, especially the propeller. Propellers painted with anti-fouling paint, especially anti-fouling which is high in copper content, may react with the metal of the propeller and cause electrolysis, rendering the propeller useless. Bronze propellers should not be covered in any way. This is because an oxide layer builds up naturally over the top of the metal which renders the propeller slightly corrosion resistant. If there is no oxygen getting to the propeller metal, then no oxide layer can be built up and thus no "self protective skin" is present. contd.....

7. .....How is electrolysis stopped? To stop electrolysis all you need to do is fit an anode. Many boat builders fit Cathodic Protection (anodes) as standard on new craft. It may be completely absent, or need renewing on older craft. There are many different types of anode available. There are anodes which attach to the hull of your craft, directly onto the rudder or skeg etc., or to the propeller shafts themselves, and also hanging anodes. .....What do Steel Developments Ltd recommend concerning electrolysis? We strongly recommend that anodes be fitted to all craft. Installation of anodes to GRP and wood boats is simple and straightforward and can be undertaken by any owner or boatyard when the craft is hauled out. The anodes must, however, be correctly fitted to the boat or it will not protect the propeller and stern gear, etc. Every time the craft is hauled out, the anode should be checked and, if corroded, then replaced. The propeller should also be overhauled ready for the next season ahead. PROPELLER CARE AND SERVICING Why have your propeller Serviced and Repaired? Roughness, Cavitation, Corrosion and surface damage to a propeller reduces its efficiency and hence raises fuel consumption. Steel Developments have compiled a list of useful hints about propeller care and maintenance: Propellers are made usually of either Bronze, Aluminium or Stainless Steel but it is vital that all are maintained properly. A propeller not only pushes the boat along but regulates engine rpm of which the rpm is directly related to horsepower and the propeller pitch is related to rpm. An example of this would be if your engine should have an rpm of 2500 but you can only get 2300, your propeller has too coarse a pitch. This can be altered by having the pitch reduced by 1" which will give you the needed 200 rpm to bring the engine to its full revs and efficiency and so reduce fuel costs. On your propeller there will be the propeller's measurements. If these are, for example, 10 x 12 then this means the first number (in this case 10) is the diameter, which is determined by doubling the distance between the blade tip and centre of the hub. The second number (which is 12 in our example) refers to the pitch. Pitch is the blade angle, and the 12" pitch indicates that in each propeller revolution the boat theoretically would advance 12" - but due to slip loss the actual advance is somewhat less. Using a damaged propeller will not only reduce the boat performance but can cause costly engine damage. To obtain the best possible performance from your vessel you should have your propeller serviced at least once a year - and every time you damage it - by an expert. Trying a "do-it-yourself" repair could well cost you more in the long run. The following hints should be followed in order to achieve the best possible performance from your vessel: 1. ALWAYS CARRY A SPARE PROPELLER TO USE IN EMERGENCIES. 2. Propellers and stern gear must NEVER be coated with anti-fouling or metal-based paints, to avoid problems of severe corrosion. 3. A suitable propeller puller should always be used when removing an inboard propeller. 4. NEVER run a vessel for long periods with a damaged propeller as you may cause some severe damage to your engine and stern gear. 5. Make sure you have an anode fitted to your vessel so you reduce the risk of your propeller and stern gear from electrolysis. CRUISER RACING Now that we are working up to a new season, it is time to give som serious thought to what type of sailing will allow us to obtain the most from our yachts and from our time available. Often, due to pressures of work and family commitments, we find we are forced to plan our sailing and we are not always able to go as far, or for as long as we would like. Racing on the Blackwater is an excellent way of having an enjoyable day out and of using your yacht to its full potential whilst developing your sailing skills. The B.J.R.C. (Blackwater Joint Racing Committee) run a series of ten races through the season from May to September, aimed at the family cruising man and woman as well as at those who are committed racing helms. Races are timed to go out to sea on the ebb tide and return on the flood, having sailed around a series of navigation marks in the Blackwater and Colne estuaries. Entry for the B.J.R.C. race series costs £5 regardless of whether you enter one or all ten races. This nominal charge also includes all the information necessary, such as the basic rules and race courses. You must, of course, comply with a few safety rules. Races are run using the P.Y. handicap system. Yachts without a recognised handicap would be rated by the B.J.R.C., and therefore no yacht is excluded. In addition to this, there is also our Marconi Barnacle Points. This year there will be two races held on the weekend of 23 - 24 July. With more than 100 cruisers in the Club, I am hoping for a good response. Don't forget, racing is a good discipline. It checks your ability and sorts out those weak points, boat and personal, as well as being good fun. BOSUN'S LOCKER Much work has been done on Jack B during the winter. The less obvious items are that the propeller has been repaired and rebalanced and new sacrificial anodes fitted. Not very exciting, but necessary. From the safety point of view the most important job has been to change all the windows (which were only ordinary window glass) for safety glass. Thanks are due to Doug Brown and to the lads at Highway Windscreens at Witham, for providing the new glass, cut to size, Free of Charge. A marine, parallel sweeping, windscreen wiper has been fitted and works well keeping the centre window clear of rain and spray. (Rumours that cockpit heating and GT car seats are to be fitted for the crew are unfounded). Malcolm Stuart arranged for a cockpit cover and that, together with a lick of aint and varnish had Jack B looking very smart at launch time. (Pity about the ddy wellies, mine included, which have clambered over the boat since then). The club name has been put on the side of the boat, but unfortunately the stick-o lettering is not proving equal to the scuffing received - further thought required on this. Thanks are due to Geoff Josey for servicing Jack B's machinery as well as the Club's outboards and to Dennis Dear for becoming Club Radio Officer. On the subject of Jack B's Radio the VHF set on the Jack B has a ‘dimmer' control which can be operated to completely cut out the control panel illumination, giving the impression that the radio is not working. Of course you radio buffs would know about that, but it took me same time to rumble it - so be warned. The offending control is marked 'dim' and is located with the squelch control - clever eh? A final note of thanks to all those who have assisted me over the winter/spring with sandpaper, brushes etc. etc., in particular Malcolm Stuart and Gordon Golding who both spent a very physical afternoon reglazing the cuddy, (the Instant Windscreen _Replacement firms have nothing to fear from us). Finally a plea to all users of Club Boats: Please report any defects or missing gear to me or the OOD so that repairs/ replacements can be arranged. Ray Ball, Bosun. Chelmsford [redacted]

Malcolm Stuart, Rear Commodore SAILING IN ROUGH WEATHER In the spring and autumn at Stansgate we frequently experience strong winds and. when these blow against the tide we can get very choppy and confused water, particularly between Stansgate Point and Osea Pier. In such circumstances the Race Officer, the OOD and all members who have turned up to race will be faced with a decision. Firstly, irrespective of what the Race Officer decides, members remain responsible for their personal safety and should not sail if they judge the conditions to be well beyond their present level of competence. The Race Officer will, in reaching his decision, assume that members have considered the weather conditions and have reached the decision that they can survive them when they sign on. fee Race Officer's job is therefore not that of deciding what is suitable for the least experienced and worst equipped member, but only that of deciding whether or not it is safe to start a race for the more experienced members. We must recognise here that the only way of getting experience in sailing in rough conditions is. to get out and do it and we are only going to improve our skills by pushing ourselves a little. The Race Officer has therefore to make the difficult judgement on how far to let those who sign on for a race push themselves. In circumstances such as this the Race Officer will consult with the duty Coxswain, the Fleet Captains and the oOoD. Any course set for racing must take account of the ability of the rescue facilities available on the day to recover crews who may get into trouble. He may therefore restrict sailing to the shorter courses, and faster boats like the Catamarans will have to put up with having their wings clipped. The ultimate authority for all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of club members is the OOD, however in practice he will normally only exercise this authority in response to a request from the Race Officer for guidance, and would in any case take any decision affecting racing after consultation with the Race Officer. fo summarise what is a cautious justification of racing in conditions that prompt thoughts of more comfortable hobbies: 1. Competitors must decide themselves whether or not they are competent to go out in rough weather. 2. The Race Officer must consult the duty Coxswain, Fleet Captains and OOD and set a suitable course or postpone until such time as a suitable course can be set. CONTE ask

Malcolm Stuart, Rear Commodore BOSUN'S LOCKER I would like to add my personal thanks to Murray and Peter for replacing Jack B's prop. shaft bearing, and re-aligning the engine. To replace the bearing (a 5" bronze cylinder with rubber lining), without removing the engine and shaft was a tricky operation requiring considerable thought. As well as spending a couple of evenings planning the job, Peter and Murray gave up a day's leave to do the work, I confess to having had doubts that the job could be done, and certainly did not expect that Jack B would be ready for the Bank Holiday weekend. (I even went as far as phoning a local marine engineering firm for a quote - THEY did not want the job). When an item of club equipment is found damaged one weekend, but is ‘miraculously' repaired and back in service a week later, it must seem to many members that the club has a ‘fairy godmother' with a magic wand. I hope the above notes will dispel such thoughts. The Club's ‘fairy godmothers' are usually, guys in boiler suits wielding, not wands, but tool kits (or on the admin. side, lounge suits and pens)..... That was the enjoyable part of my article, now for a gripe! The failure of the shaft bearing was a ‘mixed blessing' because upon hauling Jack B out for that repair it was found that the boat had suffered some damage to the hull. Damage to the port bow had removed some of the glass fibre covering the edge of the foredeck, exposing an area of unprotected and splintered plywood. Chipping of the gel-coat on the corner of the transom had laid bare small areas of glass-fibre, None of the damage was in itself serious and a few hours' work and a fiver's worth of materials put things right. BUT despite requests in Navigans I was not actually informed about the damage. If Jack B had not been brought ashore and repaired, rain and spray would have soaked into the damaged areas possibly causing delamination, etc., etc., Please, if you damage a Club boat, or notice a fault in it or in its gear, please let me know as soon as possible. I know it's embarrassing confessing to making a mess of things and I will probably growl and mumble in my beard, (I enjoy a good moan before getting on with the job), but at least I will be able to put in hand the necessary ‘stitch in time'. ‘nuff said. End of gripe. Ray Ball, Bosun Chelmsford [redacted] SAILBOARD RACK ACCESS Please keep the area between the sailboard rack and the otside stairs clear of hardware. No harm was done and Georgina didn't appear to be bothered at all in this (her first) race. Lucy Boreham with Jenny Ball as crew maintained an upright stance throughout to make up the quintette of Mirror Maniacs. The afternoon race was won by Janet Keeble (single handed) to end a day which very definitely belonged to the Keeble family with Steve and Melanie finishing 3rd, just behind Alec Pembleton's 2nd place. Spring Points 5 and 6 were sailed in very strong winds and and adverse tides. Again a good turnout with 6 and 5 entries respectively. This time, Damian had his crew, Katy Rutherford, with him and they won both races . Janet Keeble was 2nd, Lucy 3rd and Jack and Diane Rusbridge 4th in race 5, whilst Lucy finished 2nd in race 6 and the others suffered disasters of various sorts and all retired. Spring 7 and 8 were held on Sunday, 24th April, which was bright and windy - and cold. Just how cold that wind really was showed after the races with everyone complaining of numb hands, blue feet, pinched faces and wondering if a sunny, but sheltered, spot in the garden picking up weeds would have been a more sensible plan for the day. However, pleasures are relative; how wonderful those hot showers were -- you have your choice and takes your pick. It just proves how essential a wet or dry suit is for dinghy sailing at this time of year. Race 7 was postponed until 12.15 because the Jack B was out of action ('prop shaft bearing' gone - or something), and then a short course using 'F' mark was set. Only two Mirrors took part with Damian and Katy finishing 1st with Lucy and Jenny in 2nd position. This was repeated in Race 8 with Lucy reckoning she was a little closer to her brother this time - but not a lot. For both races, the wind was quite brisk, around 3-4. A good start to the season and hopefully more of you Mirror Mariners (makes a change from Maniacs) will join in the fun and games of racing with Steve, Janet, Melanie, Alec,P, Alec G , Georgina, Jack and Diane, Lucy and Jenny, Damian and Katy in what is, undoubtedly, a marvelous place to sail. Maggie Boreham Mirror Fleet Scribe Stop Press! Our Fleet Captain, Mike Battle, with Richard as crew, won his first Mirror Race!! It was Race 2 of a series of 4 over the Weekend May 1st/2nd.

6 Jolly Boating Weather or The Spring Bank Holiday Cruise The Cruiser Fleet's first Cruise-in-Company of the season was a visit to Brightlingsea over the Spring Bank Holiday Weekend. The organiser/flotilla leader for this event was Malcolm Yeoman in VARUNA II. TARA's crew consisted of myself as skipper/cook, Cadet David Ball as First Mate/Washer-Upper and Cadet Stuart Golding as everything else. Having a small boat and a young crew I intended to be quite choosy about the weather so, like a responsible yachtsman, I visited the London Weather Centre on the Friday before the cruise and paid £1.50 for a 5-day weather forecast. The forecast was for predominantly southerly winds until Bank Holiday Monday, when the wind was to strengthen from the south-west. Malcolm had called a pre-cruise meeting for 10.30 on the Saturday morning but unfortunately our car chose to have a flat tyre so our arrival at the club was somewhat delayed. However we arrived in time to load the boat, make a quick phone call to the Colne Yacht Club order dinner and to depart for Brightlingsea in bright sunshine at about 1pm. The southerly wind ('Super, a reach all the way to the Colne') lasted as far as Bradwell when it went easterly and freshened - right on the nose! Waves getting bigger - to go on or turn into West Mersea or Bradwell was the question. Decided to put in a reef and plug on (once again I blessed the day I fitted slab reefing). We soon settled down to the motion and devoted ourselves to a bit of navigation. None of this 'Down to the end of the Blackwater and turn left for us! To be honest, one bit of sea looks much the same as another to me so we used charts and compass to find the cardinal mark marking the 'Molliette' wreck on Mersea flats and were then able to bear away for Brightlingsea. By 5pm we were safely tied up alongside another yacht in Brightlingsea. Another 10 or so Marconi boats were already there. At 8pm we all gathered for dinner in the Colne Yacht Club and as usual the Colne laid on an excellent meal. On Saturday night the wind freshened and the rain came down. The boat inside of us wanted to move out at 8am on Sunday so it was a reluctant sortie to move out at 8am into wind and rain to let him out. The rest of Sunday was spent in Brightlingsea eating and taking the occasional walk ashore. The weather forecasts were unfavourable for days ahead and I was beginning to think of leaving the boat at Brightlingsea until the next weekend. Watching a small yacht being towed in by the Lifeboat at Sunday lunchtime did nothing to inspire me to leave the shelter of Brightlingsea creek. By Sunday evening the crew of the good ship TARA were getting a bit 'cheesed off'. The midnight shipping forecast was for more of the same (strong south-westerlies) on Monday so I resolved to have a lie-in on Monday morning. I awoke on Monday morning at 7am to find the friendly face of Niel Pembleton peering through the hatch. It appeared that there was to be an easing of the wind for a few hours, did I fancy heading back to the Club? The initial reaction (from a warm sleeping bag) was No! However a sense of nautical responsibility prevailed and rapid arrangements were made to leave - no time for breakfast. We broke the good news to the boat on the outside of us and they let us out. The wind was southerly which meant plugging against the wind and tide down the Colne but a reach up the Blackwater - not a bad bargain. An hour was spent motoring down the Colne against the wind and rain, and as soon as we could set a course for the Blackwater, the mainsail was set, double reefed, and about half the jib unrolled. A very brisk, if bumpy, sail was enjoyed until Bradwell was reached, when the wind dropped! Was this the lull before the storm? Engine on for a quick dash back to Stansgate, and still it rained! The mooring was reached about 11am when a hearty breakfast was enjoyed before tidying up. The cooker heated the cabin and allowed my long-suffering crew to thaw out. Thanks are due to Malcolm Yeoman for organising the cruise and the evening meal at the Colne Yacht Club. This was a well-supported Club event which was only marred by the weather. Let's hope for better weather next time. Ray Ball, TARA Cruiser Fleet has now appointed its new Fleet Captain, Mike Smith of 'Rubicon of Osea' Tel. Brentwood [redacted].

8 GONE FISHIN'... On Regatta Monday after motoring back to their mooring from Brightlingsea, Joajo's crew discovered a dead fish in their tender which they assume jumped aboard escaping from some predator. So without bothering with rod and line the Royle family ended up in possession of a fish whose length, if displayed by the outspread hands of a boasting angler, might not be too readily believed! Very long and thin, it looked at first sight like an eel, but the presence of some fins and a tail sent us to our reference books when we got home. He proved to be a Garfish or Garpike and measured 25", the usual adult measuring 30". The books say its bright green bones make it look unappetising but it is quite edible. It swims in surface layers of the sea feeding mostly on young fish and crustacean larvae. It has long beak-like jaws and the head is one-fifth of its whole body length. It is found in the southern and western coasts of Britain in early summer when it moves into shallower warmer water to breed, laying eggs with long sticky threads which tangle in seaweed and flotsam. In late summer it is more common off the northern coasts. Ed. 10 Rescue Boat Competition -— Saturday 28th May 1988 This year saw the introduction of what we hope will become an important annual event giving some recognition to the valuable service provided by our rescue boat coxswains and crews. We were fortunate to get a very professional judging panel led by Dick Townsend (Bradwell Coastgard), two representatives from the Essex River Police and David and Ione Saunders from st Johns. David went out on the water to monitor closely how the casualty was treated. The brave casualties James Brill, Emma Henderson and Debbie Yorston jumped in from the scrubbing post two or three times each and stood up well to the manhandling. Its not often you see a drowning person smile. The seven teams demonstrated a variety of different techniques for recovering the casualty but the most impressive by far was Trevor Milton in his catamaran whose very smooth pick up brought a spontaneous round of applause from the spectators. This years entries and the first three placings awarded by the judges were:-— Malcolm Grant MSC Jack B Dave Onyons MSC Jack B Brentwood Sea Cadets Baddow Star Trevor Milton MSC Stampede 1st John Chandler MYC Jacomar 3rd Barry Parker MSC Jack B Bill Fletcher SSC Zodiac 3 2nd Next year I anticipate a much bigger entry from local clubs and our Regatta visitors from Fishers Green are going to bring their rescue boat with them, so what has started as a local event for BJRC clubs could blossom into a Regional Competition. id REGATTA '88 I could get wildly enthusiastic about the way everyone got involved in making REGATTA '88 one of the friendliest and most enjoyable Regattas on record. However, as my old school reports used to say "this boy could do better if only he would apply himself", so lets look forward to an even better REGATTA '89. Mike Battle gave our predicted entry of 100 boats in the Essex Chronicle May 27th — he was one boat out, we only achieved 99. Our publicity officer more than made up for this error in getting 24 column inches of write-up on the Regatta into the Essex Chronicle on June 3rd, and 17 column inches in Yachts and Yachting. Frank Saville and Mike Hellewell played computer games on the hard over the weekend in the dry half of Charles Anderson's caravan, and came up with race results in record time. No problems with power failure thanks to the new cable provided by Malcolm Grant. Mike Battle's new token system also worked well, and avoided the problems of interpreting soggy signing on sheets. The reception girls Pat Harper, Mary Greygoose and Pat Stuart never had such an easy time - they were even seen sunbathing on the Saturday. Mike Turner took on the daunting task of following Robbie Sims as race officer acquiring Robbie's old team of Joan, Malcolm and Alastair Sims in the process. - Mike, Frank and Robbie coped very diplomatically with the GP14 and Enterprise Fleets who sailed the wrong course for Race 4 after a general recall and were (or. at least some of them) understandably upset. The Clubhouse extension, after passing the EEV destruction test, stood up well to the gales on Sunday, and the new outside bar worked well thanks to Dave Payne who got us the plastic material, Pete Clayton who welded the tubes, Murray Bates who acquiried the fixings, and Eddy Yorston who gave us a new set of noon lights. The erection team were Mike Clark, Norman Taylor, assisted by Colin Willsmore who load tested the framework, and Maurice Brill who put it together again. The extension cost the club less than the hire charge for a marquee and its cost was more than covered by. Regatta profits. With care it should last five seasons. We will use it mainly for Regatta, Barbecue, Cadet Week and Open Meetings but the downstairs bar in No 2 Garage can be used any weekend when it is too hot to stagger upstairs. The garage bars worked well thanks to Dave Payne's expert advice. What a lot of effort we have wasted in the past through not keeping it simple. Andrian Wright was plunged into the job of head daytime barman and grabbed hold of anyone who wasn't moving quickly enough to reward them with the dreaded yellow sweat shirt. MIRROR REGATTA REPORT Where were you all ? The turnout of Mirrors was either apathy or charity - apathy because you weren't interested or charity because you all thought it was about time your fleet captain had a chance to win something. A meagre five Mirrors entered the Regatta, four club boats and one visitor. Liz Ballard and son Adam from Maylandsea Bay joined Janet and Melanie Keeble, Jack and Diane Rusbridge, Elizabeth and Anne Goodwright and yours truly, who with a choice of three crew decided to opt for the heavyweight version, Janet, due to the prevailing strong southerly wind on Sunday. Capsizing was the order of the day on Sunday with both the Keebles and the Ballards taking a dip. Again this was a charitable jesture I'm sure, to give Janet and me a good chance in both races 1 and 2. The Monday however was not the day for the more portly crews and helms. Having said that, the first wins must have gone straight to my head because on the first mark at A buoy, I decided it was best to sail back through the cruiser lanes rather than head out towards No.1. Both Janet Keeble and Liz Ballard stormed away and on the long haul from C to B they tussled against one another to gain tactical advantage with Liz just coming out on top. With 2 wins and a third place for Battleship we decided to sit out the final race, which started in the lightest of breezes. Mike Turner (RO) put in an extra mark off Osea Island for the Mirrors. The conditions were a westerly wind (such that there was) and an outgoing tide. Having conquered the Stansgate spit, the Mirrors had to sail almost to Osea pier to take A mark and E mark to starboard. Liz Ballard came out the winner in this the final race but with Janet Keeble second, her fourth in the series, Liz Ballard was beaten into 3rd place overall. So the Battles marked up their first major win and collected first prize - a bottle of Gin! Not that we are ungrateful to win anything, and that it is the competing that counts not the winning, but I do think bottles of booze for winners of the "premier" event in the club's calendar is a bit OTT, especially for a fleet primarily made up of cadets. I've scoured every page of "Clubs and Classes" in the last three editions of Yachts and Yachting and in not one article or photograph have I seen winners presented with alcohol. Perhaps the Sailing Sub-Committee believe that it should be consumed and Che CompletelieDed 3 sealed again with a message saying "' I won Saltlor this at Marconi's Regatta" and then Lee thrown into the Blackwater as a promotional campaign. eres Eye (Foe Tort I jest, but I do think that we could do ) SPRAY DEFLECTOR better, next time? WELL DONE AND CONGRATULATIONS Talking of next time, I must put out a grate big CONGRATULATIONS to Malcolm Stuart. Regardless of individual views on whether we should or should not hold a Regatta, nothing can detract from the enormous effort Malcolm put into the event. (If all BR employees had his vigour to achieve results I'm sure I wouldn't swear and curse twice a day

trying to travel to and from work.) On behalf of the Mirror competitors, thanks for a great weekend to all those involved in the preparation and the duties on the day. I for one feel extremely guilty at times for taking part, but not having the time to help with the physical preparation and dismantling of such an event, an issue so easily taken for granted. CADETS DO THEIR BIT TOG Three brave cadets "came to the rescue" on the Saturday prior to the Regatta event. As the lead into the weekend, intrepid Malcolm Stuart had organised a Rescue Boat Competition. As I understand it, the plan was to have a number of nubile young females scantily clad negotiating a greasy pole on the scrubbing post, to be rescued from the water by various competing crews. The last bit was OK, just that there didn't appear to be any willing ladies, and the greasy pole turned out to be one of the flood boards. However, Malcolm persuaded Debbie Yorston, Emma Henderson, and James Brill to each act as concussed bodies, to,be manhandled from the water to a plethora of various rescue craft -— twice. The competition over, which had its serious side, each cadet received a token of appreciation - a variety of blow-up animals. The mind boggles at the possible token of appretiation had three nubile young ladies turned up..? CONGRATS to Trevor Milton, the winner. Mike Rattle PS Please excuse the "typos" ... this was a 1 ate entry typed by a very sore fingure. Sorry Malcolm I've just noticed "grate" not great big CONGRATULATIONS

SAILBOARD NEWS Summer Points Racing: This has now started and it's fun, so where are you all?! So far, of the 20 registered Board sailors, only 6 have actually competed to date. Our earliest starting time is 11.50am on a Sunday and there are 10 races in total (see Yearbook for dates). There is no need to enter them all to do well. If there is sufficient interest, there should be no problem in participating in the Autumn Points as well. Procedure is very simple: entries need to SIGN ON and identify their sail (not the board) by any visible marks or colours (so far this has proved sufficient, but if the numbers increase I will see about acquiring some stick-on numbers). On finishing or retiring, SIGN OFF. The race start is preceded by a 10-minute warning gun when our class flag is raised - a yellow and blue vertically halved flag. Lots more information in the Yearbook - read it! NOTE: I have been infommed that it is etiquette to keep out of the way of other classes starting before us - races usually start at 5 minute intervals. So far a certain Darcy Robarts is doing rather well with 2 wins out of 2 and Ian Savage, after an initial demonstration of his board's unique reverse gear, has now picked up al, 2 and 3. Rescue Boat Facility: I have been advised that the only really suitable boat for even moderately rough conditions is the Jack B. To handle any boat in any conditions requires a certain amount of seamanship and has to be learnt. Anyone who wishes to do so can learn to use the Jack B and would then be able to operate it when they felt appropriate Those sailboarders who are interested in doing this should contact either me or Dave Onyons, the’ Coxswain, directly. If there are a few interested people then I will arrange some group training sessions. Experience on the Jack B can be obtained most Sundays and Wednesday evenings - just ask the helmsman of the day - he will probably be willing to take an extra crew. It is the long term aim of the MSC to acquire a semi-rigid inflatable for rescue work ice would be much more suitable for sailboarders, but unfortunately this will not kr pen yet! Buoyancy Aids: I have agreed with the Club Canmmodore to make it clear that when the red flag is flying, all sailors are advised to wear personal buoyancy, and furthermore those participating in Club races will not qualify unless they do so. NOTE: Personal buoyancy does not include nappy- or waist-type harnesses which, whilst they might keep your most important parts above water, will not stop you drowning. Boat and Mast Racks: The area around these has now been cleared of lumber - many thanks to Pete Clayton. Both racks are now nearly full so if anyone desires a place then let me know and I will see about constructing another. Adrian Wright, Sailboard Fleet Captain.

CADET SERIES Helms and crew had to face a fair old wind on Saturday, 2nd July, for Cadets Races 1 and 2, and sailing conditions were both exciting and testing. In Race 1, Richard Battle capsized (twice I believe) but David Ball (crewed by Janet Keeble) sailed into a good 2nd position behind Lucy Boreham (1st) and Debbie Yorston (3rd but catching up fast as they approached the finish). In the afternoon, the number of entries increased to 6 when 'the morning mob' were joined by Greg Hall (sailing PATCH) and Damian Boreham (released from duties at his local Gateway Supermarket). David Ball got a superb start, trapping Damian to leeward and spilling dirty wind onto Lucy astern. With the course of 'Jack B' mooring, D, F, and 'E' (somewhere near B) David held the lead to E with Damian 2nd and Lucy third; unfortunately, tricks of the tide got both David and Damian into trouble and, much to her surprise, Lucy found herself in the lead which she held to the finish 1½ laps later. On the way, Greg hall's mast fell down and Damian provided a spectacular spinnaker capsize with screaming accompaniment from his crew, Maggie Boreham. Richard Battle finished but retired (hit mark) and again Debbie Yorston was catching up fast in 2nd place, Damian was 3rd and david Ball 4th. Debbie's crew for both races was Melanie Keeble.

3. CAMPING FORTNIGHT So many things happened worthy of mention that I will apologise here and now for any tit-bits I forget to include in the following paragraphs. Special thanks are due to our Commodore Robbie Sims who worked solidly from beginning to end of the 2 weeks (without any break that I'm aware of!); and to Joan who didn't see much of her husband during that time, but who was also there to be called on for any problems or questions that came along, which they frequently did. The early part of the first week was too windy for comfortable sailing so Ray Ball spent some compulsory shore-based time installing permanent plumbing behind the downstairs bar for the glass-washer (he'd had some practise for this at home during the winter!) and a nice neat hand wash basin basin was installed, which work should benefit us for some time to come. The Sea Cadets who were on the site for the first week turned to on more than one occasion and provided us with manpower for various jobs of work. My Tuck Shop was so popular that it was necessary to go back to Chelmsford for a full second load of goodies. This meant I had my first drive of the M.A.S.C. Van, with my sister Patsy beside me for much welcomed moral support. She reminding me in the built-up areas to keep more to the left, and on the country roads not to try to drive into the ditch every time I was overtaken - which was a fairly frequent occurence as I was too terrified of the monster under my control to do more than 40mph. All nervous learner-drivers will know exactly how I felt. Passenger and driver both welcomed the ready cup of tea and cake prepared by Leonie and Elsie up in the Galley when the safety of the Club was reached! This year for the first time we had a St John Ambulance first-aid caravan on the site, with Ione as our resident first-aid expert (with a couple of other certificate holders on the site also). Ione sent 4 people to hospital, 4 to a GP and dealt with 30 other requests for first aid, one of which was a request from me for some soothing spray for the relief of sunburn which catches me out every year. Our grateful thanks go to Ione & family for being there. It made for a certain peace of mind, and it was nice to know we were well equipped for emergencies on the morning of the East Coast Piers Race when a microlight aircraft, whose engine cut out, ditched off Osea, and the pilot was picked up by a speed-boat and brought across to us, fortunately not too badly hurt I believe, and sent on to hospital. The Boating Group of the Camping & Caravan Club, many of whom have been to our Camping Weeks several times before, set to and did their share of the duties, including manning the bar on most evenings. Chris & Rob Boustred acted as Camp Marshalls and Leonie Golding and Janet Keeble shared some of the work of cleaning the clubhouse each day. The Club had its Annual Barbecue during the middle weekend of Camping, organised by Conrad Barnard. The poor weather kept the numbers of tickets sold rather low, but those of us who were there put on our warm gear and enjoyed the event anyway. At least it didn't rain. Warmest Thanks go to the team of cooks and servers, and to the youngsters who spent their evening (with evident enjoyment) gathering glasses into baskets ready for washing-up by the machine, which wonderful toy was, I'm told, under the care of Rob Boustred. The middle Sunday had extra excitement for Leonie Golding, her mum Elsie Carlisle, and for me, who were doing Galley that day, when the water supply to the whole site (and to the neighbouring properties) was reduced to just a useful trickle from the outside tap. The Water Board investigated and it turned out that a farmer somewhere in the region had broken the water main while doing some digging. The supply of water getting through was just enough to keep essentials going, and the water was restored by the end of the day, so it could have been worse. During Cadet Week Derek Hall had a record size class of 30+ beginners to teach, with the assistance of some parents. The more experienced of our Cadets - seventeen of them - were taught the principles of racing rules and tactics by Mike Turner. On shore in the evening during Cadet Week there was an enjoyable and noisy

The fortnight ended on the Sunday with a big event - the East Coast Piers Race - whose success in the marvellous weather we had that day almost ensures that it will now become an Annual Club Event. so CATAMARAN NEWS The more observant amongst you will notice that this is the first Catamaran newsletter this year, entirely due to the fact that the scribe's duties have been delegated by the Fleet Captain. This allows him more time to indulge his propensities for amour, female wrestling and amateur radio, not necessarily in that order. The Cat Fleet is undergoing a healthy resurgence in numbers. A recent count showed a total of thirty boats, not counting those which the writer has never seen on the water. of these thirty, nineteen are regularly sailed. By far the largest class is, of course, the Dart 18, of which there are currently seventeen. Has anyone noticed the phenomenon amongst our Dart 18 sail numbers? We have 2626, 3131 and 4747. The Dart 20 (Stampede) section of the fleet has recently doubled its numbers, no less. That is to say that we now have two instead of one. | Whilst on the subject of numbers, it must be noted that whilst we have this large fleet . the boat park, rarely do we get many boats on the water at race time. So come along, helms, you will never discover your true talents until you pit them against others. It gives us great pleasure to welcome the newcomers to the Fleet, namely, Clive from Leigh Sailing Club, Keith an ex-Windsurfer, Graham Baker and Steeve Keeble. Before someone else says it, I am well aware that there are newcomers that I have missed. Some I do not know about, some I am aware of but do not know names and origins. So my apologies to those. Please come and give me the facts and you'll get a mention next time. Graham Baker and Steve Keeble are the more notable newcomers for the fact that they are recruited from other classes within the club, Graham graduating from Mirror to Dart, and Steve from Solo to Hurricane. (The wind of change?) Now the Hurricane has_ the reputation of being very sophisticated, amongst other things. So ‘hi tech' is it, that we hear it will be christened "Fly By Wire" (but only in very small letters.) The word is that once the in-mast water ballast system system is sorted it will be something to watch. Go for it Steve and Dave. Qn the racing front the summer points season is upon us, although there do not seem to many races taking place or people taking part. Nothing changes does it, and Trevor Milton seems to win them all (well, almost all.) Within the Dart class the normally all-conquering Duckmanton boat has developed a tendency to couple with racing marks. The age-old remedy of a well directed bucket of water hardly seems appropriate here. At the time of writing the Piers Race is almost upon us and by the time you read _ this, will be over - God and meteorology willing. Barrie Palmer will then be free to answer queries on next year's race. There will be one more order of commemorative sweatshirts, and orders, complete with ten pounds cash should be passed to the writer. The writer would also be grateful for any items of interest to the Fleet, e.g. news, requests for information, rumours, lies and scurrilous gossip; you know the kind of thing. As an example where are the photographs of Regatta Days promised by Andy Rimmer? Your roof-top reporter, Peter Flook (Dart 4747)

ADULT TRAINING 1. - 5 AUGUST 1988 As an alternative to the arduous routine of the full Cadet Week course we offered this year a rather laid-back course for adults which attracted a total of 17 with the four men well outnumbered by the fairer sex. We spent a very pleasant five days drinking coffee, socialising and, when the mood took us, learning how to handle sailing dinghies. 8. SOLO NEWS I have hardly visited the Club in the two months since my last notes so have very little home news to report. However one event I did manage was the Solo Team Racing Day on 25th July. This was once again very well supported with eleven Solo helms present plus, in the afternoon, Steve McCulloch guesting to make up 4 teams of 3 boats. Each team raced the other 3 in turn and the result, determined on a league table basis, gave victory to Roger Smith, Steve Rutherford and Janet Keeble. Special thanks are due to Ray Ball who coxed the rescue boat for us all day, and to _ the Battle family who did more or less everything else including the race management, thus ensuring a very successful day. Latest and very welcome addition to our Club Fleet is Peter Collis who has procured Steve Keeble's boat. There has been quite a bit of activity away from base involving fleet members. Firstly back in June Dave Nixson and I attended a sail pumpers convention at Chew Valley Lake near Bristol. In mostly light and tricky winds we battled gamely but not very successfully to get some undisturbed wind in a fleet of 75 (Inland Nationals). I finished 36th overall with Dave 56th (write out 50 times - I must practise my pumping!) Three weeks later were the ‘real' Nationals at Harwich, which this year received the best Marconi turn-out ever of 6 boats, although the total entry was a disappointing one of only 50. Malcolm Gandy did well to reflect his usual club form in his first Nationals, the rest of us also ran. Ken Falcon won the event (again), and Marconi's results were as follows: Malcolm Gandy 23rd Dave Nixson 29th John Salmon 32nd Janet Keeble 41st Dave Payne 42nd Roger Smith 43rd Special mention deserved for Janet who battled gamely through some fairly heavy conditions despite some gear failure and for Dave Payne who put in a lot of overtime in the dinghy park as chief boat fixer. Even as you read this your Fleet representatives will be once more locked in combat,this time at the Worlds at Uitdam, Holland. Races 3 & 4 - the weatherman certainly had it in for the Cadets when he ( presumably a ‘he' ?) followed up the fairly stiff winds of Races 1 and 2 with even stronger winds of Force4-5 plus for Race 3. The Race Officer set a prudent course of Jack 'B' mooring buoy, ,OD_ (three times around), thus keeping the boats within a confined area within the lee of the Clubhouse and sea wall. 12. The Ladies Cup - 1988 For the second year running the Ladies Cup was contested as a series of 3 races on a single day (ie. Sunday, 31 July) and some 14 lady helms signed on for the first race. The classes of boats taking part were Stampede catamaran (1), Dart Catamaran (2), 420 dinghy (3), Wayfarer (1), Solo (1), Mirror (5) and Embassy (1). Our thanks to the Race Officer, Rescue Boat Driver and their assistants. Race 1 - a somewhat short race (KF1) of about 1½ miles taking approximately 20 minutes to complete. The 'sausage' course meant that the race was sailed pretty well in the lee of the sea wall with a dead run to Breezy and a beat in the reverse direction. This course was a severe handicap to the catamarans and they finished well down the list, two retiring and the remaining Dart finishing 10th out of 11 finishers. However, the course and short duration did have the advantage that all boats sailed in similar conditions of wind and tide and this resulted in a close finish with only 101 seconds on corrected time covering the first 8 places. Those helms who took the inshore course up to Breezy (in order to cheat the incoming tide) found they had to gybe to reach the mark - a manoeuvre which appeared to worry their menfolk ashore more than it did the lady helms. However, the men needn't have worried - most of the ladies competing have helmed before but (as usual) give up the driving seat to the men for the 'serious' racing. Janet Keeble (Solo) kept very close inshore up to Breezy and won the race by 7 seconds from Lucy Boreham (Mirror) who, in turn, finished 11 seconds ahead of her mother Maggie Boreham (Mirror). Debbie Yorston (Mirror) must have thought she had got 3rd place ahead of Maggie because, as they both raced neck-and-neck for the finish line on a dead run, Debbie's bow was actually ahead of Maggie's bow - but Maggie was flying her spinnaker and presumably it was the spinnaker which reached the finish line first. If you've read Eric Twiname's book on the sailing rules, he illustrates a similar situation in his definition of 'finishing'. Race 2 - the problem with a single lap race is that you don't get a chance to correct the mistakes you made on the first (and only) lap. Thus, Race 2 with its course of KT2 was welcome news - not only for the two laps but also for being able to get away from the lee of the sea wall and sail some reaches. Certainly Rosie Duckmanton (Dart) found this course more attractive to sail and she came 1st, 31 seconds ahead of Maggie Boreham (Mirror). Lucy Boreham finished 3rd (23 seconds behind Maggie) and Debbie Yorston sailed consistently to again finish 4th (12 seconds adrift of Lucy). Then followed the two Janets - Janet Battle (Mirror) in 5th place and Janet Keeble (Solo) in 6th place. Race 3 - this time the course was further extended to 3 laps (KT3) and Rosie Duckmanton again came 1st - this time by a rather bigger margin of 2 mins 20 secs ahead of Caron Stuart (420) and Charlotte Burck (Wayfarer) Caron and Charlotte always look as though they enjoy their sailing and both improved considerably on their previous results. An interesting (and significant) deadheat for 4th place between Irene Hellewell (420) and Janet Keeble (Solo) meant that they shared the combined points for 4th and 5th places, each having 4½ points to their credit. The much slower Mirrors and Embassy found the extended course of 3 laps too much as they battled with the increasingly adverse ebb tide on the last lap. None managed to finish the course, the best being Lucy and Maggie who managed to struggle round No.1 but couldn't get round 'A' mark; none of the others managed to get around No.1 and all retired. Overall result - Rosie Duckmanton (Dart) was a very convincing winner with two 1sts to count and the 10th position from the 1st race as her discard. Lucy Boreham and Maggie Boreham both scored a 2nd, 3rd and Retired and so tied for second place overall, just 1/4 point ahead of Janet Keeble. Had Janet managed to beat Irene Hellewell for that 4th place then she would have come second by 1/4 point ; as it was, that extra ½ point made all the difference. It is not often that a dead-heat in the lower ranking places plays a real part in the overall result but, on this occassion, it made a difference. For those interested, IYRU Rule 11 applies. Full results listed elsewhere in this issue of Navigans. Sue Fletcher (Embassy) was probably the youngest and most inexperienced sailor taking part but, nevertheless, had a good sail and came ahead of her mother, Val Fletcher, who was sailing the family 420. Irene Hellewell usually serves at the sharp end but, having swopped places with husband Mike Hellewell, no doubt enjoyed the experience and was pleased with her =4th with Janet Keeble. Pat Stuart (Mirror) had Adrian White as crew and one wonders if Adrian was tempted to stand on the gunwale, grab the boom and try to crew the boat 'sailboarder-wise'. Family Note - did this year's entry establish some sort of record ? Have you noticed the three sets of mother and daughter helms ? In order of mother/daughter, they were Val/Susan Fletcher, Pat/Caron Stuart and Maggie/Lucy Boreham . How about trying to break that record next year ? Report by Lillie of Lagoona and Little Annie Fanny

COMMODORE'S NOTES It is some considerable time since I put thought to paper and produced a few more notes. My only excuse is that I never seem to be able to synchronise my times with your Editor's deadlines! I am making the effort now, however, and I hope you will think it worthwhile - although, perhaps, you may not like some of the views expressed. We have had a varied season so far wherein I can safely say that the lasting feature has been rain! That apart we have nevertheless had some very good times which, as far as I am concerned, were: New Members' Night, Regatta, Rochester Visit, Camping Fortnight & Barbecue, and the Fun Day. Sailing has been good (though personally you don't give your Commodore much opportunity to indulge!) and I had a very invigorating trip up to Walton Pier with John Hooper while we sampled the potential route of the inaugural Piers Race, which subsequently took place under nearly ideal conditions. If we can iron out just a few logistical problems we will have the makings of a very successful, I hope annual, event for the future. At this time of year we are very concerned with the arrangements for the running of the Club next year and are very anxious to find people prepared to contribute their time and effort towards helping their fellow members for one or more years on the various management tasks/committees - to make the same sacrifice that members before them have made and which has enabled them to do 'their thing'. This we are finding more and more difficult a task - particularly to find Ordinary Members. We must have Ordinary Members to fill certain posts to comply with the rules - but that aside , if it was not for the enthusiasm and sacrifice of our Associate Members, our Club would be in a very poor state and I wish to express my personal and the Club's gratitude for their efforts - and long may they continue. Committee work in its broadest sense is something which, frankly, anyone who puts their mind to it can contribute. So never say "I can't do it" because I don't believe you - you just need to decide that you would like to try, and I do not care if you are a new member this year or go back to the Fleetwind days. So please search your consciences and contact me or any Committee member with your offer of help or of the help of anyone too shy to put themselves forward. This is urgent - we must have names, particularly of Ordinary Members before the end of September. The Committee will be putting forward a change of rules at this year's AGM wherein the Main Committee will consist of persons elected to fill certain posts and will act in detail through Sub-Committees whilst representing their interest on the Main Committee. It was felt that this was worth trying rather than having a 'general' Committee Member and then at the first meeting of the new Committee, trying to dole out the various tasks. Do not worry if sameone is already doing a job you would not mind trying - a replacement designate is a very valuable commodity, so please, please, please, make contact. The Sailing Club has finally concluded a contribution deal with the MASC which gives us financial visibility up to 1992, so now what we want are ideas on how you_ want your Club to progress - a 5-Year Plan. Some ideas, like a full-time steward, will necessitate funding changes, perhaps partially offset by increased utilisation of our existing assets, e.g. more members, more activities/functions, longer season, etc. More working volunteers will, however, inevitably help to maintain existing or reduce increased costs. CATAMARAN NEWS The event looming largest in the memory during last north must, of course, be the Piers Race. The event will, no doubt, be well chronicled by other correspondents but we have some comments of our own. It is reported that those left behind were somewhat disappointed at the end, when, joyously greeting the returning sailors, they were met with deflated, perhaps disinterested, attitudes. It should be remembered here that the spectators saw two peaks of frenzied activity and in between nothing was happening. The sailors themselves had been on the water for around eight hours, and when returning to dry land the sensation of getting a sore backside off the hard deck led to relief rather than elation. So we apologise for not seeming to appreciate your support. For my own part the lasting impressions of the race are how long it seemed to take from Clacton to Walton on the way out. There are wide spaces of open water out there. With other boats only visible on the horizon it was hard to suppress feelings of fragility and insecurity, particularly as the last rescue boat seen was at Bradwell. This was not helped when, at the turning mark, the sea-fret descended and a Visibility was severely reduced. For all that, it was a great day and all seemed to have enjoyed it, courtesy of the weather. I won't attempt to re - thank all those helpers who have already received their thanks. However, I am asked by the fleet to say a special thank you to Mike Battle and his army for the sterling services that they provided. Last Sunday saw the final two races in the Summer series, when we actually had ten Catamarans racing. Someone must read this column. Congratulations must be offered to Graham Baker for winning his first race. Next Sunday sees the opening of the Autumn series, so let's keep up the numbers racing. Don't forget the approaching Solo open meeting (Sat/Sun 17th/18th September) when we are duty fleet. Lots of bodies will be needed so please leave these dates open and communicate your availability to the Fleet Captain as soon as possible. Your Catamaran correspondent, Peter Flook - CAR PARKING IN CAT FIELD One of the Cat Fleet members has asked for a note to go in Navigans - and it's a request very much from the heart! Cars parked along the edge of the field are OK, but those parking in the next row in, near the Cats, are asked would they please leave a gap in the row, wide enough for a Cat to pass through. At the moment some Cat sailors are having to pull their boats a considerably longer way round the field than necessary, whenever they want to take their boats to the Hard or return them to their space after a sail. Please look out for a couple of posts which will mark the space required to be kept clear. Ed.

7. CADET SERIES The conlusion of Race 7 (on 7th August left the Cadet Series very much 'wide open' with 4 competitors in with a chance to take the trophy for 1988. Best chance was that of Lucy Boreham who needed only one more win to make sure of being the overall winner but other possible winners were Ian Fletcher, Stuart Golding and Damian Boreham, all of whom needed to win the last 3 races to win the series. For Lucy, the cancellation of one of the remaining races would have been good news; alternatively, if she could not get a win then the remaining races being won by different people would also have guaranteed her overall first place. However, it was not to turn out that way...... Race 8 was scheduled to follow the Jackpot but the Club's rescue boat was so busy dealing with capsized dinghies that it could not cover the Cadet race and it would have been unwise to set a course without adequate rescue boat cover. Given the presence of a rescue boat, it would have been possible to set a course in the lee of the sea wall which would have been a good test of sailing ability, and certainly there were Cadets willing and able to take part. However, given the wind strength and the fact of the Jack B being fully occupied with the aftermath of the Jackpot, the Race Officer wisely decided to postpone Race 8 until Sunday 21st August, when the last three Cadet races could be completed. Races 8, 9 and 10 - come 21st August, the wind strength was predicted to be Force 5-6 rising to Force 8 offshore, but at the Club it was nearer Force 3-4 and sailing conditions on the water were really quite flat. Although the number of Cadets present promised some 6 boats, only 3 actually entered for the three races 8, 9 and 10. They were, Stuart Golding (crewed by Richard Carlisle); Lucy Boreham (crewed by Jenny Ball); and Damian Boreham crewed by Katy Rutherford); all of them sailing Mirror dinghies. Damian won all three races quite clearly and so ensured his hold on the Cadet Cup for 1988; as crew, Katy secured three more wins to put her at the top of the Mug's Mug league table for the crew who sails most times in a prize-winning boat. The interesting bit was the close racing between Stuart and Lucy with some good tactical moves by both - plus some errors. Although Stuart took 2nd place in Race 8, Lucy reversed the position and got two 2nd places in Races 9 and 10. Overall Result - the overall result was the closest for some years with Damian just winning the series by ¼ point over his sister, Lucy, whilst Stuart got his well-deserved 3rd place. MIRROR FLEET NEWS. I am afraid I've been very lazy about writing for Navigans this year - somehow the time flies by and, before you know it, another navigans dead-line has passed by. As you read this, the Summer Points Series will probably have been completed and we can look forward to the Autumn Points Series before finally putting the boats to bed in mid-October. Congratulations to Mike and Janet Battle on winning the Mirror Class in the Regatta - it was quite windy at times so I am told. I wouldn't really know because I must confess that we were on a canal boat holiday with another family and, I must say, it was one of the nicest, most restful and most peaceful holidays I have ever spent. Congratulations to Damian and Katie for winning the Spring Points Series; hard luck to Lucy and Jenny for coming 2nd but getting no prizes - the Mirror Class was the only one which didn't manage an average of 4 entries for the series and so lst place prize only was awarded. The camping fortnight (inclusive of Cadet Week) was, aS usual, very enjoyable and equally most successfu 1. This was the 7th (or was it the 8th) Cadet 'Week' we've attended and all have been well-worth the effort This year 'the effort' not only covered teaching sailing to the very young, but also the somewhat older members who, in their spare time, carry out the duties of being parents to the Cadets. Although the lst week was a bit windy at times, the weatherman was kind to us for the following Cadet Week with its programme of sailing instruction. The wind was just enough to sail pleasantly, the sun hot enough to give us a tan and the number of people enough to keep things lively. Even our ‘traditional' thunder- storm (yes - we usually have one at night) was a very muted affair and hardly anyone noticed the rather weak lightning and the low-level growl of thunder which followed it. . More significantly for cadet Week was the large number of Mirrors which took to the water - there must have been 12 -15 sailing .. At one time, as I looked towards Osea Pier, there seemed to be so many Mirrors sailing there thatI thought Maylandsea Bay must have been holding an open meeting but not at all - it was our members having a fine time sailing on the mighty river Blackwater. The point is, if you can get your boat on the water every day for the ‘once a year’ week of sailing tuition, it seems apity not to consolidate what you've learned by taking part in the Sunday racing programme. So don't pack your Mirror away until next year's Cadet Week - keep it sailing and join in the Sunday racing. The club's Mirror 'open' event is to be held on 10/11 September. This is an event that definetely needs your active participation and it's worth having a go. We usually only get a few visitors from local clubs so you are not going to find too many Mirrors buzzing around. In fact, most will be the same people you sailed with during cadet Week. DON'T FORGET - OQUR MIRROR OPEN NEEDS YOU 10/11 SEPTEMBER Happy sailing _ Maggie Boreham (Honorary Scribe to the Mirror Fleet) Note: The above article was intended for September Navigans, but it just missed the bus!

9. SOLO NEWS The massed support pledged at the fleet AGM last year for a visit to Holland for the Solo World Championships failed to materialise. Instead only Roger Smith and I embarked on this adventure, but it was thoroughly enjoyable, both the event itself, and the picturesque little fishing towns along that section of the Isselmere shore around Monickendam. We had bags of wind for most of the 4-day event and the short disturbed seas were very reminiscent of wind-against-tide on the Blackwater - a real home from home. Back home the big deal has been the Up-River Open at Hullbridge where the entry was dominated by Marconi members. THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE (Through the Eye of a Hurricane) Having been the sole source of amusement for the CAT fleet for the last few weeks, I thought I would get my own back by describing one boat's view of the inaugural East Coast Piers Race which was held on August 7th, starting and finishing at our Club. Let me go back to the beginning. Our story starts on a Sunday in late June when the wind was blowing force 6 and sailing had been abandoned. The first meeting of the Piers Race Committee was taking place and Dave Payne and I sat in, out of interest. By the time the meeting had finished Dave had completed the entry form although we did not yet have a boat! On the day of the race I was up at 5.30am to rig the boat and move it round onto the Hard as I had offered to lead the way to the beach at Osea should we need to use a Le Mans start. We wondered how many of the younger sailors knew what a Le Mans start was! The boat was rigged by 7am and from thereon we suffered the usual found of comments before the briefing at 8am: "Have you fitted halyards to the centre boards?" "Why are you studying the chart? Are you checking the bottom so you can find your way?" "If you get a chance please check the underwater piles on the piers as you drift past." Obviously the other fleet members had little confidence in our completing the course, but as we had set our objective as just getting around the course we were confident. We, along with a number of other club members, spent the hour before the start lazing in the sun on the beach beyond Osea Pier. With 15 minutes to go we launched into the general melee of the start area. A starboard start was favoured and we thought that we were the only ones who believed this as most of the other Cats were at the port end. We were wrong for within two minutes of the start, the No.2 Buoy had disappeared amongst a solid mass of boats. Of the 64 starters, at least 60 were grouped around the starboard end of the line. We were about 50 yards behind this group, determined not to become involved in a bumping match. Several boats collided and a number bounced off the mark. Nobody seemed to do any 720 penalties. The gun went and the fleet charged forward. We crossed about 2nd from last and immediately tacked onto port to get clear wind. The nearest we got to the leaders was passing Reg White before the start. We were going one way, him the other way. One boat had gone outside No.2 and it took several calls from us before he turned back. He had mistaken mooring buoy for No.2. This buoy is not normally there so it added to the confusion. Dave was out on the wire and I shuffled up to the shroud and we bore away across the back of Barry Palmer. Our first tack took us onto starboard and we found ourselves crossing the fleet having gained about 20 places. The next tack saw us headed back towards the Club. We combed our hair, brushed our teeth and tried to get close to the shore to give those with cameras good photo opportunities! Lindsey told me that we got so close to the Hard she thought we were coming in to retire. Dave and I would be grateful for copies of any photos taken. By the time we reached Fisherman (F) we must have been in about 30th place and were ahead of two of the the three Hurricane Specials. Although we were sailing fast we were not pointing very well and 3 other Hurricanes passed us. As we approached Thirslet Spit, we found ourselves tacking amongst the BJRC Cruisers waiting to start their race. We met a Cruiser on starboard and I had to bear away to miss the stern. Owing to the angle of our cont....

11. approach, I didn't see the tender until the last minute and Dave fended it off with his backside. You could say that they both had a tender behind! Fortunately the tender was an inflatable but the sound of the contact was disgusting! We misjudged the gate at Bradwell and had to put in an extra tack. By now the fleet was well spread and the only boats I could identify were Trevor Milton and Tom Duckmanton in the Stampede and the 13' wide Hurricane Turbo. They were both behind us, but not too far. Our inability to point as well as the other Hurricanes was most noticeable as we tacked across the West Mersea Shore. On one tack we gained a 200 yard lead on another Hurricane, but at the expense of dropping 300 yards to leeward. We tacked across towards Bradwell again and found ourselves regaining our loss on the other Hurricane and we tacked next both ahead and to windward. What we didn't know was why! We presume that it was the tide which helped us, but why not the other boat? At this point we found ourselves overhauling a Hobie 18 called "Dire Straits". We were sailing faster, but again dropping off to leeward. We tacked again and headed out to clear the Dredgers moored towards Clacton. Out we went, further and further. The further out we went the more the wind lifted us towards Clacton. I am not sure how far out we went but Dave wanted to open the duty frees and stop at Zeebruge for a newspaper. We tacked back to find Clacton Pier and spotted Hobie 18 "Dire Straits" tacking up the shore. He must have gone between the dredgers and the shore, or must have passed very close to them on the seaward side. We passed through the gate at Clacton about ½ a mile behind the Hobie and slowly began to catch him. Just beyond Clacton we suddenly found ourselves surrounded by Windsurfers. We passed behind a moored Cruiser and then realised we had just gone through the Windsurfers' finishing line. Luckily we beat the leader to the line. We still hadn't managed to get in front of the Hobie, but were only about 100 yards to leeward and were 100 yards ahead. Coming towards us was a Naval Patrol Boat. it was going at about 20 knots. I was sure that it would alter course and pass behind us but it kept on coming. It passed about 25 yards ahead of us and the bow wave was about 7' high. Krackatoa - East of Java sprang to mind as this tidal wave approached. We leapt the wave with us both on the wire and Dave taught me a few new words, for which I offer my apologies to those on Walton Beach. Every time we tacked we got closer to the Hobie 18, but every time we went close inshore the wind lifted him and the distance between us remained constant. About a mile from Walton pier we split tacks with the Hobie. We went close inshore and were lifted almost up to the pier. At this point we passed Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton. They were on their way back! We followed the Splashdown/British Airways/RWO Hurricane through the gate and around the turning mark. In fact we turned as 22nd boat, and started the long journey home. During the turn I noticed the video camera on Kingfisher, so after waving, we did probably our best gybe ever. As we headed back Trevor and Tom were coming through the gate. The RWO boat headed out to seaward and we gybed inshore. "Dire Straits" was rapidly left behind. In the distance we could see a group of boats, but they were difficult to identify and probably 3 miles ahead. On our way towards Clacton we passed close to a number of Club boats. We saw Paul Metcalfe first, then Peter Flook. "Keep going, Grandad," we cried. Mick Jones was not far behind. We kept gybing along the shore and again passed through the (Windsurfers'?) race finish line. This time we passed just ahead of a fleet of Toppers. Suddenly it all went wrong. I must have been day-dreaming for suddenly right between the hulls was a large yellow mooring buoy. it bounced off the dolphin striker and struck the port rudder hard enough to knock it out of alignment. From then on we had to fight very severe weather helm. It never occurred to me to lift the port rudder! By the time we passed through the Clacton gate we were up with the boats which had been mere specks at Walton. cont....

12 these boats were Hobies and Prindles and we began to slowly pass them one by one. At this point we were regularly lifting the windward hull downwind although the tell-tales were touching th brindle wires. Dave was out on the wire although afterwards everybody told me that we must have been pointing too high. Nevertheless we continued to pass the boats in front. We followed the Hobies between the Dredgers and the shore and headed in towards the mouth of the Colne. We took this route because the mist had closed in and we could not see Bradwell Power Station. "This trapeze belt is kna***ring me!" stated Dave in a falsetto voice, "Can we have a 5 minute rest for a drink and food?" I turned the boat directly downwind and we let the sails right out and drifted. One drink and Mars bar later I started to beat my hand on the deck like a drum. "What are you doing that for?" asked Dave. "I'm the slave driver telling the galley slave to get back to work. The skipper wants to carve up some more Hobies!" Dave finished his apple whilst on the trapeze. That short break eventually cost us about 3 places. We could now see Bradwell and we passed the last of the Hobies as we approached the Power Station. As we passed inside the Baffle we saw Trevor and Tom back at West Mersea and the 13' wide Hurricane Turbo was about ½ a mile behind, but in the middle of the estuary. Our next target was a Hurricane about a mile ahead, but the wind kept dropping away, whilst the Hurricane Turbo, now using his reaching kite, was overhauling us. We used our knowledge of the tide and kept close to the south shore but the Turbo crept past us at Stone. The Hurricane (077) was close to the Thundercat and they passed through the finish as we reached 'F' mark. The Thundercat gybed off and came around behind us. Evidently he had missed the "D" mark and had not finished. This lucky break meant that we crossed the line in 14th place, having gained 8 places on the downwind leg. Our elapsed time was 6 hours 35 minutes and 49 seconds, which meant that we finished 51 minutes behind the first boat and 46 minutes after the eventual winner, Robert White. We were 8th production Hurricane out of 11 but the 7th boat only finished 1 minute 59 seconds in front of us and the 6th just a few seconds over 5 minutes. Overall it was enjoyable, although it was a very long way. I have calculated that most boats probably sailed in excess of 60 miles, with those who stood well out to sea to pass the Dredgers, sailing nearer to 70 miles. Next year a number of us are aiming to compete in the Round Texel Race in Holland. We must need out heads examining!! Lastly our commiserations go to Maurice and Luke who broke the THAICAT off of Clacton and limped home to retire. Maurice lavishes loving care on the boat and for its age it is a credit to his efforts. Hard luck, chaps, but I'm sure you'll be there again next year; we will. As to the rest of you Club sceptics: Watch out! Watch out! There's a Hurricane about! Steve Keeble and see next page for some more....

14. The Jackpot 1988 This year's Jackpot started its 1st leg (to the Jolly Sailor) in Force 3/4 plus and finished the 2nd leg in Force 4/5 plus. Most of the Solo entries (except for Ron Greygoose) capsized sometime or other and 'hairy' moments were 'enjoyed' by most participants. Unlucky duo were Mike and Janet Battle (Mirror) who were caused to capsize after a close encounter of an alarming kind with a port-tack boat from a neighbouring race. Their exhilarating journey back towards the clubhouse on a glorious starboard-tack planning reach was suddenly and unexpectedly brought to an end near Osea and they finished in the drink and were thus deprived of a good 2nd leg result. As the Solos approached the end of the 2nd leg, the view from the racebox was, to say the least, interesting as we saw various helms capsize at high speed. Colin Willsmore and Ron Greygoose looked set for a neck-and-neck finish as each approached the finish from opposite sides of the river but Colin capsized as he reached the cruiser lines - only a little short of the protective lee of the sea wall. Barry Newboult suffered similarly, whilst Malcolm Gandy and Peter Collis capsized a little further up river between the pier and Steeple Point. Perhaps the thought of being so near the finish (after an exciting ride) caused a momentary lack of concentration; any suggestions of over-indulgence at the Jolly Sailor is strenuously denied. Remember, the Jackpot is one race sailed as two legs, the times for each leg being added together to give the final finishing elapsed time.
