16. Mona's Cup 1988 This year's Mona's Cup was rather sparsely populated with entries, only 6 boats taking part compared to 16 in 1987 and 26 in 1986. The Mona's Cup is an 'all-in' race (ie. cruiser and dinghy) and, for this reason, the 'long line start' is used. The 'long line start' is indicated by the letter 'L' after the course code letters and means that you must start between 'D' mark and No.1 but in line with the triangle on the race box and the mete pole . Those with long memories might recall that in the 1986 race some 21 out of the 26 entries were disqualified because they started between the mete and 'D' mark; this year only one boat made this mistake. Of the 6 starters, 4 were catamarans and 2 were Mirrors, thus the entries represented the very opposite ends of the 'speed spectrum'. In fact, it was reminiscent of the Hare and the Tortoise fable and could well have been a re-enactment since Mirrors often do quite well in this race. The wind was Force 4/5 (forecast rising to 6), the water was rough and there were plenty of 'white horse' to be seen off Osea. Mike Battle and Derek Holroyd (Mirror) found their weight both an advantage (keeping the boat flat) and disadvantage (slower speed, no spinnaker) whilst similarly Damian Boreham and Jenny Ball (Mirror) found themselves having difficulty in keeping the boat upright and consequently they shipped water up to the gunwales (without capsizing) and had to 'sail' into the shelter of the smoother water by Osea Pier in order to bail out. Their lightweight advantage was boat speed - plus spinnaker. The catamarans had a fine old time and they didn't take too long to get up to Heybridge and back. The finish leg was to round Breezy to starboard and finish into the wind between 'D' mark and the mete. Graham Baker showed distinct signs of not being able to find Breezy and, in the race box, we were taking bets on whether he would (a) sail to Stone (b) round Breezy to port or (c) capsize. However, he did none of these things and finished correctly having, as always, thoroughly enjoyed his sail (this time crewed by Dave Onyons). Rob Stahl was the unfortunate cat disqualified for incorrect start and it seemed a shame to have to deprive him of a finishing 'hoot' having sailed all the way up the river and back again. However, he was 'timed in' and would have finished third. Steve Keeble shows every sign of mastering the techniques of sailing his Hurricane every time he goes out and he certainly looked as though he was enjoying himself, as was his crew Dave Payne. Trevor Milton found the going very much to his liking and won the race; if he can tell me the name of his crew then he/she will get a 'credit' in the Mug's Mug League Table. CADETS - BRADWELL FIELD STUDIES & SAILING CENTRE My daughter Jenny and Lucy (Boreham) went to the Bradwell Sailing Centre for a week in August with the aim of achieving their RYA National Dinghy Certificate Level 5 to top up on their qualifications earned with Derek Hall's excellent tuition of our Cadets over recent years. They succeeded in gaining their Level 5 certificate, and enjoyed their week so much that they intend going back again next year if possible. In case there are other Members who might be interested in their Cadets trying this course I have typed out below all the relevant information on what the Centre offers, taken from its own literature. Jenny's one week residential course cost £60 which we considered very reasonable for 6 full days at the Centre - from 11am Monday till 2pm the following Sunday (though Jenny and Lucy did leave at 10am to hurry back to the Club to take part in a vital Cadet Race! The Centre is situated beside the Creek at Bradwell Waterside on the River Blackwater. There is a main residential and administrative building, boat yards, workshops and a laboratory for field studies. The Centre can house 40 students plus six accompanying staff. Accommodation is in centrally heated rooms with full toilet, shower and drying facilities. There is also a lounge, dining/lecture room, and a recreation room with table tennis and juke box. The meals are cooked by permanent catering staff but the students are required to assist in other domestic duties. All equipment, including protective clothing for the various specialised activities, is provided by the Centre. (Ed's note: You'd need to take along your own wet suit if you usually wear one for dinghy sailing, they are provided by the Centre for those doing the Boardsailing Course only.) SAILING Instruction is given in Toppers, Yachting World Day Boats, Oysters, Wayfarers, 505's and Bradwell 22's. Teams of experienced helmsmen and instructors enable complete novices to receive expert tuition. A safety boat is always in attendance. The Centre also has a 26' auxiliary sloop, in which all off-shore sailing, coastal and foreign cruising is done. Basic equipment for courses in seamanship, navigation and meteorology, covering the theory of the RYA/NSSA Proficiency and Coaching Scheme is also offered. The Centre is recognised as a Royal Yachting Association/National Schools Sailing Association Examination Centre. CANOEING instruction is given in a variety of single-seater kayaks. Expeditions by canoe can be arranged on request. CAMPING: Sailing and canoeing camping expeditions are also arranged, using modern lightweight camping equipment and craft suitable for sleeping aboard. All the necessary equipment is supplied. BOARD SAILING. The Centre is equipped with a variety of boards, also with junior and intermediate rigs for the beginner. CATAMARAN NEWS Event of the north this time goes to the Catamaran Open held on the weekerd of lOth/llth September. An overall entry of 23 Cats. looks encouraging until it is realised that 14 of them are Club entries. Our Cat men must be complimented on this turnout whilst bemoaning the lack of visitors in any numbers. The weather was not kind to us over this weekend, bursts of reasonable wind strengt always quickly abating to nothing at all for long periods. This weather of course did nothing at all to assist the administration of the event which was being run by our Solo colleagues and the courses can only be described as interesting. Thank you, Solos, for a job well done in difficult circumstances. Results as follows: First: Stampede 63 Trevor Milton Second: Dart 4469 D. Lloyd (Stokes Bay) Third: Tornado 290 John Nickalls An interesting innovation was the donation of a new trophy for Marconi Sailors participating in this event by Steve and Janet Keeble, entitled the "Old Codger's" Shield. Its concept is brilliant, Steve, quite the best thing you've done this year. Modesty prevents me from publishing the names of the first winners but carn I just add that if anyone knows of a 72-year-old trapeze artist, please put them ir touch with me. The following weekend gave us the chance to be useful at the Solo Oper Meeting wher we hope we ran a successful event. On both days we were able to field 3 rescue boats which were not needed because, once again the wind did not appear. Thanks to all Cat men and women who turned up to help. By the time this appears in print, sailing will have officially finished (although rumblings are heard of a potential winter Cat series.) It is to be hoped that everyone has enjoyed the season and looks forward to the next one. Do not forget the winter's social events, the first of which is the Laying Up Supper on the 19th November. Let's have a good attendance and show that we are surely now the largest class in the Club. Your Cat correspondent Peter Flook More Cat chat on next page......

THE MARCONI CATAMARAN OPEN MEETING - 10/11 SEPTEMBER (through the eye of the hurricane) (This is not meant to be an unbiased view of the evert, as from on the water it is impossible to see all of the action throughout the fleet.) Saturday dawned bright with a force 2 wind blowing from the West. Owing to confusion over first race start times the meeting was reduced from 4 races to 3, but to keep the troops happy Ron Greygoose, our intrepid Race Officer, set a practice race up to No.8 Buoy. The race got under way after postponed start, and Janet (my better half who was crewing in place of Dave) and I had an excellent view of the rest of the Fleet streaming from us towards the first mark. By the time we got to No.2 we were in the lead and pulling away from the Fleet. The run back from No.8 to No.1 was fairly uneventful except that the wind was gradually fading. A quick reach to C and back “brought us into contact with Paul Metcalfe who was just rounding No.1 on his way to C. We reached across to round A only to find that the wind had died completely and we were forced to slowly tack up the shore by the Club. As we reached the middle of the Hard, a voice cried out 'race abandoned!' and there on the Club flagpole was a limp ‘abandon' flag. At least we didn't have far to go to get ashore. Paul Metcalfe crept ashore about 15 minutes later ard most other boats drifted in on the falling tide. After a leisurely lunch we dragged ourselves onto the water for the second race. Again the wind was very fickle and we made one of our yet to be forgotten lousy starts. John Nickalls_ shot straight into the lead. He started to cross the river towards the Club but the wind died and he tacked to the Osea_ shore. We were following a similar course but the wind held up and we made it across. We were accompanied by two Darts and the three of us spent the next ten minutes trying to get around the corner. The Fleet was now divided into two halves. One on the Osea shore and one in the bay. The wind made the race a lottery as it varied from force nil to force 2 and boats ten yards apart could experience the extremes. We swapped places with our little group, losing out by our slow tacking. A Dart led the way round No.2 eTMclosely followed by John Nickalls and Caroline. Two more Darts followed and then us, closely followed by another Dart. As we drifted with no wind towards No.1 we watched Trevor Milton and Tom _ sail serenely up and round No. 2 with their own personal breeze. They must have gained 600 yards on the leading boats and then continued on towards the leading group containing John and the first 3 Darts. The rest of us? We still had no wind, just tide. Rounding No.1 and heading for C the leading group were in line astern. The wind was very localised with both Trevor and I managing to lift hulls at some point whilst others were just coasting slowly towards the mark. The shallow water forced me _ to bear away as the rudders were grunching on the bottom. This forced me to put in a tack at C and the yellow hulled Stampede shot past on his own personal gust. From C to B was again a procession and then followed the usual short tacking duel to the Club finish line. Although we overhauled the yellow Stampede, it was a race in which the Darts took the honours. CONT.

10. Cat Open contd. Sunday was a lot better with the wind blowing 3 gusting 5. After a much delayed start, the Fleet headed to No.2. This was our most disastrous start, with me actually falling off the boat! John and Trevor made their usual good start with Rob and Matthew not too far behind. We had Graham Baker and Dave Onyons for company as we set off to catch the rest. By the time we got to No.2 we had passed everybody except John, Trevor and the leading 2 Darts. Mike Duckmanton and Rosie were trying to make life difficult by trying to catch us on a port/starboard meeting. At No.8 just John and Trevor were ahead. JI do wish Johr would get a more colourful sail as it is almost impossible to pick him out from a distance, and a distance is about the closest we ever got! Downwind to No.1 we chose a different route from Trevor. We were behind him and had nothing to lose. It paid off as we were first to Osea pier, where we promptly found @ hole in the wind. John and Caroline were well on their way to the E mark and the end of the first lap as we crossed them when tacking between No.1 and C. "They will Finish after one lap," we thought. We had been racing about 90 minutes and the Sparks were a long way back. But no! There was John and Caroline goirg around again! By now the river was filled with boats and as we headed for No.2 we thought we could see the Committee Boat. But alas no. As we came up towards No.2 we found ourselves slightly to windward of an echelon of cruisers. We were all on starboard and in front were 2 Windsurfers crossing on port. "Starboard!" we cried as one. "Starboard!" again. No reaction from the Windsurfers. "Starboard!" we cried. - "You don't own the river!" came the reply. They were very lucky, as a Hurricane is 8ft wide and they must have been $8ft 6ins apart. The cruisers were all trying to take evasive action as well, but we were clear so we left them to have an accident with some other unfortunate boat owner. The rest of the race was uneventful, except that as we passed Osea pier on the way back, there were Sparks still heading for No.2. Janet and I were pleased to finish ahead of Trevor although he beat us on handicap (28 seconds in 3 hours). Race 4 was a short affair and after our usual bad start we did not see the leaders at all. We spent the first part of the race trying to get through Peter Flook's dirty wind and the second part catching and passing Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine and _ the yellow hulled Stampede. Although we crossed the line ahead, they murdered us on handicap. JI understand that Trevor beat John across the line by 1 second, which gave Trevor and Tom the meeting overall. John and Caroline finished 3rd overall with Janet and me 5th. Typical, they only had prizes for the first 4! The highlight of the presentation was the award of the 'Old Codger' trophy to Peter Flook. It couldn't have happened to an older (and nicer) man! Thanks must go to the Solo fleet for running the event and to the people who manned the Galley and Bar, and we look forward to returning the compliment with a couple of 3-hour races in a force 5 wind. Steeve Keeble (fly by wire) P.S. I understand that those little wooden wash tubs with the red flannels on a broom pole were also racing. Did anybody see them?

MARCONI SAILING CLUB - 1988 A.G.M. Commodore's Report Fellow members - friends - another year has gone by since I last gave you my report. Little did I know then what a traumatic year it was going to turn out to be both personally and Clubwise. Over the past year we have had quite an eventful time which started with the retirment of Claude Emerson to some well earned rest in the middle of England. This resulted in two abortive attempts to recruit a single replacement, with us finally finding two people to share the job viz: Dave and Darren, with all its attendant difficulties in effective control and we are back to one again now! For some time past now, members have been increasingly suggesting that the load of work, or rather chores, falling on their shoulders was becoming unacceptable and as a result we asked the MASC to investigate the possibility of being able to offer a full-time steward accommodation. As a result, planning permission for a house was sought - rejected - and is now on appeal. Whether, if the appeal is successful, the house is ever built will depend entirely on us the members because the cost will not be insignificant. The only help against this will be increased membership and -~if you remember, this was one of my messages to you last year - each of you recruit one member and our financial worries sink into the background. As Pat will no doubt be telling you, the recruitment drive was beginning to show some success, but we do need more. Over the years I have always been adamant and vehement that our Club was successful because the members belonged and they belonged by being involved and were involved by supporting the essence and spirit of self help. This support must continue and we will remain successful - BUT I think the time has now come, because of our size, when we must seriously consider removing the burden of chores from our members by having a full time steward. If you agree then give your new Commodore your support by recruiting one more, at least, new member each by Easter. Remember though, I said CHORES - not Working Parties - you are and will continue to be essertial work units for these belonging activities! We have made a start in trying to drain the Cruiser Park - but it obviously still needs some more work done on it - but at the end of the day I think we will have to spend a great deal of money and have it done properly. um There were for me three highlights this year. First we had a Regatta which, with Malcolm's energetic input should continue to improve over the years especially if we build on the new conditions and procedures we introduced this year. Second, I actually managed to spend the whole of the camping fortnight at Stansgate which I found very instructive and enjoyable despite never having a minute to myself. z think a lot more members should consider attending this camp. Third we had an inaugural Piers Race which, thanks to the clemency of the weather, allowed us to see and learn our mistakes without getting into a serious sailing incident. Long may it continue and become the prestigious East Coast Race it deserves to be. You will note from the papers already issued to you that your Committee has managed, I think for the first time in several years, to announce Committee nominations for all positions. This is excellent and it is essential that everyone will offer their services from time to time without being specifically asked. In particular your committee must have visibility of ordinary members who will be prepared to ‘do their bit' So do not be bashful, drop broad hints to Officers and Committee about what you may like to do. You will note that your President, Jack Pateman, is relinquishing his post and that we have been very lucky in securing the services of Martin Jay for this position. Our grateful thanks to Mr Pateman for all he has done for us in the past and a rousing welcome to Mr Jay for taking on the mantle. One note I had hoped I should not have had to announce to you. We have still failed

4. to reach a final agreement with the General Committee of he M.A.S.C. for the use of the assets. On two occasions in the past 9 months we thought we had an agreement only to find the General Committee would not ratify the plan. We were trying right up to Friday evening to come to some compromise. In this respect Gerry Wignall has worked very hard to arrive at a settlement and we have found him helpful and constructive. It is now obvious we must have some representation on the General Committee, and to this end, John Weedon offered himself for co-option during the summer, but now faces an election this coming week. WE MUST ENSURE JOHN IS ELECTED so please every ordinary member of the Club make the effort to go to the M.A.S.C. to vote. Voting is all week, so do take your MASC membership card, and take the few minutes it needs. You will have up to seven votes to cast, but you need only cast one for John. We are on the last legs of the negotiated compromise and I think that if we had not been up against an election next week we may well have had a settlement for a five-year term with an extension of two years if a new five-year term had not been agreed by the end of the fifth year. But in case of difficulty Niel and I intend to brief Mr Jay in the next week or so. What we can say is that the total figure is known to within a few hundred and this should enable us to formulate reasonably accurate budgets. I have kept you all long enough but I cannot conclude without paying unstinting tribute to the other Officers, Committee and Members for the wholehearted support I have enjoyed over the past two years as your Commodore. And finally, if I may turn to the personal trauma I alluded to at the beginning of this report. It is not unique to me - there are many others here today who have suffered; are now suffering; and unfortunately still others who don't know it, like me last year, yet to suffer. I mean of course the indignity of redundancy or redeploy ment. I mention this not to raise any oohs and aahs but to try and show you all the strength and support our Club - or which should more appropriately be called our Community - can afford to its members. The true empathy which emanates from its corporate being and which can be so effective in combating depression is priceless -guard it well -it is what makes our Club GREAT. Continue to show my successor and all his successors the same support you have shown me and you will - No, we will - have a still greater Club. I hope my family will be able to remain members for many years to come and if we can escape from Lincoln, the Sims' tent will be with you for Regatta and Camping fortnight. Robbie Sims, Retiring Commodore, A.G.M. 1988 Sailing Secretary's Report to A.G.M. ed The year started with the RNLI rowing race at Maldon, then Sailboat '88 which has attracted several good members to the Club. Events The Club has run two major events this year, both of which have been a success. I refer to the Regatta, re-introduced as a favourite local event after a break of 2 years, due to hard work and perseverance of Malcolm Stuart. Secondly the Cat fleet invented the East Coast Piers Race and that looks like being another regular. Cruisin As a dinghy sailor, one does not get too much feel for what is going on in the Cruiser world but I get the impression that this year has not seen so many ‘going foreign'. Am I wrong? Let us see your log in Navigans and win the Mamgu Trophy - also open to dinghy sailors. Cruiser Fleet have been very supportive of the dinghy open meetings by providing Committee Boats, back-up rescue services etc. Disappointing - the Barnacle Points was not run this year. Dinghy Sailing Another increase in the number of entries to Club events - a lot of that due to the Cat Fleet who also provide a significant input to the Club

5. activities generally. Solos continue to have highest average entry despite attempts by Cats to decimate the Fleet if a good number of boats get on the water. Good to see Handicap up this year. Sailboards have started racing with a Summer and Autumn points series and they are another group who contribute to the running of the Club. Open Meetings Solo, Cat, 420 and Mirror well supported, others not. It does cost the Club money to run these events so we must work hard to get 12+ entry or not hold them. Team Racing In a word abysmal - we lost the Boothby Cup (again), the Rochester visit and made no impression on the MBYC Challenge Cup. Must do better next year. Representation Cat fleet and Solos, plus 420 of the Cunningham's have been travelling. Robin Smith puts MSC's name in Yachts & Yachting regularly. Malcolm Gandy was a creditable 23rd in Nationals at Harwich. Overall it must be considered a successful year with more boats on the water, more big events and more enjoyment of Sailing. Finally having done the job for 2½ years I shall miss it - both good and bad. SOLO NEWS At the end of another successful sailing season I would like, on behalf of the Solo Fleet, to express my appreciation to Dave Onyons and the other Rescue Boat Drivers for the excellent support provided for the racing this season. Our thanks also go to those members of other Fleets who supported our racing programme with Race Officer and other duties. The Fleet AGM took place at MASC on October 12th and I will summarise a few of the key decisions taken here: 1. The Fleet would support the Eastern Region's attempt to field a team for the Inter-Region Championship at Littleton S.C. on 6th November, even though this clashed with the Club AGM. For this and other reasons the Fleet felt that it would be more appropriate to hold the AGM at MASC midweek. 2. The provisional 1989 sailing programme was found to be generally acceptable although it was felt that pursuit-type racing on a Sunday should be kept to a minimum. 3. More Sunday evening barvecues would be organised in 1989 - Ron Greygoose to arrange. 4. John Salmon agreed to continue as Fleet Captain for a third and final year. Dave Nixson agreed to continue as Vice-Captain. 5. The September 1989 Solo Open meeting should be a single day event (on a Sunday) with three races in a day. In order to achieve the tight timing of such a programme it was felt that the meeting should be for one Fleet only. 6. John Salmon (Fleet Captain) and Malcolm Gandy (Spring Points Series Winner) were charged with deciding who should receive the Frank Savill Trophy which is awarded each year to the Fleet Member showing most improvement. The 1988 winner is Janet Keeble. 7. The January Solo Supper should be repeated, preferably at the Cross Keys again - Pat Stuart agreed to investigate. 8. A provisional date of April 8th was fixed for a repeat of the Solo Fleet Dinner Party at Stansgate but this event will only be held if someone volunteers to organise it. Any Fleet member who would like to take this on should let me know. The final Eastern Area Open Meeting of the season took place at Fishers Green on 2nd October with the usual minimal breeze. The event was won comfortably by John Reece from Broadwater SC. Seven MSC helms competed, gaining finishing positions of: 2nd John Salmon, 3rd Ron Greygoose, 5th Malcolm Gandy, 6th Dave Nixson, 8th Roger Smith, 10th Janet Keeble, 14th Colin Willsmore. This left Alan Burrell of Half Way YC as Eastern Area Champion with MSC helms filling the next five places in the order: Malcolm Gandy, John Salmon, Ron Greygoose, Dave Nixson, Roger Smith. Pembleton, Chelmsford [redacted] or Clubhouse Secretary, C. Davies, Chelmsford [redacted], if you have a problem. MIRROR NEWS The Mirror Fleet AGM was held at MASC on Friday 11th November. 1. Mike Battle agreed to continue as Fleet Captain for one more year only, with Debbie e~Yorston as assistant, Debbie to take over as Fleet Captain at the end of the year. 2. To encourage a larger turnout for Mirror Racing, it was suggested that a Mirror Teach-in would be held in the summer - less confident sailors to be put in with experienced ones to help them improve their skills and learn about racing. Also it was proposed that advanced sailors could be shown tuning of their boats for best performance. 3. Mike Battle said he would like to put up a Prize for the lst ‘Beginner Cadet' over the line in the Mirror Open to encourage Cadets to enter the race who have not done so in the past as they felt they had no chance of winning the race. It was also suggested that the Mirror Open should be a series of 3 races on one day, instead of over a whole weekend. 4. It was decided that the Cadet Races should no longer be held on Saturdays because this can be less convenient and makes the Cadet Series seem not as important as that of other Classes - which of course is not true! It is intended that on each of two Sundays there would be 3 Cadet races, with the rest of the Series fitted in as normal. On these two Sundays it was proposed that Pursuit Races would be held for the other meTMFleets. It was also hoped that a Mirror Fleet Barbecue be held after sailing on these two Sundays and that the Mirror fleet might hold one or two other social activities. 5. The Fun Day during Camping Fortnight was a success and it was hoped it would be an annual event. The Club's Regatta had also been a great success though Mirror involvement was disappointing and it was hoped that more would take part in the future. Finally, it was generally accepted that 1988 had been quite a good year, but next year we are going to boost our numbers and get more of those sixty-or-more Mirrors sitting in the park out on the water! Jenny Ball, Mirror Scribe. CADETS CADETS CADETS All Cadets........Keep watching Navigans for Cadet News and information on Cadet Winter Meetings in future Navigans. 10. EDITORIAL continued Once again Many Thanks to all Members who turned out on the last Working Party and worked so hard both inside and outside the Clubhouse. It did look a lot neater at the end of the day. The Christmas Working Party this year is on Monday 2nd January, making it a New Year Working Party, and once again we need our Members to set to and help. Details of work to be tackled will appear in next Navigans. This Navigans has gone a little later to the printers for various reasons, and so far I've received entries amounting to a total of 29 pages! This is usually a busy time for the Magazine with the Club AGM Reports, a couple of Fleet AGM reports, Sailing Results for the end of the season, Membership Renewal Forms, and the Discount Offer on Boat Paints. I have had to live up to my name this time and severely edit out anything that I didn't think urgent, but the material held back will appear as soon as possible, though with so much of it still in hand I hope members will bear with me if I arrange for it to appear in smaller print. The Diary of Jenny's and Lucy's stay at Bradwell Sailing Centre is a victim of the cut, but that can appear in one of our thinner winter issues, perhaps when we are all beginning to turn our hopeful thoughts to next summer's sailing. LOWESTOFT COLLEGE - SURVIVAL COURSE FOR SMALL BOAT USERS This is a one day basic Sea Survival course designed for the small boat user. Instruction is divided into two main Parts: a) Theory and demonstration of raft and equipment in classroom. Survival problems and solutions! b) Practical wet drills with liferaft and jackets. The course is based on the inflatable liferaft, but it also covers aspects where a liferaft may not be available. The actions required at any particular stage during an incident are dealt with so that threats to life are minimised. Courses are normally held at Lowestoft College where there are purpose facilities, including a heated training tank and a wide selection of survival equipment. The course starts at 0900 hrs and finishes at 1700 hrs with a lunch break of about an hour. A lounge area is available for use at coffee and lunch breaks, and coffee machines are on site. Meals are not normally available. A swimming costume and towel are required and if you would like to test your protective clothing and lifejacket please bring them along provided they are clean. There are lifejackets etc, available at the College. The cost of the course for up to 16 persons is £280 - (£17.50 per person) - and the choice of dates are: Saturday 25th February 1989 or, Saturday 11th March 1989 The original deadline was December 10th, but if any members are interested there is still time so please contact as soon as possible: Ron Brobson, 24 [redacted], Gt Baddow, Chelmsford Tel. 6. NAUTICAL BRAIN TEASERS Below are some nautical terms and an imaginative attempt to describe their origin. These attempts bear no relationship to reality. Why not send in a few of your own. Jib Sheets : Named by a bosun, in Nelsons time, who compared the quality of the rope to bed clothes in a Gibraltar doss house. Mizzen Mast : Caused by confusion at English Harbour, Antigua, when a short sighted local talking to the captain of a ship of the line, mistook his ship to be a 2 masted vessels and said, "If you've got a 3 masted ship, you've got a mast missing!" King Post : When sailing ships transported Official letters to the empire they used to store the sacks close to the main deck support beams for increased stability. As the term Royal Mail had not yet been coined, the area became known as the King Post. Fore Deck : In the sixteenth century it was common practice for ships to have bow and stern castles. The purpose of these castles was to give the best advantage to the ships weapons (arrows). Each castle had many floors (decks) but for stability reasons four was considered to be the maximum. Hence the exposed deck at the front of the deck became known as the Four Deck. Tiller : In early times it was considered that a ship travelling through he water made a motion like a plough through the soil. The man who steered the plough was called the Tiller as that is what he did, and this name was applied to both the man and the steering device on the ships. HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR FINAL Saturday 8th October saw the top Helmsmen from the four major fleets in the Club assemble at Stansgate for the 'High Noon' of the season to decide the Marconi Sailing Club Helmsman of the Year 1988. Damian Boreham represented the Mirror Fleet, Mike Boreham was to have represented the Handicap Fleet but pulled out to be substituted by Mark Savill, Malcolm Gandy was the Solo Fleet representative and John Nickalls from the Catamarans. The contestants are the helms who achieve the most consistent performance throughout the season up to the end of September. Again this year the Sailing Sub-committee agreed to sail the Final in Lasers, arranged that each helm has a sail in each boat. Boats were provided by Mark Savill, Mark Strong, Derek Webb and Derek Holroyd. I would like to thank the owners on behalf of the Club and the Contestants for making the event possible. October 8th saw a Force 4-5 Westerly making life difficult. All except Malcolm Gandy had an involuntary swim to freshen themselves up and John Nickalls enjoyed it so much he kept going back for more. Either that or he was looking for the other hull! Malcolm and Mark had a close race with Mark getting line honours and Damian battling to a gallant 3rd. At this point, much to the disgust of the Race Officer, the combatants decided that gardening was much more fun on such a day and downed tools to come back another day. Needless to say Murphy's Law applied and as soon as the boats were put away the wind dropped to a benign 3. So episode 2 of this mind-warping suspense thriller was staged on 22nd October when the weather was Southerly 1-2 at most. Thanks to Graham Baker, Colin Willsmore and Debbie Yorston for rescue and race-box duties. John Nickalls jetted in from the States to participate but obviously had difficulty in adjusting to the time zone. Race 2 was easily won by Damian and we all thought that his skill combined with the lighter weather would make it his day. All apart from Mark Savill who won Race 3, which was a particularly well contested race. This made race 4 almost a formality but Mark came in first once more to confirm his status as 'Helm of the Year 1988' Helm - Race 1 P'n - Race 1 Pts - Race 2 P'n - Race 2 Pts - Race 3 P'n - Race 3 Pts - Race 4 P'n - Race 4 Pts - TOTAL Damian Boreham (Mirror) - 3 - 3 - 1 - ¾ - 3 - 3 - 2 - 2 - 8¾ Malcolm Gandy (Solo) - 2 - 2 - 3 - 3 - 2 - 2 - 3 - 3 - 10 Mark Savill (H/cap) - 1 - ¾ - 2 - 2 - 1 - ¾ - 1 - ¾ - 4¼ John Nickalls (Cat) - R - 5 - 4 - 4 - 4 - 4 - 4 - 4 - 17 Roger Smith

5. BRADWELL SAILING CENTRE Lucu (Boreham) and I spent a week at Bradwell Sailing Centre where we were trained and tested for our Level 5 (this now replaces Seamanship 2). However, we got a fun holiday out of it as well which you can see in the following write-up of our week there. MONDAY We arrived at the School about 10.45am having had some trouble finding the entrance. Lucy had arrived already and had managed to get hold of a room for just two. All the other dormitories in the girl's section were for four people and these were mainly taken up by the Basildon Swimming Club who were there on their week off from training At about 11.30 we all met in the TV room where the warden told us about the school and the rules about meals and the fact that the girls' rooms were out of bounds to the boys and vice versa! In the afternoon we all went out for a sail with the instructors in Wayfarers and Oysters. There was a strong breeze at first and we all sailed to Stone where the wind conveniently dropped totally, leaving us all to drift (or row) back with the tide. seTUESDAY Breakfast was at 8.15 and so by 9.30 we were all down at the boat-yard across the road to get our gear. Lucy and I were put in a Dayboat and left to get on with rigging a boat we'd never even heard of before, let alone sailed in. All the dinghies there are moored up on the water making rigging quite difficult as you have restricted space. Luckily, two boys who were also doing their Level 5 were on the next Dayboat and they had sailed in it the day before. This meant they would be able to tell us what to do if we could not work it out. However we did not have too much trouble and the only questions asked came from the bovs wanting to know how come we had ended up on the best Dayboat and why had they got stuck in the one that was the worst? There was barely any wind so we rowed out of the creek and drifted along with about four other boats. (Most of the Swimming Club had gone in the Toppers, canoes and sail boards.) We drifted about a bit and then had lunch after which a sea breeze came up and we sailed all the way out to sea just past Bench Head and back agair: in about a Force 4. WEDNESDAY Today was when Lucy and I really took our Test. We went through everything; sailing without a rudder (not as hard as it sounds), sailing without a centreboard, @sailing a triangular course, man-overboard drill, hove-to and sailing backwards. We managed everything except sailing backwards which we just could not master. What made it harder was that the sail has to be pushed out against the wind and as the wind had increased from a steady Force 4 to a strong 5 it became almost impossible to hold the sail out against the force of the wind. However we completed the other tasks without difficulty and with much more success than the two boys in the other Dayboat! All the people involved in the Level 5 testing had lunch (the others in the Toppers had eaten ages ago!) and we set off again to practise coming alongside and sailing a tight circle around the rescue boat. Both Lucy and I were now very cold and tired having fought the elements all day, and the boys were too. We were all sent ashore to swap round (Lucy and I were supposed to be showing the boys how to sail without a rudder, however the wind was too strong) and we just sailed all the way out towards sea, turned round and came back again. As we were nearing the entrance to the creek I heard several voices calling my name and I saw our very own Jack B motoring past with my family aboard and a couple of my brother's friends as well! I though they had come all the way just to see me but I was wrong, they had come to fetch 'A' mark after it had wandered downriver and been towed for safe keeping into Bradwell Marina. We moored up and went ashore very tired after a long day. CONTG :0::«:«

-..- Bradwell continued... THURSDAY The boys had been told, much to their relief, that they were not good enough, so now it was just Lucy and I doing the Level 5. We had spent all the previous evening poring over a chart of the river, phoning up Lucy's parents for the weather forecast and tides, and asking the advice of one of the instructors, working out where we would go for a day's cruise. We had worked it all out as a part of the Level 5 and set out, with one of the adults from the swimming group as ballast, in a Wayfarer expecting to have to actually go on the cruise, but we did not have to in the end which was a relief! During the morning we finally mastered sailing backwards as it was only a Force 3 breeze. By this time Lucy and I were sick of dinghy sailing, we both wanted to go in the Toppers as everyone else was really enjoying themselves so we were pleased when we were told that we could go in the Toppers in the afternoon. During lunch there waS a massive shaving-foam fight where everybody, including the instructors, got totally covered! After we had washed ourselves off in the water (which incidentally is not warm at all, despite the rumours!) we sailed about in the Toppers. The wind had steadily increased and was now a Force 4 - 5. This and the fact that there were not enough Toppers to go round meant that there were two people to each Topper. Everyone was capsizingall.round but Lucy and I stayed upright without much difficulty. That is until my helm (i.e. Lucy) slammed the tiller across too hard when tacking and we went straight into irons. I am not sure quite what happened yy (probably something my helm did) but the next thing I knew was that I was floundering in the freezing water while my helm had struggled over the top in an attempt at a dry capsize. However, while standing in triumph on the daggerboard it bent under her weight and she slipped off and fell into the water which saved me the job of pushing her in! By now we were thoroughly enjoying ourselves and were not too happy when everyone was told to come in because it was too windy. Reluctantly everyone packed up the Toppers which were towed back and we all walked back along the sea wall, back to a nice Silower. FRIDAY We woke up to what seemed a howling gale on Friday morning. The forecast was for a strong Force 6-7 and there was a gale warning until Sunday evening. On days like this the Bradwell 22s are used and so all of us rowed out and rigged these massive dinghies. As the name tells you they are 22' long and are built at the School's boat yard across the road from the school itself. They have the foredeck of a Wayfarer, a huge steel centreplate and four sails (two jibs, a mainsail and a mizzen), and are very sturdy and strong. Lucy and I ended up doing most of the rigging as the Instructor decided thar if we were good enough for Level 5 then we should do all the work. We motored OUw - each Bradwell 22 has am outboard engine for emergencies - and then began the struggle down towards Osea. In all my time on the river I do not think I have seen anything like it. The waves were enormous, there was spray everywhere and the wind was howling fiercely. The wind was so strong that even the Bradwell 22's were heeling (gasp!) and the Instructor heartened us by saying that one had even capsized before (double gasp! ) Apparently it took three people oan the centreplate as well as two on the skeg to stop it from turning turtle!!! Our destination was to be Osea Island, and although we enjoyed it at first, by the time we had been thrown about, continually soaked to the skin by the spray and been out in the freezing wind for ten minutes, we were all ready to go back. However, the powers-that-be in the nice warm cabin of the safety boat, with their cups of coffee, had other ideas! Tacking was an awkward affair. The centreboard case is just below waist height so getting over it was extremely difficult, and trying to control a flapping jib that was determined to catch itself on the other jib, the mast fittings and everything CON EG + 35.6

..-Bradweli continued... else, was almost impossible. In the end we worked out a system of two people either side of the centreboard case (one for each jib), and when we went about we just unwound the jib sheet from its bollard and handed it to the person on the other side. It got so windy that in the end all three boats took down their mainsails, (another job for Lucy and me) and just relied on the other three sails. When we got as far as Stone we beached, because our safety boat had spotted someone in trouble. Just off Osea we could see a dinghy on its side (hardly surprising) and our safety boat spent a good half an hour before they had even got the boat upright, and it took a long time then to tow it back. These two totally mad people had set out from Stone in this wind, which personally I thought rather stupid because if we had not been there, no-one would have been there to help them out and they could have ended up a lot worse than just spending a long while in the freezing water. Nobody could face turning out again, even for the short part of the trip just across to Osea as we had all slowly frozen up just sitting there cold and wet waiting for the safety boat to bring our lunches across. After lunch we back on a broad sailed reach. By now the sun had come out and because the wind was us, we all felt behind a lot warmer and everyone fell asleep, including the Instructor, apart from the four of us who were watching the jibs and the poor boy who got lumbered with helming. I do not think that I have ever enjoyed a hot shower as much as I did that day and wmI hope I do not get as cold as that ever again! SATURDAY As everyone had been so cold on Friday and the weather was still rough it was decided that we take the motor boats and go across to West Mersea. The ex-Liverpool class Lifeboat had broken down (sob!) so we all piled into three motor boats - one similar to Jack B but smaller; one similar to the work boat but bigger; and another that was a cross between the two. However the boat similar to Jack B broke down outside the Power Station which meant that those on board crammed into the other two boats which were already well loaded. We went up the river to West Mersea and were just working out where to moor up along the slipway when we ran aground on it. Local teenagers had struck up a good trade ferrying people from the shore to their Cruisers in huge tubs with engines and one had just zipped before us into our selected space and as we turned around we grounded on the slipway. It did not help when another lad came by in his boat and said "Don't hang around here or you'll go aground!" We all scrambled out and waded ashore to have lunch and spent part of the afternoon looking around before we motored back to the Sailing School. The broken-down boat had been repaired in time to come and collect us. On the last evening it is the tradition to march off to some woods nearby and have a Barbecue, but because it had been raining, the food had been pre-cooked and we took it into the recreation room to have our feast there. We all played silly games like passing waterbombs along a line from under chins etc. and needless to say it turned into a waterbomb and shaving foam fight that involved everybody - this of course took place outdoors so we did not make a mess! After we had washed and changed into dry clothes, most of us went to the TV room and watched TV until bedtime. SUNDAY Lucy and I left early to get back to MSC in time for racing. The others were due to be collected at 2pm so they went sailing again in the Bradwell 22s for the morning, so even on the last morning you get a sail. We thoroughly enjoyed out stay there, and you can just go for a week's sailing, without having to do a certificate. If you want to know anything else at all about the week, just come and ask me or Lucy. Jenny Ball

9. A TRIP TO ETAPLES If you are looking for somewhere different to explore why not try Etaples? We went there rather by accident, having been stuck in Boulogne by gales. Etaples is a fairly small French town situated on the River Canche some ten miles south of Boulogne. The entry must be made within an hour either side of high water because the Canche estuary dries out. It should also be made in fairly settled weather because fairly nasty seas can build up in the shallow water of the estuary. The entrance is very winding but is well marked by both buoys and marker posts. Normally you will see fishing boats which use the entrance and which provide a good guide to its location. Once established in the channel do not be put off by the line of breakers which appear to block your passge, the channel goes very close to the beach to avoid the shallow water. Having passed the breakers, one should stay as near as possible in mid-channel and certainly avoid going outside the marker posts as they mark the end of training walls which lead out at right angles to the shore. After this it is merely a matter of following the course of the river with Le Touquet and its airfield to starboard until you reach Etaples when further progress is barred by a low road bridge. Immediately before this bridge you will see a small marina where, provided you can obtain a berth on the outside pontoon, you will find enough water to stay afloat at low tide. Failing this it is possible to dry out against the quay taking care not to take up the positions used by the fishing boats. One quirk of the drying estuary is that all the tide seems to come in at Etaples in the two hours immediately prior to high tide and does so at a rate of up to five or six knots which is quite an experience. However the tide soon slackens off and you have plenty of time to reach the sea before the water starts to recede at any great rate. The town of Etaples itself is quite charming and well worth a visit, particularly so because it is off the normal yachting route and in fact most of the pilots do not recommend entry. One of the main features is a large fish market with a huge variety of fresh fish and shellfish for sale. This market is immediately underneath a fish restaurant which is reported to be excellent. The countryside behind the town is also quite pretty and is easily accessible especially if you carry bicycles on board. So, next time you are stuck in Boulogne with nowhere to go, why not give Etaples a thought. It is certainly worth a visit. Dave Beane (Rodrigon) THE LAST FLING - (Through the Eye of the Hurricane) Like most members of the Club intending to put in an appearance at the AGM, I was not impressed to wake up to a misty morning with no wind (I must remember to shut the bedroom windows!) However, the lure of the final race of the season was beckoning and I could not resist it. This 'Final Fling' was "arranged" by word of mouth at the previous Working Party so needless to say there were a lot of people who did not know about it. The plan was for a race, starting on the Hard and going around Osea. Start time was to be 10am giving time for a decent race before the AGM in he afternoon. The wind was about force 1.5 at the Club with the occasional gust of 1.500005 and the visibility was down to about 150 yards, but we were determined to start. By 9.30am the fleet consisted of Dave Payne and me, Graham Baker and Malcolm Gandy (providing the ballast) and Damian Boreham and Debbie Yorston in the 420. By 9.45 we had acquired one Mirror dinghy, Colin Wilsmore in his Solo, Maurice and Sarah Brill, Mick Jones and the Osprey. Spot on 10am Malcolm Stuart arrived. Lucy Boreham volunteered to be Race Officer and at 10.20 we started en masse from the Hard. the course was 2s, Osea s, Fs and finish by the scrubbing post after passing inside the mooring barge. The start was organised in PY order with the Mirror nearest to number 2. A mass start from the Hard means that the back boats have to go out a long way before they can tack towards the first mark, whilst those starting from the beach (those pebbles at the end of the Hard) could go straight on course. Dave and I were in a difficult position as we had kamikaze Jones next to us. Mick has a slight hearing problem which seems only to occur when I call starboard on him. He claims that I don't shout loud enough but nobody who knows me could possibly believe that! Mick gave us a chance by sailing single handed which meant that we out-accelerated him from the beach and were able to tack around the back of Jack B. contd...

10. (I am allowed to 'have a go' at Mick after he dumped 2 tons of cold water down my wetsuit when he took me for a ride on the trampoline of his Dart!) Malcolm Gandy had gone a funny purple colour when he put the trapeze belt on, and he and Graham decided on a leisurely start to give Dave and me a chance. "We don't need to worry about the course" quipped Graham, "as we will be close behind you and can follow you around." Who was he talking to? One of the Solos? The Mirror? No, Us! The fleet was fairly closely bunched as we rounded the corner into the bay. It was obvious that Malcolm Stuart, Colin Wilsmore and Damian were in for a close tussle as they sailed together in a tight group. The first tack took us into Mundon (Steeple?) creek and Dave and I seemed to have a commanding lead. We tacked to clear Mundon Spit and passed just in front of Graham and Malcolm, the Osprey, 2 Solos, a 420, 2 more Darts and the Mirror. So much for the commanding lead! We all short tacked up the shore to stay out of the falling tide in a gently dying wind. Our fourth tack took us across to Osea where a nice lift took us around the Island. By this time we could only see Graham and Malcolm in the Dart and even they were disappearing in the glow of a very low sun. Maybe Graham is now employing fighter tactics. Attack out of the sun so they don't see you coming. You have to get a little closer, Graham! The tack downwind was exceptionally boring with the hardest part being guessing where the wind was coming from. Sometimes it came from in front and sometimes from behind but there was so little as to make no difference. The tide was the main form of propulsion. The water behind Osea was crystal clear and we could see the bottom long before we reached the shallows. As we rounded the eastern end of Osea, the wind direction fluctuated wildly. First to a northerly, then easterly, then back to westerly. The latter was ideal as we were able to lay the finish on one tack from F Mark. As we finished the 3 Darts were all rounding the eastern end of Osea, followed too closely by the Osprey, with spinnaker in full bloom. The two Solos and the 420 were still battling it out close together. The Mirror had retired because of the lack of wind. The wind had now backed to south westerly and this meant that the fleet was forced to tack against the tide in very light winds. Graham and Malcolm finished second and Dave and I stood on the scrubbing post armed with the hose to give them a welcome, but they stayed craftily out of range. The Osprey and the other 2 Darts were in trouble and making no headway against the tide. Meanwhile the Solos crept towards the finish. Colin Wilsmore had the lead and was short tacking towards the finish as close to the shore as possible. About 10 yards off shore was a slight breeze and Malcolm Stuart sailed straight up this into the 3rd finisher spot. Was Colin sick! Damian and Debbie were the last boat to finish as the Osprey and the Darts retired. The result: Dave and I were first, beating Malcolm Stuart on handicap by 2 seconds. Colin Wilsmore finished 3rd. The 'Final Fling' is to become an Annual Event, complete with trophy, so make sure you all attend next year. Steve Keeble

5. RESCUE DRIVERS Roll up! Roll up!.... Once again the sailing season is upon us and it is time to think about planning and resourcing the Club's Rescue Services which, thankfully, have so far enabled our activities on the water to continue in relative safety and with the reassurance that assistance is near to hand. Whether one is venturing out for a tentative first try or is a hardened competitor, the knowledge that the Club is providing these services is a much welcomed aid to one's confidence. Last year the response to my ‘recruitment campaign' was first class, and has enabled me to establish a solid nucleus of experienced Rescue Boat Drivers. To enable us to provide an even better service this year, it will be necessary to recruit additional volunteers and organise further training sessions. Aside from providing a wider service - perhaps by having two boats out at a time - with sufficient manpower we will also be able to lessen the burden on the _ stalwarts who have provided the service to date. At present there are four boats which are used for rescue purposes and training: Jack B Baddow Star The Workboat The Fisherman Primarily we use Jack B, with Baddow Star as back-up. It is the Club's intention to complement the above with a fast inflatable in the near future. The communications are by CB and VHF, and although there is an increasing array of equipment, the maintenance is taken care of for us. All we have to do is drive the boats - although obviously there is a training programme to enable would-be drivers to attain the required level of competence. Further to this I intend to arrange some training in the correct use of the Communications Equipment and some First Aid sessions with the help of the St John Ambulance Brigade. It is envisaged these will be held both at the MASC and at Stansgate (more news on this in a later edition of Navigans.) We will also be sending some representatives to the Bradwell Field Studies Centre for specific training in handling rescue craft - although places are very limited. In a lighter vein, there will be the Annual Inter-club Rescue Boat Competition which last year served as an excellent opener to the Regatta. If anyone is interested in entering a team please let me know. Finally, if you haven't already, you will soon be receiving a copy of the Sailing Schedule. This once again promises to be an eventful mix of Opens, Regatta, Team Races and, of course, the East Coast Piers Race, not forgetting all the normal Points events. As a small Club the organisation of these events necessitates a great deal of work by a small number of people. Let's get things moving - IF YOU CAN HELP by driving or crewing a rescue boat, please contact me now! , Dave Onyons, Coxswain, Tel. 7. JURY RIG FROM ST PETER PORT Some of you know that Geoff Vines was unfortunate enough to lose the mast from Seabrume last Summer. He was entering the Big Russell between Sark and Herm and the wind was SW 5 when a lower port-hand shroud parted at the deck causing the mast to buckle at the cross trees and fall to starboard. The mast was recovered and Seabrume limped into St Peter Port under engine. Most of us would have put the boat into a yard at that stage and left it for the insurance company to sort out. There followed a period of several days of much telephoning and letter-writing when the extent of the damamge needed to be surveyed and negotiations with the insurance company started. By this time Mike Vines had joined his father and the decision was taken to set a jury rig and sail the boat back to the mainland. The boat would be much more accessible in Portsmouth than it would be in St Peter Port. The remains of the mast were cut in two and the upper portion rigged with cordage salvaged from the original rig and other bits and pieces which were on board. The genoa was rigged so that the foot was set to the improvised forestay and the peak led aft to the jib track with a sheet to the winch. The rig was evidently sound because Geoff and Mike arrived safely at Portsmouth having sailed across the Channel in 5's and 6's. Now Geoff Vines is a member of the RNSA and a fellow member had observed his activities in St Peter Port. It turned out that he left at about the same time as Mike and Geoff and was also headed for Portsmouth. The result of this coincidence was that Geoff's efforts and successful voyage back to Portsmouth had been monitored and Geoff was subsequently nominated for a seamanship award of the RNSA which was duly presented at a ceremony in January. I feel sure that the Club would wish to congratulate Geoff on his well deserved award. Incidentally the trophy, now in pride of place on Geoff's mantelpiece, is known as the Sex Pot. I have been repeatedly assured that it really is an award for seamanship. Seabrume is currently being repaired and fitted with a new mast and it looks very much as though Geoff will be in the water well before the rest of us for the 1989 Season. Dave Steward

COMMODORE'S NOTES m*oe. Last year Jack Pateman retired and the Club invited Martin Jay to became our President. For those who do not know Martin, he started sailing at the age of two with his grandfather in dinghies. In the 60's he owned various dinghies leading to a wooden Folkboat and an Iroquois Catamaran in the 70's. Since that time he has sailed extensively in the UK, France, Spain and the Mediterranean. 5. CAT CHAT THE PINOCCHIO TROPHY For those of you who didn't know, it was my 40th birthday in early January. As befitting such an august occasion I was treated to a surprise birthday party, cunningly arranged between my devious wife and that 'snake in the grass' Dave Payne. The Party, of which I had not the slightest inkling, was full of surprises, least of all being a package hand-franked 'Grafham Sailing Club'. On opening the package I found two small shields, one for me and one for Dave, engraved 'Pinnochio Trophy, 1st, 1.1.89' So what is the Pinocchio Trophy? Our story starts the previous week on Monday of the New Year. Along with Robin and Lisa; John and Caroline; Trevor and Christine; Tom and Mike Duckmanton; we dragged ourselves to Grafham to compete in the Grafham Grand Prix. Meanwhile Janet went to my mother's for the day. Dave and I were back home by early afternoon and about 6pm Janet rang me to find out how we had done. "We were up-wind of everybody right from the start. Trevor and Christine got close but were just behind; Paul Smith (a friend who sails a Hurricane) was about ten yards behind...." When Janet had finished talking to me, she rang Dave to sort out the surprise party. She also asked him about Grafham and he told her the same things as I had. From all of this Janet believed that we had won the Grand Prix, but was surprised to see that we had left the boat at Grafham. After intensive interrogation the following day, I finally admitted the truth. "There was no wind and racing was abandoned without the boat ever going in the water." But every word we had said was true. We were furthest to windward of all the boats waiting to launch; Trevor and Chris were next to us, but our bows were slightly ahead: Paul Smith was parked behind us, etc.... I didn't think any more about it until we received the trophies. The significance of the 'Pinocchio Trophy' was that Dave and I told the most believable pack of porky pies Janet had ever heard, and that she was completely taken in by our consistent stories. The 'Pinocchio Trophy' was her revenge. It has pride of place on the shelf amongst all of her genuine trophies. Steeve Keeble, Fly-by-Wire. CAT CHAT Captain Keeble on his yacht, found his crew a Payne So decided, singlehanded, to sail his Hurricane Said Steve, "I'll follow Chichester and Chay I'll sail both Capes and Roaring 40's on the way." Preparation over, dawned the long-awaited day To see our Steve afloat, and safely on his way. A man whose name was Hobie shouted same advice "If your mast fills up with water, send for us in a trice." The sail progressed quite smoothly when alas, alack and zap The compass, map and sextant fell from poor Stevie's lap As if this was not enough for any man to face, A Tornado had been forecast, Stampede-ing at a pace. "Oh, Dave. Oh, Dave, Where are you? Wish you were here with me. There's Shearwater everywhere, just me the boat and sea." No Spark of inspiration, No 'A' Class thoughts were there, Nacred into the bargain, Steve started to despair. Just then a gust filled the sail right to overflowing. He Catapulted in the air, oh where , oh where's he going? He Darted here, he Darted there, but to no avail, He lost all his provisions, 'cept for same olde tyme ale. They found poor Steven later upon a desert isle, Alone, shipwrecked and legless, but still he had a smile. The moral of this story, if to sailing you aspire, Don't take your 'cat' to sea alone, takes two to FLY BY WIRE. Christine Milton, Cat Fleet

en SAILING IN SAFETY _ About this time last year Malcolm Stuart wrote an article for Navigans on Sailing in Rough Weather. The article is reproduced here as advice to new members and a reminder to existing ones. Malcolm's notes are mainly directed towards racing, but much of the advice is relevant to non-racers as well. Adrian Wright also offers Similar advice to Salboarders (see Page 8). Do remember at all times that, although the sun may be keeping things warm ashore at this time of year, the water is still very cold, and this could put life in danger for the sailor who is in the water too long. If you are inexperienced, do let saneone ashore (e.g. a friend or the OOD) know that you are going out. The moral is: Get out there and enjoy your sailing but do make sure that you and your boat are properly kitted out and that the conditions are suitable for your own level of experience. SAILING IN ROUGH WEATHER In the spring and autumn at Stansgate we frequently experience strong winds and when these blow against the tide we can get very choppy and confused water, particularly between Stansgate Point and Osea Pier: In such circumstances the Race Officer, the OOD and all members who have turned up to race will be faced with a decision. Firstly, irrespective of what the Race Officer decides, members remain responsible for their personal safety and should not sail if they judge the conditions to be well beyond their present level of competence. The Race Officer will, in reaching his decision, assume that members have considered the weather conditions and have reached the decision that they can survive them when they sign on. The Race Officer's job is therefore not that of deciding what is suitable for the least experienced and worst equipped member, but only that of deciding whether or not it is safe to start a race for the more experienced members. We must recognise here that the only way of getting experience of sailing in rough conditions is to get out and do it and we are only going to improve our skills by pushing ourselves a little. The Race Officer has therefore to make the difficult judgement on how far to let those who sign on for a race push themselves. In circumstances such as this the Race Officer will consult with the duty Coxswain, the Fleet Captains and the OOD. Any course set for racing must take account of the ability of the rescue facilities available on the day to recover crews who may get into trouble. He may therefore restrict sailing to the shorter courses, and faster boats like the Catamarans will have to put up with having their wings clipped. — The ultimate authority for all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of Club Members is the OOD, however in practice he will normally only exercise this authority in response to a request from the Race Officer for guidance, and would in any case take any decision affecting racing after consultation with the Race Officer. To summarise what is a cautious justification of racing in conditions that pramnpt thoughts of more canfortable hobbies: 1. Competitors must decide themselves whether or not they are competent to go out in rough weather. 2. The Race Officer must consult the duty Coxswain, Fleet Captains and OOD and set a suitable course or postpone until such time as a suitable course can be set. 3s If these two points have been properly addressed, then racing will only be abandoned in the most extreme conditions, or in the absence of rescue cover.

GATE LOCK Though the Gate Lock broke down completely on 7th May (design fault), it is hoped it will be repaired by the time you read this. When it is back in action the following accumulation of knowledge might be useful to help prevent difficulty in operating the lock: 1. Make sure the gate is firmly shut hame before you begin, and avoid pulling, pushing or leaning on the gate in any way while you are operating the lock. 2. Insert key fully -= and remove it in one continuous motion, (ensure that the key cames to a stop against the reader frame before removing it). 3. Listen for the distinctive sound of a 'click' from the lock mechanism, which will tell you the lock has operated, allowing you to open the gate. (This is more useful sometimes than looking for the green light which can be difficult to see in strong sunlight.) 4. If the lock fails to operate at the first attempt, wait a short time before inserting the key again. (The instructions with the keys say: Do not insert the key into the reader if the red light is on - which is probably saying the same thing.) Ed.

SAILBOARD NEWS May Bank Holiday Series Congratulations to Greg Goodrum, one of our new members, who was the outright winner of this 4 race event, beating dinghies, catamarans and the rest of the Sailboarders with positions (after handicapping) of 1,2,5, and 2. John Smith also did well with two firsts out of two sailed - good job for the rest of us that he has to work in the mornings! These races did raise the question of the correct rules we should be using when racing, especially regarding "pumping". The problem is that whilst pumping is allowed for any type of funboard racing, it does seem fairer to restrict boards to the same rules as dinghies when racing against them. After a (very amicable) protest the decision was made that in future, in mixed class racing, pumping is bannned. It was prompted by Malcolm Stuart's rather serious article in the last Navigans about safety and the responsibilities of the inidvidual, the Race Officer and the OOD. What Malcolm said was absolutely spot on, but don't let the serious side of officialdam spoil the fun you can have if you are Race Officer. The Race Officer has the ideal opportunity to get his own back on all of his rivals, both within the Fleet or in other Fleets. What is a good course for one Fleet can be a B...... awful course for somebody else. So - if you are Race Officer, what must you consider when setting the courses: The relative speed of the Fleets. Obdviously the Cat Fleet proceeds around the course at approximately twice the speed of the Mirror Fleet, (difference in PY numbers indicates this), but that is not always the case. If there is an average wind and a strong tide, then the speed differential between the fast and slow boats will increase. e.g. If the tide is 3 knots and the Mirrors can only do 5 knots then their speed will vary between 8 and 2 knots, depending whether they are sailing with or against the tide. (In fact the boat speed will vary also with the tack of the boat, but for the purpose of this explanation we have taken a fixed speed). If a Cat can do 10 knots then its speed will vary between 7 and 13 knots depending on the angle to the tide. The ratio is now not 2:1 between the Fieets. contd....

6. This example highlights that a course with legs into the tide favours the Cat Fleet (ratio 3.5:1), but that a course with lots of down-tide legs favours the slower boat (ratio 1.625:1). Unfortunately life is not this simple, as courses are a combination of up, down and across tide legs, and boats vary their speed with the legs of the course. So that it is at best an indication that strong tides favour fast boats. However, light winds favour slow boats. If a fast boat is stationary for any length of time then it has to make up that time on the slower boats by the ratio of their PY numbers. However, if the Race Officer shortens the course, the fast boat will find it almost impossible to make up the time. e.g. If the Fleet is windless for twenty minutes at the start of the race, and the race is shortened to one hour, then the Cats need to make up that 20 minutes (times the difference in PY) plus the difference in PY for the forty minutes sailed. This means that a Hurricane would need to beat a Mirror by approximately 55 minutes in 40 minutes of sailing! Time ticks faster for fast boats when there is no wind. But then again, a dying wind favours the fast boats and a strengthening wind favours the slow boats, for obvious reasons. Having disposed of the impact of the wind and tide, let us consider the sea state. Flat water favours the boat with the least wetted area, as there is less friction with the water. This is why it is important to lift the stern going upwind, and to plane with the bows clear going downwind. If you look at the record-breaking Windsurfers, they are designed to have minimal wetted area when planing downwind. I have heard quotes of as little as 200 sq cm being in contact at any one time. That is about 2/3 of the sole of your foot! As the waves become steeper and the wave tops closer, then the longer boats are favoured, as they do not dip into the thoughts as much. If the distance between the waves is 12 feet, then a Mirror will fall into every trough, but an 18-foot Cat will generally ride across the peaks. The hull shape also is impacted (just the word) by the waves. A pointed bow will cut through the waves, whereas a flat bow will slam and slow the boat down. A flared bow will lift the boat over the waves, whereas a sharp bow will tend to nosedive into the face of the wave. The final part of the equation is the characteristics of the boats themselves. Monohulls can tack more quickly than Cats, so a course that requires a lot of tacking favours a monohull. Trapeze boats are favoured by long legs in strong winds as the crew expends less effort in keeping the boat upright. High aspect ratio sails are favoured in light winds, but can be difficult to manage in strong winds. Fully battened sails are favoured in light winds as they hold their shape better. Spinnakers are favoured in light winds as they provide extra drive. So where does this bring the fun into being Race Officer? Well, it depends on your point of view. If you hate the Cat Fleet you set a course with lots of tacking. If you hate the Mirrors the course has legs into the tide or the waves, etc. However if you want to set good courses, then the Cats want long legs in good winds and the tide can generally be ignored. The Mirrors want legs where the tide assists them to the next mark and where they are out of the waves. The Solos want similar courses to the Mirrors but with less emphasis on avoiding all of the tide; while with the Handicap Fleet you pays your money..... The Windsurfers prefer to avoid downwind legs in steep waves. Setting courses can really be fun, especially in Club racing where the Fleets can be given courses suitable to them individually. It only becomes difficult in a Handicap race where the boats are mixed. One other thing, some helms/crews have poor memories, so you can always send them around odd-shaped courses to further confuse them. Sailing the same old courses, week in week out, becomes very boring! I love it when my turn for Race Officer comes around. I like to see the Fleets work, so the courses are always unusual. I look forward to seeing what courses you set. Steeve Keeble, Cat Fleet

NEW RACING RULES Every four years the International Yacht Racing Union revises the Racing Rules. The last changes in 1985 were mainly to clarify the existing rules, this year however the changes will affect every sailor. These new rules came into effect on lst May this year. A brief description of the rule changes that effect yachts at this club is’ given below. The new RYA rule book (YR1/89) should be consulted for a more detailed and definitive description of the rules. Rule 4.1 The individual recall signal is now the display of the 'X' flag instead of lowering the class flag to the dip. Rule 5.4(c) The Race Committee may now abandon or cancel a race when it considers that to continue would be unfair, even if this has come about due to a change in the weather conditions. Rule 25 This rule, which defines the sizes of class insignia and sail numbers, has been changed but will only apply to sails made after lst January 1989. Rule 26 Advertising and Sponsorships: This rule has been rewritten. A further description of this rule and how it will affect this Club will be given in a future edition of Navigans. Rule 32 Avoiding Collisions: The change to this rule has put a new obligation on the Protest Committee when serious damage has occurred. The Protest Committee MUST now penalise the right-of-way yacht if it finds that the right-of-way yacht had the opportunity but failed to make a reasonable attempt to avoid the collision. Rule 42.3(c) This rule which was about luffing another boat the wrong side of a mark has been deleted. For a boat to be allowed to luff another boat the wrong side of a mark, the leeward boat must have luffing rights and the leading boat must not be about to round the mark. Rule 43.2 When two yachts are approaching an obstruction close-hauled on starboard tack, and the yacht to leeward or ahead needs room to tack and hails the other yacht for roan to tack; if the other yacht shouts "you tack” and the yacht requiring water tacks - under the old rules the hailed yacht (on starboard tack) had to 'keep clear' - now she simply has to give room for the hailing yacht (on port tack) 'to tack and clear (the starboard tack yacht.)' Rules 45, 52 and 51.2 A yacht is now required NOT to touch a mark, this was not actually specified before. If a yacht does however touch a mark, the standard exoneration procedure has changed from re-rounding to doing a 720° turn. The offending yacht is required to sail well clear of other yachts to do the 720 as soon as possible after hitting the mark. Rule 54 The ‘pumping and rocking rule has been reworded and a definition of sailing added. Ooching (sudden movement of the body forward or aft) is now always prohibited. When roll tacking or gybing the mast must now not move away from the vertical more than Contd

Racing Rules (continued) once. A Protest Committee may now disqualify a yacht for infringing rule 54 without a hearing, although if one is requested by the yacht, one must be given. Rule 68.4(b) Protest flags. If after a collision oe of the yachts involved displays a protest flag but does not subsequently lodge a protest, a third yacht having witnessed the collision may lodge a protest even though she herself did not display a flag. Appendix 3 The 720 rule has been rewritten such that a yacht that infringes a rule in the preparatory period must take the penalty as soon as possible after the infringement, instead of waiting for the starting signal.
