Maldon) of the site; these boats need to be moved into the dinghy park so that the grass can be cut ready for the various camping days.SO PLEASE would the owners move their boats into the dinghy park URGENTLY. On the racing side, the nice weather of the Easter Series was followed by winds of Force 4-5 for Spring Points 1 and 2, making the water very choppy. The weather and wind has been sometimes hard, sometimes light since then and we've had some interesting racés. Jenny Ball (my usual crew) borrowed my boat LARS TINN to sail a couple of single-handed races whilst I borrowed Damian's boat BUMBLE. James Brill has joined us on the water as has Jenny's brother David Ball; also with us has peen Ben Hoiroyd and Paul Mander. The good weather is with us now so come and join us and make the most of the sunshine. your Mirror Scribe Lucy Boreham On the record - but off the wire ! ed During the May Day Bank Holiday Handicap Series, Richard Willmot ‘slipped his leash' on the trapeze of Graham Baker's Dart and plopped into the water. Rumour has it that Graham sailed on all unknowing and engaged in lonely conversation with himself that is the hallmark of those who choose to sail solo. Having finally realised he had lost the 'helmsman's best friend', Graham returned to pick up his errant crew and, all now safely gathered in, continued the race and no doubt wondered whether ‘the rules' would have allowed him to finish without the company of his companion-in-arms. I can certainly ‘feel' for Richard since, many years ago, I did the self-same things whilst crewing in Suva harbour. The problem was that I fell off just a few yards short of the finishing line; I still held the rather Tong length of jib sheet and was dragged over the line mindful of the fact that, very occassionally, (small) sharks were to be seen in the harbour. I must admit I got back in fairly sharpish. The above reminiscence was sparked off by a snippet in The Times which reports that the Royal Naval Sailing Association (organisers of the Whitbread Round the World race) has apparently decreed that any boat finishing without having picked up, ‘dead or alive', a crew member who has been swept overboard will be disqualified. Time was when such a boat wold have been generally expected to respectfully retire but obviously times have changed. However, the mind boggles at such a situation; does a disqualified yacht appeal against the Race committee ? what comes first, the coroner's inquest or the race committee meeting ? Could a helm, having lost his crew ‘dead or alive’ in an inland reservoir race, wait for an uncomfortable race committee to disqualify him (unlikely to be a ‘her' I’think) if he chooses not to retire ? I must admit that when avidly reading the descriptions of the Round the World races I've never considered the terrible dilemma facing skipper and organisers - it makes you think. MPB

It is with deep regret that the Club has learned of the recent deaths of Roger Smith's wife Wendy and of Eric Royle. On behalf of all the Club, I would like to offer our sympathy and condolences to Roger and his daughter Caroline; and to Eric's wife Wendy, his son Julian, daughter Sally, and to all their families and friends. Their warmth and friendship will be greatly missed within the Club. COMMODORE 'S NOTES Regatta. What can I say? The sun shone; the weather was dry and warm; there was a magnificent amount of help and support from within the Club; we didn't even seem to have a last minute panic to find Spotters. Even the sailing was reasonable - although I can probably hear those who wished for more wind on the Monday - but because of the fantastic degree of co-operation we still managed two Races that day. The additional race arranged very quickly by the Cat Fleet provided both amusement and same very much needed light relief during the frustrating wait for wind. In view of the vast amount of help received, I would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who helped in any form to make it such a success. I would also like to thank Malcolm Stuart on everyone's behalf for taking on the not inconsiderable co-ordination role and for overseeing all the individual effort. The only blot on the horizon was the Water Supply. After struggling for many years at events like these to dispose of the Waste (before installing the new sewage disposal system), we now see that the Supply is insufficient. I would like to thank you all for co-operating with the crash action that had to be taken and can oly apologise for the necessity to supply only cold showers. However, this did reduce the consumption sufficiently to keep both the toilets and Galley supplied with water, and I promise that by the start of the next Season we will have a much improved Water Supply, and in the meantime every attempt will be made to reduce the problem for the camping weeks and the East Coast Piers Race. We also have the MIDSUMMER PARTY on SATURDAY 29TH JULY, another attraction arranged by the Social Committee which promises to be an enjoyable event. Finally, I would like to express my thanks again to all who helped at the Regatta. N.T. Pembleton, Commodore

7. MAYDAY AT MAPLIN The omens were bad from the start. The bank holiday cruise was for at least a week to posh places - and I'd forgotten my shaver. As is well known, it is almost impossible to get bits of rope like moorings, painters, etc. hooked up around a saildrive with folding prop; and we managed to avoid this, but a deep spade rudder and shallow skeg can be lethal for mooring buoys which are too buoyant to depress to free. It was freezing cold in swimtrunks battling with the buoy and the elements, and in the end it was a knife job. We motored down to a mooring in Bradwell Creek which seemed preferable to bouncing about on the Club moorings, so at least the first night was OK. Next morning we rejoined the fleet near the Bench Head Buoy for the beat to the Spitway. Once through the Spitway it was a more-or-less dead run in the direction of the Medway and Thames, but the wind reduction hoped for when everything was going the same way was not very obvious. I had chosen my largest Genoa (a lightweight cloth) for the season and once on the headfoil this was not likely to be changed as the joins in the foil luff groove were no longer perfectly aligned. In order to protect the nearly new lightweight cloth I decided to use the main only and make a series of donwind tacks after controlled gybes. The conditions were such that it could easily be described, after a few drinks at any Club bar, as a Yachtsman's Gale but realistically it was only a good Force 5. My crew on this occasion was the better half, who now sails only against medical advice due to an assortment of mechanical problems. This meant I could not leave the tiller in such conditions and no way would I trust the Autohelm. My previous practical experiences have included strong wind and an uncontrolled gybe and, yes, it does bring the mast and supplementary gear down to deck level. Apart from the occasional change of tack when the echo sounder suggested it, the only other excitement was the antics of the Avon being towed astern. The three main modes of behaviour were: steadily filling up with water and acting as a good sea anchor if only the painter glue joint holds; upside down; and airborne, attempting a fly-past. Nevertheless there was no apprehension and the use of harnesses or the washboard to shut up shop was never considered. Anyway, at this rate, it would soon be peaceful again. The conditions were modest compared to a never-to-be-forgotten incident, surfing in on enormous breaking waves some years ago in Holland, when precise rudder control and hence my ability to take the seas just slightly on the quarter (Cape Horn style, never dead square,) left me with 100% confidence in the underwater details of my boat. At the Maplin Bell Cardinal I gybed for a port tack about due south. The echo sounder, mostly on 10' flashed 8' a couple of times, but the alarm set for 7' (twice our draft) was not sounding. The waves were looking nasty and we were rising and falling more than the 2' indicated by the echo sounder. Then it happened. About three horrendous crashes. Nothing else occurred to me other than that we were aground on sand as hard as concrete and no boat would take that for more than a minute or two in such waves. The fact that I spotted the remains of the rudder astern and the crashes had ceased should have told me we were still travelling forward, but I'd lifted the engine hatch and saw water coming in from the direction of the transom. The Prospect has many attributes, that's why I chose her. Among them are the inner mouldings in the hull and topsides; super for insulation, but it does mean that it contd....

MAYDAY contd... 8. takes a lot more than lifting the berth cushions to see the inside of the hull and confirm the presence of keels - or otherwise. Frantic activity inside while upside down, attempting to evaluate the problem, also caused seasickness and I subsequently abandoned the task to despatch what must have been an unusual Mayday format. My brain had just about managed to work out that if we were breaking up and about to sink, the rest of the fleet could not approach us in such seas, and taking to the Avon would have been difficult for me and impossible for Joyce. With hindsight I'd probably do the same things again, as to delay until it was too late could have been an even greater mistake. The crisis lasted about 10 seconds, but I managed to pad it out for a couple of minutes. Derek Hall of 'Staggers', with a calmer appraisal suspended the 'Mayday' action until the need was confirmed and since we were still afloat and not aground, he managed to carry out a difficult tow to Thames Haven Yacht Club, where I could dry out and assess the damage and temporary repairs necessary. Many thanks once again to Derek and also to Peter Bloomfield for standing by. The plywood, saws, drills, clamps, Isopon paste etc. were ordered from home, promptly delivered and after a night-shift duty spent sitting and lying in the mud, 'Tekin Two' returned to base the following Monday. A new rudder is required; the hull/transom join requires a complete new section; the port bilge keel needs rebedding and tightening up; but it could have been a lot worse. The sounder was used for a survey of the area on the return trip, without result. I have not learnt anything from the incident I didn't know before and I am still uncertain about the possibility of a large log in the water, or some similar obstruction. In a sudden crisis, time is vital for major decisions, 10 seconds or even a couple of minutes are inadequate unless you have all the facts. I have been once before adrift without any form of control or propulsion. The elements were the worst ever recorded in the area, anna domini was not a factor in September 1951, and I had 9 full days (and, worse still, nights) to consider the only variable, for all the use it was. This long-ago incident does throw up some analogies for the small boat scene, so I pass them on for what they are worth: 1. Once out of control, ships and boats are beam-on to the seas and that's the worst attitude. 2. Roll angles of over 90° (over 45° heel) can occur and can never be got used to. 3. Revise your Physics. The future depends on the relative positions of the ship's (and its cargo) centre of gravity and its centre of buoyancy, which is called the Metacentre.* 4. Always have a large reserve of fuel on board for long trips, in bad weather it is possible to use it all up with no progress over the land. 5. The last 10-15% of fuel in a low tank is generally unuseable, sediment and sludge on the bottom become disturbed and that's your lot. contd....

9. MAYDAY contd... 6. Never rely on outside help in extreme conditions, sometimes even aeroplanes can take days finding you. 7. Oil on troubled waters, sea anchors, even lifeboats (if they are still in the davits) are useless, they are only for story books. A small boat sailor may try a sea anchor from the bow if he's not too paralyzed to move. See, I've experienced all that and I still don't know what happened! Here's to the next time, Father Neptune. Ron Phillips, Tekin Two. Ed's Note - I believe there is an automatic membership of an Association for people who have used a parachute to save their lives. I wonder if an equivalent group for those who have ever been rescued as a result of a Mayday call would be very popular. Perhaps the numbers qualifying would be too great. Or would those eligible very much prefer to keep their heads down and not take part in an annual get-together when hair-raising yarns could be swapped! * The following from the Oxford Companion to Ships and the Sea: Metacentre. The point of intersection of a vertical line, in relation to the ship's structure, drawn through the centre of gravity of a ship when she is lying upright and a vertical line drawn through the centre of buoyancy when the ship is heeled. To make certain that a ship is stable so that a righting moment comes into play when she is heeled, the metacentre must be above the centre of gravity. 100 CLUB DRAW Dave Harper won the £50 prize and Malcolm Yeoman won the £5 prize in the June Draw.

We all look forward to your frequent participation in Sunday racing. Two of our boats will be travelling abroad soon to take part in the round Texel race. With a little improvement we could have, for instance, class racing for Darts alone without all that messing with handicap numbers. So if you know of another Catamaran owner who likes to race, bring him along. And all you new members, don't be nervous about joining in, it's the quickest way to polish your act. 4. SAILBOARD NEWS 1. Seavets Event, 24th June This proved very successful with 34 competitors taking part, and ages ranged from 35 to 78! Four races were sailed and a great deal learnt by all concerned about the organisation of such an event. Over £200 was raised for the charity 'Research Into Ageing'. Ian Crumpen must be praised for obtaining so much pre-publicity, and together with his father, Joe, for operating 'Kingfisher' as a Rescue Boat-cum-TV platform - many thanks to both of them. Nigel James' help was invaluable in organising the food; producing superb recording forms; registering entrants; and running the Race Box. (Any complaints about the start of the 3rd race to me - I'm not very sure about all those flags - very confusing!) Guy Chevenix-Trench, the sponsor, provided Les who worked hard all day, as well as prizes and a trophy to be competed for on an annual basis. My thanks also to Bob Leeder, Graham Baker, Malcolm Stuart, Jean Flook, Lee Tridini and Barry Marke, all of whom helped make the day go very well. (Anyone I've omitted - kick me when you see me). 2. Board Identification The Seavets event did make apparent to me the reason for the increasing number of complaints we have been getting about identifying Sailboard race competitors. There seems to be one effective solution - sails must be clearly marked with a number on both sides. Please can those who race, or intend to do so, set about this as soon as possible. For the purpose of internal Club racing it doesn't matter what letters/numbers are used - the only rule is that no two can be the same! I will compile a list of existing Sailboarders and numbers and place a copy on the Club notice board opposite th signing-on counter. Please let me know of any additions. If you wish to get an official RYA 'K' number, you will need to pay £12 per annum for membership of the RYA, and this will also provide 50% off 'Boards' magazine and free third party insurance. Phone the RYA (0703 629962) to obtain a registration form. 3. Class Flag Racing sailors should note that the Sailboard class flag has changed to 'O'. The reason is that the previous 'K' was too similar to the Catamaran class flag. 'O' is a diagonally halved, red above yellow, flag (and also signifies 'man overboard' - not entirely inappropriate!) Adrian Wright

5. CATAMARAN NEWS Recollections of the last weeks seem to be a haze of hot sunshine and sparkling waters. Can you remember a time when you had to take so much care to protect against the sun? So hurry along with your orders, remember, all proceeds to Charity. Your Catamaran Correspondent, Peter Flook CAT FLEET NEWS - ROUND TEXEL AND ALL THAT Whoops! Someone in the Hurricane Fleet really stood on Peter Flook's toes by the sound of it. A pity to see a petty personal disagreement brought to Navigans though. A third Marconi Cat went to Texel and in spite of being forgotten in the "well-wishes" list, it was Hurricane 101 'Flying Colours' that put Marconi SC high in the honours list. Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton crossed the line 5th behind the 'Specials'; were first production boat to finish and when the prizegiving was finally held at 12 noon on Sunday, were placed second overall from 950 starters. Texel is the first Friesian Island off the North coast of Holland, is only 3 miles from Den Helder on the mainland at its southernmost point, and is served by a good, if not expensive, ferry service. The event started some 12 years ago when 5 boats challenged each other to a race around the Island on Catamarans. From there it quickly escalated. In 1980 there were 410 Cats in two starts. Now the format is for one mass start. 1988 saw 870, and this year a massive 950, to race the 100 kilometres - 60 miles - around the Island. The biggest Cat Race in the world without doubt.

6. Round Texel contd... The island is long and thin, surrounded by shallow water and shifting sand banks. The western shore is straight, runs approximately North-South, and has long, sandy beaches pounded by the North Sea surf. At the top of the Island is a lighthouse at the entrance to the sound between Texel and the next Island, Vlieland. Here the water is very shallow but with a very strong current. As the shore curves around the back of the Island, the course follows a line of withies eastward same 15 miles to the 'VC' buoy, where the Cats turn southward to close the shore again about one-third down. The water is too shallow to navigate inside the line of withies. From here to the bottom of the Island the shoreline is very much like the edge of the Blackwater, marshy, but like everywhere else in Holland, backed by a sloping dyke or sea wall. The course then goes back up the western shoreline to the finish about half-way along at Strand 17. The organisation is superb. On arrival at the beach road, competitors are marshalled on to a hardstanding area where trail©&TMS are unhitched from the cars and immediately picked up by oe of a fleet of 20 tractors, to be towed along the beach where each class has its own area. When you are ready to leave the beach you simply queue a few minutes at the marshalling point for a tractor and direct it to your trailer. The start line is between two huge trawlers and is over a mile long. At the ten, five and start signals a helicopter flies along the line with white, blue and red smoke respectively to complement the signals from the Cammitttee boat. There are no general recalls. With strategically placed video cameras at both ends, and in the air, they get your number. The weather was glorious with a breeze of around 12 to 15 knots from the north-east, which meant that everybody started om the same tack of the close fetch up to the lighthouse. This drastically reduced collisions compared with last year's event, but the start was delayed for 1 hour because the wind was holding the tide out around the top of the Island, across the shallow sands between Texel and Vlieland. Most of the Hurricanes and faster boats started at the outer end of the line, which had a slightly favourable bias. From here these crews were able to twin trapeze immediately. showing amongst the early leaders was Rob White and Jeremy Newnan while 100 yards to weather, Robin Smith & Lisa Gatton tailed the Dutch team of the Hoekstra brothers. Slightly further ahead the Hurricane Turbo with wing mast and new extra-long racks sailed by Reg White and Steve Olle was doing battle with the giant Roberts 27s. ew Towards the lighthouse a number of singlehanded 'A' classes, Hurricanes and Tornadoes, that had started further inshore, found a band of stronger wind just off the surf line, and these boats led around the light to start the beat across the top of the Island. Robert White and Robin Gnith steadily worked their way through the pack, and in fact passed the Roberts 27s when they ran aground near the 'VC' buoy. Robin & Lisa were the first Hurricane round the mark on to the long downwind leg behind the Island, in 5th place behind 3 'A's, a French Formulae 20 and a Tornado. Down the back of the Island Robin & Lisa overtook two of the 'A's, the Formulae 20 and the Tornado, but were in turn passed by the faster 'Specials', the Roberts 27s and the Hurricane Turbo, when they hoisted their huge spinnakers. At the bottom of the Island Robin & Lisa started the twin trapeze beam reach back to the finish same mile behind the leading 'A'; and with helicopters clattering overhead and chase boats to leeward, ‘Flying Colours' was pushed to the limit as the gap was reduced. But at the line the 'A' Class was still 50 yards ahead. A few moments earlier, Reg White &

Round Texel contd... 7. Steve Olle had crossed in 2nd place after their spinnaker had exploded while just leading a Roberts 27 to the line for line honours. Some 2 hours later, between 4.30 and 5.00 pm, some 500 boats crossed the 100-yard-long finish line. Even with video cameras running at both ends, the Race Committee had a major headache and at 11.30pm announced that the prizegiving was delayed until 12 noon on Sunday. The results were worth waiting for. Robin & Lisa were 2nd overall, just over 4 minutes behind the A Class on corrected time. Third place was a Nacra S.S. There were 4 Hurricanes in the top 11 boats, the next British boat being Robert White & Jeremy Newman. Other Marconi Positions: Trevor Milton & Rob Stahl - Dart 20 - 123rd Paul Ellis - Dart 15 - 204th Steeve Keeble & Dave Payne - Hurricane - 238th HURRICANE EUROPEANS OUD NARDEN - HOLLAND 17 - 18 JUNE Just one week after the Round Texel Race, Robin Smith & Lisa Gatton beat the best in Europe to win the Hurricane Europeans, and became Marconi Sailing Club's first European Champions of 1989 with 'Flying Colours' Racing took place on the 'Gooimeer', 10 miles east of Amsterdam, and to the south of the new town of Arlmere. The huge waterway, once part of the Zuider Zee, is renowned for its unpredictable windshifts and is also very shallow with the occasional drifting reed bed. The Dutch Hoeksbra brothers were out for revenge after being beaten the previous weekend by Robin & Lisa in the Round Texel, but the Marconi duo sailed a very consistent series, with one first place, two seconds, a third and a fourth position, to accumulate 11.7 points to the Hoeksbra's 17.0 points in second position. Third place was Robert White & Huub Lambrieks. Steve Keeble & Dave Payne did not disgrace themselves with a 28th in their first European Championship, especially when Dave returned home to find out he had one broken rib and two cracked, caused when the boat hit him while launching through the surf at Texel. (We thought the Grolsch at 28p a bottle might have something to do with it....) Robin Smith, 'Flying Colours' CONGRATULATIONS... belatedly to Yvonne and John Weatherley on the birth of their first grandchild, Matthew, born on 8th April 1989. I'm sure it won't be too long before Matthew has his first sail in 'Viridia'.

The Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championship. (Through the Eye of the Hurricane) This event is held annually at Stone Sailing Club and consists of a number of different races. On day one, there is the Stone Dinghy Challenge, which is effectively a practice race for the following series, followed by the first race of the championship proper. Day 2 has the rest of the championship and is followed by the "Cock o' the River" race. This last race is a pursuit event between all of the class winners in the championship event. Many years ago, the two premier sailing events on the Blackwater were the Marconi Regatta and the Blackwater and Colne championship. However, in recent years the Stone event has seen a falling off of entries, although a revival is taking place. It was disappointing to see so few entries from Marconi, although I do not believe that we had any entrants at all in recent years. This year, the Marconi fleet provided entrants in the Cat Menagerie andw the Laser fleets. Mark Savill was our sole entrant in the Laser fleet and despite some excellent and consistent sailing was unlucky to place only third. Mark scored two second places and a forth out of the three races but was beaten by a first, second and DNS by the winner, and a first, third and fifth by the eventual second overall. That is close racing by any standards, and I am sure that we will see Mark amongst the pots ( and not just beer and toilet) in the very near future. Well done Mark! The Cat fleet was represented by Fleet Captain, John Nickalls accompanied by the ever blushing Caroline (It's not often that a good looking young lady gropes my thigh under the table!); Current European Hurricane Champions Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton, myself (wearing the loudest trousers in the competition) crewed most ably by Mike "Crocodile' Duckmanton and on the Sunday Trevor Milton crewed by Chris and Paul Ellis. Trevor was taking the opportunity to test drive the demo Hurricane. Race one on the Saturday afternoon got off to a bad start, as John had broken the goose neck on the Tornado and everybody (thanks Darcy) was trying to help get him on the water in time. The effort did not succeed, but did mean that Mike and I missed all of the signals and were about 50 yards behind the line when the gun went. It was only because we saw Robin screaming in, that we were even facing the right way. Needless to say Robin and Lisa screamed into the lead, followed by a couple of Unicorns and about 4 Shearwaters. It was a reach to the first mark and Mike and I had passed all except the leading Unicorn, who we passed at the second mark. It was then a chase after Robin and Lisa. We maintained our distance on them to the next mark, after which we had a long reach up to the Baffle. At this point John and Caroline joined us and we both chased Robin and Lisa. John stayed down to leeward and claimed after the race that he was under powered, whilst Mike and I tried to pitchpole on several occasions. Unfortunately, we had knocked

Blackwater & Colne contd... the port rudder back and every time I tried to bear away, the rudder just acted like a brake, sending up a spectacular plume of spray. Meanwhile Robin and Lisa had reached the paffle and fallen into a hole in the wind. Both John and I had been gaining on Robin, but when he reached the Baffle the distance was dramatically reduced. However, despite our best efforts, we both fell into the same hole! The wind was going through all points of the compass, but Robin snook round and was off on the reach back to Stone. John rounded second and raced off, and after two involuntary gybes Mike and I began the chase. There is no way you can catch Robin and Lisa when they have got a 100 yard lead, so Robin took line honours, John crossed second and we were third. Meanwhile the leading Unicorn seemed to sail straight around the Baffle without stopping. Robin won the race, the Unicorn was second by 7 seconds and we were third. Race 2 was on Sunday morning. Robin got to the line a little early and consequently had to dip back. John Nickalls and I made perfect starts and John led by about 10 yards at the first mark. Around the second mark we went, with Robin and Lisa breathing down our necks. You just can't keep that man back, and he sailed over us on the reach. John kept him at bay, and the two of them fought tooth and nail (or is it forestay and tiller) around the course. Mike and I held our position about 100 yards back until about halfway around the second lap, when two ‘dead in the water tacks' lost us about 400 yards. We had just passed Mark Savill when we did the first bad tack and he proceeded to sail effortlessly passed as we floundered about. He had requested a tow as we overtook him; we could have done with one when he went passed. John managed to hold Robin off to the finish, but Stone were sailing the Tornado off of a lower handicap than the Hurricane, so Robin took the race on handicap. Trevor Milton had taken the Demo Hurricane (Robert Whites Boat!) out to race, but was forced to retire at the first mark when the tiller , extension broke. He's a strong lad that Trevor! A liberal application of brute strength and lashings of adhesive tape meant that Trevor, accompanied by Christine, were out for the second race. The one advantage of a fast boat is that you are back with plenty of time for lunch. When the second race times were reached, a large portion of the monohull crews were still in the galley queue, so a postponement was signalled. Unfortunately, 3 out of the 4 Marconi cats were already on the water, so for 30 minutes we practised heaving to. John Nickalls claims he is faster than me even when he is hove to! Mike and I made a dream start to the third race. Well, anyway, I woke up when I hit the water after bouncing off of the mainsail! Robin and John rushed off into the lead again, whilst Trevor rushed ashore to pick up Paul Ellis in place of Christine. (Sailing is now getting like football, with substitutes on the touch line). Mike and I pulled the Hurricane up and proceeded to chase Trevor around the course.

10. Blackwater & Colne contd... Robin won again, with John close behind. A Unicorn finished third, with Trevorfourth and Mike and I fifth. The Shearwaters were no longer racing in the same fleet as us, as they now had enough boats to have a class of their own. Overall, with three wins, nobody could touch Robin, but John and Caroline finished second and proved that Robin isn't unbeatable. A Unicorn from Stone finished third with Mike and I forth. Next year we intend to make it a clean sweep for Marconi. The final race was for the "Cock o' the River", but Robin did not realise that he was eligible, so he was back at our club when racing commenced. The race was won by a Shearwater. I am sure that Robin could have collected that trophy as well. Well done to Robin and Lisa, and John and Caroline. Maybe next year a few more Cat sailors will make the effort to 'beat up the Blackwater’. Steve Keeble, 'Fly-by-Wire ed

COMMODORE'S NOTES 3. I cannot remember the last time that the Club enjoyed such warm and dry weather for the Camping Fortnight, we almost made it through the evening of the Mid Summer Party as well. Although I was not able to be present for the Camping Weeks, I understand that a very enjoyable time was had by all. My grateful thanks to all who helped make a success of the event. Similarly to those who helped at the Midsummer Party which was a tremendous success, especially the band, many thanks Pete, and others. It will soon be the Annual General Meeting and amongst other items will be the election of Club Officers for next year. Following the rule changes last year, the list of Officers who are elected at the Annual General Meeting are: Commodore Secretary Vice Commodore Sailing Secretary Rear Commodore Social Secretary Treasurer Clubhouse Secretary In addition to the above there are a large number of other positions to be filled, some of which are elected by the individual fleets. A full list of all positions will appear in a later Navigans, along with the request for nominations. However, can I appeal to everyone to start to think now whether they can help to fill any of the posts. The next major event for the Club is the EAST COAST PIERS RACE over the August Bank Holiday. I know that John Nickalls and the others involved in organising it will welcome all offers of help. The sight of all those 'Cats' last year was really impressive and I hope that the weather is kind and that this year's event will be even better. N.T. CAMPING WEEKS One interesting spectacle that hasn't been at our camps before was the presence of a dolphin amongst the moorings. He had already been seen in the river earlier in the season and during our fortnight spent time up at Stone and also visited our own moorings on most days. If we were at the right place at the right time (perhaps about an hour or two before low water) we might see him leap right out of the water a times, and fall back with a huge splash. I've been informed that he (or they - for there may have been two of them) was probably feeding on fish who graze am_ the weed growth on mooring chains and boat bottams. Perhaps the warmer water attracted him or it may be a more desirable spin-off from the grossly overpriced and totally ineffective new environment-friendly anti-fouling the yachtsman is now legally obliged to use! There was lots of interest playing 'spot the dolphin’ by people both afloat and ashore. He usually kept a respectful distance from boats but if you kept stationary and patient afloat you could get quite a good view of him. Peter's cartoon arose from the frequent discussions among us on whether we were seeing a porpoise or a dolphin - I'm sticking to dolphin! Our fortnight's weather was warm and dry except for the middle Sunday which was rather grim. For the rest of the time, though it varied occasionally from too much to too little wind for enjoyable sailing, those of us mm site had enough variation to allow everyone to have same of the sort of sailing they liked. Calm hours allowed everyone to safely swim, paddle and generally play around in the water. contd....

Camping Weeks.... 6. Thanks to the Workers: My personal thanks go to Leonie and her mm Elsie (Supergran) Carlisle for stepping in to help me in Galley om the first Sunday which proved to be quite a busy day. Thanks also to Jill Fowler and Phillipa Anderson who stepped in at the last minute to do Galley on the middle Sunday which proved to be a far busier day, and they simply sold out of all their stocks in the end. I believe the bar was manned by different volunteers every evening - thank you to all those, and as for the Tuck Shop which didn't happen, I reckon the considerable reduction of litter om the site, and ame parent saying it was a relief not to be nagged for money for sweets - well perhaps it was a service not too much missed! I must remember this time to mention Mr & Mrs Greenhalgh who this year, as well as in previous years' camping weeks, did various little jobs on Idle Vice to see that she was fit for the water - there are always same little odds and ends to bring up to scratch. The Boustreds worked hard as Camp Marshalls and planned the layout of the site for us which made quite a difference. The Hoe Down was a great success, and the rain stayed away till it was nearly over. I know many people helped in the bar, and Jean Flook led the team doing the laying out of the food, thank you to all involved in these tasks. All in all a great camp and, with co-operation of campers and forward planning by the Committee and our Clubhouse Secretary Chris Davies, we managed not to run out of water, and the facilities and supplies kept up with the usage we made of them. Also Darren, our Caretaker, came twice a day to clean up, his first visit of the day ending before 5am, so _ few of us saw him then, the restocked handtowels and toilet rolls being the most noticeable evidence of his early visits. Ed. CADET WEEK Cadet Week followed the patter established over the last few years with dry land instruction, capsize drill in a dinghy attached to the moorings barge, a trip to Maylandsea for lunch, a trip to Osea for lunch, and a First Aid lesson for sane younger Cadets. On Tuesday there were two separate Raft Races organised, one for younger Cadets and one for the older oes. Each of two teams were given 2 long pieces of rope, 3 barrels, 4 planks, and the task of assembling a raft and propelling it out to the moorings barge and back. The whole task kept them busy for some hours. The last day, Friday, was rather short of wind but there was no rest for the Cadets who had a busy programme of organised games on the water all day. All their activities during the week were videoed by Maureen Bigden and Janet Battle, and there was just time for the results to be shown on the Friday evening after the Presentation of Prizes. The Presentation was made more interesting by the use of a 'Sin Bin' - any Cadet who had supposedly ‘stepped out of line' during the week had his nose held over a barrel containing seaweed liberally dosed with, I believe, pickled onion vinegar. The audience decided how long the poor victim suffered by electing how long the count should last - anything up to a (sometimes very slow!) count to 20. And by the end of the evening there was a new saying - if anything at all to do with sailing ever goes wrong it's now always “Ben's Fault" (Holroyd, that is). Thanks are due to Ione & family and her friend who came along with their First Aid skills and the St John Ambulance Caravan for Cadet Week. Ione was much less busy last year, but there were one or two custamers, and it was peace of mind for us CONG 660%

Cadet Week.... 7. Thanks go to Mike Turner our Cadet Fleet Captain, his wife Rosemary, and his assistant Mike Battle for all their hard work in organising the Cadet Fleet - it does take a lot of planning beforehand as well as hard work at the time. And thanks are due to Dave Gibb, Dave Fletcher, Alec Goodwright and Derek Holroyd, who all spent a lot of time out on the water following the fleet of cadets, giving advice and support and supplying rescue services. Many other people helped out when the occasion arose, thanks to all for supporting the events. I understand that the number of cadets taking part this year was 46 - more than ever before. I do hope we will see lots of you coming to the Winter Meetings at MASC, it is a good way to get some theory under your belts ready for the new season. Ed. ADULT SAIL TRAINING, 31 JULY - 4 AUGUST 1989 8. Repeating last year's laid back style we attracted eleven adults of whom nine saw the week through. The course fell into the usual pattern of coffee at 10am followed by a bit of theory and a lot of practice. After two years' experience with this course the most useful aspects seem to be the basic seamanship points of getting the dinghy away from the shore and back again without hitting anything on the way. We also picked up a very useful idea from Mike Duckmanton's race traing programme using two buoys close together and setting a figure-of eight-course round them. Much of the work this year fell on Mike and Maggie Boreham when I suddenly disappeared off site with a gammy leg. Many thanks also to Janet Keeble who helped with the sailing tuition. Look out for our new adult helms who, I hope, we will see out on the water - Clare Savill, Alistair Sims, Derek Hymass, Michele Fraser, Rosanne Canith, Linda Chaplin, David Pennington and Richard Range. The other three girls had also done the '88 course but liked it so much they came back for an MoT - Zohra Gibb, Eileen Jolly, and Philippa Anderson. Finally, many thanks to Mike Turner and Mike Battle who organised a superb Cadet Week this year and invited the adults to join in the Friday Treasure Hunt. Malcolm Stuart, Rear Commodore, [redacted] SOLO NEWS As I write we are preparing for the trek go Plymouth for the Solo World Championships, where I think we will have six Marconi boats representing the Club. Four of the seven Eastern Area Open Events are now completed though I'm a little short of results details, since I missed the last three myself. However the Club has achieved a reasonable representation at all of them and Malcolm Gandy has predictably been our best performer, particularly at Downs S.C. (Deal in Kent) where he scored an outstanding victory despite the presence of several star names. The Inland Championships at Grafham at the end of June was an excellent event this year, blessed with sunshine and a reasonable breeze, as well as an entry of 107 boats. Final positions after four hard-fought races for your Marconi representatives were: Maldolm Gandy - 21st John Salmon - 43rd Dave Nixson - 47th Colin Willsmore - 54th Janet Keeble - 77th Janet also finished in 3rd place in the ladies competition and very close to the 2 above her. A good effort all round. But what of the domestic scene? All the points series races have been well supported and the Solo Team Racing day on July 22 was an outstanding success with 13 helms taking part in ideal weather. Particular thanks are due to Steve Keeble who was Race Officer and to Alan our rescue boat Coxswain, who both put in a hard day's work in managing an excellent event. Must just mention the winning team (since I was in it!)

with brilliant Captaincy from Dave Nixson, ably supported by Doug Eyles and yours truly. Finally, a word about the Cat Weekend (26-27th August). CADET SERIES The Cadet Racing went very well this year and had a pleasing turnout. The first day of racing was 'good weather', force 3, but the entry of a Dart in with the Mirrors posed a problem for the Race Officer who had to fit in three races. All these races were won by Lee Harrison and Debbie Yorston in the Dart. The next set of races were due to be held om the first Sunday of the Camping fortnight. There was barely any wind and plenty of tide and everybody retired except Damian Boreham who finished the course eventually, and won. In the afternoon there was a bit more breeze but not much. Only 3 boats entered, Damian (Mirror), Lee & Debbie (Dart), Lucy Boreham & Jenny Ball (420). There was not enough wind and too much tide for the Mirror which got into trouble at A Mark and ended up drifting round the corner and finally retired. However the 420 did well and managed to cross the line before the Dart and therefore had a clear win. The 3rd race was put off to the next Sunday due to lack of wind. The next Sunday the 2 races were again postponed, this time due to too much wind, it was blowing a Force 5-6 gusting occasionally to 7. The next Saturday when the 2 races were due to be sailed, there was again no wind but by the afternoon it had picked up enough to have a race. At very short notice Ray Ball, and Mike & Maggie Boreham stepped in to provide rescue cover and Mike Battle agreed to be Race Officer - many thanks to them. More boats joined in the races and by the 2nd race the wind had picked up to a force 3-4. Both races were won by Damian Boreham am_ handicap. The winner of the Cadet Series was Lee & Debbie in the Dart with Damian coming a very close second by just one point and o countback. Jenny Ball

LADIES SERIES - 1989 The winner of the 1989 Ladies Series (hence winner of the Ladies Cup) is:- MAGGIE BOREHAM (MIRROR) If the 'Average Entry' is the criterion by which a series is judged to be successful then surely this Ladies Series must be the most successful club event of the year; the Average Entry of 11.7 will be hard to beat - even by the Catamaran Fleet which has established itself as the most active of our fleets, at least in terms of numbers taking part in the racing programme. The wind (at Force 2 +) was strong enough to give good, enjoyable, sailing whilst the tide served to pose some problems for those who strayed too far from the recommended route between the buoys. Caron Stuart (crewed by friend Denise) and Lucy Boreham (crewed by Jenny Ball) had a close private battle in their 420s whilst Val Fletcher was not far behind them in her 420. Caron lacked a spinnaker and Lucy lacked 420 experience; each scored a 'win' over the other and an honourable draw can be declared. Jane Crawthern (Osprey) had a good sail and enjoyed some good results but no doubt wishes she'd not stayed out in the tide in the hope of getting a stronger wind. Melanie Keeble did particularly well in her borrowed Topper and not only achieved a 2nd place in the 2nd race but also secured 3rd place overall and thus features in the prize list. She also coped very well with a much larger non-racing boat which, by all the recognised rules and courtesies of sailing, should have kept clear of her - but didn't. The Mirror Fleet was well represented by Kirstie Jolly, Janet Battle, Pat Stuart, Clare Savill, Phillippa Anderson, Leone Golding and Su Fletcher. CADET SERIES, 1989 The winner of the 1989 Cadet Series is:- LEE HARRISON (DART 18) Many congratulations to Lee Harrison (Dart 18) on winning the 1989 Cadet Series in what turned out to be a ‘nail biting' finish and all hinging on the last race. This is what a race series should be like and the 1989 Cadet Series must rank as one of the best for some years. Cadet Races 1,2 and 3 were raced on Sunday, 2 July, in Force 4-5 with at least 5 entries in each race. Lee Harrison won all three races very handily and, truth to tell, the Cadet Series looked to be well and truly ‘wrapped up' for 1989. Apart from Lee, the other entries were Jon Yorston (Dart 15), Jenny Ball, David Ball, Lucy Boreham and Damian Boreham (all Mirrors). Cadet races 4,5 and 6 were scheduled for Sunday, 23 July. For race 4, the wind was somewhat lacking in strength, very patchy and very variable around the course, so much so that only Damian Boreham (Mirror) and Michael Fletcher (Topper) managed to round Breezy mark to complete a shortened course. Unfortunately, Michael inadvertently infringed a rule at the start and was disqualified. There were only three starters for Race 5 which was sailed in slightly windier conditions but was still pretty light and made it difficult to make way against the tide. This race was won by Lucy Boreham (420) with Lee Harrison (Dart 18) second. This time it was the turn of Damian Boreham (Mirror) to be frustrated by lack of wind at 'A' mark and he eventually retired. The Race Officer decided to postpone Race 6 until 30 July (when Cadet Race 7 was scheduled, together with the Jackpot for the club's senior citizens). The gods deceeed that Sunday 30 Ju'y brought with it a wind of Force 7 - occasionally observed to touch Force 8. Problems with the Jack B delayed the start of the Jackpot and eventually the Race Officer postponed the Jackpot to a later date and the Cadet Races 6 & 7 to Saturday, 5th August. Despite Lee's three previous wins,the Cadet Series was now still far from over ; Lee could be beaten by Damian if he (Damian) won both races 6 and 7 and Lee finished no higher than 4th in each race. Thus Cadet races 6 and 7 promised to be very interesting. Cadet 6 was raced in Force 3-4 and was won by Damian (Mirror) with Lucy Boreham (420) 2nd, Ian Fletcher (420) 3rd and Lee (Dart 18) finishing 4th. Clare Davies (Mirror) and Sian Caruth (Mirror) both retired whilst David Stewart (Topper) unfortunately missed out a mark and was disqualified. So, the scene was set for a nail biting finish with all depending upon the last race. Cadet Race 7 was sailed in Force 4 and, although Damian again won the race, Lee won the series by finishing 2nd with Lucy 3rd, Ian 4th, David Stewart 5th and Kirsty Jolly 6th. The Final result - since both Lee and Damian had 4 1 ' points each, the series was decided on countback; Lee's vital 2nd place in race 7 overtook Damian's 3rd place in race 2 and so Lee emerged the overall winner. The 1989 Cadet Series came to a marvellously exciting end , having been sailed in a wide variety of condition of course, tide and wind, thus providing a good test of all round sailing skill and knowledge. Lee dealt with the varying conditions with great competence and thoroughlydeserved his win but he had to fight hard for it. Lucy Boreham (helm) and Jenny Ball (crew) discovered they liked sailing the 420 and came 3rd overall; alas, no prize because the Average Entry fell just short of the magic number of '6' required for the award of 3rd prize. With 4 races to count, only Lee, Damian and Lucy competed all 7 races. David Ball and Jon Yorston each competed 3 races, Jenny Ball 2 races as helm (but she also crewed for Lucy) with Ian Fletcher and David Stewart also competedin 2 races. Stuart Golding, Richard Battle, Michael Fletcher, Kirstie Jolly, Clare Davies and Sian Caruth all sailed one race, some of them taking part in their first race ever. A total of 14 helms took part in the Cadet Series which is not a bad total compared to some previous years. However, in view of the large number of cadets taking part in the Cadet Week training programme it would be nice to see more cadets taking part in 1990. lst Lee Harrison (Dart 18) ala pts 8th David Stewart (Topper) 37 pts 2nd Damian Boreham (Mirror) 4 34 o 9th Kirsten Jolly (Mirror) |: 3rd Lucy Boreham (Mirror/420) Richard Battle (Mirror) Ap 4th David Ball (Mirror) 25 i =10th Sian Caruth (Heron) 42 " Sth Jan Fletcher (420) 29 . =10th Clare Davies (Mirror) 42 " 6th Jenny Ball (Mirror) 30 " =10th Michael Fletcher (Topper) | i 7th Jon Yorston (Dart 15) 32 " =10th Stuart Golding (Mirror) 42."

Five Go On A Sailing Adventure On Sunday 28 May, five people - Luke (skipper), Kim, Peter, Adrian and Maureen (that's me) - embarked on 'Bluenose' for a week's sailing course in, on and around the Solent. The following is a record of what happened during that week. It's not about the technical side of the sailing but what we 'got up to'. I think I can safely say we all had a great time and learnt a great deal from Luke. I know I had a wonderful holiday - not least because I had four delightful sailing companions. Sunday pm After a long train journey across South-east England, I arrived at Jack's home where a warm welcome was waiting. While we waited for everyone to arrive we made endless cups of tea and coffee and met the various members of Jack's family, the family pets and anyone else around. Eventually Jack sorted us into the various crews and boats. For us it was a Rival 34 named 'Bluenose'. We then sorted out food (which was already prepared for us), foul weather gear and sleeping bags etc. which were then packed into Peter's car while the rest of us walked to the Marina. I personally have never seen so many boats in one place, and got quite a surprise at the size of the Marina. Before we started any sailing we had a thorough and necessary tour of the boat. We were allocated lockers and berths - Kim and Peter in the forecabin, I and Adrian in the saloon, and Luke in the skipper's berth. Once everything was on board and settled, we set off under power for Cowes. The evening weather was dry and calm but nippy. The number of boats at Cowes surprised us all and we had to search hard for a mooring for the night. Eventually we found Club UK, and after a quick meal we went there for a drink and this gave us the chance to get to know each other and settle into the boat. I slept well that night - although I can't vouch for the rest of the crew. Monday We were up early for the shipping forecast and lovely hot showers at Club UK. After a cooked breakfast we got down to some serious sailing which proved interesting, entertaining and hard work - not necessarily in that order. After sandwiches for lunch, we spent more time learning how to handle the boat under power and then under sail. We also tried our hands at tacking, gybing and man-overboard, which was hard work but the fairly decent weather made it much easier, and we certainly learnt a great deal. Soon it was time to decide where to spend the night, and after due consultations, Kim decided we were going to Marchwood. (The rest of us agreed to this!) After an extended sail we found Marchwood. Now, why people should want to go there I shall never know. Oh, what a lovely place!! We eventually picked up a buoy just off what we thought was the Yacht Club. This was at 9.30pm and we were all hungry. Kim's comment for the diary was, and I quote, "picked up a buoy off Marchwood Yacht Club. They supposedly welcome visitors, but we couldn't find a way over or around the barbed wire." So we stayed put for the night. Tuesday After another good night's sleep (well, at least for me,) we were up early again for the shipping forecast and a cooked breakfast. The weather was cloudy and a bit chilly. We did some more practice of boat handling, this time picking up a mooring under sail. We all did pretty well at this. It was then over to Husbands Yard (which we had passed on the way to Marchwood.) Luke and Kim were keen to get better information about this area as the pilots are pretty useless. I helmed 'Bluenose' (sail, then motor) and got us in first go - I have to be honest, more by luck than by judgement. We moored up against another boat and Luke and Kim disappeared. It was then that the three of us remaining on board discovered that the other boat wanted to move out at 11.00am - would the others be back in time? It was a great relief when they returned and we moved off towards Calshot. By the time we picked up a small buoy at Calshot the tide was dropping and the wind was getting up. We decided to leave and head for Yarmouth. Unfortunately the buoy became stuck between the the rudder and propeller which led to an impromptu training session on freeing obstructions under boats. Discussions were held on how best to sort the matter out. Finally it was decided to use the rubber dinghy to put out a kedge anchor. By sheer brute force from the male members of the crew, we finally got the buoy clear when I pushed the rudder back and forth and freed it. A big sigh of relief from us all and we headed for Yarmouth. Luke and I decided a kip would be in order. Kim and Peter were helming and piloting. It would appear (and I

13. only have the men's word for this) that Luke had a short kip and I slept for most of the afternoon. I'm pleased to say that I woke before we got to Yarmouth because although it was crowded, it really is a beautiful place. We saw the harbourmaster who said we could tie up against the quay for a short time and we found that Yarmouth itself proved to be small but quaint. We were then back on the boat for a short hop to our night's mooring past the swing bridge. While we waited for the bridge to open, Kim was able to say a quick hello to some friends on another boat. We found our mooring which was much quieter than the main quay. After stopping off for a very short time, Luke decided we were going to Freshwater - and thereby hangs a tale! I have sailed up some narrow creeks before but I don't think I'll ever sail up one as narrow or as pretty again. It seemed to me that the echo sounder alarm was sounding all the time, but having said that, I enjoyed getting us through. The scenery was quite superb. After twisting and turning our way up (or down, I don't know which,) we found Freshwater. Mind you, we didn't have any choice as to where we went because we came to the end of the water! I grounded 'Bluenose' briefly which was not really surprising as there's not much water here and we were almost at the bottom of the tide. It was decided that we had enough time for a drink at the local before we had to leave. Using the dinghy, we clambered ashore, much to the surprise of a mother swan and her babies. On our way to the pub a passing motorist stopped and asked us if we were from the boat. Considering we were all clad in sailing gear and that there was only one boat and no-one else around it was a daft question! His further questions amused us: Did we know it was almost low water? Yes, we replied. Did we know we would ground? Yes, we replied. He then advised us he would never risk taking a boat this far. Perhaps he's in need of a week's sailing course with the Southern Sailing School! We found the pub easily along a leafy country lane and round the corner. It was beautiful. One of the things I love best about cruiser sailing is mooring in obscure creeks and finding the local pub. After our one drink it was back to the boat before we really did get stuck. Adrian helmed us back to our mooring which was much quicker this time. After a hot meal we decided to walk into Yarmouth for showers at the Yacht Club and then drinks in a local pub, (we're not really alcoholics - we just give that impression.) We left the dinghy tied up against the pontooon and started walking to town. It was then we discovered we had to cross the water again and none of us had boots on. It proved to be only a few inches deep so we hopped, skipped and jumped across and managed to stay upright. Once at the Yacht Club we headed for the showers and made use of them just before they closed and then it was over to the pub. It was dark when we left the pub, and it was only then we learnt that Kim was the only one with a torch, which meant the walk back to the dinghy was rather interesting as we couldn't see where we were going and the surface was very uneven. We eventually found the dinghy only having got lost once. Kim, Adrian and I were the first across to the boat, and I cannot recall what started all the giggles but it was nothing short of a miracle that I got aboard the boat without falling in. It had been a long and eventful day and we were all glad to climb into our sleeping bags. Wednesday Luke had promised us a quiet day (ha ha!) The weather was lovely so we were up early for re-entry to Yarmouth quay via the swing bridge. While we waited for the bridge to open we watched a red car having its roof re-arranged by the barrier across the bridge - quite the funniest moment of the day, that! We tied up against the quay again and took the opportunity for some shopping while Luke hunted for bait as we intended to go mackerel fishing. For the better part of the morning while we hopped along the coast to Poole we sunbathed, read the papers (the first we'd seen all week), and generally relaxed. Luke tried fishing but caught nothing but seaweed. As we got further towards Poole, the wind freshened and we were sailing at a fair rate. As was usual by now, I started preparing the mid-day meal. Having purchased some fresh rolls in Yarmouth, I endeavoured to make lunch which was not easy as we were heeling at a sharp angle and the only thing to do was to strap myself in and pray. I must say the men appreciated my efforts, and I their thanks. The last leg of the journey to Poole was proving very interesting. Once past Bournemouth, concentration is needed on both piloting and helming because the inshore waters cover hidden dangers, i.e. rocks. Once or

14. twice we came close to seeing just what those rocks look like, however, thanks to some super teamwork by all the men we got through to the outer section of Poole Harbour. It was then Luke decided to take us up some of the more obscure creeks just off Brownsea Island. I had a good look at the pilot and thought I knew where we were going and Adrian was helming, with me giving directions past the buoys. We had just passed the entrance channel for Blood Island when we grounded. This time we were really stuck - I'm not sure if "what to do when grounded" is in the RYA syllabus, but it ought to be. We used the motor, jib and almost the entire crew hanging as far as possible out on the boom to try to get us off the bottom, but at first 'Bluenose' did not want to know. It took repeated attempts before we were free. We motored to an anchoring just off a small island, whose name will remain a mystery because I forgot to write it down! We went below for a kip - this time it was a short one, and after a brief rest and a cup of tea we decided to find a quick and direct way into Poole for the night, It was interesting watching a Hercules making masses of passes overhead and then dropping heavens-only-knows-what by parachute onto the island below. The journey through the outer reaches proved uneventful, but finding a place for the night in Poole quay was a different matter altogether. We came alongside one boat only to be told that they were preparing to go. Okay, we said, and moved on. We came alongside another boat only to be told by the harbourmaster (a woman!) to move on further down the line of boats. It was then we noticed markings on the quay wall which showed where you went depending on your boat length. We found a berth and tied up alongside 'Cameo'. Everything was going fine, the food was being cooked at last and it looked like a pleasant evening was in store. Then the high jinks and a game of musical boats started. Luke had been told by 'Cameo' that the boat inside of them was moving out. The meal was put on hold and we prepared to move again. However, this gentleman (I could call him something else!) was not ready to move yet - he was waiting for somebody. So, I started to get the meal ready again - two or three times I had to put that meal on hold. Finally he decided to go and we and 'Cameo' moved out to let him go. What fun we had! There were boats coming and going, and tankers appearing from nowhere. 'Cameo' got herself back into her berth, and we were preparing to do the same, when 'Starling' nipped in under our nose leaving us high and dry with a tanker bearing down on us. Thanks to some skilful helming by Kim we made it into our berth in time - just. We enjoyed our dinner finally, although I don't mind saying, I almost threw it at a certain 'gentleman' as he went past. Another boat came alongside us for the night - Poole's a busy place. After dinner Luke and I decided to go for a walk to find fishing bait and showers, we found neither, but enjoyed the walk. It was then time for our usual trip to a local pub where discussions were were held on what to do the next day. Our aim was to get to Keyhaven which meant leaving either very early or in the late afternoon because of the tides. We left the pub almost at closing time and went back on board to finalise details for the next day. It was decided to leave at 3.30am at the latest. Luke duly informed the boat on our outside who promptly said they were leaving at that time as well, and would we wake them? I proceeded to make some sandwiches for the morning as I did not fancy making breakfast for five at 4am! Peter and Luke 'ummed and aahed' about whether to go to bed or not, it was well past midnight and it seemed pointless for only a couple of hours - we were to get up at 2.45am. I went to bed as did Kim and Adrian. I could not sleep and got up, thinking Luke and Peter were still up, but the only sound was Luke snoring so I went back to bed. It had been a long day. Luke had promised us a quiet day and if this was a quiet one I would love to know what his idea of a busy one is. Thursday The alarm went off and it was time to get up. We woke up the boat next door and off they went. Just as we prepared to slip our lines a boat came in looking for a berth, I warned him not to come alongside as we were just leaving. We were away on time. It's a lovely feeling sailing at that time of the morning. I was a little anxious but my fears soon went as we eased our way out. Kim was helming, Peter piloting, Adrian and I were picking out the buoys and Luke was keeping a careful watch on proceedings. This was a good thing because we went aground again, but it did not take us long to get free, after all, by now we had had plenty of practice at freeing grounded boats. My sandwiches were eaten quite early and I was pleased I'd made the effort to prepare them. Kim came off watch and I went on (Luke had already sorted us into the various watches.) I enjoyed my stint on helm.

15. Thanks to Peter, I knew where I was going and it was wonderful watching the dawn come up. The only disappointing thing was the weather, it had started raining, but as all of us on deck were wearing foul weather gear and our safety harnesses (Luke had insisted,) we didn't get too wet. I finished my watch and went below for a kip. That, unfortunately, was not possible because Luke was asleep on my bunk with my sleeping bag and shoes in my locker underneath. So I sat around for a while until a certain person woke up and let me have my bunk back. I crawled into my sleeping bag and asked to be woken in thirty minutes so I could do my stint on stand-by watch. By using the motor and sail we had made very good time and we ignored Keyhaven and went to Lymington instead. Somehow, I ended up spending the rest of the trip asleep and only woke up when we actually picked up the mooring in Lymington quay. Lymington is lovely. Luke, Kim and Peter went ashore, Adrian and I just pottered about and fed the baby ducks (well, I did anyway.) Once the others came back I took the chance to go ashore and do some shopping, as it was to be our last night on board and I wanted to do something special for the meal. I got back on board and suggested breakfast - but wasn't it dinner time? None of us seemed quite sure. We felt as though we had been up all day, yet it was only mid-morning. Getting up so early had sent our internal bio clocks up the creek (excuse the pun, please.) We had our meal and decided to move off for Beaulieu so we could get to a mooring before the pubs closed. Luke decided I would be pilot and Adrian would helm. This was not the best navigation exercise I have ever done and I'm thankful Luke was on hand to check my courses. Still, we made it to the outer reaches of Beaulieu Channel. This channel is narrow and very long and it took time to reach the first of the two marinas, by which time the heavens had opened. The rain eased and by the time we reached the main marina it had stopped. This was a lovely and well-run marina, and the harbour master showed us our berth for the night. Luke decided he wanted a walk to Beaulieu before having a shower, and did anyone else want to go with him? I, mad fool that I am, was the only one who said yes, and we set off for what I thought was a short walk (I had to get back to cook that meal!) We walked on and on and on. Eventually we got to the pub at Beaulieu where I thought we going to have a drink - and we would have if it had been open. We started back, I was getting concerned about the time - it was getting late and I was worried about that meal. Luke said surely they would start cooking it without me, but I wasn't so sure. By the time we reached the boat Luke and I were soaked - the heavens had opened again. It was a good job we had kept our foul weather gear on. Kim, Peter and Adrian had to some degree justified Luke's faith in them. They had put the oven on ready for the cooking. Why hadn't they started to cook? Because they thought I wouldn't be pleased and they would be told off. Although at the beginning of the week Luke had said I would only spend one day cooking, I ended up doing most of it! I enjoyed doing it and did not mind in the least. However, Peter, Kim and Adrian nobly offered to cook our last main meal. Luke and I went off for a shower, and what a wonderful surprise awaited me when I returned to the boat! The three served up a superb mushroom soup and roast pork with all the trimmings, and I supplied a fresh fruit salad for afters. A huge bottle of wine stood ready. It was easily the best meal of the week and also the noisiest. We ate, drank and laughed till we cried. The bottle of wine, which had been unopened, was finished before we went to the pub! It was a lovely evening. The weather cleared up and we were able to sit back in the cockpit and watch everyone arriving and trying to get into their berths. A Frenchman in a steel boat provided some entertainment. We walked over to the pub and found that Beaulieu is a really beautiful place. There is a museum there and we decided to visit it the next day (Friday). The pub was crowded but we managed to find ourselves some space, and the cabaret was a one-man-band who obviously had a few fans (or were they family?) in the audience. It was clear that a lot of Sailing Schools use this pub, and apparently Beaulieu is a popular place for the Schools on a Thursday night. A lot of people wore clothes which showed that they were with a School. Southern Sailing doesn't do this I am very pleased to say. It was then back to the boat for some supper and reflections on the past week. Friday We awoke to a beautiful morning, and a cooked breakfast and a shower were the first duties of the day. It was decided we had enough time to visit the museum before we had to leave for home. The museum was a wonderful place and certainly worth a visit. All too soon it was time to leave - but I'm definitely going back to Beaulieu one day.

16. We arrived back at Swanwick Marina in plenty of time, and while Luke went off to find Dave the engineer to sort out the problem of the water tank, the rest of us cleaned the boat inside and out. Back at Jack's house, Luke gave us our certificates and we said our goodbyes. Reflections The weather was not bad at all - in fact it was very good. The only times it rained were early Thursday morning and Thursday evening. My sailing confidence has shot up because of this course and it was nice to put into practice what I had been taught in the classroom during the winter. I'm certainly going on to do my Coastal Skipper, and it will be with the Southern Sailing School. ......and it's not every woman who gets to spend a week with four men, not one of whom is her husband. They were all super and I enjoyed sailing with them. Most of the girls at work were quite jealous and couldn't believe my luck! Maureen Bigden, 'Gemma'

COMMODORE'S NOTES It is extremely unfortunate that the fine weather of the summer broke on the August Bank Holiday weekend when we ran the second major event of our calendar - the East Coast Piers Race. While Malcolm Stuart, John Nickalls and the rest of the organisers tusselled with the problem of the course to set, I was at Walton listening to the wind howling in the rigging and I whole heartedly support their decision to _ shorten the course despite the pressure of the event and the natural desire to sail the course. We still have the Autumm Series to be sailed, the Solo and Mirror Open on Sunday 17th September and the Helmsman of the Year Final om Saturday 7th October. All of these should provide good sailing and I am sure that the Helmsman Final will provide interest for any spectators who are there. Following the pattern of last year, the Main Committee will be contacting each Fleet Captain to arrange for them to carry out a specific task and the Fleet Captains will be looking for your support. By using this method last year, a great deal was achieved. The Laying Up Supper is on Saturday 11th November. Because of the increasing number of people attending, we are holding it at the Heybridge Moat House at Ingatestone this year. Peter Bloanfield has succeeded in booking the same popular band as we have had at the last two events. Please book your tickets early to avoid disappointment, either via your Fleet Captain or the normal ticket sellers (see below). Finally, to round off the year we have the 'Last Fling' race on Sunday 19th November followed by the Annual General Meeting and Prize Giving. N.T. 6. COASTGUARD COMPLIMENT Having survived the rigours of Marconi's East Coast Piers Race, I was aroused from reasonably deep slumber to answer the telephone. In a matter of seconds I was briefed with the details of an incident at the Club by the Duty Officer of Thames Coastguard at Walton. I was requested to rendezvous with the Bradwell Marine Rescue Unit (MRU) at the Sailing Club. Mersea Inshore Lifeboat had been launched and an ambulance had been requested to stand by from Burnham-on-Crouch. As I pulled into Stansgate Road, I was aware of the blue lights of the MRU fast approaching and we both arrived at MSC together, approximately 6 minutes after the initial call, quickly followed by the ambulance. Having identified the yacht involved, which was on its mooring, the casualty was a 44-year-old male who had been loading stores from the boat to the dinghy alongside, had inadvertently slipped, upturned the dinghy and ended up in the water. The only other person on board the yacht, the Master, quickly threw the main sheet to the casualty who tied himself securely under the arms to it. The Master had made several attempts to raise the casualty by using the boom, but because of the physical exhaustion of the casualty, was unable to get him on board. A call was made to Thames Coastguards who raised the initial alarm and hence our attendance at the Sailing Club. The Lifeboat arrived some 8 minutes after us and put the casualty ashore, where he received immediate medical assistance. My reason for writing this note is that it may serve as a lesson for all - the casualty was fortunately all right although hospitalised for the night, but in the space of a very short time he became close to hypothermic on a flat calm night while the yacht was at anchor. It had been impossible to get him aboard and it was only through the skill and presence of mind of the Master, who attempted in every way to recover the casualty, acted in text-book fashion to ensure that he was safe and secured to the yacht and called for assistance, all of which, had he not done so, could have ended in a very sad evening. I trust he is not embarrassed by my mentioning his name, but credit must go to the Master, Mr Derek Hall, for his commendable action in saving the life of his crew. Charles Anderson

10. EAST COAST PIERS RACE 1989 (or "Thank Goodness we didn't go to Clacton......") With a forecast of "Force 6/7 occasionally 8" one has to look on the bright side; a wind direction of NNE, whilst not bright, was at least less gloomy, so we took the plunge by setting the full course. The buoys were already in place, the spotters had set off for the four gates, and Roger Smith prepared to tell the competitors that they were to sail down to the mouth of the river, up the coast to Clacton and Walton, and then back to Marconi's. Perhaps the competitors had suspected what we were going to ask them to do and found an excuse to be elsewhere, or perhaps their families had simply demanded their presence at some other Bank Holiday activity - either way, there weren't as many faces at the Briefing as we'd have liked, and the reasons for this are still a subject for some conjecture. The preparations had been based around accomodating 150 boats, trailers, cars and tents - the site looked quite empty as a near-gale rattled through the dinghy park. As the fleet gathered for the Briefing the so far unaccomodating weather did us a favour. A particularly strong squall threw itself at the clubhouse, the water turned streaky-grey, and the race committee's hearts fell. A quick rethink, the course was shortened, and the Commodore in Titchmarsh Marina became ten years younger in a trice. Even with the strong wind course in use only 38 of the entrants were adventurous (foolish?) enough to venture out to the start, but the race set off a few minutes late from Osea Pier, with the boats fetching up toward No.1 before beating up Goldhanger Creek. This first beat saw the first real evidence of the wind strength as Reg White's Hurricane Special's mast broke in two - it wasn't to be the White family's weekend. The reach from Goldhanger to Mill Beach threw off most of the 'fast' rescue boats, and they rejoined the leaders as the fleet emerged having passed behind Northey Island. By this time Rob White had assumed the lead in his standard Hurricane - Will Sunnucks, also sailing a Hurricane, was lying second, and we'd let our Tornado drop back to third place. Past the club in 31 minutes and on toward Bradwell the cats with less sail area were able to pick up valuable time against the more powerful boats struggling to stay upright on the tight reach. The wind increased as the leaders passed through Bradwell Gate, and the spotters watched as half a dozen boats capsized in quick succession. With a multitude of rescue boats having volunteered their services for the day all the casualties were quickly attended, although a number of boats suffered minor damage and several retired. The beat across the river to the Nass Beacon gave a brief respite from the stinging impact of high-speed salt water and a chance to re-establish communication with the crew - even if this was limited to the expression of mutual interest in keeping the mast out of the water. Bearing away at the Nass was exciting, and the downhill ride back to the Club gave the water a chance to numb the other side of the face. Downwind, the cats lost their tendency to lift one hull clear of the water in a gentle attempt to deposit slow-witted sailors in the water; instead they adopted a more effective bow-down attitude. Every gust pushed the lee bow further under the waves, threatening to trip the boats (now travelling at over 20 knots) forward into the spectacular, but most disconcerting, "pitchpole". On our boat, Caroline took the helm, leaving me with both hands free to haul on the mainsheet, and with four eyes glued to the port bow we careered upriver. Rob White was leading as we passed the Club, and Will Sunnucks was still ahead of us, but the second White mishap of the weekend happened as Rob rounded No 2 mark in the belief that it was a large inflatable near No 4. The Race Officer didn't approve of this - indeed I understand a mild panic set in as Will Sunnucks followed Rob on the wrong course and visions of the entire fleet failing to complete the race arose in the organisers' minds. Luckily (mainly for us !) we spotted the mistake, rounded the correct mark, and screamed back to the finish line. Although Paul Smith very nearly passed through our lee as we pinched up to the windward end of the line (anticipating a second lap), a scream from Caroline sent us reaching down to a two length lead over the line. Was the event a success? Well I certainly think so. All those who sailed enjoyed the race: several thought that we ought to have had another lap, but we were very pleased that we hadn't! The organisation seemed to go well - several visitors observed that we had clearly planned for a lot more entrants, and that we'd have been able to cope without any real difficulties with over a hundred boats. Whether to hold any future Piers Race on the Bank Holiday weekend must be a critical question, and we've learnt a lot to apply in the future. However, several aspects were particularly satisfying - not the least that we had 24 rescue boats of assorted types covering the course.
