Sincere thanks are due to all those who helped out at the weekend: to the cat fleet members who helped with the setting-up and taking down; to the other Club members who put in a lot of time and effort to provide rescue cover, to marshall the competitors, to staff reception, and to make the event run smoothly in a hundred and one other ways; to the Solo fleet (and in particular Roger Smith and his team on the Piers Race day and to John Salmon for providing the additional races); to all the Club members who weren't directly involved yet tolerated the inconvenience that the race inevitably involved; to all our sponsors for removing the financial burden and allowing us to make a generous donation to the RNLI and Sailing for the Disabled; and to all those members of the other clubs who willingly gave their time and services to bring us all safely back to shore. My own special thanks must go to Malcolm Stuart, who (as always) was tireless in his efforts for the event, to Charles Anderson who put all his local knowledge and organisational skills into making sure we achieved such an effective rescue cover (and what a seductive radio voice he has!), and to Mike Duckmanton whose calming influence rescued me from many a panic! And what of next year? Well, we have a good foundation on which to build. We've built up a broad range of contacts, and we've seen many (but I'm sure not all) of the pitfalls. The final decision remains to be made, but personally I hope 1990 will see the best Piers Race yet. It's unlikely to be faster (we averaged 16 knots), but a warm sunny day, flat water, and an on-board store of cold beer would let me forgive that! 12. THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE - (Through the eye of the Hurricane) Sunday morning came with the crowing of the farm cockerel. I'll wring its neck if I get my hands on it as it was only 5am! I turned back over, collided with the wife (her being on starboard and me having no rights) which caused me to sit up with a start. As I was sitting up, I pulled back the curtain and looked out of the window at the weather. It was fairly calm inside the awning with little prospect of any rain. Reaching over to another window, looked out once more. It was overcast and WINDY!!! No fool would want to go out in that wind, I thought, so I lay back down and tried to sleep. My eyes closed and I dozed off for what seemed no more than 30 seconds, but the clock indicated that it was about an hour, so who am I to argue? Time to go. A quick check revealed that that it was still windy! My enthusiasm underwhelmed me as I set about my morning ablutions; taking the opportunity to inspect the anemometer on the way past. A steady 7, GUSTING 8! A mere bagatelle to a foolhardy catamaran sailor. No sweat, I thought, Dave will convince me that discretion is the best course and I will safely return to the warmth of my bed. Dave arrived at about 7 o'clock raring to go. He looked at the anemometer, asked me if this was Datchet, and when I replied no, said that we were racing, so we rigged the boat. Walton here we come. Boat rigged, we made our way to the briefing at 8 o'clock. What a briefing! The only thing that was missing was crosses marking the spots at which many of us were to capsize. Everything else was marked. We were to stay within the estuary, but having helped put the Bradwell gate buoy out on Saturday, I knew that the beat to the Nass was going to be no picnic. Dave had rigged the boat for heavy weather, maximum tension on the diamonds, spanner set tight along the boom, jib sheet blocks back to open the jib leach. The top three battens were reversed to allow the top of the sail to fall away more easily. Safety equipment checked as we went onto the hard. Rubber band collected, we were ready. One last check on the clean underwear situation and we launched into the Northerly onshore wind. A QUICK reach up to Osea Pier and we practised our tacks and gybes ready for the real thing. Postponement flag down, ECPR flag up, we sailed around trying to decide where to start on the line. Close to Osea the water was relatively calm, but the wind was less; further out the wind was better, but the water was rougher. Our choice was influenced by John Nickalls who was close to Osea. John is a master at good starts so we knew that if we were near to him we would not be far wrong. The only problem was that we were a long way away from the committee boat and the signals. Blue Peter up, then both flags down and we were away. Hold on, where did the Darts come from? There, just ahead of us, was Crocodile Duckmanton and Rosie. It must be his underwater stealthy approach which we missed. Through the Cruisers off Osea, the leader about 50 metres (1992 and all that) ahead. Close behind was a group of Hurricanes who were effectively stopping us from tacking. Paul Metcalfe tacked early, whilst the leaders sailed on. At last we had gained sufficient to windward to tack. At this point we were close to the Hurricane 4.9 and in about 12th place overall. We clawed our way past the Darts but could not get past the 4.9, who seem to have as much boat speed as us. In fact we were grossly over-powered and only the bottom 5 panels on the main were shaping correctly. The top three panels were completely backed, but even then the telltales were still streaming parallel! The remaining panels were nicely 'S' shaped. Around the back of Northey we went, almost in line astern, and by now in about 9th place. As we passed the corner by number 9 buoy the leaders were just turning across the causeway. As usual something has to go wrong. We turned to cross the causeway and there was a loud thud and the starboard rudder shot up. Why? There was nothing we could see. Whatever we had hit was below the surface. After the race, the boat following us told us that they had hit something with their centreboard, but had missed it with the rudder. However, the impact was strong enough to push the blade back and I knew that steering was going to be hard work for the rest of the race. Down the south side of Northey we reached, still not able to overtake the 4.9, but being overtaken by another Hurricane 5.9 which sailed through to leeward. On reflection he probably sailed a shorter course rather than being any faster. On our way back to Osea Pier we put a lot of distance between us and the next boat, so we were now sailing as the back marker of a group of four. Three Hurricane 5.9s (110, 112 and 082) and the 4.9. Past the Club we went, twin wiring, and spilling wind like crazy. Off Stone, the leading Hurricane in the group (110) decided to go for a swim. Now up to about 9th place. We headed for the Baffle, overtaking both the other 5.9 (112), which then also went for a swim, and the 4.9. Now in about 7th place. The waves were coming in from the quarter and Dave was getting bumped about all over the place and the spray was blinding both of us. **Behind the baffle. HELLS..glug..BELLS..glug..WHERE....glug....IS..glug..glug..THE WIND! Both Dave and I were swimming with the boat trying to fall on top us us. Steering the boat whilst facing away from it is extremely difficult, and if Dave hadn't unhooked we would have pulled the boat down on top of us. As it was, we sailed the boat in almost a half circle around our position in the water and then managed to scramble on

13. board. The 4.9 had learnt from our mistake and kept well away from the Baffle, whilst the following boats, which had been about 500 metres back, were now almost alongside. Off to Bradwell gate, where we hardened up onto a beat. Steve Dodgson, who eventually finished 11th overall tacked off, whilst we and Dave Williams, 10th overall, stood on. We tacked, travelled about 100 metres and then we were hit by a real gust. Up went the boat. Dave and I dumped everything, but it just kept going. At the point of no return it stopped. Slowly it began to fall back. SAFE! No, another gust must have hit the trampoline as the boat lifted again and I did a one and a half twist with inverted pike just aft of the mainsail. Dave tells me that he did a pinball dive, colliding with various bits of the boat before landing on the main and sliding under the boom and into the water. Quickly up onto the hull; out with the righting line; weight out and the boat started to lift. Would it, wouldn't it? Slowly around and up it came. Slide into the water, the hull now at a foot up from the sea. Another big gust, hull rising, being lifted out of the water, boat back over!!!!(expletives deleted.) Back on the hull to begin again. Success this time but about 10 minutes lost. We were now almost sideways on to the waves and it was difficult to get forward motion as the waves were picking us up and slamming us down. Eventually, after 2 or 3 abortive tacks, we succeeded in turning into the waves and continuing the race. We were now back behind one of our original group of four (112), the 4.9 had not capsized, and we never saw the other boat (110). Strange that, considering that this boat (110) finished 8th overall, beating boats which did not capsize at all. I wonder, did he sail the full course? Around the Nass beacon we went, with the Club Darts not too far behind. The reach back to Osea was as painful for Dave as the reach down, with him bouncing off the hull on a number of occasions as the waves knocked his feet from under him. We were sailing closer to the northern shore and the wind did not seem anywhere near as strong. In fact, we found it easier for a tme to sit inboard close to the shroud whilst Dave trapezed behind me. By now my arms were beginning to ache from the strain of steering with and out-of-line rudder. There was another Hurricane in front which was receiving a heavy dose of gusts, as we could see the white water shooting up from the bows as the nose dived into the start of a pitchpole. He didn't succumb, but we were gaining on him rapidly. However, if anything, we seemed to be underpowered, or sailing in a relative hull, for the Darts seemed to be gaining. As we passed the finish line, John Nickalls and Caroline were just finishing. In the confused chop off number 1, the Hurricane in front went over and almost immediately turned turtle. The Police 'Alert' was quickly on the scene, unfortunately forcing us to alter course as he was on our direct course. As we came into the lee of Osea, the leading Dart was passing in the opposite direction, so we were about the distance from the pier to the turning mark and back, behind him. There was a Condor and a Hurricane ahead, but we had fallen into a lull and they began to draw away. The Condor slowed as well, but the Hurricane just sailed on and away. We were about 50 metres behind the Condor at the mark but he accelerated away, whilst we sailed steadily back to the finish. As we passed the pier, Mike Duckmanton and Rosie were close behind Graham Baker and Richard Wilmot. This was about the same distance that we were behind the leading Dart, but where we finished about 12 minutes behind the Dart, they only finished about 6 minutes behind us. Either the wind had died as we passed Osea, or I was sailing like a PLONKER! I'll let you make up your own mind about that. Having crossed the finish we returned to the beach at Osea to lower the main and have a drink and a Mars Bar, before making our way back to the Club under jib alone. So overall we finished 18th out of the nineteen who completed the course, beating only the Thundercat, whose crews' combined weight was probably no more than mine alone, and "but for the....." we might have finished in the top 10! Ah well, I suppose we will have to try again next year. Well done to John & Caroline; Trevor (who was disappointed that they had shortened course as he was just getting warmed up) & Keith; Graham (do you think I'll get round?) Baker & Wilmot, and Mike & Rosie. Hard luck to those Club members who started but retired. It was an achievement to be out there at all! The end of an exciting day, and I must express my thanks to all those people who were involved in the organisation before and on the day. Without you, these events would not happen. STEVE KEEBLE, Fly-By-Wire ** Ed's note: This event was witnessed by half the contingent of Bradwell Sailing School who were out on the water for the last sail of their week's course. Jenny, David and Stuart informed the audience who the unfortunate sailors were - and pupils and instructors all liked your trousers, guys!

16. WEIL'S DISEASE The national rat population is increasing and between 50 to 60% of rats carry and excrete the organism Leptospira ictero-haemorrhagiae in their urine. Infection with the organism causes an illness which has been known to result in death of 10% of cases. There has been a recent increase in the incidence of the disease - 133 cases were notified in 1988 compared with amily 68 in 1987 and 32 in 1986. Formerly occuring mainly among sewage or abbatoir workers and miners, recent records show that the majority of fatalities are now related to water activities. In 1989 there have been 19 deaths of which no fewer than 13 were associated with water users. The nature of leisure water activity means that the average age of this at-risk group is fairly young with most cases occuring in the 13 - 42 age group. ABOUT THE ILLNESS The organism enters the human body through breaks in the skin such as cuts, blisters and abrasions or via the lining of the nose, throat or alimentary tract. The incubation period is 7 - 13 days and the disease starts with a fever, muscular aches and pains, loss of appetite and vomiting with prostration. It is vital that the doctor be told of any water-borne activity as the symptans are easily confused with those of flu and if the patient has a 'clean' occupation the possibility of Weil's Disease may be overlooked in the early stages. Subsequent bruising of the skin, sore eyes, nose bleeds and jaundice may occur. The fever lasts about five days and may be followed by significant deterioration. Laboratory testing of blood will confirm the diagnosis but this may take undue time — in an ordinary hospital. Send samples direct to: The Leptospirosis Reference Unit, Public Health Laboratory, County Hospital, Hereford, HR1 2ER. Tel. [redacted] here they will be tested within 24 hours. Treatment is usually by Penicillin Antibiotic. RATS AND THE ILLNESS The rat is a creature of the water's edge. The leptospira organism is passed in urine and, while it does not live long in dry conditions, can survive for same time in water. Salt water soon kills off the organism but there is a significant risk in tidal waters such as lower parts of the Thames and other rivers. The risk increases upstream and is greatest in canals, ponds or areas of slowly draining water. There is a significant risk to users of river banks or reservoir edges. WATER USERS Sailors, board sailors, canoeists, oarsmen, swimmers or fishermen are at risk in any area with a population of rats. Any skin wound or blister, old or new, may be infected if immersed in water polluted with the organism. GENERAL CARE Handrails, steps and walkways should be checked for gaps, nails or rough edges that may Cause minor wounds. ALL MEMBERS: Every effort must be made to see that food residues are removed from the Clubhouse, boat and trailer parks or picnic areas. A happy well-nourished rat will produce more rats. Wear shoes to protect the feet from cuts. Don't allow water to collect inside your dinghy, it may be wet but it may not all be water! (Ed's note: The same caution also necessary with pools of water collected on the outside of boat covers i.e. don't let it come into contact with any wounds.) Cruiser Owners: Don't think it is solely a dinghy sailor's problem. If you ever have to come ashore clutching at the jetty from your tender, you too are at risk. Waterproof surgical plasters of an adequate size should be used to cover old skin wounds before going afloat or to the dinghy park. Such protection will also apply to club workingparties when members may be clearing old structures or other hazards. Every sailing club should have available to members at all times a supply of clean fresh water to wash wounds and a shower for those who may have fallen into suspect water.

2s COMMODORE'S NOTES As the Sailing Programme draws to aclose it is time to start to think about the future. This begins with the election of next year's Committee at the Annual General Meeting and there is a nomination form elsewhere in this issue of Navigans. The only restrictions that apply are that the Canmmodore, Secretary and Treasurer must be Ordinary Members and that the Canmodore, along with the Vice and Rear Commodores, must have served at least one year in the last three on the Main Committee before being elected to these positions. Under the Constitution and Rules of the Club the Main Committee can, via Rule 10.7, make nominations for any position and increasingly over the last few years, these have been the only nominations. Whilst this helps with continuity, it should not exclude others from seeking nomination. Early next year I will attempt to give an indication of those people serving on all the Committees who may be intending to retire, so that others can came forward. You will see from the nanination form that very few of the positions are elected if you compare the list with the Committee in the front of the Year Book. Again, volunteers are always required to fill these positions and if you are interested, please contact the relevant Sub Committee Chairman. Regarding this year, I an pleased to say that members have came forward to fill all the positions. There are however a number of other positions to be filled by election, namely, the Fleet Captains and the Dinghy and Cruiser Representatives on the Clubhouse and Social Committees. These are elected at your Fleet Meetings, so do consider volunteering and attend the meetings. I hope that the dates of these meetings will be published in Navigans. Winter Tasks Over the winter there is a considerable amount of work to be carried out, ranging from erecting the Tractor Shed and Tender Rack through refurbishing the Entrance Hall, redecorating the Galley and Bar, to work to replace the old sewage-system covers and remove the trees to increase the size of the dinghy park, and same work on the road; these activities will be arranged on a Fleet basis as last year, when we made a tremendous improvement in the site. In addition to these, there are a number of items which will be carried out using professional help, which includes an electric shower in the Ladies' Changing Roan, and an updating of all the radios to allow us to use Channel M2. Beyond these activities, the Main Committee have made a definite committment to a second Rescue Boat and the Sailing Sub Committee are producing a proposal so that we can approach the MASC for the funds. At the same time we will be asking the MASC to replace the water pipe. Finally, next summer a series of working parties will be needed to start work on the Cruiser Park drainage. Obviously the costs of all these schemes are much less if we, the Members, carry out as much work as possible, but it does require help from everyone and not just a dedicated few. 8. THE 1989 JACKPOT - Through the Eye of the Hurricane Sunday the 1st of October was the day scheduled for the rerun of the 1989 Jackpot. The original race was abandoned owing to a battery failure on the Jack B, but many people were relieved as the wind was at force 6 and the gusts were stronger still. However, the rerun could not have been a greater extreme! Despite a forecast of northerly winds of force 3, competitors were welcomed at Stansgate with a northerly force zilch! Nevertheless, a large group of intrepid adventurers slipped gingerly onto the water, to pick up what breeze there was. By the scheduled start time of 11.30am the wind was up to a whole force 1, and with a storng tide under the boats, care had to be taken not to be carried over the line. The outer end of the line was favoured, if only because the tide was strongest there, and accordingly, that end was a mass of monohulls , jilling about close to the line. The Cats were hanging back, as they are not as manoeuvrable, but were being forced to go for the middle of the line where there were gaps. The gun went and off went the fleet. The outer end of the line was crowded, but from out of nowhere came Rob Stahl and Keith Gurney (Hurricane 136) slipping through the monohulls to take the lead. Dave and I were right behind them, with Graham Baker on our inside. "Up, up, up," shouted the Gull at Graham, who started to luff in response. His bows passed behind my transom as I responded with a firm "Mast abeam". Suddenly we were clear of the cruisers and, looking back, I was amazed to see that Rob and I had a clear lead. A large Sailing Barge was heading up to Maldon, so Rob and I headed to windward, unlike some others who fell into its wind shadow! By Osea Pier, Rob and I were side by side, with Steve and Rosie (Prindle 18-2) about 100 yards behind. Trevor and Christine were close behind them, followed by a gaggle of Darts. Unfortunately I had to sail a slightly longer course than Rob to No.3, and he lead by about two boat lengths at this point. The wind was rapidly dying and Rob and I took turns at getting individual gusts to help us on our way. Meanwhile, the people behind were getting closer and the Solos were amongst the Darts. We almost caught Rob when he almost failed to see No.7 mark, and was forced to bear away sharply to get to it. Near to Northey, Rob tacked to stay in the main current whilst Dave and I stood on as we had found a little wind. In the end we were forced to tack and we only just crossed ahead of Steve and Rosie who tacked themselves shortly afterwards. We overstood the course to the mark (No.8) knowing that we could bear away if the wind died or went forward as it was prone to do. This paid off as we regained ground on Rob and pulled away from Steve who had tacked back earlier. At No.8 Rob had a 50 yard lead with Steve 20 yards behind. Rob, followed by Steve, gybed across to Northey to remain in the current, whilst Dave and I found wind on the Heybridge shore and crept along overhauling Rob. Alas, our wind disappeared and we were forced to gybe. Rob retook the lead, whilst Steve gained an overlap at the mark (No.10) and rounded second. We had to go the long way round but were able to bear away more and we slid through to leeward of the Prindle. Meanwhile Trevor and Chris had rounded No.10 just behind us and the leading monohulls were well amongst the Darts and only 100 yards from No.10! By bearing away we passed to leeward of the Prindle to cross the line some 4 seconds ahead, but about 40 yards behind Rob and Keith. Now came the fun! All the way from the Club, all the boats had had the advantage of the tide under them and when the wind dies all boats travel at the same speed, thus the slower boats have an advantage on handicap. However, the last leg was into the tide and the slower boats began to struggle. What had been a mere 2-minute difference between the boats up to No.10 increased to 15 minutes on the last leg to the finish. But even 15 minutes was not enough on handicap! Some people were confused as to the placement of the finish line and they concentrated on keeping close to the Heybridge shore rather than use the whole river. This meant that they had to tack, and lost some time. The boats came ashore next to the lock, and what looked like a small sand and shingle beach turned into a knee-deep quagmire of smelly gooey mud! However, the sight of all these boats did attract a small crowd and at least one onlooker who was concerned for his moored boat, lest it be damaged. After light refreshments we all gave a mighty cheer as Mike 'Crocodile' Duckmanton crossed the line as last boat. As the Cat Fleet qualifier in the 'Helmsman of the Year'Final he was practising his single-handed Mirror sailing. Whilst we were ashore they opened the lock gate, giving us a healthy dose of algae, and possibly a helping of Weil's Disease! Dave had bought me a pint of best knowing that I rarely drink, and I don't like bitter very much at all! Most of it ended up in the river, thus preventing any chance of disease striking! I am not sure what tastes worse, the river water or the beer.

9. The second race, at 2pm, was to start between Channel Mark 9 and the Jack B. Unfortunately, other clubs were using that part of the river and some boats were turning around No.9. After a postponement, the start sequence got underway. A port tack start was favoured, near the pin end, and this meant that a continuous stream of starboard tack boats came down the line. Everyone planned to tack onto port at the last moment and go. If only a Cat was as manoeuvrable as a monohull! The Cats hung back again, or chose to start at the Committee Boat end. With 10 seconds to go, the line was just a stream of starboard-tack monohulls, none of whom could tack onto port because of the boat behind. Dave and I were already on port and we bore away to pass behind the end of the line of boats, but to do this we were being forced into the middle of the river. Peter Flook, Clive Shenton and Rob Stahl were all to windward of us, but had to wait for the starboard monohulls to pass. Trevor and Dave Onyons had started nearer the Committee boat and therefore had the best start, but were not in the best place to lay the first mark (No.8). However, the postponement meant that the tide had turned and being in the middle had some advantages. Although Trevor held a slight lead, we were closer to the mark. We tacked about 10 yards to leeward of the mark and rounded about 30 yards ahead of Trevor. Dave Onyons called 'starboard' as he came in from overstanding the mark. ".......," I thought, but the words came out as, "Hold your course!" We passed about 2 feet from him and he mumbled about a protest opportunity. To have touched me he would have had to bear away, which would have been illegal! However, I understand that there was a general melee at the mark and Dave ended up being protested and disqualified. It was hard luck on anybody in those conditions, especially when the local cruiser fleet are trying to pass as close to the buoy as possible at the same time and from the opposite direction. Trevor rounded second with the Prindle and the other Hurricane close behind. The wind(?) was dying again. Rob went to the Northey shore, Trevor stayed in the middle and we tried vainly to follow the telltales all over the river. The inclusion of No.7 on the return leg (remember No.7 - the green cone that seems way out of line!) meant that we had to gybe to keep in the channel. Trevor was forced to do the same whilst Rob crept through without a gybe. This brought him to within about 40 yards of us, but we gradually pulled away to finish almost 2 minutes ahead. No wind and a falling tide again was of benefit to the slower boats and they followed home in a tight procession, too close for the Cats to win on Handicap. I thought that the Hornet would win, but it was not to be. Although I do not know the full result, I believe that Colin Wilsmore won in his Solo, followed by the Gull. Congratulations to Colin, who had avoided going to Fishers Green with the rest of the Solo Fleet. Colin is buying a new boat so we had all better watch out in future. Maybe next year we can arrange with one of the Maldon Clubs to finish the race at their finish line, use their facilities (Galley etc.) and restart from their line. Thanks must go to all those who organised the race, and to all competitors who supported this event. Steve Keeble REMEMBER THE AGM ON SUNDAY 19th NOVEMBER!

Mind you, some of them have the tanned and weathered look of those who have spent a life-time in sailing (or something for which a mis-spent youth is now taking its toll). It's just as well none of the lady helms took part otherwise it might have cramped this writers literary style a wee bit. Whilst talking about the ladies, why no lady helms this year ? Are they all too shy or have they secretly decided to leave the field clear to the poor old lads ? All I can say is I'll be glad when I'm old enough to join in ! N.J. JAMES Many old friends in our Club were saddened to hear of the death of Norman (Jimmy) James, Jimmy had not enjoyed good health for several years and passed away on 14th September. He had a long association with Marconi's, at Baddow and then at Witham, with the Marconi Microelectronic Company. With his family he sailed a GP 14 for many years and more lately enjoyed cruising in his Centaur "SONYA" which unfortunately he had to sell because of his health. Jimmy was a very popular Club member, always willing to help. He will be missed very much by his fellow mariners, and we send our condolences to Peggy and his sons Roger, Peter and Nigel. COMMODORE 'S NOTES This issue of Navigans has been brought forward so that the Annual General Meeting Notice can be sent out with {ts By doing this we will achieve a considerable saving on the expense of the Annual General Meeting paperwork normally incurred by the Club, We have been granted permission for the tractor shed which can now be erected during the winter. In addition eethe MASC have provisionally agreed to fund the replacement of the water pipe. The subject of the Officer of the Day has been discussed at length by the Main Committee, particularly regarding the Winter Period now that more use is being made both of the site and the sailing. As a result it has been decided that there will be an OOD every Sunday during the year and both Saturday and Sunday during the main Sailing Season (late March to early November), This obviously requires more OODs and it has_ been agreed that in future members who have been in the Club for a minimum of three years will be eligible for OOD duty. In practice this will mean doing a duty about every two and a half years. After my first year as Canmodore, I would like to offer many thanks to ALL the members who have supported the Club during the year, whether this has been on Canmittees, in the Bar or Galley, helping at Working Parties on major Club events or in any other way. It is certainly true that 'many hands make light work' and that we could not have achieved all we have this year without so much support and help. N.T. BLACKWATER '89 5. The Marconi Sailing Club have been trying to win the Colwyn Stone Challenge Trophy since it was first awarded in 1981, However each year Rochester have managed to win by a mixture of good luck and good sailing. On Saturday 24 June 1989, the luck finally ran out. On a warm sunny day the combination of a fickle wind, a strong tide and a well sailed single-handed Mirror finally managed to do what world champions, fast boats and national level sailors had failed to do: Damian Boreham won the Colwyn Stone Trophy for MSC, It was like John Bertrand winning the America's Cup for Australia. The MSC team was: Ron Greygoose in a Solo, John Weedon in a Laser, Mike and Maggie Boreham in a 420, and their son Damian in a_ single-handed Mirror, The Rochester team was: Richard and Sharon Stone in a Wayfarer, Christopher and Alexander Jibb in a Mirror, and Peter and Gordon Belcher in Lasers, On paper it was a strong team - Richard had won the trophy four times; Peter had won it three times; Gordon had sailed in the event for fourteen years; whilst Christopher showed great promise last year. The wind was light and from the West, the tide was coming in from the East. The Rochester team made @ good start and on the second leg were in first, second and third places. However the wind stayed light and as the fleet ran downwind against the tide, the single-handed Mirror was too close for comfort; Damian somehow managed to control three sails and kept close to the fleet, staying out of the tide, to win. Rochester packed well with Peter Belcher second - first on the water but just eight seconds behind on handicap. Richard Stone was third, Gordon Belcher fifth and Christopher Jibb sixth, At lunch Rochester were 4? points ahead and ready for the sea breeze to cane in and blow the single-handed Mirror's chances, rm, was not to be - the wind for the second race was even more fickle, After a long beat with the tide the fleet had to run against it along the island shore; John Weedon, now in a Kestrel crewed by Lucy Boreham, pulled away and appeared to have an unassailable lead, Peter Belcher and Richard Stone were chasing him hard and Gordon Belcher was trying to keep Ron Greygoose under control. Damian Boreham was out in the tide and appeared to have blown his chances. Once again the final run against the tide changed everything. The boats at the front of the fleet sailed into a hole with Peter Belcher and Richard Stone overtaking John Weedon; then the wind changed direction to the East and freshened as, belatedly, the sea breeze came in, Peter and Richard were first and second over the line, but the slower boats were now sailing in a good breeze and easily beat their handicap, Damian won the race, with Ron Greygoose second (despite almost capsizing at the last mark). Rochester's placings were three, four, five and eight with MSC placings one, two, six, seven, thus MSC won the second race by 4% points, Overall Damian Boreham won the Colwyn Stone Challenge Trophy with two firsts, whilst Rochester retained the Medway Cup for the team event, Again a very pleasant visit with good interesting sailing, good company and good food. -- The results of the 'HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR! Final for 1989 The winner of the 1989 'Helmsman of the Year' series :- MALCOLM GANDY Congratulations to Malcolm Gandy who won the Helmsman of the Year trophy after what must rank as one of the closest and most keenly contested H.o.Y finals for many a year. MalcoJm.saw an almost certain runaway victory suddenly turn into near defeat - only to snatch a well deserved but-hard-earned success in the last moments of the competion. Certainly, those of us who were able to watch the 1989 final witnessed a fine performance by all who took part, with victory and defeat being governed by the capricious activities of the wind and tide - aided and abetted (as always ) _ by the helms making the wrong decisions at the wrong time. Enough of poetry (poetry ? what poetry ?), let's get on with the report. Those taking part in the H.o.Y were :- Malcolm Gandy (Solo Fleet) Lee Tridini (Sailboard Fleet) Mike Duckmanton (Cat Fleet) Mike Hellewell (420 Fleet) Damian Boreham (Mirror Fleet) John Weedon (Handicap Fleet). All races were around 2 laps of the course D, A, E, No.1 and F marks, all passed to starboard with.a N-Nl! wind starting out at Force 4 - 5, later dropping to Force 1-2 and then picking up again to Force 3-4. "E' mark was placed near Osea island and directly to windward of 'A' mark and I reckon Graham Baker, driver of the Jack B, made a good job in positioning it just about right. It certainly provided a choice of route on the windward leg between A and E which undoubtedly proved crucial to the outcome of the Elimination Rounds. The formula for 1989 was that the 6 finalists were divided into two groups of three, each to race an Elimination Round of 3 races in Mirrors (swopping the boats for each race). The winner of each group would then meet in the final as a Match Race sailed in lasers, the winner to be the first to score two wins. The Elimination Round (single-handed Mirrors) - the two groups were :- Group 1 - Malcolm Gandy, Mike Hellewell and Lee Tridini Group 2 - Mike Duckmanton, John Weedon and Damian Boreham For obvious reasons, Damian was not allowed to sail either of the Boreham-owned Mirrors (Bumble and Lars Tinn) and these boats were allocated to Group l. Malcolm, John, Lee and Damian had all had experience of sailing Mirrors and Mike Duckmanton took the wise precaution of getting some Mirror experience during the Jackpot on the previous Sunday. Just as well - a Mirror handles somewhat differently from a Dart 18 catamaran ! Mike Hellewell stepped into the Mirror for the first time but was well used to mono-hull sailing in his 420. He did wonder why the jib kept failing to tack, that is until he realised he didn't have his usual crew (Irene) to do it for him. Races 1 and 2 provided much sport for the spectators as near victory turned into even nearer defeat with each tack and gybe. Mike Duckmanton capsized in Race 2 and Mike Hellewell spoiled a brilliant start in race 1 by going back because he thought he was over the line. At the end of race 2, the Elimination Round was still wide open with:- (a) Lee Tridini needing a win the the 3rd race of Group 1 in order to beat Malcolm Gandy and (b) John and Damian needing to finish ahead of each other (but not necessarily win) in the 3rd race of Group 2. Race 3 was a fine race with much swopping of the lead and lesser places all the way around. The outcome of the Elimination Round was that Malcolm (Group 1 winner) and Damian (Group 2 winner) went forward to face each other in the Match Race Final. The Match Race final (single-handed lasers) - Damian won the start of Race 1 but was soon overhauled by Malcolm who went on to win by almost 2 minutes. Race 2 saw Malcolm in the lead from the start and soon well ahead at the finish of the lst lap. These races were really a procession and, to be honest, a bit of a bore after the thrills and interest of the Mirror racing. So confident were we in the rescue boat that Malcolm would win the 2nd race (and the H.o.Y) that we planned to pick up 'E' as soon as both had passed it . Then an apparent miracle happened - the wind started to drop and Damian started to catch up. Gradually, inexorably, Damian caught, matched and then overtook Malcolm to win the 2nd race by 30 seconds. One win each and all to play for on the last race. Malcolm lead the 3rd race initially but lost the lead on the broad reach and run legs. An incident at 'F' mark on the first lap saw Malcolm doing a 720 which enabled Damian to establish a handy lead. Now another miracle - the wind started to increase again and Malcolm gradually whittled away the lead until, as Damian rounded 'F' mark to start the beat for the finish line, Malcolm was not many yards behind. With 156 yards to go they were level and the previous victories and defeats now counted for nothing. Malcolm eased his way ahead and won the race, and Helmsman of the Year, by 8 seconds. A MAGNIFICENT SERIES - A FINE WIN - A PLEASURE TO WATCH
